title: Mexican peso strong, but not stronger than Colombian  currency
text:
Most emerging currencies have gained ground during the first seven months of the year against the US dollar, with the Colombian peso and the Mexican peso being the currencies that have appreciated the most, but the context of this appreciation between the two Latin American countries is explained differently. So far this year, the Colombian peso has appreciated 17.3%; the Mexican peso, 12.8%; the Brazilian real, 9.2%; the Chilean peso, 6.9%; the Hungarian forint, 6.7%; the Polish zloty, 6.6%; and the Peruvian sol, 4.8%.

Why is the Mexican peso strong? During the semester, the Mexican peso appreciated 12.8% and is already close to breaking the level of 17 units per dollar, due to the timely intervention of the Bank of Mexico to control inflation since June 2021, according to analysts. The differential between Mexico's rate and that of the United States has generated an attraction for peso assets, in addition, record levels of remittances and the attraction of investment have supported the local currency. Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, mentioned that the fact that the peso remains strong raises the probability that the exchange rate will continue to show a downward trend. In fact, if the exchange rate shows the same trend observed since July of last year, this 2023 could reach a minimum quotation of 16.74 pesos. "The strength of the peso is not due to the government's economic policy, it is due to the flow of dollars coming in from exports, remittances and foreign direct investment, in addition to the monetary policy of Banco de México and the preference of foreigners to invest in pesos. What has helped the current administration is that the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico has been respected and the investment grade of the sovereign debt has not been lost. Plus the factor that the golden opportunity of nearshoring has appeared, which implies a greater flow of foreign currency to Mexico", added Siller. What about Colombia's currency? The appreciation of the Colombian currency is due to internal and external factors. On the domestic side, the political climate has had an influence, as Gustavo Petro's government's reform proposals on labor, pension and health issues have encountered many debates and obstacles in Congress, which sends a signal of confidence to the market regarding the autonomy of the country's institutions. On the external side, the strength of the Colombian peso has been influenced by a greater appetite for emerging currencies, due to the expectation that central banks, especially the U.S. central bank, may end its restrictive policy. "When the idea that there will be no more interest rate hikes and that external agents have a little more appetite for risk is consolidated, surely capital will continue to arrive to the Colombian economy but not in the same way as it was seen at the beginning of the year; in such a way that not much appreciation of the exchange rate is expected but not much depreciation either, since the markets are calmer and above all inflation and interest rates in the world are ceasing to rise", Scotiabank Colpatria analysts indicated in a report. One Colombian peso to one Mexican peso The exchange rate conversion between these Latin American currencies is one Mexican peso for 242.81 Colombian pesos. Conversely, for one Colombian peso you would be paying 0.0041 Mexican pesos.

title: The strength of the Mexican peso
text:
After a brief period of weakening triggered by the financial turbulence in the United States in early 2023, the Mexican peso has resumed an appreciating trend. During the course of this year alone, our currency has strengthened by more than 12% against the US dollar. This has generated concern in some sectors for its potentially harmful effects on the competitiveness of our economy, as well as fears that the peso's appreciation may continue for a prolonged period of time.

My impression, I believe, like that of most private sector analysts, given the trajectory they project for the peso's parity against the dollar in the coming months, is that the trend of appreciation of our currency will not last long. Why?

The strength of the peso has several determinants. I believe that three stand out among them. The first is the combination of a high level of interest rates in Mexico and a moderate volatility of our currency's exchange rate, which makes domestic financial instruments more attractive than those observed in other emerging economies. The above encourages a strong demand for peso-denominated assets, albeit of a very short-term and highly volatile nature.

Remittances from Mexican workers abroad represent another important source of pressure on the peso. The growth of these inflows over the last few years has been formidable. From 2018 to 2022 remittances increased by more than 70%, reaching in the last of these years just over 4% of GDP. What explains this evolution? The strong demand for labor in the United States, driven by measures to deal with the ravages caused by the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, but also the inability of the Mexican economy to retain these workers.

The third determinant of the peso's recent appreciation that I wish to highlight is Mexico's macroeconomic position. In particular, a small balance of payments current account deficit, a comfortable international reserve position, prudent monetary policy and reasonable public debt to GDP ratios, which together place the Mexican economy in a favorable position in the emerging economy environment.

I would like to note that, contrary to what is often argued, the latter is far from being indicative of sound economic fundamentals. The strength of the current account of the balance of payments is mainly the result of high remittance inflows, i.e., of deficient public policies that have prevented a significant part of our country's human capital from being tapped. On the other hand, while public debt is moderate today, government finances are characterized by very low revenues and spending rigidities that make them worryingly fragile over time.

What information can be drawn for the future trajectory of the peso from the outlook for these determinants?

The interest rate differential favorable to Mexico is likely to narrow in the coming months. As inflation declines, the ex ante real policy rate (i.e., the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation) will tend to increase. At a time when economic activity is also expected to weaken, this opens up the possibility of nominal interest rate reductions. The interest rate differential may also be diminished by its external component, as the U.S. Federal Reserve (FED) has suggested that its interest rate may show one or two additional interest rate increases before the end of this year.

Additionally, remittance inflows to Mexico are likely to weaken. The U.S. labor market remains strong. However, it is difficult to believe that the sharp adjustment in U.S. interest rates will not have an impact on U.S. economic activity. In fact, in its most recent projections, the FED anticipates GDP growth rates of only 1 and 1.1% for 2023 and 2024, respectively, and the possibility of a recession remains latent.

To the above, we should add the risks derived from the important electoral process in Mexico next year. In addition to the nervousness that this may cause in financial markets, the peso could be affected if there is a relaxation of macroeconomic policy, aimed at counteracting the possible weakening of the economy and the consequent political costs.

Nor should we forget that the Foreign Exchange Commission, made up of representatives of Banco de México and the Ministry of Finance, has the tools to intervene in the foreign exchange market, without affecting the floating regime, if the exchange rate reaches levels considered inappropriate.

Finally, I believe it is important to point out that, although it is important to carefully monitor the implications of the trajectory of our currency, we must keep in mind the enormous benefits that the flexible exchange rate regime has brought us, and be aware that in the search for a competitive position in the markets, exchange rate policy cannot act as a substitute for improvements in productivity.

title: Global  Forex  and Fixed Income Roundup: Market Talk
text:
The latest Market Talks covering FX and Fixed Income. Published exclusively on Dow Jones Newswires throughout the day.

1641 ET - The IPC stock index closes up 0.2% at 55033 points, with financial group Banorte shares up 1.5% and conglomerate Femsa advancing 1%. The peso slips to 17.80 to the US dollar from 17.76 Friday. Last week the peso ended at its strongest level since September 2017. DBRS Morningstar affirmed Mexico's sovereign rating at BBB, saying government commitment to fiscal sustainability "should help preserve stable macroeconomic conditions, even as the global environment becomes more challenging." Kroll Bond Ratings Agency also ratified Mexico at BBB, the Finance Ministry says, adding the government seeks to maintain favorable access to domestic and international markets through solid handling of public finances. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1602 ET - The banking turmoil "doesn't appear to have triggered a severe further tightening in credit conditions," Capital Economics' Paul Ashworth ways in a report about the Fed's April Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey. "Although there was only a modest post-SVB additional tightening in lending standards on [commercial real state and commercial and industrial] lending, banks do appear to be more concerned about household lending," Ashworth says. "Higher interest rates are now weighing heavily on the demand for credit." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1551 ET - Treasury yields rise as markets digest Friday's surprisingly strong labor data ahead of inflation data due later this week. The 10-year gains 0.073 percentage point to 3.518% and the two-year rises 0.089 pp to 4.009%. The benchmarks weakened after the Fed indicated last week it could keep rates unchanged in June. April payrolls, however, raised the prospect of another rate increase, fueling a Treasurys selloff, while the risk of bank failures and the debt-ceiling standoff could still trigger a run for safety. CPI inflation Wednesday is expected to show prices still resilient. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1534 ET - The Brazilian government nominated two new members to the central bank's monetary policy committee, including one who is close to the government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, which could generate some friction within the committee, said Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos in a research note. Da Silva has called for the bank to cut interest rates to boost economic growth. Gabriel Galipolo, one of the two men nominated, is currently an official in the Finance Ministry. Galipolo is also seen as a possible replacement for the central bank's current president, according to Ramos. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1534 ET - Brazil's motor vehicle production fell in April from a year earlier amid weak demand, according to the Brazilian Association of Automotive Vehicle Manufacturers, or Anfavea. Production declined 3.9% from the same month a year earlier and dropped 19.4% from March, the group said. But even with high interest rates in the country slowing sales, 14% more vehicles have been sold in the year through April than in the same period of 2022, Anfavea President Marcio de Lima Leite said. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1528 ET - The US labor market is gradually softening, but not fast enough to support market bets on Fed cuts this year, Apollo's Torsten Slok says. He notes that total nonfarm payrolls are below their six-month moving average, while saying that inflation "is sticky because of continued high wage inflation and the housing market recovering." Slok adds that "the market is underestimating the Fed's commitment to get inflation down from currently 5% to the FOMC's 2% inflation target." Markets are pricing rate cuts starting in September. "I don't think the Fed will cut rates in 2023," Slok says. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1525 ET - Brazilian exports of pork rose in April from a year earlier as some Asian countries battled outbreaks of African swine fever, said the Brazilian Animal Protein Association, or ABPA. Exports rose 16.6% to 104,500 tons of the meat last month, while export revenue jumped 29.9% to $251.3M in the period, the ABPA said. China continued to be the biggest importer of Brazilian pork in this year through April, buying a total of 143,200 tons in the period, according to the ABPA. Hong Kong was another big buyer in the first four months of this year, with imports of 42,200 tons, ABPA said. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1430 ET - Rising social tension increases credit risk for Latin American issuers "via governability; policy shifts, including regulatory changes and government intervention; economic performance and financial volatility channels," Moody's researchers say in a report. They point to financial volatility a risk in Argentina, while policy shifts in Brazil "may lead to government intervention in state-owned enterprises." Changes in Mexico's energy policy "have dampened private investment," Moody's says, and social protest in Peru is a potential threat to the country's sovereign, banking, tourism and retail issuers. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1302 ET - The market's pricing of a pivot to Fed cuts is out of sync with the FOMC's commitment to bringing down inflation, say Bank of America's currency strategists. But if the hiking cycle is indeed at an end, they say it shouldn't imply dollar weakness. "A common thread to past pause periods has indeed been dollar depreciation at the onset, but the direction is less clear over the full duration of the rate hold," BofA says. The strategists say the past three periods where the Fed paused rate hikes produced differing results for the USD, and they expect the dollar to find near-term support. "Inflation has remained sticky and should keep the Fed committed to holding rates at terminal into 2024, well beyond market pricing," they say. The ICE US dollar index is little changed. (patrick.sheridan@wsj.com)

1259 ET - Retailers are signaling that a slowdown in imports is deepening. The National Retail Federation's Global Port Tracker forecasts imports at the nation's busiest container ports in April and May will be 23% to 24% lower than the same time last year. Ben Hackett, of Hackett Associates which produces the report, says his group is revising down forecasts as economic uncertainty weighs on retailers. Import volumes during 3Q peak shipping season are expected to be 7.2% below last year's levels. "Our view is that imports will remain below recent levels until inflation rates and inventory surpluses are reduced," Hackett says. (paul.berger@wsj.com)

1203 ET - Retail gasoline prices swung sharply in both directions last month, adding some uncertainty as to what the BLS's overall US Consumer Price Index for April will reveal Wednesday morning. Volatile fuel prices are often a key factor in the overall CPI number that's expected to be up 0.4% month-over-month. Gasoline prices surged by 5% during the first few weeks of April after OPEC-plus's surprise production-cut announcement, and reached a 2023 high of $3.68/gallon April 23, according to AAA. But recession fears and other issues caused crude-oil prices to fall in late April, and fuel prices at the pump quickly followed with steep declines of their own, leaving gasoline prices to finish April not much higher from where they began. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

1200 ET - Risks pressuring investment-grade spreads are likely to dissipate next month, Bank of America's Yuri Seliger says in a report. "We look for IG spreads to remain biased wider in May due to a combination of three risks: 1) heavy supply, 2) a resurgence of bank stress and 3) the upcoming US debt limit x-date." Seliger says issuance seasonally slows in the summer, while "more elevated bank stress increases the likelihood of a solution." Similarly, the approaching of an X-date in which the government won't be able to fully pay its bills increases the possibility of a compromise in Congress, he says. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: World  Currency  Map: Mexican peso, among the oldest  currencies  in the Americas
text:
The Mexican peso is the official currency of Mexico, and one of the oldest currencies in America, since it began to be used in the XVI century, after the arrival of the Spaniards to the continent, with a wide variety of bills and coins, the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) is in charge of the issuance and distribution of the currency.It has bills of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000 Mexican pesos, as well as coins of 50 cents and one, two, five, 10 and some commemorative coins of 20 pesos.In World Coin Map we will share with you the essential data of the most important currencies in the global market, we have already written about the Euro(?) and the US dollar ($), and we will continue with the Mexican peso.History of the Mexican pesoAccording to the Bank of Mexico, the history of the peso dates back to the 16th century, after the arrival of the Spaniards to the country, when the colonizers introduced the royal coin of eight, which was the silver coin used in Europe and ended up becoming the 

currency of New Spain.After Mexico's independence in 1821, it was established as a federal republic and it is right at that moment that the first official currency called Mexican peso was created, which was based on the value of the old real de ocho.The Ministry of Finance assures that, during the 19th century, the Mexican peso suffered multiple devaluations due to the economic and political instability Mexico was going through.In 1864, during the French intervention in Mexico, a paper currency called "Peso Fuerte" was issued, whose value was greater than that of the Mexican peso. However, after the restoration of the republic, the use of paper currency was discontinued.Creation of the Banco de MéxicoYears later, in 1925, the Banco de México was created, a central body whose main objective continues to be the regularization of the country's currency issuance and monetary policy.Along with the creation of the also called Banxico, the gold standard was introduced, which meant that the peso could be exchanged for gold at a fixed value.Today, the Mexican peso remains Mexico's official currency and is widely used in trade and tourism, and the Bank of Mexico remains in charge of regulating the country's currency issuance and monetary policy.The peso vis-à-vis the worldThe Mexican peso is a currency that is considered stable and relatively liquid in international financial markets.However, in times of global economic uncertainty or volatility, as occurred during the 2008 financial crisis or the covid-19 pandemic, the Mexican peso can be affected by capital flight and devaluation against other strong currencies such as the U.S. dollar.In addition, domestic factors such as inflation, insecurity, corruption and political uncertainty can influence the perception of the Mexican peso.In general, macroeconomic stability and fiscal policies are considered fundamental to maintain confidence in the currency and strengthen its position in international markets.Elements of the currencyIn the Political Constitution of the United Mexican States, it establishes among its paragraphs the functions of the Central Bank, also known as Banco de México, and it is exclusively responsible for minting the currency and issuing banknotes.Mexico's banknotes feature a series of designs and motifs that represent the country's history, culture and biodiversity.The obverse of the banknote features the image of an important figure in Mexico's history, while the reverse features an image of a historical site or monument, a natural landscape or an emblematic animal of the country.Below, we will analyze the banknotes that are produced by Banco de México (Banxico), which has been responsible for their production since their creation in 1925.The $20 bill, issued for the first time in 1977, presents on its obverse side the consummation of Mexico's Independence, and on its reverse side you can see the mangrove ecosystem with the Mexican crocodile and the chocolate heron of the Ka'an reserve, in Quintana Roo.The $50 bill, issued for the first time in 1992, depicts the historical period of ancient Mexico on its obverse side, while its reverse shows the ecosystem of rivers and lakes, with the salamander and corn in Xochimilco, Mexico City.The $100 bill, issued for the first time in 1994, presents the image of the Mexican poetSor Juana Inés de la Cruz and on its reverse side the ecosystem of temperate forests with pine, oak and oyamel trees, in the Monarch Butterfly Reserve, in Michoacán.The $200 bill, issued for the first time in 2002, presents on its obverse side the process of Mexico's Independence, with Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla and José María Morelos y Pavón, and on its reverse side the El Pinacate Biosphere Reserve and the Gran Desierto de Altar, in Sonora.The $500 bill, issued for the first time in 1994, shows Benito Juárez, former president of Mexico, on its obverse and the El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve in Baja California Sur on its reverse.The $1000 bill, issued in 1983, shows Francisco I. Madero, Hermila Galinda and Carmen Serdán, revolutionary drivers, on its obverse, while its reverse shows the jaguar ecosystem in the ancient Mayan city of Calakmul, in Campeche.Mexico's banknotes also include a number of security features, such as watermarks, micro texts, holographic elements, serial numbers and special inks that change color when tilted or viewed under different lights. These security features help prevent counterfeiting and protect the integrity of the banknote.As for coins, it is the Mint of Mexico that mints and markets coins and medals, through processes that comply with quality standards for the Bank of Mexico and public and private, national and international institutions.Although there are coins of five, 10 and 20 centavos, in Mexico's economic framework they are not really used in the monetary flow. The 50 centavo coin, originally issued in 1992, shows the National Coat of Arms in relief in the center, while the reverse shows the number fifty together with the cent symbol "¢". The one peso coin shows on its reverse the value and a stylization of the Ring of Radiance of the Sun Stone.The two-peso coins show on their reverse side their face value, as well as a stylization of the Ring of Days of the Sun Stone. The five-peso coin shows on its reverse side the face value, accompanied by a stylization of the Ring of Serpents of the Sun Stone. The ten-peso coin shows in the central part the circle of the Sun Stone, which represents Tonatiuh, god of the sun and leader of the Mexica people, using the mask of fire.As part of the security features of the coins of this currency, we find the embossed engravings that can be felt with the fingers, the perimeter rings found on the edges of the coin and the magnetic ink, which can only be detected with special equipment.Commemorative coinsAccording to the Banco de México, the Mexican peso has had several commemorative coins throughout time. Some of the most outstanding are the following:Five-peso coin commemorating the 75th anniversary of the oil expropriation, minted in 2013.100-peso coin commemorating the bicentennial of the beginning of the War of Independence, minted in 2010.20-peso coin commemorating the centennial of the promulgation of the Political Constitution of the United Mexican States, minted in 2017.10-peso coin commemorating the centennial of the birth of Octavio Paz, minted in 2014.Five-peso coin commemorating the 50th anniversary of the founding of the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), minted in 1989.Two-peso coin commemorating the bicentennial of the birth of Benito Juárez, minted in 2006.The Mexican peso has been a historically volatile currency due to various internal and external factors.Despite fluctuations in its value, the peso has managed to maintain relative stability in recent years thanks to the implementation of responsible monetary policies by Banco de México.However, global economic uncertainty, trade tensions and the domestic political situation in Mexico continue to be factors that may affect the peso's strength in the short and medium term. MO

title: Mexican peso declines on Fed officials'  interventions
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 8 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso depreciated on Wednesday, but continued to hover below the barrier of 19 per dollar, in a market awaiting the interventions of several officials of the Federal Reserve in the course of the day.

The local currency was trading at 18.9264 units, with a loss of 0.27%, as investors continued to evaluate comments from the head of the U.S. central bank, Jerome Powell, who showed in a speech on Tuesday few signs of an aggressive stance on the strength of employment.

"During the session, the performance of the exchange market will depend mainly on comments from Federal Reserve officials," the firm Banco Base said in an analysis note.

Speeches were scheduled throughout the day by New York Fed President John Williams, central bank Governor Lisa Cook, Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic and Minneapolis Fed chief Neel Kaskari, among others.

Investors' attention was also focused on Thursday's release of local inflation figures for January and on Banco de México's first monetary policy announcement of the year.

For the time being, the currency was expected to oscillate the rest of the day in a range of 18.81 to 18.95 per dollar, according to analysts at CI Banco.

title: Breakfast with Carstens: a central banker in the eye of the storm
text:
What would you ask Agustín Carstens? The former governor of the Bank of Mexico is in the eye of the storm that central bankers live in. The eye of the storm is the region of the calmest weather conditions, around which there are fierce winds and heavy rains. Agustín Carstens lives in Switzerland. He is the head of the Bank for International Settlements, the BIS, known as the central bank of the world's central banks. There, the global inflationary crisis is processed in a unique way. It is an unprecedented phenomenon, which is hitting hard in rich and poor countries alike. It is something that puts in tension the relationship between central bankers, the political class and societies around the world, "these are difficult times, and the autonomy of central banks was conceived for circumstances like these. Not for times when everything is fine and calm. It is in difficult times that autonomy can make a difference.

 It is important for central banks to provide a vision that goes beyond the short term".

He is sitting at the head of the table. It's a Mexican breakfast and he orders a barbacoa taco for dessert. He has lived in Basel since late 2017 and you can tell he misses Mexican food. He was in CDMX to celebrate a regional BIS meeting. He has a bit more gray hair. He is sparing and cautious when talking about Mexico, but he is in front of a group of journalists who put pressure on him. He praises the role played by Alejandro Díaz de León and Victoria Rodríguez Ceja at the head of Banxico, "each one has done an excellent job. Each one has his or her own style".

Topics come and go in a conversation that lasts two hours and overlaps with Mexico's match against Poland. Martinoli's voice reaches us in waves and sometimes floods us, but we don't miss anything. Carstens' x-ray of the Superpeso is much more interesting than a scoreless game. Agustín Carstens has had a front row seat to Mexico's recent economic history and has the ability to put things in perspective. In 1994, there was also a very strong peso, but the situation was very different, he recalls: "the Bank of Mexico was committed to defending an exchange rate level and the government was willing to do almost anything to prop up the value of the peso, for example, issuing billions of dollars in Tesobonos... now, the strength of the peso is not related to government interventions. The Bank of Mexico does not spend reserves either..."

The topics are chained together and minutes later we find ourselves talking about the rate differential between Banxico and the Fed, is it necessary to maintain the six points? His answer goes far beyond the short term, "it is likely that in the coming months we will first see the effects of the rate hikes on the slowdown of the economy rather than on the reduction of inflation. It will be very interesting to observe what will happen then... I am optimistic that we will soon see lower inflation, I think we could be at levels of 4 or 5%, but it will be complicated to go from there to 2% or less".

Agustín Guillermo Carstens has just turned 64. He has received many awards, including Best Governor of a Central Bank, by The Banker magazine in 2012. In the next few days he will receive the King of Spain Economics Award. Thirty years ago, another Mexican received this distinction, Miguel Mancera. He recalls that at that time he participated in the elaboration of the reception speech. The theme was the role of economic openness in controlling inflation. "The Bank of Mexico was a promoter of that opening, it brought more competition and market discipline in many branches of the economy". He anticipates that his speech will deal with the challenges facing central banks. One of those has to do with cryptocurrencies. "People expect central banks to play a bigger role in innovation-related issues. What is happening with Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, with the bankruptcy of FTX makes it clear that in many cases the supposed monetary decentralization is false. Companies like FTX play a central role and are not subject to any rules.... At the BIS we have innovation labs and we are working with central banks to respond to a reality where many people want digital currencies. The challenge is technological and regulatory, it is very important to solve the balance between privacy and the obligations that there may be in tax or security issues." Last night he flew to Switzerland. That quiet place that is so close, in the very eye of the storms.

title: Mexican peso loses on Fed officials  interventions
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso depreciated on Thursday in the face of a global strengthening of the dollar amid mixed signals from the U.S. economy, while investors awaited comments from several Federal Reserve officials later in the session.

The domestic currency was trading at 19.4473 per dollar, down 0.57% against the Reuters reference price on Wednesday, in line with the rest of the region's major currencies.

"In the absence of relevant local economic indicators, the Mexican peso is influenced by external factors," said Luis Adrian Muniz, analyst at local firm Vector.

According to data released in the morning, the number of people who applied for state unemployment benefits in the U.S. fell last week, while the Philadelphia Fed index fell????? in November?? more than anticipated.

Meanwhile, St. Louis Fed President James Bullard said that even under a "generous" analysis of monetary policy, the Fed should continue to raise interest rates probably by at least another percentage point.

Later in the day, other U.S. central bank officials are expected to speak at various public events.

For the rest of the day, the currency is expected to oscillate in a range of 19.25 to 19.50 per dollar, according to Monex Grupo Financiero.

title: Is Bitcoin the recipe for Mexicans to face their inflation and pay their debts?
text:
Inflation rises and Banxico would take action, a mix that may plunge the population into debt, although many might be thinking about bitcoin.

Key facts:

57% of households in Mexico have some kind of debt.Not only is inflation rising in the Aztec country, bitcoin adoption is also on the rise.Inflation is unstoppable in Mexico. The National Consumer Price Index (INPC) presented an increase of 0.41% during the second fortnight of September, bringing the annual rate to 8.76%, just below the inflation reported in the second fortnight of August, of 8.77%. Given this scenario, bitcoin (BTC) appears in the recipe for Mexicans to contain the rise in prices, and also to pay their debts.

Mexico's economic outlook for the remainder of the year is not encouraging. On the one hand, the Anti-Inflation and Deficit Package (PACIC), implemented by the government of Manuel López Obrador since May, has been ineffective, according to media reports.

On the other hand, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) considered that the inflationary environment in Mexico will continue to be complex, and therefore expects the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) to intervene.

The same is expected by 20 analysts consulted by Reuters, who anticipate that the Central Bank (Banxico) will raise its key interest rate from 8.5% to 9.25% to contain inflation, following in the footsteps of the Federal Reserve (Fed).

More than 50% of Mexicans are in debtRising interest rates coupled with crippling inflation is sending more and more Mexicans into debt using credit cards to pay for everyday needs.

In fact, 57% of Mexican households, or nearly 21 million people claim to have some type of debt.

Among them, most have outstanding credit card commitments, while others have personal or payroll loans. This was revealed by public accountant Melisa Murialdo, who analyzed statistical data on the Mexican population.

The data analyzed by the expert shows that Mexicans are borrowing more and more money to pay for essential items such as food and gasoline, necessities that have increased in cost much faster than average earnings. And with interest rates poised to rise again, it could be even harder to get out of crushing debt.

However, Mexicans have a particular perception about their level of indebtedness, as only 8 out of every 100 people feel they are very indebted, while the majority perceive themselves to be debt-free and only a small percentage of the population has enough to save.

Is Bitcoin part of Mexicans' anti-inflationary recipe?In the face of Mexico's bleak economic outlook, bitcoin has begun to appear on the horizon, as the country has raised its level of cryptocurrency adoption.

According to Chainalysis' Global Cryptocurrency Adoption Index 2022, Mexico is in the Top 30, climbing from 44th to 28th place globally in the last year.

Chainalysis measures the performance of countries based on their population's use of different bitcoin services and other cryptocurrencies. According to its report, Mexico obtained a score of 0.323; which now ranks it 28th among the 159 countries analyzed.

Analysts note that poorer countries are adopting bitcoin more. And although it does not include Mexico among them, it seems to be clear that the population sees the cryptoasset as a way out of the economic adversities resulting from government monetary policies.

However, what is the realistic position of liquidating levels of indebtedness with bitcoin? according to Ibrahim Martinez, Financial Analyst at Key to Markets.

Martinez believes that despite its adoption in Mexico, bitcoin has suffered a decline from its all-time high of more than 73%. Considering the market structure, bitcoin is still far from breaking price limits that potentially put it above USD 30,000, let alone recovering this loss of more than 73% of its market capitalization. So buying and holding cryptocurrencies in the short term may not seem sufficient to mitigate the debts of each household's equity.

title: Mexico is well positioned to weather the risks of a turbulent global environment: IMF
text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) considered that Mexico is well positioned to weather the risks of the turbulent global environment, which has been generated by inflation, high interest rates and currency depreciation.

"Faced with increased risks in a more turbulent global environment, the (IMF) Directors agreed that Mexico is well positioned to weather the challenges, due to the soundness of its macroeconomic policies and economic policy frameworks," informed the Bank of Mexico (Banxico).

The central bank noted that the Executive Directors agreed with the thrust of the IMF staff's assessment of the Mexican economy in 2022.

They also welcomed the authorities' prudent macroeconomic policies in the face of a rebound in inflation, according to the International Monetary Fund's annual assessment of the Mexican economy in 2022, which was published by Banxico.

The IMF evaluates the economic situation and outlook of each of the Fund's member countries, generally on an annual basis.

As part of the assessment, an IMF staff team visits the member country, collects and analyzes economic and financial information, and meets with the relevant authorities, as well as with private sector analysts and representatives of civil society.

The issues reviewed are not limited to macroeconomic and financial policies, but also include those elements that may have an impact on a country's economic performance.

The IMF's assessment expects Mexico's economic growth to slow in the short term due to slower U.S. growth and tighter global financial conditions.

"Directors welcomed the Bank of Mexico's proactive approach to dealing with rising inflation," explains the document published by the body led by Victoria Rodríguez Ceja.

Given the significant uncertainty about the inflation trajectory in 2023 and upside risks, IMF Directors agreed that further increases in the target rate and the maintenance of a tight policy stance for some time in Mexico may be necessary.

They also generally stressed the importance of clear communication of economic policy.

IMF Directors recommended aligning wage increases more closely with expected inflation and the productivity of lower-paid workers, as well as the neutral fiscal stance planned for 2022 and 2023 is appropriate.

"The easing of retail fuel prices (in Mexico), while reducing cost pressures, came at a considerable cost to the budget and, in general, they urged the authorities to choose more targeted supports to protect other priority spending in the event that oil prices rise again," the IMF said.

It added that contingency plans should be prepared for a rapid policy response should downside risks materialize.

"It would be important to increase fiscal buffers in the short term and reform the institutional framework for greater flexibility in the longer term," it added.

IMF Directors noted that the floating exchange rate in Mexico should continue to act as a buffer, although intervention in the foreign exchange market could be considered should there be a significant worsening of market liquidity.

They agreed that the financial system remains resilient post-pandemic, welcomed the favorable assessment of the effectiveness of Mexico's financial stability framework, and generally supported the key policy recommendations of the 2022 Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP).

"Additional measures, including an update of the financial sector supervisory and crisis management frameworks, are needed to keep pace with a changing regulatory and risk landscape," they concluded.

title: ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL TRENDS : The heavyweight
text:
The exchange rate remains around 20.00 pesos per dollar, which makes the Mexican peso one of the strongest currencies worldwide so far this year, at a time when the euro is already below 1 dollar, the Japanese yen went from 115 to 150 yen per dollar and even the Chinese yuan went from 6.70 to 7.20 yuan per dollar.

The reasons why the Mexican peso has remained strong against the dollar is due to the free floating of the currency. Unlike the economic crises of the last century when the President decided whether the peso should be devalued or not, as of April 1, 1994, the Bank of Mexico is autonomous and the President of the Republic cannot intervene in its decisions.

Since the December 1994 crisis, Banco de México opted for a free float of the peso against the dollar, so the peso can wake up one day at 19.80 pesos and the next day, due to something that happens inside or outside Mexico, the peso will wake up at 20.20 pesos and then go to 20.50 pesos and return to 20.00 pesos the following week.

In the past, when we had a fixed exchange rate, if domestic and foreign investors bought large amounts of dollars, commercial banks would turn to the Bank of Mexico, which was forced to sell its reserves, and when they were about to run out, there was no choice but to devalue. Today that does not happen, Banxico does not sell its reserves and consequently they are already at a level of around 200 billion dollars.

Particularly in the last few months, the peso has remained stable, as a result of the inflow of foreign currency from exports, tourism, remittances and oil sales, as well as investments made by foreigners in Mexico.

However, if during 2023 Mexico does not grow at 3.0% as estimated by the Ministry of Finance and tax collection falls, there will be the possibility that the rating agencies will lower the sovereign rating and in doing so, a large amount of dollars invested in Mexico will leave the country, which will cause pressure on the exchange rate.

There is no problem if the debt increases, as long as tax collection increases in the same proportion, which can only happen if the economy really grows significantly next year, which will probably not happen due to the bad moment the United States is going through, as well as the reduction in local consumption due to high inflation.

For 28 years the President of the Republic has not intervened directly in the peso-dollar parity, although his decisions can trigger a strong depreciation, if he makes happy accounts and also increases strongly the public debt, as will happen in 2023.

title: Fintech law falls "short" of regulating cryptocurrencies; experts call for outlining tax and data protection issues
text:
Four years after the publication of the Law to Regulate Financial Technology Institutions, better known as fintech law, and on the eve of the construction of a digital currency issued by the Bank of Mexico (Banxico), specialists and industry participants agreed that although this regulatory framework regulates virtual assets, it is not enough for the full and healthy development of the ecosystem that operates these instruments.

During the Bitcoin, Mexico and the Digital Economy Forum, organized by the association Legions, different specialists gave their point of view on how the issue of cryptocurrencies should be regulated given the potential they have to advance financial inclusion and therefore the economic development of the country.

"There is a Fintech Law in Mexico that is the legal framework, but it is not enough to be able to talk about all the issues regarding cryptocurrencies. What do we have to do? I invite the administrative authorities to have a uniform criterion regarding the use of cryptocurrencies, to reach this we have to make an interdisciplinary and equally that dialogue is opened," detailed Rebeca Álvarez, founder of the Loxical firm.

In Mexico, with the publication of the Fintech Law , the issue of virtual assets took on regulatory relevance. For the financial system, Banxico indicated that it would not allow institutions to offer these instruments to the general public and they can only use the technology for internal matters.

At the same time, the Tax Administration Service (SAT) took on anti-money laundering supervision for those platforms outside the financial system and for the purposes of preventing money laundering and terrorist financing.

For Vanessa Solis, director of the firm Vconsulting, the current regulatory framework that applies to cryptocurrencies does not cover the tax treatment on the operation of these instruments and although the Procuraduría de la Defensa del Contribuyente (Prodecon) has issued guidelines in this regard, the fact that the issue is not within the law causes uncertainty.

"There are countries that, without the need to compromise the financial system, have created measures or regulatory frameworks in tax matters. It is important to adapt the frameworks to the business models, but we must be very careful because any excess of the law can slow down growth," commented Solis.

Solis explained that although the Prodecon has suggested the payment of Income Tax in the operation of these instruments, the reality is that there are several aspects that must be considered for this to happen, because, for example, sometimes trading is done in other parts of the world or in centralized or decentralized platforms, which makes it impossible to talk about withholding this tax.

In her speech, Silvia Matus, vice president of External Practice of the Mexican Institute of Public Accountants (IMCP), detailed that, if the cryptocurrency trading operation generates profits, it is necessary to pay ISR despite the fact that it is not contemplated as such in the Mexican tax framework.

"The authority does not care if we have income from trading or, for example, selling tables. If you have legal profits you have to pay," Matus explained.

Rebeca Álvarez emphasized that, in the event of contemplating to adapt the regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies, it is necessary that the concepts addressed by the law be as broad as possible so that new business models such as non-fungible tokens or other types of tokens can be covered.

"We need concepts that are as broad as possible, that are flexible and that go along with business models.... It's not only putting the legal framework in place, it's also applying it. Today we have regulators in Banxico, the National Banking and Securities Commission, the National Commission for the Protection and Defense of Users of Financial Services and the Ministry of Finance, who need to understand the business models and that is extremely important," Alvarez said.

Treatment of personal data During the event that took place in the Senate of the Republic, Rodolfo Guerrero, legal representative and partner of the firm Coffee Law, highlighted the urgency of regulating the issue of digital assets and their relationship with the protection of personal data, as well as cybersecurity issues and digital rights.

"A principle of homologation must be followed.... The fact is to recognize what we have in the law, as well as the necessary reform paths so that those points that are part of this digital transformation, are clear and generate this famous democratization of technology," Guerrero said.

The specialist highlighted that, in terms of privacy of information in digital assets, it is necessary to reform the Federal Law for the Protection of Personal Data, especially so that there is a path on what to do with the digital identity of a deceased person.

Likewise, Guerrero highlighted the need to approve a general law on cybersecurity, in addition to being clear about digital rights in the context of the traceability of blockchain technology and the treatment of personal data.

"What we have to take care of is privacy and recognizing as part of a digital right, the right to anonymity because if we do not take into account those two figures, we are going to generate a major debate on privacy coins," Guerrero noted.

Anti-money laundering regulations, the complement In different parts of the world, such as Iceland, India and China, cryptocurrencies are prohibited; however, in other countries such as Japan, Sweden and El Salvador, these instruments have freedom of use.

For the specialists who were at the forum, a concern of governments that restrict the use of cryptocurrencies is because of the risk of these instruments for money laundering and terrorist financing, which they are working to limit before the requirements of the Financial Action Task Force.

"The issues (of cryptocurrencies) that matter at the moment are the FATF rules and the issue is that of cybersecurity, so that the funds are properly protected," detailed Etienne Luquet Farías, leader of Regulatory Affairs for Mexico at Bitso.

In his intervention, José Rodríguez, director of Talent Land Blockchain, severely criticized the narrative that cryptocurrencies are a focus of risk for money laundering, since, most cases of money laundering happen in the traditional financial system.

"Mexico sadly has the largest money laundering cases in the history of mankind and it's all been done in regulated financial institutions.... If FATF, authorities, central banks, all politicians are really interested in combating money laundering, why haven't the licenses of these big money launderers been cancelled. On the other hand, in cryptocurrencies you have a system that is born regulated and transparent", said Rodriguez.

For the director of Talent Land Blockchain, this narrative about the use of cryptocurrencies for money laundering causes authorities to focus on excessive policies against companies or platforms that operate these instruments, which causes a brake on the progress they can give to financial inclusion.

"If we look at it like in El Salvador, today more people have a Chivo wallet to access bitcoin and remittances and for the first time they have access to international payments.... In six months, that country managed to implement a system that has surpassed all the banks combined," Rodríguez explained.

For Ricardo Lechuga, partner of the firm Garrido Licona, in order to have an adequate regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies it is necessary to take into account the government's stance on monetary policy, financial security, structure for financial inclusion and even the environment.

"In Mexico we are in a process of financial inclusion, which so far has not been achieved (less than half of the population is banked), cash is still used as the main method of payment, that is a very complex issue to be able to enter into the regulation of these issues," Lechuga added.

title: The West vs. Russia
text:
To Ian, for sharing his knowledge

MEXICO CITY (Proceso) -At the beginning of the year I wrote in Proceso about the beginning of a new Cold War due to the tension between Russia and Ukraine. I alluded to the political division of the world for several decades. The polarization is now between Europe and Russia, but it is a game in which the United States has the final word. What I did not imagine is that it would not become a conventional war between two countries, but the war of all Western countries against Russia. Ukraine aroused a unanimity that I do not recall had ever been reached.

The regrettable US invasion of Iraq in 2003, far from provoking an outcry over the senselessness of a war that would soon cause more than 1 million deaths, hundreds of thousands of wounded and maimed, millions of displaced persons and refugees in other countries, was supported by England, Germany, Spain and other countries, which now condemn Russia's incursion into Ukraine whose damage so far is not comparable.

No action of war is justifiable, but the unanimity aroused with the leadership of the United States, whose president, Joe Biden, thus resorts to distraction about his inability to govern his country, is strange. His interference in other countries has been demonstrated by the disasters he has left in Iraq and Afghanistan, but there are also the sanctions with serious social consequences. It has done so on more than 115 occasions (1918-1998), 64 of which occurred in the 1990s. And in 1997 alone, half of the world's population suffered from its sanctions (Hélène Richard and Anne-Cécile Robert, Le Monde Diplomatique, March 2022). There are also the trade embargoes on Kuwait, Syria and Lebanon regardless of the famine and deaths.

What had happened before February 24 when Russia advanced on Ukraine? In 1991 the Soviet Union was dissolved. Since 1997, NATO has given accession to several countries of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. George Kenan, the renowned diplomat who contributed to the détente between the United States and Russia, said: "NATO enlargement is the most fatal mistake in U.S. foreign policy since the end of the Cold War".

In 2014 in Minsk, the capital of Belarus, the protocol was signed to ease the tension in eastern Ukraine and cease its attacks in Donetsk and Luganks, a war that reached 10,000 victims. In 2015 Minsk was reactivated with the signatures of Germany, France, Russia and Ukraine, but peace was never fully established and in the Donbas area fighting continued. On February 22, Russia recognized the independence of these regions, which it had encouraged. President Volodymir Zelensky criticized the Western allies for leaving Ukraine alone because he did not want to lose those regions, although he did not achieve peace.

Russia had already asked NATO to stop its eastward expansion, to withdraw Western troops from the new countries and to repatriate deployed nuclear weapons. The opposite happened, because military-technical cooperation with Ukraine was intensified. Obviously, its entry and the possible installation of nuclear bases of the Western countries and the United States were sponsored. The objective was to encircle Russia and Putin used the image that for Russia it was the same as if Russia were to place bases in Mexico. This was reminiscent of the missile crisis in 1962, when it tried to establish bases in Cuba.

The crisis has favored Ukraine by opening the doors to NATO, despite the previous commitment of the United States to avoid it, and it will also be able to accede to the European Union. The situation is reversed when Ukraine appears as the beneficiary of the Russian incursion. Why is it that what seemed to be a Russian strategy for non-explicit purposes turns against it and is slammed by the Western countries that allow the United States to regain its hegemonic position as leader of the West?

Russia is condemned by all. Biden haughtily affirms that Putin will be punished for his aggression. The head of NATO accuses him of destroying peace in Europe. Countries agree to criticize it in the most extreme manner. The resources denied to alleviate humanitarian crises magically appear and Ukraine receives millions of euros to buy high-powered weapons and even machine guns distributed among civilian militias.

Europe and other countries seem to have no memory as they join the unanimous narrative with a single perspective, that of the official voice to not only bend Russia but to humiliate it. And then comes the most severe sanction since the globality that allows, with the use of the swift, to deprive the country of its monetary reserves, preventing the use of 640 billion dollars frozen in the Central Bank. The banks of New York, London and even Switzerland have been closed for the Russians, in contravention of the political neutrality maintained even during the Second World War. 268 billion dollars have been frozen for private companies in Russian foreign currency banks, as well as 400 billion dollars invested in Russia. Citizens are unable to dispose of their 12 trillion euro cash and must stand in endless lines to get some of their own savings. They are betting that the ruble will collapse -it has already fallen several points- and the recession will provoke distrust and even an uprising like those designed by the United States to bring down governments in other countries.

Russia is losing the economic war and is also humiliated with numerous actions. Unanimity was expressed at the UN when the Russian Foreign Minister, Serguei Lavrov, when speaking, the room was abandoned by 100 delegations, depriving them of hearing another argumentation. Why, if his judgment has already been pronounced. Zelensky also wins the majority support of the European Parliament for Ukraine's accession to the European Union because "we are fighting for the freedom you have".

Russia has to be put down and it does not matter if traditions and ways of acting towards others are set aside, and the Hague Tribunal is already preparing to prosecute it for war crimes, when denunciations of other nations have been disdained for years. FIFA, breaking what kept it above politics, has deprived Russia of all its powers. So have other supposedly sporting organizations. In addition, Apple has decided not to sell its products in Russia. Film companies will not exhibit their films. The Cannes Film Festival has announced that it will not accept the participation of Russian productions. In the extreme, a ban on the purchase of scientific inputs and products is being induced. And despite Mexico's stance on non-intervention, it has suspended the Sputnik vaccine that was being applied. But that's not all, because Putin himself must suffer the humiliation and, although it makes one laugh, the International Taekwondo Organization has withdrawn his black belt.

All this looks like a program from the old TV series The Twilight Zone, because only one language is spoken and nobody listens to another. In the past different opinions were known, there were arguments, different positions, and now with the conflict in the making, the same voice is always heard. It remains to be seen whether Russia accepts the condition that is being imposed on it because its response could change the course of history. This analysis is part of the 2366th issue of the printed edition of Proceso, published on March 6, 2022, whose digital edition can be purchased at this link.

title: Mexican Stocks Close Lower; Peso Firms Against Dollar -- Market Talk
text:
1635 ET - The IPC stock index closes down 0.2% at 51045 points, well above its session lows, with America Movil shares off 0.9%, and Cemex shares down 2.5%. The peso firms to 20.66 to the US dollar, which was broadly weaker following gains of recent days. The government placed MXN15B in a syndicated auction of 3-year peso-denominated bonds due March 2025. The yield was 7.18%, 8bp above the previous close of the existing September 2024 bonds, says Banorte. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1427 ET - Mexico's Finance Ministry welcomes Fitch Ratings ' decision to affirm the country's BBB- sovereign rating and stable outlook, which it says will "help to preserve favorable access to international and domestic financial markets for the public and private sectors." Fitch cites "stable and robust external finances," and notes that Mexico's debt-to-GDP ratio has increased less than those of other triple-B rated countries. On the downside, the ratings firm says limited fiscal spending to address the pandemic could constrain future growth and employment, while government policy intervention affects investment prospects. Fitch forecasts economic growth for Mexico of 5.9% this year and 2.8% in 2022. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1401 ET - Deutsche Bank now expects the Fed to begin raising rates in July, or even earlier, rather than its previous forecast of December 2022, with another increase in November followed by three in 2023 and three more in 2024, eventually bringing the Fed funds rate to 2.1%. "Relative to our baseline expectation, we see greater risks of three rate increases next year than one," DB says. The move reflects higher-than-expected inflation and DB acknowledges the liftoff could be delayed if it weakens. Labor tightness is another factor. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1359 ET - A portfolio manager says he is betting on housing stocks as he sees supply issues easing next year. "I like those stocks," says Andrew Slimmon, the head of the applied equity advisors team at Morgan Stanley Investment Management . "You could have really good earnings growth for these companies because there is clearly a secular demand for those stocks, and their margins probably do quite well." Fresh data showed that housing starts, a measure of US home-building, declined 0.7% in October from September amid rising material costs and labor shortages that drove up home prices. (dave.sebastian@wsj.com; @depsebastian)

1357 ET - The US dollar weakens a touch against the euro and by 0.7% against a broadly stronger yen. The WSJ Dollar Index falls 0.2%. Minh Trang, senior FX trader at Silicon Valley Bank, tells WSJ today's moves are "a bit of profit taking given the recent run of the dollar.... Today you're seeing yields drop a bit and the dollar moving in unison." Trang says the dollar has had a great run, up nicely yesterday and this week overall. Retail sales numbers yesterday support the dollar's strength, he adds. (jonathan.vuocolo@wsj.com; @jonvuocolo)

1346 ET - Investors are likely anxious about the uncertainty about the Fed's incoming policy decisions, but Christmas, buoyed by strong spending, is coming, says Andrew Slimmon, the head of the applied equity advisors team at Morgan Stanley Investment Management . "I think the market is near term overbought, and there's some pretty high bullish sentiment readings, and I wouldn't be surprised that the market takes a breather from now until ... the week after Thanksgiving," Slimmon tells WSJ. He also notes that corporate fundamentals gleaned from earnings reports have been better than expected. (dave.sebastian@wsj.com; @depsebastian)

1315 ET - The stock performances of retail companies that reported earnings this week have been mixed. TJX gains 7.9% after the retailer posted earnings that exceeded analysts' expectations, while Target falls 4.6% even though results topped Wall Street estimates. Nevertheless, any pullback in retail stocks are buying opportunities, says Andrew Slimmon, the head of the applied equity advisors team at Morgan Stanley Investment Management . "If a company beats estimates, but the stock drops, I would not run out and sell those stocks," Slimmon tells WSJ. "Stocks don't go down for long when companies are doing better than expected." (dave.sebastian@wsj.com; @depsebastian)

1154 ET - Preliminary data shows US airlines carried 58.4M passengers in September, above the previous year's figure but still below prepandemic September 2019, the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics says. In September of this year, airlines carried 53.6M domestic passengers and 4.8M international passengers, according to the data. Airlines carried 72.6M passengers in September 2019 and 25.1M passengers in Sept. of last year, the BTS said. Final September data will be released on Dec. 16. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)ING sees the euro falling to $1.10 by 4Q 2022. "ING Sees Euro Falling to $1.10 by 4Q 2020 -- Market Talk," at 1554 GMT, misstated the year in the headline.

1122 ET - The Canadian dollar falls as October's inflation data was largely disappointing for the currency despite consumer prices rising at the highest rate since February 2003, Monex Europe says. Canada's consumer price index increased 4.7% year-on-year in October, which was in line with forecasts at time when U.S. CPI rose to levels not seen since the early Nineties, while other October inflation readings are outstripping economists' already high expectations, Monex forex analyst Simon Harvey says. "Secondly, the core-common measure of CPI, regarded as one of the better measures of underlying inflation, stayed stable at 1.8% despite many expecting it to show increased underlying inflation pressures." USD/CAD rises to a five-day high of 1.2599 after the data from 1.2552 beforehand. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1054 ET - ING expects the euro to fall to $1.10 by the fourth quarter of 2022 from $1.1302 currently as it sees the Federal Reserve raising interest rates before the European Central Bank . The Fed may raise rates by next summer while the ECB is likely to hold rates, ING analysts say. U.S. rate rise expectations are some 40-50 basis points below the Fed's projections, they say. For ECB rates, nearly 30 bps of tightening was expected for 2022 at one point, they say. "We view that pricing as extreme and unlikely, although it may take eurozone inflation dipping into next spring--the German VAT hike rolling out of calculations helps--before the market backs away from that kind of pricing." (renae.dyer@wsj.com) Correctiond & Amplifications

This item was corrected at 11:49 a.m. ET. An earlier version misstated the year in the headline as 2020.

1036 ET - Hackers linked to the Iranian government are launching cyberattacks against critical infrastructure including hospitals, local governments and transportation systems, according to a joint advisory from the US, UK and Australian governments. The state-sponsored group has broken into victims' computer systems using vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange email servers and tools made by the cybersecurity firm Fortinet . The governments' advisory, which warned of data theft and ransomware, urges companies to back up their data and update their computer systems. (david.uberti@wsj.com)

title: Despite covid-19 pandemic, Arturo Herrera said that Mexico is in a good fiscal position
text:
On June 9, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador announced a new change in his cabinet. Arturo Herrera, who had headed the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP), will be proposed as governor of the Bank of Mexico (Banxico). Instead, Rogelio Ramirez de la O will be in charge of running the country's finances.

Thus, a month after leaving his office in the National Palace, the official received journalist Hernan Gomez to talk about his management at the head of the agency. He explained that his intervention in Mexico's public finances was interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, a situation that afflicts everyone.

Nevertheless, Herrera Gutierrez said that the federal administration has been able to overcome the adverse conditions generated by the disease, because in addition to the fact that the transmission of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has decreased, the secretary stressed that the country's fiscal position is favorable.

"What is going through a difficult time is the world, because of the pandemic and because of the economic impact on the pandemic. But it seems to me that in these complex conditions, we managed to get this out of the way. We have the pandemic today at very low levels, with relatively lower levels of contagion, and the fiscal position is coming out much better."

According to his explanation, there are countries that bet on debt trying to overcome the crisis soon, however, today they are involved in serious fiscal problems.

As for his candidacy to head Banxico, the official said he feels very flattered, since for an economist, "being in the Treasury or being in the Central Bank is like for a footballer to play for Barcelona or Real Madrid."

As a balance, he recalled that one of the main challenges he faced at the head of the SHCP was the task of making sure that there were sufficient resources to combat the presence of the virus and, in addition, to maintain stable public finances.

"You don't choose the circumstances, but what you have to be is to know how to face them, so the most important thing is to make sure that we could contribute to keeping the country afloat in an extraordinarily painful process. We had to make sure that there were resources for the hospitals, for the vaccines and that we could keep the public finances stable."

On the other hand, he made it clear that his working relationship with President López Obrador has worked on the best terms. "The president listens, but requires and demands arguments, it is not giving a blank check," he said. In addition to this, he defended that he has the necessary experience to assume the position for which the president has nominated him.

Surrounded by buildings of historical, political and cultural value, the office of the secretary of finance is located facing the Zocalo in Mexico City. Before taking the nineteenth-century elevator to get to his cubicle, Arturo Herrera recounted what a morning is like for someone who occupies his position.

The first thing it monitors upon awakening are the economic variables that affect the country. According to the secretary, these are the price of oil and the exchange rate.

"The exchange rate in general has been fine except just as the pandemic started. The pandemic brought an exacerbation to investors' risk because no one knew what was going to happen, how long it was going to last, and what they did is: they pulled their investments from emerging countries, including Mexico, into hard currencies, particularly the dollar. Then, in February of last year, the Mexican peso went from 18 pesos per dollar to 25.3 pesos per dollar in just five weeks," said the graduate of the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana (UAM).

title: What do the markets expect for this Wednesday, May 12th?
text:

Mexico

The information will begin at about 6:00 a.m. when INEGI publishes indicators of industrial activity during March.

United States
