Later, at 7:30 a.m., the Bureau of Labour Statistics will publish inflation indicators during April; analysts estimate that the price increase is around an annualized rate of 3.6 percent, above 2.6 percent earlier and above the U.S. central bank's target. At a monthly rate, forecasts estimate that inflation is around 0.2 percent.

At 8:00 a.m., Richard Clarida, Vice President of the Fed, will give a speech on the economic outlook.

At 8:05 a.m., Eric Rosengren, president of the Boston Fed, will speak to Harvard Law School about the central bank's outlook and digital currencies.

Later, at 9:30 a.m., the Energy Information Administration (EIA) will release oil inventories and their derivatives as of May 7.

An hour later, at 10:30 a.m., the Treasury Department will reopen a short-term bond auction (T-Bills) for $35 billion liquidity management in a 119-day operation; another 41 billion will be auctioned at noon, but this time it will be 10-year Treasury Notes.

At noon, Raphael Bostic, president of the Atlanta Fed, will speak at a webinar.

At 12:30 a.m., Patrick Harker, president of the Philadelphia Fed, will participate in an event to discuss higher education.

At 1:00 a.m., the Treasury Department will have monthly budget data during April.

Europe

The information to be followed will be data on business investment, trade balance and industrial production in the United Kingdom in March, and in that country will also highlight the GDP data in the first quarter of the year.

For the Eurozone, there will be data on industrial production in the third month of the year, where a 1% vs. February progress and 11.5% annual growth are expected.

Inflation figures will be revealed in Germany and France during April; there will also be interventions by economic authorities in the Eurozone.

title: US launches "first warning" to Mexico over peso price against dollar
text:
Joe Biden's government fears that fiscal austerity and hostile investment climate in Mexico will impede an adjustment in the trade balance with the country, which has a negative balance for the US.

Mexico's growing trade surplus with the United States has already aroused the strangeness of Treasury Department officials, as Janet Yellen's entity decided to give a "first warning" to the neighboring country with the start of monitoring of trades by pesos per dollar.

The criteria for the US to have decided to include Mexico in its "close monitoring" list are alleged intervention in the foreign exchange market, current account surplus of at least 2% of GDP and/or a bulging trade surplus.

Mexico closed 2020 with a trade surplus with its main partner at nearly $112.722 billion (mdd). A trend that continued during January and February of this year, with a cumulative of about 15,940 mdd, indicate data from the US government.

For Alfredo Coutiño, director for Latin America at Moody's Analytics, while acknowledging the existence of a foreign exchange market for free floating and minimal interventions by mexican authorities, Joe Biden's government is "concerned" about policies implemented by the Mexican government that have an indirect effect on foreign exchange parity and current account surplus

"Specificly, the northern neighbor's authority is concerned about the persistent policy of fiscal austerity and the hostile climate for private investment that together hold domestic demand depressed, thereby promoting a persistent trade and current account surplus, hampering an automatic rebalancing of Mexican external accounts to the detriment of Americans" , he commented in an interview via email.

"Mexico has had a trade surplus of more than 20,000 mdd with the United States since 1999 and by 2020 the current account surplus averaged 2.4% (relative to GDP). This would lead to Mexico being included in the list, but not for the first time, because the trade and current account criteria are not the first time Mexico has reached them," Gabriela Siller, Director of Financial Economic Analysis at Banco Base, said.

However, Felipe Hernandez, Economist for Latin America at Bloomberg Economics, considered the possibility that the United States sanctions Mexico is much lower in a Biden administration than under the Trump administration.

"The trade relationship is very important and I don't see sanctions in this administration," the expert said.

The Ministry of Finance ensures that this surveillance will be transitional and that the bilateral balance will be adjusted to pre-pandemic levels as the economic recovery occurs.

"Once we look at the effects associated with this set of policies and be clear how many are related to the foreign exchange market is when it will be possible to determine whether Mexico actually falls into a category of country that manipulates the exchange rate or not and I think in that sense it is very rare for it to act in that regard," said Víctor Gómez , deputy director of economic analysis of Finamex Casa de Bolsa.

For Moody's economist, the signal sent about Mexico is not positive and adds to the negative factors that can cloud the country's economic future as the US is particularly concerned about fiscal management.

The Treasury's report also advanced that with AMLO's government policies, U.S. renewable energy exports to Mexico are expected to shrink, and this in turn will mean a bilateral trade surplus for Mexico.

"Mexico's economic policies jeopardize the trade relationship with the United States. Not for trying to generate more growth for Mexico (which would be a positive thing), but for changing the rules of the game and affecting the interests of other countries," Siller said.

Janneth Quiroz, deputy director of analysis at Monex Casa de Bolsa, said that considering that the United States is Mexico's largest trading partner with more than 80% of exports, it is the country that will be most interested in Mexico practicing a regulation that is established internationally.

For Quiroz, the US announcement is a call to the Mexican authorities to remember that Mexico is not isolated from the rest of the countries and is part of an international community.

"It has signed trade agreements that must comply with and comply with these pacts must be a priority for economic authorities in the country," she said.

Quiroz considered that respecting trade agreements will give investor guarantees and improve the investment climate in the country.

"The United States somehow raised its voice to say 'we are watching over the economic policy that our trading partners also implement' and it is certainly important for Mexico to comply with these regulations and it is certainly news to ensure and try to ensure that Mexico does not deviate from all these reforms of the policies that have been implemented" Said.

The peso closed Tuesday's session with a depreciation of 0.62% or 12.2 cents, to be quoted at 19.94 units per dollar, due to good economic data and US business performance and despite an environment of worsening the coronavirus pandemic globally.

The US entry launches a "first warning" to Mexico for the price of the peso against the dollar appears first in I-Xport.

title: Why a "treasure" from porfirio Díaz's era could turn Mexico into a world power
text:
A "treasure" of more than 830 billion pesos could make Mexico a world power, assured Infobae México Rogelio Amparan, a member of the Joint Private Fund for Autonomous Heritage.

We're going to check it out, because if this is real. or we have it, Mexico is really going to become a power, because to do everything you want, you need resources

Since the country achieved its independence from the Spanish Crown, in 1821, a series of "out-of-book" deposits have been generated to compensate the legitimate owners of the Mexican territory, the original communities, for the extraction of natural wealth at the hands of nations of great economic importance.

"So, what is a fact, because we came to know all these deposits at some point, when we do a compliance with England, they throw away all the information and it is amazing, was the confirmation a few years ago that there were so many gold deposits of different denominations and weight, that the Mexican state made to concentrate them and, at the time , to compensate the entire Mexican population through the administration of their central bank," Amparan told Infobae Mexico.

However, it was until Porfiriato, a thirty-year period in which General Porfirio Díaz was president of Mexico, that such contributions became more relevant.

This moment in history is characterized by political, social and economic stability, as it opened the door to important foreign investors who managed to accelerate commercial activity. Mexico's Gross Domestic Product from 1877 to 1910 was impressive for its time; real GDP per capita remained at levels of 2.1% per year.

Compared to other more developed countries, according to economist Timothy J. Kehoe, "[...] Porphyriato was the period - except for the 1950-1981 import substitution period - in which Mexico is comparable to the United States."

Already with Plutarco Elías Calles at the head of the Federal Executive, a decree is issued to begin with the compensation of indigenous peoples in the future, an amount that was formed by the accumulated deposits and an appraisal of Mexican lands.

"The deposits themselves form something called the Single Support Capital Account (CUCA) from which the entire population becomes an active partner, three generations of 33 years have passed and Mexico has the right to collect it up to the fourth generation, but Mexico should be receiving dividends from that unique contribution account to distribute them to its entire population," explained Mauricio Montijo spokesman Lucero , single administrator and liquidator agent of the FMPPA.

Montijo Lucero acquired the right to manage the fund for the appointment given to his family, when Elías Calles, in 1928, began the registration process from the updating of particular committees of all the indigenous communities of the country.

"It was Grandma, Dad and then Mauritius who has been following up. This right was granted to it when those 33 years expire, after those deposits in that third period Mexico can now automatically access through its common representative the yields generated by that account and those huge yields, Mauritius talks about 822 million initially, but right now we go in eight hundred and thirty-somethings," he said.

It has been proven that everything Mauritius says is real, that Mexico has a great treasure

It would take the intervention of the Mexican State, with the support of a diplomatic corps, for the Joint Private Fund of Autonomous Heritage to initiate a process of repatriation of resources. For this reason, the members of that body took with optimism theinitiative of Andrés Manuel López Obrador on indegar about the "treasure".

At a morning press conference on January 19, the Mexican representative reported that Arturo Herrera, Secretary of Finance and Public Credit, was given the instruction to investigate the fortune he would be abroad.

"We have heard this version on other occasions, but we have no evidence, there is no evidence that this is real, of course we do not close any files that have to do with these facts, with the possibility that there is money abroad that is from Mexico, that does not prescribe; if investigated, if you have elements, if tested, if it is real; then the government would act to demand the return of that wealth for the benefit of the people of Mexico, but there is now no information on that," he said on January 19.

With these resources, rogelio Amparan said, Mexico gained financial independence. In addition, an investment in four main axes could be generated among the country's 2,458 municipalities: education, health, economic development and food.

"If we give that money to each inhabitant, because we are going to collapse the country and that is not the idea, it is a smart financial action that should apply that investment and make the whole population work for their communities, under that case let's say hypothetical the amount towards each inhabitant generates a source of investment because the stock market does not withdraw , it is maintained and what it produces is what is being withdrawn and is being invested in the four areas of sustainable development," he said.

However, this information has not been disclosed to the population. According to the FMPPA member, there are political and business domes that Mexico does not want to regain its value in the foreign exchange market, investment development. "[...] that part is the one that the public administration doesn't like very much because it thinks we're trying to generate an alternate government and it's not."

"Our intention is not to be in confrontation with anyone, let alone the president of the republic, the intention is to give him the most powerful tool that the president of the republic can access, to access the whole plan he brings to develop this country and is genuine," he added.

title: Interventionist  policies in pandemic could exacerbate credit risk: Fitch Ratings
text:
MEXICO CITY (apro).- Qualifying agency Fitch Ratings warned that interventionist policies amid the pandemic could exacerbate credit risk for financial institutions in Mexico and Latin America.

According to the firm, the increased risk of government intervention arising from legislation may expose banks to international sanctions.

"Mexican lawmakers delayed the debate on a controversial bill recently passed by its Senate of the Republic, which requires the central bank (Banxico) to buy excess foreign currency in cash until February 2021," notes the report entitled "Non-Orthodox policies in Latam would stress financial institutions in the midst of the crisis."

Fitch warned that while this bill is intended to benefit people receiving remittances or cash dollars from tourist activity, this exposes Banxico to the risk of buying U.S. dollars from illegal or un traceable sources. In the meantime, major banks support efforts to combat the proposal.

According to the rating agency, the implementation of these initiatives is currently at very early stages, either in simple initiative or bill, in countries such as Mexico, Panama and Peru.

However, Costa Rica has had interest rate limits since July 2020 and Fitch expects that to negatively influence the financial and credit profiles of private banks.

The effects on Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador, Bolivia and Argentina are varied and some have experienced slowdowns in loan growth, deteriorating credit quality or pressure on margins, as a result of interest rate caps and government tariff restrictions.

According to the analysis, these policies are unlikely to push the credit ratings of large banks in the short term, as they benefit from the scale and diversification of their portfolios.

However, he clarified, they could extend the time required for small and medium-sized banks and non-bank financial institutions (IFNBs) in specialized sectors to recover from the economic consequences of the pandemic.

For Fitch Ratings, unrthodox and populist policies, such as limiting interest rates on products -- such as consumer or microfinance loans--, reducing commissions, requiring loan deadlines, and implementing foreign exchange legislation, have been discussed with Latin American authorities since before the pandemic crisis.

However, the authorities have increasingly used these policies to support debtors and promote credit expansion to respond to the region's severe economic downturn.

Compulsory loans to sectors could result in greater risks to banks. They could also involve a reduction in IFNB's appetite to extend credit to risky segments.

The report highlights that larger and more diversified banks should be able to offset the margin pressure of interest rate caps through cost-cutting measures and the use of alternative channels, such as digital and online, for the origination and collection of credits.

However, small and medium-sized banks and IFNBs in specialized sectors such as microcredit or consumer loans will be more affected by higher operating, lending and funding costs.

"Commissions and fees could help mitigate the impact of margins, but commission collection is being restricted with proposed reductions insome Latin American countries," Fitch added.

title: The reform that the Bank of Mexico does need
text:
Central banks in the world can have one or two of these main objectives; the first is to maintain the purchasing power of the currency, that is, to avoid inflation and the second is to avoid unemployment.

The two phenomena of both inflation and unemployment are regarded as the greatest enemies for society economically. Inflation, the widespread increase in prices, extracts, erodes, eliminates the purchasing power of money and has regressive effects because it affects the most humble people they least have. On the other hand, unemployment is also a major enemy for the economy for obvious reasons.

Central banks are the bodies responsible for exercising a country's monetary policy and can deal with these two terrible phenomena; inflation and unemployment. If the Central Bank implements an expansive monetary policy by increasing the monetary supply in the economy, it can thereby promote the activation of the economy, which will ultimately result in job creation, and in the same way to avoid an inflationary process it can contract the money supply to achieve it.

The point is that in our country the Bank of Mexico has only one mandate that is to maintain the purchasing power of the currency, but it does not have the mandate to avoid unemployment, which must be corrected as soon as possible by allowing the Bank of Mexico with its very powerful monetary policy to intervene in the economy to combat unemployment while always taking care to stay within an inflation target previously set by the Bank itself.

Within the central banks that enjoy this dual mandate, controlling inflation and avoiding unemployment we find the influential Federal Reserve of the United States of America, so it would not be a proposal for reckless but well-founded reform. The important thing is to put the central bank's monetary policy to work in a dual mandate, to avoid inflation and also unemployment, which would be very much in line with the current administration focused on improving the well-being of citizens, especially the most unfortunate.

Mtro. Jesús Torres Gómez

Professor at the International School of Law and Jurisprudence.

title: Banxico Law Changes Put Country Note at Risk
text:
Mexico's credit quality could be at risk with the adoption of changes to the Bank of Mexico Act, which will now be voted on in the San Lazarus plenary, Moody's warned, which currently assigns Mexico a note of "Baa1" with a negative outlook.

The main one of these risks, they detailed, is that resources of illicit origin could enter, with the implications that this would have, including international sanctions, but also with impacts on the local financial system and the economy.

Unprecedented in the worldHéctor Grisi, executive chairman and CEO of Santander Mexico, stressed that there is no precedent in the world, that a central bank is the ultimate taker of some country's resources, which would pose a risk, because it is transferred to the State, responsibility for the purchase of cash and is also exposed to interventions that may be from the U.S. Department of Justice , which could lead to the freezing of international reserves.

title: Banxico, willing to help financial institutions meet law requirements for  foreign exchange
text:
The Governor of the Bank of Mexico,Alejandro Díaz de León,proposed three alternatives to the LXIV Legislature of the Union Congress to resolve the management of residual cash currencies of financial operations, rather than the reform to Articles 20 and 34 of the Law of Bank of Mexico that is currently under discussion in the Chamber of Deputies.

At an extraordinary meeting convened by the Finance and Public Credit Committee of the Chamber of Deputies,the central banker stated that measures can be implemented to help open more correspondent doors for all Mexican intermediaries, such as the creation of a kind of Council, where Banxico and the Ministry of Finance would participate.

A second alternative would be for the Legislature to promote in law the use of technological tools developed by the Bank of Mexico itself.

And the third would be the holding of financing operations between the same Central Bank and the multi-banking institutions that face difficulties in placing the foreign currency they capture in the country of origin.

The proposals are included in a document that was already submitted and delivered by Banco de México to the chairman of the Finance Commission of the House of Senators, Alejandro Armenta Mier,on December 8, a day before they approved the reform of articles 20 and 34 of the Law of Bank of Mexico, where they explain in detail each of them.

This same document with comments could already be in the hands of the Finance Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, taking into account the commitment of the central banker to support them in their deliberations in order to take longer to analyze the proposed changes in the minutes approved by the Senate. Time where they could listen to more experts and authorities in the field.

Alternative 1: The CouncilAs described in the document before the Senate Finance Commission, the copy of which is in the possession of El Economista,the first alternative is to implement measures that help open more correspondent doors for all Mexican intermediaries.

Correspondent operations are those contracted by one bank to authorize another to make low-cost transfers outside the territory where the former operates.

"Given the complexity of the phenomenon, its solution requires the coordination of all relevant authorities (...) it would also be useful to consider the relationship to be had with the foreign authorities affecting the cross-border operation of their currency."

If addressed, the initiative could be strengthened by creating a special coordinating authority to address this problem and could operate as the Financial System Stability Council,the Financial Inclusion Board and the Financial Education Committee.

Alternative 2: Technology PlatformThe Legal Team of the Bank of Mexico proposed as a second alternative that could be raised to the rank of law: the use of tools developed by the Central Institute to support institutions in carrying out their operations with instruments considered to be of greater risk.

"The Bank of Mexico can help mitigate the cause of the problem by creating a technology platform that centralizes currency transaction information infinancial institutions can know statistical data on the operations their clients carry out with other entities in the financial sector."

This "would aim to enable them to make a deeper and more complete due diligence process. Financial institutions would consult that platform to complete their customer knowledge process using the information they receive."

Using it "reduces the possibility of cash dollars that cannot be repatriated to the United States and thus the need for the Bank of Mexico to intervene as proposed in the initiative."

Banxico's legal team clarifies that if this proposal is advanced, "Mexican entities providing such services will be in a position to demonstrate to their counterparties that they serve as correspondent banks in the United States that their customer knowledge and due diligence processes are robust enough to maintain financial relations with it."

Alternative 3: FinancingThe third alternative proposed by Banco de México's legal team is "to hold financing operations with multiple banking institutions that face the conditions that make it impossible for them to place in the country of origin the foreign currency they capture, derived from the services they have been offering on a daily basis".

"This in order to avoid ingesting the acceptance of this currency by such institutions thereby avoiding public impacts on access to foreign currency cash transactions."

In turn, these transactions would mitigate the impact of the institutions' foreign exchange transactions by the conditions described above and, on the other hand, would prevent Banco de México from taking the risks acquired by such institutions that have resulted in the inability to place in their country of origin the foreign currency acquired by them.

title: Banxico is exposed with meaningless law
text:
With changes to the Bank of Mexico Act passed Wednesday by the Senate, the goal of achieving a better exchange price for users will not be achieved, but international reserves are put at risk.

The initiative, which was taken over by Deputies, aims to force Banxico to buy the cash currencies that financial institutions fail to repatriate through their correspondents abroad and it would be the same institutions that define how much they did not repatriate and should buy from the Central Bank.

The flow begins with currencies - mostly dollars - that arrive in cash in the country and are exchanged in financial institutions, which subsequently seek to sell them either to people in the country who require those currencies or abroad.

The main argument for changes to the Act points out that by not being able to repatriate all currencies, institutions face higher costs than moving to the exchange rates they offer.

However, in a technical note sent to the Senate, Banxico clarified that financial institutions have mechanisms to repatriate through correspondents, and a total of $4.732 billion raised in cash between January and September, only 2% have not been repatriated and is kept in bank vaults.

The Central Bank has rejected the reform and warned that by buying the dollars in cash it takes the risk that these resources will be of illicit origin, which it would have to integrate into its reserves, as would be required by the new Law.

It detailed that 99% of remittances reach the country through wire transfers, so the measure would be aiming to serve only that remaining 1%.

"This risk would not only be limited to the amounts of cash currency captured by the Bank of Mexico in accordance with the above, but could extend to the operation of international reserves in the possession of the Institute," he said.

title: 12,500 mdd local bond market left in three months: IMF
text:
Mexico is characterized by being one of the emerging countries with the highest participation of foreigners in financial markets, which is a risk factor in the face of financial uncertainty and volatility is a report from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The Fund states that over the years, emerging and border markets have become more dependent on foreign capital flows. Specifically since the global financial crisis, 10 years ago, the participation of foreigners in emerging financial markets has grown significantly.

The stock market highlights, where non-resident participation has traditionally been smaller and that investors now own a significant share of stocks traded on stock exchanges in emerging economies.

Risks related to portfolio flows may be sharper in a context of high levels of global debt in emerging markets.

Two separate expert analyses of the Fund emphasize that proportions are "exposure factors in the event that financial conditions and investor preferences continue to be tightened".

In their "Covid-19 Response Policy Tracker," developed by the IMF for 191 countries and updated daily, they estimate that between February 20 and May 21, foreign investors settled Mexican government bonds for $12.5 billion or 1.2 points of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

This proportion has increased since March, when the cumulative exits since the pandemic began in Mexico were equivalent to 0.4% of the product.

There they emphasized that in periods of high risk aversion, such as those experienced in March and mid-April by Covid-19, currencies have weakened as a result of sales by foreign investors who want to reduce their exposure and prefer to move to safer assets.

Within the second part of its Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR), IMF experts propose to limit risk from strengthening the emerging capital recipient, in this case Mexico or Hungary.

They propose to the authorities the development of efficient money markets, strengthen primary market practices to improve transparency and predictability of issuance, strengthen market liquidity, develop a strong market infrastructure as well as ensure compliance with the law and respect for contracts.

By ensuring certainty they fuel the confidence of investors who even in volatility can wait before selling or turmating securities, they said.

They emphasize that increased foreign participation in emerging debt markets exposes them to changes in global financial conditions through the behaviour and preferences of foreign investors.

They emphasized that in periods of risk aversion, when local currencies weaken and domestic assets are topped off, investors continue to reduce their exposure, triggering capital outflows that could disrupt bond markets.

The risk lies in the economies that were financed in foreign currencies, generating what is called "original sin," they stressed.

Upward riskIn the Response Policy Tracker, Mexico chapter, they emphasized that the risk paid by 10-year sovereign titles rose from 131 points on February 20 to 434 basis points at the peak reached on April 28.

This"driven by Pemex's deterioration in risk" which reached 1,186 basis points from 377 starting points.This perception of uncertainty about Mexico and its state production company, led to a depreciation of the Mexican peso from May 18 to 21, which has eased from the peak reached of 25% at the end of last March, they detailed.

These capital outflows from Mexico led to interventions and a monetary-rate stock package implemented by the Bank of Mexico in conjunction with the Ministry of Finance, to try to order movements that are documented by the IMF and which is one of the most modest of those collected in the world, equivalent to 0.7% of GDP.

title: Aeromar suffers over-the-charge for trial, SAT  intervention
text:
The Mexico Exchange Commission raised the amount of the foreign exchange program it has to expand the mechanism it has been using over the past three years by $10 billion to the usability to secure the price of the U.S. currency and thereby avoid the risks of volatility facing the Mexican foreign exchange market by international financial turbulence.

Thus, the Commission, which is composed of the secretary of the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, Arturo Herrera, and the governed Bank of Mexico, Alejandro Díaz de León, in addition to two undersecretaries and two members of the governing board of the Mexican central bank, decided to increase the available amount of that program in order to auction exchange rate coverage of up to 30 billion dollars.

Until now, the maximum amount of exchange rate coverage that the Mexican government could issue through Banco de México was $20 billion. To date, Mexico's financial authorities have auctioned $5.5 billion auctions, which in the face of the program's increase would allow them to issue 24 billion more in exchange rate hedges.

By purchasing the foreign exchange hedges issued by the Government of Mexico, purchasers will be able to secure the value of the U.S. currency in pesos in the future at a price determined at a certain price at present. Thus, if the exchange rate is at a weaker level than the acquired hedging, the Mexican government will buried the difference in the price of the dollar in pesos so that the economic operator can buy the dollars without having to disburse more resources.

If, on the other hand, the exchange rate depreciates less than expected in hedging, then economic operators will have lost the value of the hedging as they will be able to buy the dollars on the market at a lower price than they expected.

Thus, hedges cause foreign exchange market participants to not have to suffer volatility by being able to secure a future value for the U.S. currency.

"Over the past few days, global financial markets have shown marked volatility due to the economic and social impact that could result from covid-19 contagion, as well as recent energy announcements by major crude oil producers globally," the Exchange Commission said in a statement. "In this environment, the foreign exchange market in our country has also been more volatile."

So "with the aim of . . . maintain an orderly functioning of the exchange market . . . [the] Commission has decided to increase the size of the liquidable exchange hedge programme by difference in national currency," the unit added.

The objective of hedging is not, nor was it in the past, to defend a currency contribution level, but to ensure that the market trades with sufficient liquidity by providing a tool to economic operators to better plan their future dollar operations.

The exchange rate hedge programme began in February 2017 to provide foreign exchange market participants with a foreign exchange toolplanner against the volatility that the weight experienced at the time by the arrival of Donald J. Trump in the US presidency. The protectionist stances of the then new U.S. representative generated nervousness in Mexican financial markets, hitting the peso.

Since then, multiple auctions of these hedges have been held, something the government will be doing in the future.

"The Commission may convene at any time and immediately carry out auctions of these instruments," the Commission added. "The Exchange Commission reaffirms its commitment to continue to assess the conditions of operation on the exchange market and, if necessary, take additional actions."

The announcement by the country's foreign exchange authorities gave a slight respite to the Mexican peso in after-hours operations. The peso wholesale price against the dollar was strengthened from 21.06 units per dollar prior to the announcement to 20.7 units.

However, the Mexican currency officially closed with a 5% drop from Friday's close, a second crash after Friday's 6% fall.

title: Mexico weathered the storm over the peso and increased its reserves
text:
When the Mexican peso fell to historic lows earlier this year, the central bank remained on the sidelines, saving ammunition. It's a policy that may be starting to pay off.

The Bank of Mexico refrained from using its foreign exchange reserves even when the peso led down to emerging market currencies in late March. This action was very contrasting with that of its peers in developing countries.

The bank seems to have weathered the storm. After losing 25% of its value until March 23, the peso stabilized, even as oil prices fell and the coronavirus pandemic threatened to cut off to 12% of gross domestic product. By comparison, Brazil—which has spent $48 billion on spot market interventions—has seen a 27% depreciation of its currency this year, while the president, Jair Bolsonaro, usded a political storm.

"Banxico continues to choose to use its swap program for currency management," said Ilya Gofshteyn, a Strata at Standard Chartered in New York.

The policy has left Mexico in an almost unique position among emerging markets, as it registers an increase in its foreign currency reserves this year. Reserves reached $186.1 billion in May, the highest since August 2015.

The country has the lowest share of gross reserves on average annual imports among major Latin American peers.To provide liquidity to the market, Mexico's central bank used a Federal Reserve swap line of $60 billion twice in April and sold a total of $10 billion in the market in the form of dollar credit. The country also supplies non-deliverable forwards settled in pesos, a measure similar to Brazil and Chile.

The peso "remains the preferred emerging market indicator among investors and Banxico will hesitate to intervene directly through selling," Gofshteyn said.

Mexico may have had few options. The country has the lowest share of gross reserves on average annual imports among major Latin American peers. In relation to its reserves, Mexico's potential financing needs in the event of a major external shock will be high, according to Marcelo Carvalho and Luiz Peixoto, emerging market analysts at London-based BNP Paribas. South Africa, Egypt, Chile, Colombia and Turkey are also among the vulnerable nations.

After simulating a global crisis in exports, tourism, remittances, foreign direct investment and emerging market portfolio flows, Carvalho and Peixoto found that the impact on the balance of payments could reach 6.9% of Mexico's GDP and 4.7% of Brazil's GDP. Assuming a 90% renewal of short-term external debt, total external financing needs would reach about 5.1% in Brazil and 7.5% for Mexico.

title: López Obrador to speak to Banxico about remnants of foreign reserves
text:
Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador will meet with the central bank about unexpected remnants of the bank's foreign currency reserves after the peso crash this year.

At a morning press conference, the president said he would talk to the bank's board members about the remnant, raising speculation that he will now request a payment of this year's earnings, even though they would normally be paid in April 2021.

The problem for the president is that there is no remnant in 2019 as the weight was regained that year. Given the 27% drop in weight this year and the current level of reserves, Benito Berber, chief economist for Latin America at Natixis North America, estimates that around 866 billion pesos (US$36 billion) could be paid to the Ministry of Finance. This would represent a significant entry for a government suffering from liquidity problems.

"It would be very controversial if they made some kind of breakthrough," Berber said. "It would be very close to government financing by the central bank. But given the shock, the market might not take it negatively, especially if the funds are used to support the economy."

Banxico has the final say on how much is actually sent, and the money goes to debt reduction (Photo: REUTERS/Daniel Becerril) (DANIEL BECERRIL/)A presidential spokesman said the meeting will take place Thursday after AMLO initially said it would be today.

Banxico has the final say on how much is actually sent, and the money goes to debt reduction. The bank may refuse to send a prepayment as the final figures for weight depreciation and reserves are not included.

"They don't have to transfer everything," said Eduardo Suarez, Scotiabank's strata in Mexico City. "You can't, partly because at this time you don't know how much it will be."

However, for López Obrador, who has made fiscal strength a priority even in the midst of the coronavirus crisis, additional central bank funds will be attractive.

"This surplus will help us avoid debt growth," he told reporters during the conference.

title: Strengthens Banxico international reserves
text:
If the Bank of Mexico were to make direct intervention in the foreign exchange market from international reserves, it would have $185.509 million at its disposal.

This, incorporating the $1.334 million increase that was completed in the week of March 20-27.

This weekly increase in the international reserve is the result of a change in the valuation of international assets of $884 million and $450 million sold by Pemex to the central institute.

Asset valuation is the movement resulting from the foreign exchange appreciation of the national currency with respect to the various currencies that make up the international reserve.

So far this year, the central bank's dollar acquis, i.e. international reserves, completed an accumulation of $4.631 million. This is the fastest rate of accumulation for a similar period since 2015, only beyond the history reached in 2014, when reserves were strengthened by $6.163 million in the same period.

In the 13 weeks of the year, the Bank of Mexico has recorded eight weekly accumulations of reserves totaling $5.965 million. However, this increase in reserves has been affected by the cumulative reductions in four weeks, which totalled $1.634 million.

In this year, Pemex has contributed 1.733 million of this provision of dollars, as by law it must exchange the currencies resulting from its oil sales in the Banxico. Since the fall in hydrocarbon production began in 2015, targeted reserve accumulation has been limited.

IMF strengthens dollar acquisSince 2009, Mexico has had an open credit line at the IMF, which guarantees access to a certain amount of dollars, currently $61 billion, if required by the Banxico.

This IMF facility for Mexico guarantees the central bank the possibility of putting together a strategy in the event of a high volatility episode, as it could complement international reserves with this FCL.

So by adding up to the $185.509 million that are part of the international reserves, with the $61 billion open line at the IMF, the Bank of Mexico can count on liquidity in dollars of up to $246.5 billion.

Notwithstanding Banxico's arsenal of dollars that represents access to this Flexible Credit Line, its use comes at a cost, because even if they are resources that would be available they would have to be documented as public debt. Mexico has ceased to be an IMF debtor since 2000.

title: 4 Banxico measures to guarantee liquidity for banks
text:
The Bank of Mexico (Banxico)released four measures that seek to guarantee liquidity for banks and corporate companies that may even require U.S. dollars in the face of deteriorating global financial conditions, because of the contingency caused by the spread of Covid-19 coronavirus.

Measures involving the use of the $60 billion that Bank of Mexico will exchange with the U.S. Federal Reserve(Fed)on the swap line announced Thursday, March 19.

The first action is to reduce the Monetary Regulation Deposit (DRM) held by the multiple banking and development institutions at the Central Institute, amounting to 50 billion pesos.

The objective of this measure is to improve the liquidity and ability to provide loans from banks, as well as to maintain or expand lines of credit. Currently the total amount of the DRM is 320 billion pesos, and the Bank of Mexico will sterilize the monetary impact of this measure that will take place on April 1 of this year.

The second action is also aimed at multiple banking and involves the cut in the cost of loans or reports between the central bank and financial institutions, which currently fluctuates between 2 and 2.2 times the objective of Banxico'sone-day interbank interest rate. The measure is to halve this cost and place it at 1.1 times the rate target. This measure is called Ordinary Additional Liquidity Facility; is available since 2008 and the change will take effect from April 1.

The third measure announced by Banxico is aimed at guaranteeing liquidity in dollars,and was taken by instruction from the Exchange Commission where the Ministry of Finance also participates. This facility will be financed by the temporary foreign exchange mechanism, known as the swap line,established with the Fed in the amount of $60 billion.

And the fourth action is a collaboration with the Ministry of Finance to strengthen the Government Debt Market Trainers Program that will also come into force on April 1.

Discouraging speculationIf the Bank of Mexico had to resort to direct intervention in the exchange market, it would have $245.619 million available that it could use to try to order the sharp weight movements against the dollar.

This amount comes from adding up international reserves, amounting to $184,619 million as of March 13 and $61 billion available on mexico's Flexible Credit Line at the International Monetary Fund(IMF).

If these resources were not sufficient, thanks to the open swap line with the Fed,Banco de Mexico would have another $60 billion available.

According to the Founder and Coordinator of UNAM's Center for Model modeling and Economic Forecasting (CEMPE), Eduardo Loria, the Bank of Mexico by incorporating in the package, the auctions of dollars from the resources of the swap line with the Fed , the signal is being sent that the central bank has dollars to prevent the exchange rate from moving to the market's liking.

"It is to give a message that we have sufficient liquidity to prevent it from happening to us as 1982, 1985 and 1994. The intention is to discourage speculative attitudes against the exchange rate, because if they demand dollars and want to take them out, the BankMexico has how to offer more to arm in quotation marks and avoid larger depreciations."Message receivedBNP Paribás strategists and the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, admit that the additional measures announced by Banco de Mexico to strengthen liquidity measures as much as possible, send the signal of a central bank with robust resources.

On the decision to use the swap line to auction dollars between credit institutions, BNP Paribás' chief economist for Mexico and Colombia, Joel Virgen, says it is optimal to secure liquidity even in dollars.

He adds that leaving international reserves intact and keeping the Flexible Credit Line open, the message is sent that they have a large and robust wealth of dollar resources that they can use in case the market warrants it.

From London, the senior economist for Latin America at Pantheon Macroeconomics, Andrés Abbey, believes that these measures aim to promote and improve the functioning of domestic financial markets.

However, it underlines what the Governing Board itself said in the communiqué, in order to assert that "perseverance in strengthening macroeconomic fundamentals and in the adoption of the necessary actions in both fiscal and fiscal policies and to contribute to a successful adjustment of domestic financial markets and the economy in general."

Both strategists agree that global volatility will persist and as the next Bank of Mexico meeting is scheduled until May, there is a wide possibility that an additional off-calendar cut will be resubmitted.

title: Mexico's international reserves recorded its biggest drop in three years due to investment losses
text:
Mexico's international reserves fell last week by $952 million, mainly due to the change in the valuation of the assets that make up them, the central bank reported Wednesday.

The fall of the indicator is the largest since January 2017, when Donald Trump's U.S. presidential election took the peso to a historic low and triggered several bank of Mexico (Banxico) interventions.

"The weekly reduction in the international reserve of $952 million was mainly the result of a change in the valuation of the Bank of Mexico's international assets," the central bank reported.

Banxico Governor Alejandro Díaz de León said last week that a direct sale of dollars to the exchange market in the current context is among the tools the institution has, but that the preference is to use exchange rate hedges.

2019 could be the worst year of the decade for the Mexican economy (Photo: Pxhere)The Mexican peso depreciated on Wednesday by twelfth consecutive session to a new historic low, above 24 units per dollar, due to persistent fears about the economic impact of the coronavirus.

Due to the depreciation, the central bank announced measures such as a swap of government debt instruments, as well as auctions of foreign exchange hedges.

Peso falls to new all-time low, oversulsing 24-dollar barrier

In the current six-year age, the Mexican peso has devalued 49% against the US dollar.The Mexican peso depreciated on Wednesday by twelfth consecutive session to a new historic low, due to persistent fears of the economic impact of the coronavirus and a sharp decline in oil prices.

The local currency was trading at 23.81 per dollar, with a 3.81% depreciation versus 22.9367 of Tuesday's Reuters reference price. The weight fell in international operations during the early morning until 24,067 units, a new all-time low.

The Mexican currency accumulates a retracement of more than 25% in the year.

Oil prices fell on Wednesday for the third consecutive session, with futures falling in the United States to a low of 17 years in the face of the worsening fuel demand outlook due to the suspension of travel and social life caused by the Coronavirus.

Base said that during the session an exchange rate was expected to be quoted between 23.00 and 24.50 pesos per dollar.

The sharp depreciation of the local currency will have to influence Bank of Mexico's monetary policy decisions next week, analysts said.

The central bank soon called for a new auction of foreign exchange hedges, later in the day, seeking to "promote better liquidity conditions" in the market, as well as a swap of debt instruments.

title: Bankers, crisis and opportunity
text:
The themes originally planned for the 83rd Banking Convention were overtaken by the outbreak of a couple of black days in the world's financial markets.

The focus of bankers' concern, outside the work tables, was around a big question: what should the Mexican government do, not only to overcome the situation, but to emerge stronger and seize the opportunity offered by the crisis are generating the petroprice war and the expansion of the coronavirus?

Yesterday the annual convention of bankers began in the port of Acapulco, and from the night before and in the early morning the markets marked the beginning of what would later be considered as the worst day since black Monday 1987.

This Thursday, March 12, a day after President Donald Trump decided to close his borders to U.S. flights to Europe and vice versa, to prevent or contain the contagion of the Covid-19, and a couple of days after the Arabian price war began Saudi Arabia and Russia recorded a unique day of losses that affected the global financial market.

Wall Street had its worst day yesterday since Black Monday 1987. Markets in the US were painted red and in Mexico the BMV fell to its worst level since 2012.

Industrial Dow Jones fell 10%, the S&P 500 had a 9.5 percent decline. On Monday, 19 October 1987, US markets fell by more than 20%.

In Mexico, a severe depreciation of the peso against the dollar was observed, which closed at 21.64 and peaked at 22.87. It could have been worse.

The Bank of Mexico reacted and saved the weight of what may have been one of the strongest depreciations it has ever had, with hedge auctions

Mexico's Exchange Commission (integrated by the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, headed by Arturo Herrera, and the Bank of Mexico, ruled by Alejandro Díaz de León) announced an auction of $2 billion in foreign exchange hedges, thereby relieved the pressure on the national currency. Just earlier it was listed above 22 units.

And the announcement by the Ministry of Finance of a trade in government securities of up to 40 billion pesos for others over terms longer than two years.

The announcement, especially for the coordination between the Treasury and Banxico, had an effect that was immediate and very positive.

Also in the morning, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador issued a message that sought to build trust by ensuring that Mexico has sound finances and growing incomes. But what was most striking was when he reiterated his respect and commitment to the autonomy of the Bank of Mexico.

He assured that his government would not intervene so that the weight would be artificially strengthened.

The market should be regulated with the market, no interventionism. Not that it's the first time he's said it, but it's important when he repeats it.

And among bankers, the issues of financial inclusion and digital modernization of banking, although discussed, were overtaken by the central theme, the challenge posed by the global double crisis: the price war on the oil market and the impact coronavirus, whose impacts were reflected by the pair of black days observed on 9 and 12 March.

For Héctor Grisi, the CEO of Santander Mexico, both crises can become an opportunity for the country.

Taking the right public policies Mexico could increase its trade importance with the US, in view of China's coronavirus involvement.

The reorientation of the current government's energy policy would be strategic, said Barclays Mexico's president and CEO, RaulMartínez Ostos. From its point of view, the current government is very clear that it must open up the energy sector to domestic and international private investment.In the banking run, managers agree that Mexico is facing a double crisis and an opportunity. "Even if coronavirus fears lessen, the recent worsening in eurozone economic data threatens to keep the CHF stronger for longer," she says "It is our expectation that eurozone growth will be sluggish this year implying that EUR/CHF is likely to continue to trade heavily." Rising worries about the global economic impact of the coronavirus outbreak are "also likely to benefit the franc." Rabobank has a three-month forecast of 1.06 for EUR/CHF, which is last up 0.1% at 1.0632. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0613 ET - Some pain from the novel coronavirus will be inevitable in Germany, Gilles Moec , chief economist for AXA Investment Managers, says. Even when it is still difficult to estimate the economic impact of the pathogen, there's growing evidence of its significant negative economic effect and Germany is highly dependent on Chinese demand for goods as it is its biggest export market, Moec says. "Beyond the impact of the epidemic, we have been for a while uncomfortable with the German economy's rising reliance on Chinese demand," Moec says. From a capital-expenditure perspective, China is by far the biggest economy in the world and given Beijing's strategy to reduce the capital intensity of its economy, German industry would be at risk even without the coronavirus, Moec says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

The fiscal rules, "proving somewhat of an inconvenience, may well be broken only months after being adopted. If so, it's likely to be via some kind of fudge," says Citigroup 's Jamie Searle. Javid's fiscal rules allow for an extra GBP20 billion pounds of infrastructure spending but require day-to-day spending and revenue to be in balance in the third year of any forecast. The 10-year gilt yield trades last at 0.626%, having reached almost a three-week high of 0.660% after Javid's resignation, according to Tradeweb . (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com; @lorena_rbal)

0623 ET - The Swiss franc will likely maintain its strength against the euro in the coming months due to its role as a safe haven asset, Rabobank FX strategist Jane Foley says. "Even if coronavirus fears lessen, the recent worsening in eurozone economic data threatens to keep the CHF stronger for longer," she says "It is our expectation that eurozone growth will be sluggish this year implying that EUR/CHF is likely to continue to trade heavily." title: Llerenas and monetary policy
text:
The fundamental mistake is to imagine that central banks have the ability to determine, at their discretion, the level of interest rates. False.

In the case of monetary policy intervention mechanisms, the Bank of Mexico has control over a very short-term rate only.

The British economist Keynes wrote in his masterful treaty The Economic Consequences of Peace in Currency and Central Banking an expert in a million, but we find it every day. This is the case of the guest columnist Vidal Llerenas, who, coming out of his journalistic comfort zone (the issues of urban development) reopened a flank of vulnerability to show in writing his improvisation in monetary policy.

Great misinformation in that field and nothing else shows in writing that "the demand on the [central] bank would have to be to lower interest rates at a faster rate." The fundamental mistake in this stark statement is to imagine that a central bank has the capacity to determine discretionary interest rates in the economy. False. In the case of monetary policy intervention mechanisms, the Bank of Mexico has control over a very short-term rate only. Should such a rate be determined at a level inconsistent with the general conditions prevailing in the economy, the error would be perversely manifested in a term interest rate structure with a very steep slope. That is, with the rates with which investment projects are financed at very high levels, inhibiting economic growth.

Another big mistake in the article "El Banxico and its comfort policies" is not making the distinction between inflation and its expectations or forecasts. They're not the same. If even if inflation is in its target range, the corresponding expectations are not sufficiently anchored with their long-term goal, it is not possible to sing victory prematurely by vocingly announcing that "inflation is controlled." The fact is that those expectations are not yet sufficiently anchored.

I do not believe that any name-worthy central banker could propose that interest rates be kept at an artificially high level to be kept in a "comfort" zone. Nor do I think Werner of the International Monetary Fund would commune with such a dislate.

Werner surely knows that in order to keep interest rates down in a sustainable way, they need to be relatively high at the juncture to anchor inflation expectations. But there was no way it would support the central bank falling in haste for that purpose.

title: The Bank of Mexico, a useless white elephant?
text:
In a country with a strong, organic economy with strong institutions, a central bank could operate with the dual function of seeking inflationary stability and boosting full employment.

But Mexico is far from this economic strength and institutional strength that would allow the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) to have the dual function, without ending up as a scapegoat for the government's failures.

When some aspire to make the Mexican central bank a driver of growth, without neglecting inflation, they are thinking of the Us Federal Reserve (Fed), without taking into account the maturity of a developed economy that does not face many of the challenges Mexico today, now aggravated by the interventionism of the 4T.

In a country like Mexico, where there are controlled prices, monopoly public tariffs, an informal and illegal economy that alters price formation, where there is a government that has no slam in slamming into wage increases, assistance is a list of resources public, or the setting of off-market guarantee prices, with an exchange rate that relatively easily transfers its price weaknesses, it is very difficult to ask its central bank to behave like a first-world institution with a mandate in two Addresses.

Open the Banxico website and the first thing you will find in huge letters is the legend: "Banxico's priority objective is to keep inflation low and stable." If curiosity wins, this legend leads him to the description of article 2 of the Law of the Bank of Mexico, which accounts for its purpose of providing the country's economy with national currency, promoting the healthy development of the payment system and promoting good functioning payment system. That legend is his defense.

What we are clear about is that President Andrés Manuel López Obrador would like this article to include something like that the priority objective is also to promote full employment, which is a way of calling for the promotion of economic growth.

Now imagine that Morena's solicitous lawmakers hear the president say that the Banxico should in addition to controlling inflation, support growth, but the law prevents it.

Well, there are already some rapprochements between senators and advisers of the Banxico and the Ministry of Finance to explore the possibility of expanding the scope of monetary policy towards promoting growth, beyond putting levees to the elevation messy prices.

Mexico's economy has shown that with a strong central bank it can cope with inflationary pressures, as has happened since the mid-1990s, when Banxico gained its autonomy.

If the economy wants to grow at higher rates, more work is needed on the factors of confidence, macroeconomic stability, strength of the energy industry and consolidation of institutions, beyond personal enlightenment.

Passing the ball of growth responsibility to Banxico would only make that institution an obese, clumsy body. Come on, a white elephant unable to compete against the vagaries of discretionary fiscal policy management.

The cherry on the cake of a developed, structured, institutional economy with full attachment to the rule of law can be a Banxico with dual function. Before that, impossible.

title: They raise "indicators of well-being"
text:
The government of President Andrés Manuel López Obrador suggested to the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) to include "welfare indicators" in its economic policy measurements.

After that, last week, the Central Bank made an adjustment to the economic growth range for this year, of 1.7 and 2.7% at a range of between 1.1 and 2.1%, the spokesman of the Presidency of the Republic, Jesús Ramírez, He considered that Banxico should not only have as its mandate the management of inflation and monetary policy, but also the standard of living of citizens.

Interviewed by El Economista , the spokesperson said that it is not an interventionism in Banxico, and stressed that the autonomous body can, by itself, include the "indicators of well-being", although it left open the possibility of reforms to the Law of the Bank from Mexico. Ramírez Cuevas also reproached the measurements of the National Council for the Evaluation of Social Development Policy (Coneval) and the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (Inegi).

- The president analyzes the indicators of the Bank of Mexico, because he dismissed the cut to the growth of this year of the Banxico? (Ramírez Cuevas was asked).

-There is a debate about the indicators. As there was a debate about the Inegi, his way of measuring unemployment so that the unemployment rate was lower. There is also a manipulation of the way in which the indicators are presented. Coneval himself, when he measures poverty, may technically be correct, but as he communicates it, it already has a political effect; It is a political decision. So, they are not aseptic organisms. The Bank of Mexico itself, which has a mandate, which includes the management of inflation and monetary policy as the only macroeconomic indicators. We have proposed that the Bank of Mexico also include the standard of living, that is, the level of welfare should be part of the economic balance.

-How could I measure it?

- You measure it by changing the mandate of the Bank of Mexico, or that the bank assumes.

- With a reform?

-Yes, with a reform.

-But what is included, for example?

-Well, consumption, standard of living, well-being, income, and that if the income goes well, because inflation says we control it, and we control the price of the currency and other factors of the trade balance, but the level of people, the wellness? So, since it is part of the balance sheet of a central bank that is concerned about the nation, not only the financial and economic sectors; that is why we believe that it should have a mandate like that, and that it does not affect anything, because it is not interventionism, maintaining its autonomy, but including these indicators so that people have a reference and the leaders have a reference, and economic actors have that same reference.

- That would be with a legal reform?

-The Bank of Mexico can do it, of itself, as a decision to include welfare indicators as part of its economic policy considerations.

-It's a suggestion?

-It is a suggestion, and we have said it since the campaign, but we are not emphasizing on that; That would be desirable, we must see what path to follow, without feeling that we want to intervene in the internal life of the Bank of Mexico, but it is adequate. If the economy has a human destiny, the end of the economy is that there is social welfare, it would be logical that the Central Bank that is in charge of the variables, include the human variableas measurable to see where we are going, not only technical-economic variables. But that is part of the reflection on the economy and the changes that are going to take place. The approach is more regional and sectors are being promoted, for example, if in the field everything was oriented to production for export, now it is about focusing on the production of food and the improvement of the productive capacities of the peasants, of small and medium producers; the big ones will also be supported, but since the children have been abandoned, and (the programs) Aserca and Procampo and all those programs that were, were focused on the big ones, now they are going to focus more towards the family unit more little.

title: Rodolfo Navarrete Vargas / Will increase the rate
text:
The exchange rate continues to be a cause for concern in Mexico. During the past week, it once again observed worrying behavior not only because it was the second worst performing currency among the emerging countries, but also because it has been observing this performance for just under two months. This time could be enough to start influencing inflation, especially since it has become more sensitive to this kind of events, due to the fact that the economy is in the high phase of the cycle. Last week the Mexican peso depreciated 2.76%, just below the South African currency that did it at 3.01 percent. Since April 17, the date on which the weakening of practically all emerging currencies began, those that depreciated the most are the Argentine peso (20.65%), the Mexican peso (12.23%), the Brazilian real (9.18%) and the Turkish lira (8.72%). This phenomenon is due to the combination of two types of factors.

 One, the attraction of capital to the United States, mainly related to the Fed's monetary policy; and, the second, the expulsion of capital from emerging countries, which depend basically on the state of the economic foundations of each country. The US monetary policy runs on two lanes. One, the rise in the reference interest rate; and, the other, the decrease in the Fed's balance, which implies the reduction of the liquidity of the system, which acquires disturbing characteristics in circumstances in which the need for money is increasing as a result of the increase in the US fiscal deficit. This attracts capital from all over the world, forcing global investors to sell their risky asset positions, especially in emerging countries. On the other hand, the depreciation observed by these currencies is not accidental. It responds to the relatively vulnerable state of the macroeconomic foundations of each of these countries. Most of them have problems with their fiscal balances and with the current account of their balance of payments, as well as with inflation. However, the problem in Mexico is different. The main internal headache is the commercial relationship with the United States. Once the attempt to reach an agreement on NAFTA that the American Congress could approve this year has failed, a wide range of negotiating possibilities has opened up, which in the end only contribute to raising uncertainty. The reimposition of tariffs by the United States to imports of steel and aluminum from Mexico, Canada and the European Union, as well as the retaliatory measures adopted by these countries, increase the probability of a commercial war in the world and that Trade negotiations between Mexico and the United States will be complicated. This is the factor that internally explains the depreciation of the peso, to which probably has been added the concern regarding the elections of July 1. Finally, it should be noted that the weakening of our currency is observing some worrying characteristics. Apart from its high magnitude (12.2% since mid-April), and being the second currency with the worst performance in emerging countries, the strong increase in peso volatility has been added to it. This is relevant because apparently the pattern of Banco de México's interventions in the recent past has had to do with the correlation between these two variables. That is to say, that whenever there was a strong depreciation of the peso, accompanied by a significant increase in the volatility of the exchange rate, the central bank raised the monetary policy interest rate. This concern is even more important if we take into account the warning from the Bank of Mexico in its May 12 press release that, if necessary, it will act in a "timely and firm" manner to achieve the convergence of inflationto its goal of 3.0 percent. As a result, it would not be strange to see an increase in the benchmark interest rate before the monetary policy meeting scheduled for June 21. title: They ask to remove Bouquet 23 and Commission of Changes
text:
The Mexican Institute of Finance Executives (IMEF) presented its agenda aimed at shaping the National Development Plan for the next Administration, which includes eliminating Branch 23 and the Exchange Commission. In a press conference, Fernando López Macari, national president of the IMEF, explained that it is a project in process that will be presented to the candidate who wins the elections on July 1, and later to the new cabinet. The agenda consists of four main axes: Economic Policy; Good government; Social and Business Responsibility, as well as the Rule of Law. Among the economic policy proposals, the elimination of the Foreign Exchange Commission stands out, in order to give full responsibility to the Bank of Mexico in the determination of the exchange policy, without the intervention of the Ministry of Finance.

 The Foreign Exchange Commission is in charge of the exchange policy, it is chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury and consists of three officials from this department and three from Banxico. Another one of the points indicated in fiscal subjects is the elimination of the Branch 23, budgetary branch for the allocation of federal resources, with whose elimination the discretionality and opacity of the use of resources in that area would be fought, indicated Lopez Macari. Among other points, of the first axis, it considers macroeconomic stability, the implementation of a fiscal reform, improvements in commercial policy and promotion of productive investment.

title: UPDATE 1-Mexico readying economic response if U.S. exits NAFTA
text:
(Recasts introduction, adds comments from IMF, background)

By Ana Isabel Martinez

MEXICO CITY, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Mexico's government is preparing a macroeconomic response in case U.S. President Donald Trump makes good on threats to quit the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), an event which could wreak havoc on the Mexican economy and hurt the peso.

Mexico's Foreign Minister Luis Videgaray said on Monday the government and central bank were preparing a plan to address the possibility of a future without NAFTA, but gave few details.

The government has said it is examining how it could adjust Mexican legislation to give investors certainty about their investments if the almost 24-year-old NAFTA collapses.

Underpinning some $1.3 trillion in annual trade between the United States, Canada and Mexico, NAFTA has been a central pillar of recent Mexican economic development. Nearly 80 percent of Mexican exports are shipped to the United States.

Trade negotiators from the United States, Mexico and Canada meet in Mexico City this week to continue talks on overhauling the accord, and Videgaray reiterated the government's position that the expectation was that talks would ultimately succeed.

Mexico would continue to work on diversifying trade, protect foreign investment, review possible changes to tariff barriers, and prepare a macro-economic response from the finance ministry and the central bank, Videgaray added.

"These are the four lines a plan B must include," he told Mexican radio. "We have to be prepared for all the scenarios and one of the scenarios is that the United States leaves the treaty, and as we have said, that is not the end of the world, the Mexican economy is much bigger than NAFTA."

Separately, the International Monetary Fund said in a report on Monday that ending NAFTA would bring back World Trade Organization "most-favored nation" tariffs, which would disrupt Mexican-U.S. trade, and could crimp economic growth, dampen capital inflows and raise risk premia.

The IMF suggested that among various policy responses at Mexico's disposal, "temporary foreign exchange interventions and liquidity provision could help smooth extreme volatility."

Concerns that Trump could follow through on his threats to dump NAFTA have battered the Mexican peso in recent weeks.

Additionally, Mexico should continue to implement its structural reforms and boost efforts to diversify trading relationships, which would increase competitiveness and help economic growth over the medium-term, the IMF said.

The IMF sees Mexico's economy growing 1.9 percent next year after projected expansion of 2.1 percent in 2017. (Additional reporting by Anthony Esposito; Editing by Paul Simao)

(Recasts, adds analyst's comments)

MEXICO CITY, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso snapped back on Wednesday, gaining as much as 1.3 percent, after the central bank said it would accelerate its foreign exchange intervention in a bid to stem the currency's recent fall to six-month lows against the dollar.

The peso has been on a roller coaster ride this year due to uncertainty over negotiations to update the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), a lynchpin of Mexico's economy.

U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to tear up the 23-year-old accord, which underpins $1.3 trillion in annual trade between Canada, the United States and Mexico, if it cannot be reworked to benefit U.S. jobs and reduce the trade deficit.

After slipping to an all-time low of 22.04 to the dollar in early January, a rosier outlook for NAFTA helped the peso steadily gain to 17.47 by July 18, making it the best performing major currency in the world over the period.

But amid renewed uncertainty over the trade talks pushing the peso to six-month lows, Mexico's currency commission said on Wednesday it will raise the amount of dollars auctioned in foreign currency hedges.

In a statement issued by the central bank, the commission said it would raise the amount regularly auctioned from a pool of $20 billion set aside for the purpose in February.

"Past form suggests that the FX swap auctions should provide some relief for the currency, but that this could be fleeting," Neil Shearing, chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients.

"The prospects for the peso over the next couple of months will be determined by whether NAFTA talks can get back on track. We're increasingly concerned," Shearing added.

So far, Mexico has auctioned $1 billion in hedges from the pool in lots of $200 million. It will now offer another $4 billion through Dec. 6. in larger amounts, starting with an auction of $1 billion on Thursday, the commission said.

The central bank said it will hold three auctions on Oct. 26 for a total of $1 billion worth of peso hedging instruments due to expire in the coming months.

The auctions comprise a 32-day instrument worth $400 million expiring on Nov. 27, a 61-day instrument worth $300 million expiring on Dec. 26, and a 90-day instrument worth $300 million expiring on Jan. 24, 2018. (Reporting by Miguel Gutierrez and Anthony Esposito; editing by Susan Thomas)

title: RPT-POLL-Mexico, Brazil  currencies  set to weaken less on dovish Fed, ECB
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers with no change to text)               

* reuters://realtime/verb=Open/url=cpurl://apps.cp./Apps/fx-polls?RIC=BRL= poll data               

By Bruno Federowski               

SAO PAULO, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Brazilian and Mexican currencies will weaken less than previously thought against the U.S. dollar during the next 12 months as low interest rates abroad offset political uncertainty at home, a Reuters poll found on Thursday.               

The fresh forecasts come in the wake of a stronger-than-expected performance for both currencies in the first seven months of 2017, which drove them to their strongest levels in more than a year.               

Still, estimates from top banks and research firms suggest the currencies probably will give back part of their recent gains.               

The Mexican peso is seen at 18.115 per dollar in 12 months versus 18.5 in July, having outperformed all major emerging market currencies this year as fears of a U.S. trade war abated. The Brazilian real is expected to weaken to 3.35 per dollar from 3.42.               

Elsewhere in the region, foreign exchange strategists polled by Reuters forecast the Argentine peso at 18.865 in a year, the Chilean peso at 666.5, the Colombian peso at 3,039 and the Peruvian sol at 3.38 to the greenback.               

Emerging market currencies are expected to benefit from resilient appetite for high-yielding assets throughout the world as the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB) take their time in unraveling monetary stimulus.               

Although U.S. economic growth has shown signs of accelerating, an unexpectedly slow pickup in price hikes has made analysts skeptical of the Fed's stated plan of increasing interest rates once more this year and three times next year.               

Meanwhile, euro zone inflation remains far below the ECB's target of close to 2 percent, driving policymakers to hold off paring back bond purchases meant to stimulate activity.               

That prospect is likely to provide support to the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso, despite both countries facing highly uncertain general elections in 2018 that have stoked trader fears of a populist swing. A series of interest rate hikes and currency interventions in Mexico also have fostered trust in the strength of the local currency.               

In Brazil, concerns that corruption allegations against President Michel Temer could derail his plans to streamline the country's bloated social security system also seem to have been put off in the short-term.               

"So far, the political crisis hasn't impacted the risk perception in Brazil in any meaningful way," Ivo Chermont, an economist with investment boutique Quantitas, said. "We'll only begin to seriously discuss the elections in around six months."               

Eleven of 12 strategists who replied to an additional question said they saw no potential for regional spillovers from the political crisis in Venezuela.
