title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real rallies past 2/dlr,  Mexico  peso falls
text:
(Adds Brazil gov't sources on intervention strategy, updates prices)

* Brazil cenbank offers FX swaps when real traded flat

* Real trades below 2/dlr for first time since May 15

* Peru cenbank sells dollars for 1st time since Oct. 2011

* Real ends 1.7 pct higher, Mexican peso weakens 0.16 pct

By Natalia Cacioli

SAO PAULO, May 25 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real on Friday rallied through the level of 2 per dollar for the first time in 10 days as the central bank stepped up its market intervention, but other Latin American currencies fell on European debt fears.

In a more aggressive intervention stance, Brazil's central bank on Friday offered to sell currency swaps early in the session, when the real was practically flat from Thursday's close.

The strategy left many investors wondering whether policymakers were uncomfortable with the level of the currency, but two government sources told Reuters the interventions were only aimed at limiting volatility after the real depreciated with "excessive" speed.

The real rose 1.7 percent to 1.9937 per dollar in its third consecutive session of gains. It was the first time it closed below the level of 2 per dollar since May 14, although it remains nearly 15 percent weaker from a late-February high.

Since it resumed the sale of currency swaps a week ago, this was the first time the central bank offered swaps when the real was trading stable against the dollar.

"The central bank is willing to make regular interventions to avoid that the real returns to the level of 2.1 per dollar," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

Some analysts also said it was too early to say the central bank was trying to draw a line at any specific exchange rate.

"We can't say the central bank is defending any specific currency level yet, as this was the first time it acted like that (when the real was stable)," said Mario Battistel, currency desk manager at Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"Maybe the central bank was worried about Europe's impact on our market, so it acted early to avoid putting out a fire later."

Fears about the impact of a possible Greek exit from the euro zone continued to weigh on global markets, keeping most Latin American currencies weaker.

Mexico's peso fell 0.24 percent to 14.0340 per greenback in its fourth consecutive session of losses. A sharp drop of the peso on Wednesday caused the Mexican central bank to call a dollar auction for the first time since 2009.

The Chilean peso declined 0.12 percent to finish at a fresh 4-1/2-month low of 509.40 per dollar.

Peru's sol ended practically stable at 2.695 per dollar after the central bank sold $2 million in the spot market for the first time since October 2011.

The Peruvian central bank has also been auctioning deposit certificates and repos in recent weeks to satisfy demand for dollars and curb the depreciation of the sol, which has been trading around its weakest levels for 2012.

title: ANALYSIS-Slow and steady Mexico draws equity bets over Brazil
text:
* Fund investors eyeing Mexican stocks over Brazil

* Mexican economy might be safer bet in market rout

* Brazil hit harder in recent sell-off than Mexico

By Pablo Garibian and Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, May 24 (Reuters) - Mexican stocks are drawing investors away from Brazil as Latin America's biggest economy loses steam and Mexico's close ties to the United States render it a safer bet in unsettled times.

Although the market capitalization of Brazil's bourse is three times that of Mexico's, the Mexican stock market's standing with fund investors has been on a slow and steady rise since the end of last year, according to data from EPFR Global, which tracks funds with $16 trillion in global assets.

Slow and steady economic growth, at an annual rate of 3 to 4 percent, is also earning Mexico a second look from those with money to invest in the region despite renewed fears about the future of the euro zone and the chance of a Lehman-style global crisis.

Mexico, which has resisted the temptation to change interest rates, intervene in currency markets or battle capital inflows in recent years, is in part benefiting from Brazil's unsettling changeability in key policy areas as well as its own ties to the perceived 'safe haven' of the United States.

As risk aversion has flared again this year, Brazil's exchange suffered a bigger hit than Mexico's, suggesting investors may be more willing to hold on to Mexican stocks in crunch times. First-quarter foreign inflows into Mexican stocks were the largest since the third quarter of 2009.

"Recently I find that we have been putting more money to work in Mexico at the expense of Brazil," said Ed Kuczma, investment analyst for two Van Eck emerging market equity funds which had $275 million assets under management as of April 30.

"I think investors are starting to see a kind of top-down, favorable macro environment for Mexico and a more challenging environment for Brazil."

After an impressive 7.5 percent expansion in 2010, Brazil's economy, which is twice the size of Mexico's, slowed last year to a modest 2.7 percent, less than half the growth recorded by Peru, Colombia, Chile or even Ecuador.

Brazil's economic well-being is closely tied to commodity prices and demand from China, where growth is easing and which would be particularly vulnerable to a collapse in demand from Europe, its biggest export market. Italy and Spain have slid back into recession while France is stagnating.

Experts are concerned about the hit to Latin America's economy from a fresh euro zone crisis, a topic to be discussed at next week's Latin America Reuters Summit, which will be attended by the finance ministers of Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Chile and Mexico.

While economists have been cutting back growth projections in Brazil, many have upgraded their outlooks for Mexico, where policymakers are optimistic 2012 growth will near 4 percent on the back of stronger U.S. demand for manufactured goods and a view that the United States might hold up in the face of a fresh European crisis.

"There's a general sense of Mexico might be more slow and steady, if you like, but more stable at the same time, whereas Brazil has been on this roller coaster ride," said Neil Shearing, economist at Capital Economics in London.

"Real strains are starting to emerge in its growth model."

Still, EPFR data show fixed income funds are sticking with Brazil, where benchmark interest rates are among the dearest in the world at 9 percent. In real terms, Brazilian rates are about 4 percent, compared to Mexico's 1 percent.

TALLEST MIDGET

Mexico's stock market is shallow and illiquid compared to many of its emerging market peers, with many big companies controlled by family interests, such as Carlos Slim's America Movil and baker Grupo Bimbo.

But in an emerging market rout, fund managers said Mexico, which has so far escaped an economic hit from its war against drug cartels, would gain from being the least-worst option.

"There's so much money around, where are you going to put it?" said a strategist with a major fund, who declined to be named. "It's the tallest midget competition, everyone is tiny ... but you have to choose one, so who are you going to choose? You choose the tallest one."

Mexican officials also point to the ease of entry in the country's markets, with no need for foreign investors to register with authorities, unlike Brazil; no withholding tax; no minimum investment period and a freely convertible currency.

"We have a flexible and modern legal framework compared to other emerging markets. This makes it much easier for the foreign investor to take a position in Mexican assets," said Jorge Alegria, head of Mexico's MexDer derivatives exchange.

Foreign investment represents 32 percent of the Mexican market's cap. Comparative figures are not available for Brazil, but foreign investors accounted for about 40 percent of share transactions so far in May.

Brazil's benchmark Bovespa stock index is down more than 11 percent so far this month, on track for its worst monthly loss since the depths of the global crisis in October 2008.

Brazilian stock market data shows that between May 1 and 18 there was a net 2.543 billion reais ($1.21 billion) outflow in foreign investment in equities, although year-to-date data are still positive at $1.29 billion.

In Mexico, where the IPC index has fallen more than 5

percent this month, central bank data show foreign investment inflows in company equity of close to $2 billion between January and the end of April.

Equity investors have been put off Brazil by a tax on financial transactions by foreigners, one of the measures put in place by President Dilma Rousseff's government last year to tame the then-appreciating real.

And many feel the country has been overbought after years of frenzied interest, which drove more than 100 companies to go public between 2006 and 2007 and sent share prices above levels easily justified by economic fundamentals.

Brazil's market is seen as a play on China and top oil producers and miners are vulnerable to a downturn in commodity prices while its homebuilders, credit card firms and banks may suffer if credit expansion proves to have been too excessive.

"It's very hard to find investment ideas that are not very, very expensive," said Fred Searby, Latin America equity strategist at Deutsche Bank, adding that many Brazilian companies are trading at inflated price to earnings ratios.

Brazilian retailer Lojas Americanas is more expensive than Mexico's Wal-Mart de Mexico on a price to earnings ratio, and Brazilian brewer Ambev outprices Corona-maker Grupo Modelo.

Still, Mexican companies are more expensive than their Brazilian peers in the banking and telecommunications sectors, with Banorte and America Movil ahead of Itau Unibanco and Telefônica Brasil .

title: CHRONOLOGY- Mexico 's  central bank intervenes  as peso slumps
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 23 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank on Wednesday held its first auction of U.S. dollars since late 2009 after a sharp drop in the peso.

Last week, central bank governor Agustin Carstens said the peso was trading far below its fundamental value because of the global volatility sparked by Europe's debt crisis, but the bank was happy with its current dollar sales mechanism.

Mexico's foreign exchange commission, a joint effort from the finance ministry, the central bank and other state agencies, is in charge of setting policy affecting the peso.

Following is a list of some of board's key decisions over the past years:

October 2008 - Mexico's central bank says it will auction $2.5 billion to stop the peso's most dramatic slide since the so-called Tequila Crisis in the mid-1990s. The bank, which ends up selling $998 million in the market, also announces daily auctions of $400 million whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent before the dollar during a single session. The amount of that daily dollar auction was trimmed to $300 million in March 2009 and to $250 million in May 2009. The auction was suspended in April of last year.

March 2009 - The foreign exchange board says it will sell a daily $100 million in a new mechanism to stop the peso's decline. It will coexist with the other daily auction announced in October 2008.

April 2009 - The central bank gets a swap line from the U.S. Federal Reserve to sell dollars among local financial institutions.

February 2010 - The board resumes "put" dollar auctions to add to the country's federal reserves as a measure to cushion the economy from external turmoil. By using this mechanism, the central bank purchased $600 million between 1996 and 2001.

November 2011 - The central bank says it will resume dollar auctions to defend the peso, using the same trigger as in 2008,

after a slump in the currency caused by rising worries of a widening euro-zone debt crisis risks fanning inflation and driving investors from the country's bond market.

May 2012 - The central bank holds its first dollar auctions since late 2009 after the peso declines sharply.

(Reporting by Adrianna Barrera and Rachel Uranga; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  fall on Greece, real hits 2/dlr
text:
* Traders in Brazil speculate c. bank will intervene

* Brazil's real off 0.55 pct, Mexico's peso down 0.68 pct

By Danielle Fonseca and Rachel Uranga

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, May 14 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Tuesday w ith Brazil's real closing at a near three-year low, fueling speculation the country's bank could soon intervene.

Worries that new elections in Greece would harden domestic opposition to an international bailout and open the possibility that the country could exit the euro weighed on global markets and pushed Brazil's currency to its weakest level since July 2009.

"The market is seeing the possibility of Greece leave the euro zone as very likely," said Alfredo Barbutti, chief economist at BCG Liquidez.

The Brazilian real weakened 0.55 percent to 2 p er dollar.

Some investors have been pushing the real above the level of 2 per dollar to test the central bank's tolerance of a weaker currency that could spur inflation by raising import prices.

"We have some speculation in the foreign exchange market right now," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a manager at Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo. "The market is wondering whether the central bank will intervene, so it is pushing the currency to 2 per dollar."

The Brazilian central bank bought dollars in the spot market from February to April, helping weaken the exchange rate from around 1.7 per dollar, which was considered harmful to exporters.

Some traders bet the central bank will intervene again if the real weakens beyond 2 per dollar. Government officials have indicated they still do not anticipate meaningful inflationary pressures from the currency at that level.

"At between 2 and 2.10, the possibility of intervention is really, really high," said Diego Donadio, Latin America currency and debt strategist for BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

The Mexican and Chilean pesos hit four month lows as a ttempts to form a new government in Greece collapsed spooking investors and raising the prospect anti-bailout candidates could sweep elections, sparking a fresh round of the euro-zone crisis.

The news from Greece weighed on riskier Latin American assets that tend to sell off when investors seek safety in currencies like the U.S. dollar.

Mexico's peso weakened 0.68 percent to 13.8350 per dollar. C hile's peso fell to four month lows, nearing 500 per dollar. The currency closed 1.42 percent weaker to bid at 499.30 per dollar.

"The 500 level is really difficult to break," said Francisco Schneider, director of trading at Celfin Capital in Santiago. "If it happens the next level could be 504 but if markets calm down, don't rule out the peso's recovery to new ranges between 490 and 500."

(Additional reporting by Moises Avila and Froilan Romero in Santiago; Danielle Ramos in Sao Paulo; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: *DJ Bank Of Mexico-Government Relations Seen Positive If PRI Returns To Power
text:
4 May 2012 15:14 EDT *DJ  Mexico's Opposition PRI Supports Continued Central Bank Autonomy

4 May 2012 15:14 EDT *DJ  Mexico Leading Presidential Candidate's Party Favors Price Stability

4 May 2012 15:14 EDT *DJ  Mexico PRI Agrees With Foreign Exchange Policies - Campaign Manager

4 May 2012 15:19 EDT DJ  Business As Usual For Bank Of Mexico If PRI Returns To Power

--Bank of Mexico's sole mandate is the right path, says PRI campaign manager

--Priorities are price stability, avoiding excessive appreciation of the currency

--PRI candidate in agreement with existing exchange policies 


 
   By Juan Montes 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--If Enrique Pena Nieto of the opposition Institutional Revolutionary Party is elected president of Mexico as opinion polls suggest, the country's central bank probably won't have any headaches ahead.

The PRI, as the party is known, ruled Mexico for 71 years until it was unseated in 2000. It now appears to have its best chance in 12 years of returning to power in the July 1 election. Pena Nieto leads second-placed Josefina Vazquez Mota of the ruling conservative National Action Party, or PAN, by more than 20 points, according to recent polls.

"We have three goals: first, full respect for the Bank of Mexico's autonomy; secondly, stability of prices as a priority, and thirdly, to avoid an excessive appreciation of the currency," Luis Videgaray, Pena Nieto's campaign manager and closest adviser, said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires.

The Bank of Mexico's principal mandate is to preserve the purchasing power of the Mexican peso, and the bank uses inflation targeting as a cornerstone of its policy objectives. That single mandate has led to some criticism that the central bank neglects economic growth in favor of keeping prices down, and calls for a dual mandate like that of the U.S. Federal Reserve.

Videgaray said the Bank of Mexico should stick to price stability as the sole mandate. "In a developing country, which could be a victim of speculative attacks from global capital markets, the priority of monetary policy is to protect the currency. Part of our credibility comes from this, and when monetary policy becomes difficult to predict, that could create some incentives for financial speculation," Videgaray said.

Bank of Mexico Gov. Agustin Carstens, a former Mexican finance minister and former deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund, defends balanced public finances as a must, and considers price stability to be the best contribution the central bank can make to Mexico's prosperity. He has argued monetary policy can't be a substitute for much-needed energy and fiscal reforms to propel private investment and promote growth, two overhauls Videgaray said the PRI would have as top priorities.

The Bank of Mexico, known for its prudence and orthodoxy, hasn't moved rates since Carstens took over the helm in January 2010 for a renewable six-year term. Carstens was appointed by President Felipe Calderon, of the PAN, and ratified by the Senate with PRI support. The overnight interest rate target has been at 4.5% since July 2009.

Videgaray, who is tipped to become Finance Minister if Pena Nieto wins the election, also expressed agreement with the Bank of Mexico's soft interventions in foreign exchange markets, responding only to unusual bouts of volatility and allowing the market to determine the exchange rate. Videgaray declined to comment on the possibility of his becoming the next finance minister.

The central bank bought dollars last year through monthly put options when the peso was appreciating, and in November, in response to heightened global market volatility, switched to being a potential seller of dollars if the peso weakens 2% in a single day.

The Finance Ministry has the last word on foreign exchange policy with its tie-breaking vote in the exchange commission, which is made up of three central bank and three ministry officials.

Videgaray, who witnessed major devaluations of the peso under PRI governments in 1982 and 1994, said he would be pragmatic. "A policy based on a free-float is the right path. Mexico has already lived a lot of crises trying to impose the price of its currency," he said.

JP Morgan's chief Mexico economist Gabriel Casillas said it's improbable there would be any changes under a PRI government that could affect the peso. "In fact, it was the PRI that established the system of flexible exchange rates," he said.

Both Videgaray and Carstens studied economics at Mexico's ITAM university, which in recent decades has turned out a stream of top government officials steeped in economics, and both have doctorates from the U.S.

"Both are intelligent economists with a brilliant academic record. So, it would be difficult for conflicts to arise in a relationship that should be basically institutional," said Everardo Elizondo, a former Bank of Mexico deputy governor.

-By Juan Montes, Dow Jones Newswires; (5255) 5980 5178, juan.montes@dowjones.com

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Stronger Versus Dollar In Upbeat End To 1Q
text:
-Currency gains 9.2% against dollar in 1Q as euro-zone jitters ease

-Improved growth prospects, high oil prices support currency

-Further peso gains expected in 2012


 
    By Anthony Harrup 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Friday, ending the quarter on a positive note as investors were encouraged by news on bailout funds for Europe and remained upbeat about economic prospects for the U.S.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.7980 to the dollar, according to Infosel, slightly stronger than its MXN12.8150 close Thursday, and 9.2% stronger than its 2011 close of MXN13.9725.

Global investor worries about Europe's precarious debt situation hit all types of risky assets in the final quarter of 2011, carrying the highly liquid peso to its weakest ever year-end close.

"The world looks quite a bit different here at the end of the first quarter than it did at the end of last year," Brown Brothers Harriman said in its second-quarter foreign exchange report. "The combination of stronger U.S. growth and the aggressive liquidity provisions by the European Central Bank has effectively pushed the global economy away from the abyss that it was facing at the end of 2011."

In the emerging markets space, BBH favors Latin American currencies over Europe, Middle East and Africa, and Asia, where energy importers remain more vulnerable to higher oil prices.

Nomura this week changed its year-end estimate for the peso to MXN12.00 to the dollar from MXN12.80, citing lower risk from Europe, a positive growth outlook, the possibility of Brazilian exchange controls diverting investment flows to Mexico, and still relatively small net long peso positions in futures markets.

Within Latin America, several analysts see an advantage in Mexico's less interventionist attitude toward currency appreciation, as Brazil has already resumed measures to discourage gains in the real.

Amid the flurry of volatility late last year, the Bank of Mexico switched its position from a buyer of dollars through monthly put options, to a potential seller via a mechanism under which the central bank will sell from reserves up to $400 million on days when the peso weakens 2% against the dollar. The currency's rebound this year has meant no sales have been triggered, and Bank of Mexico Gov. Agustin Carstens said last month a return to the options mechanism to accumulate more reserves couldn't be ruled out. Exchange-policy decisions are made jointly by the central bank and the Finance Ministry.

Dollar revenue from crude oil exports by state monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos, which changes dollars at the central bank, is the principal source of reserves, which are currently $148 billion. The peso, therefore, mostly benefits from high crude prices, which also bolster federal budget revenue.

title: UPDATE:  Mexico  Watches For Effects On Peso From Brazil's  FX Intervention
text:
--Bank of Mexico watching exchange rate for effects of Brazilian actions

--Official says sovereign upgrade warranted, but unlikely before elections

--Central bank considers diversifying currencies of reserves, a slow process

(Adds comments from Bank of Mexico official, details and background beginning in fourth paragraph)

By Juan Montes and Amy Guthrie

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--A Bank of Mexico official said Thursday that the central bank is keeping an eye out for possible peso appreciation as a result of investors shifting money into Mexico as Brazilian authorities take measures to damp down the appreciation of the real.

A number of analysts have said the exchange-rate policies of the Bank of Mexico and Mexican Finance Ministry make the peso an attractive option for taking advantage of higher-yielding securities with less risk of exchange intervention.

Jaime Cortina, director of operations at the Bank of Mexico, said at an event organized by financial information company Profit & Loss that the exchange commission, which is made up of central bank and Finance Ministry officials, is keeping an eye on that and will take it into account.

"Certainly, this is something we're monitoring and we're concerned about it," he said.

The peso has appreciated around 8.8% so far this year against the U.S. dollar, after a sharp depreciation at the end of 2011 on risk aversion caused by the European sovereign debt problems. The currency recently traded in Mexico City at MXN12.8410 to the dollar.

Late last year, at the height of peso volatility, the central bank stopped buying dollars through monthly dollar put options and activated instead a mechanism where it will sell up to $400 million a day on days when the peso depreciates 2% against the dollar from the previous session. So far no sales have been triggered under the mechanism.

Mexico's foreign reserves are currently at $148 billion, and Cortina said that reserves will continue to reach new highs as long as oil prices remain high and state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos changes dollars at the central bank rather than in the open market.

The bank is analyzing investing reserves in other emerging market currencies to secure greater yield, Cortina said, but such a decision would take a long time and central banks must be very cautious to not put reserves at risk.

The global trend, and the trend for Mexico, will continue to be diversification away from the U.S. dollar and into other currencies and assets, such as gold, Cortina said.

"The problem is that many of those other markets don't have the size that many central banks require," he added.

The Mexican central bank holds some reserves in gold, and has also diversified into currencies other than the U.S. dollar, according to Cortina.

Mexico deserves a better credit rating given the country's healthy public finances, with low budget deficit and debt, and record-high international reserves, Cortina also said.

"Clearly, there's margin for an upward revision. But I don't see the international credit agencies doing anything before July's presidential election."

Mexico has a lower medium-grade credit rating, despite having a budget deficit of 2.5% of gross domestic product in 2011 and a net debt of 32.4% of the GDP, relatively low compared with U.S., Europe and other developed countries.

Standard and Poor's sovereign rating for Mexican debt is BBB, similar to that of Fitch, while Moody's has Mexico one equivalent notch higher at a Baa1. All three agencies maintain a stable outlook.

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  weakens as Bernanke enthusiasm eases
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Mexico peso weakens 0.3 pct, Brazil real 0.08 pct

* Brazil cenbank holds reverse swap auction

* Traders say Brazil cenbank may be defending 1.81 level

By Caroline Stauffer

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 27 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies mostly ended weaker on Tuesday as enthusiasm for U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's commitment to loose monetary policy eased and fears of Brazil's desire to weaken its currency hurt the real.

Brazil's currency strengthened as much as 0.3 percent early in the session as Bernanke's comments from Monday lifted higher-risk currencies that benefit from low interest rates in the United States.

But the real ended 0.08 percent weaker, bidding 1.8162 per dollar after Brazil's central bank sold 41,200 reverse currency swaps in an auction. The swaps are derivatives that mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets and are used to prevent the real from strengthening.

Investors are convinced Brazil's government and central bank will do everything they can to keep the currency from appreciating beyond 1.8 per dollar, with some traders saying the bank's target level is now a weaker 1.81 per dollar.

"That's what the traders say and the way the bank is intervening suggests it, though I still believe 1.8 is the level," said 4Cast Analyst Pedro Tuesta.

Some traders said they feared Brazil's government, which has previously raised the tax known as IOF on financial transactions and extended its scope to foreign debt maturing in up to five years, could take additional measures to weaken the real.

"It's hard to think that they'll go beyond what they have in place in a worst-case scenario they might adjust the IOF on derivatives," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky of RBS.

Other countries are also intervening in their currency markets, determined to deter hot money inflows from the developed world that have been fueled by the very policies Bernanke pledged to continue.

Colombia's peso weakened 0.16 percent to close bidding 1761 per dollar the day after the country's finance minister said the government wants to see more "aggressive" action to help stem currency gains and will ask the central bank to consider stepping up dollar purchases.

Peru's sol ended 0.08 percent stronger at 2.668 per dollar even after the central bank bought $42 million in the spot market in a routine intervention.

Mexico's peso, which had gained the most among Latin American currencies on Bernanke's comments in the previous session, lost 0.3 percent to 12.7082.

Bernanke said on Monday that accommodative monetary policy would stay in place to support demand and that the U.S. economy needed to grow more quickly to reduce the unemployment rate.

Some market participants took that as a sign the Fed could launch another round of asset buying, or quantitative easing, to inject cash into markets that in past years have fled to Latin America's fast-growing economies and high-yielding assets.

But that interpretation was questioned on Tuesday.

"The peso saw losses due to market expectation that the Federal Reserve will not launch more monetary expansion," said Economist Gabriela Siller of Mexico-based Banco Base in a note to clients.

Asked on Tuesday about the potential for a new round of asset purchases by the Fed, Bernanke told ABC News the Fed does not take any options off the table and needs to be prepared to respond however the U.S. economy evolves.

Chile's peso ended nearly unchanged against the dollar, as prices for its main export, copper, were little changed. The peso closed a marginal 0.02 percent firmer, to bid at 486.00 per dollar.

title: Mexican Peso Closes Slightly Weaker After US Sentiment Data
text:

--Weaker-than-expected U.S. consumer-sentiment data weighs

--Bank of Mexico stays on hold, offering a brighter growth outlook

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones) -- The Mexican peso weakened slightly Friday against the U.S. dollar, ending the week mostly flat after worse-than-expected data on consumer confidence in world's largest economy and Mexico's main trade partner.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.67 to the dollar, according to Infosel, compared with MXN12.6590 at the close Thursday.

In the U.S., the Reuters/University of Michigan consumer-sentiment index declined, contrary to economists' forecasts for a gain. Mexico is highly dependent on the U.S. economic prospects, as it sends almost 80% of its exports north of the border.

Recent positive U.S. manufacturing and employment data have been supporting the peso, which has appreciated more than 9% since the beginning of the year. "A continued acceleration of the U.S. data and overall economic recovery, could push the peso towards MXN12.20 fair-value level, where the Bank of Mexico could intervene," said BBVAforex strategist Claudia Ceja.

On Friday, the Bank of Mexico said the country's growth prospects have improved "in recent weeks," due mainly to the better-than-expected performance of the U.S. economy and the lower probability of a financial catastrophe coming from the euro zone. The central bank left rates unchanged at 4.5%, as was unanimously expected, and most economists keep expecting the bank to stay on hold for a long period of time.

Next week, the macroeconomic focus will be on Mexico's inflation data for the first two weeks of March, scheduled to be released on Thursday at 9 a.m. EST.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real hits 8-week low as  intervention  eyed
text:
* Speculation of sovereign wealth fund dollar spurs selling

* Real likely to keep lagging region-wide rally

* Brazil real slumps 1.29 pct, Mexico peso up 0.34 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slumped to an eight-week low on Friday on expectations of more big interest rate cuts and new intervention measures by authorities worried that a strong currency is crimping growth.

The real slumped by the most this week since the beginning of November when it was hit by panic about European banks, shedding 3.3 percent against the dollar and leading losses in March for the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Speculation that Brazil's sovereign wealth fund could soon start to buy dollars in the market spurred selling. Authorities have deployed a growing tool chest of measures designed to sap the real's strength, which is hurting local industry.

Still, analysts said global demand for higher-yielding assets would likely cap losses ahead in the real, which could soon begin appreciating again.

A recent liquidity boost of more than half a trillion euros from the European Central Bank is expected to keep driving financial flows into emerging markets offering higher yields, such as Latin America, in the coming weeks.

Europe's cheap financing adds to the global pool of money available at low-interest rates that can be invested in emerging markets.

"All this liquidity is the global force that authorities in Brazil are fighting," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York.

"The global forces suggest the real could still rally a lot. But all these measures by authorities could make it underperform the rally we are likely to see if money keeps pouring into emerging markets," Melzi said.

On Friday, the real sank 1.29 percent to 1.7835 to the dollar, paring losses that had taken it to its weakest level since mid-January.

Data on Friday showed inflation in Brazil eased in February to its slowest pace for that month in five years, reinforcing the central bank's argument for increasingly aggressive interest rate cuts. Lower rates could make investing in Brazilian bonds less attractive.

Late Wednesday, Brazil's central bank surprised analysts by cutting its benchmark interest rate three-quarters of a percentage point to 9.75 percent. After the cut, the median of a Reuters poll showed analysts see the rate falling to 8.5 percent this year, versus a previous floor of 9.5 percent.

That would still leave Brazilian interest rates among the highest in the world. Even if the return on fixed-income assets is falling, lower borrowing costs could boost growth and tempt more foreign investors to dive into the country's stock market.

Enrique Alvarez, an analyst at IDEAglobal in New York, expects the real to finish the year at about 1.70 to 1.75 to the dollar.

Other major Latin American currencies rose after the U.S. government reported that U.S. employers added more than 200,000 jobs for a third straight month, a sign the world's largest economy was strengthening.

Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States. Mexico's peso gained 0.34 percent to 12.6625 to the dollar for a third day. Earlier it reached 12.6010, its strongest in six months, before pulling back.

Rafael Camarena, an economist at Santander in Mexico City, expects the peso to trade laterally between 12.70 and 12.60 per dollar over the next week as investors look for further confirmation that the U.S. economy is improving.

Analysts said profit taking could be seen next week after Greece pushed through a bond swap needed to clinch bailout funds.

In March the peso's performance has been nearly the opposite that of the real, strengthening nearly 2 percent.

Alvarez thinks the peso could gain as much as 7 percent yet this year to reach 11.80 to the dollar, helped by investors shifting investment from Brazil to Mexico.

Brazil's intervention tactics are pushing more investors to eye the peso, since Mexico is not acting to deter speculators in its market, Alvarez said.

Mexico's central bank is seen holding its benchmark rate steady at 4.50 percent next week after inflation in February fell back into the central bank's comfort zone, below 4 percent.

Chile's peso firmed about 0.25 percent to 483.00 to the dollar from 484.40.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real gains despite capital controls
text:
* Brazil widens scope of foreign-loans tax to stem inflows

 * Mexico peso strengthens 1.1 pct; Chile peso slips 0.4 pct 

(Updates prices, adds comments)

 By Guillermo Parra-Bernal and Rachel Uranga

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, March 1 (Reuters) - Brazil's real climbed on Thursday despite the country's latest capital controls. It was the opposite of the desired effect, coming on the same day that Brazil's president lashed out at U.S. and European monetary policies she blames for inflating the real's value.

 Brazilian authorities widened the scope of a tax on corporate foreign borrowing, and the move fanned speculation that Latin America's largest economy will fight capital inflows more vigorously.

 Analysts, however, doubt new measures will be enough to halt the real's advance.

 The Brazilian real gained 0.47 percent to 1.7120 per dollar, hovering near the 1.70-per-dollar mark the central bank has been seen defending.

 "You introduce these measures, and people just back away for a little bit. But in the end, everyone knows there are a lot of flows, and it's inevitable that the currency will break that" level of 1.70, said Italo Lombardi, a Latin American economist from Standard Chartered Bank in New York.      

 Brazil's so-called IOF tax was extended to foreign loans with maturities of up to three years from two years previously.

 BACKLASH AGAINST 'CHEAP MONEY'

 The move comes on the seventh consecutive day of the central bank purchasing dollars in the spot market and on top of  Wednesday's reverse currency swaps. 

 "We cannot discount the possibility of additional measures being announced to slow foreign-exchange inflows if the currency continues to threaten breaking below (the 1.70-real threshold)  on a sustained basis," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research at Royal Bank of Canada Securities in Toronto.

 Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff has even stepped in with a high-profile speech that slammed rich nations for unleashing a "tsunami" of cheap money that was "cannibalizing" poorer countries. 

 The European Central Bank and other countries' efforts to spur their economies with low interest rates and cheap loans have fueled gains in the real, which has appreciated more than 8 percent this year. 

 Foreign investors seeking returns higher than those found in developed countries are pouring more money into Brazil and in the opinion of government officials,  hurting local manufacturers by making the country's exports more expensive overseas. 

 Brazil's effort highlights concerns that short-term dollar flows are coming through disguised as intercompany loans, said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland Securities. She said the move may do little to arrest the real's rally, since many companies borrow abroad for longer than three years.

 A report by local newspaper Valor Econômico, citing sources familiar with the situation, said government officials are mulling a potential tax on foreign direct investment inflows while they remain in cash. The report said that the tax could be refunded once the funds are applied.

 According to Valor, the government is worried that a meaningful portion of direct investment, the type of capital spending used for productive purposes, is parked in Brazil to earn returns on government debt - which pays one of the world's highest borrowing costs. 

 Finance Minister Guido Mantega, speaking at a news conference in Brasilia, denied there were plans to tax foreign direct investment. The levy "will continue as it is," he said.

 "Taxing FDI inflows will be a very risky move, given FDI is seen as helping to improve Brazil's competitiveness, productivity and capital stock, so they will have to tread lightly here," Chamie said.

  In the year through Feb. 24, U.S. dollar inflows

into Brazil totaled $12.533 billion. Much of that money has flowed into the nation's stock market, helping boost the nation's benchmark Bovespa stock index by 16 percent in the same period.

 But Brazil's increasing use of interventions and capital controls has spooked some investors.

 "If I am bullish on emerging market currencies and I am bullish on Latin American currencies, I would much rather play Mexico than Brazil because there is no fear of intervention," Lombardi said. 

 The Mexican peso gained 1.05 percent to 12.7270 per dollar, while the Chilean peso weakened 0.35 percent to bid at 481.50.

text:
* Brazil cenbank intervention beats back real's surge

* Brazil real weakens 1.2 pct, Chile peso declines 0.6 pct

* Mexican peso trades flat

By Rachel Uranga and Asher Levine

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Feb 29 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real slipped sharply on Wednesday after the country's central bank stepped into currency markets to beat back the real's surge beyond the 1.70-per-dollar mark.

The real, which has appreciated more than eight percent since the beginning of the year, weakened 1.2 percent to bid at 1.7190 per dollar. Other Latin American currencies traded mixed.

"With foreign capital entering the local market, it will continue to get more difficult to hold the real at this level," said Maurico Nakahodo, an economist at Brazil's CM Capital Markets.

A flood of foreign investors seeking returns higher than those found in developed countries has helped strengthen the real, hurting local manufactures by increasing the cost of the country's exports.

Brazil's central bank said on Wednesday that U.S. dollar inflows to the country totaled $5.251 billion in the calendar month through February 24.

"Both the intervention as well as expectations that the government could employ other tools to hold back the real's gains helped weaken the real," he said.

The central bank used reverse currency swaps and spot dollar buys to cool the real.

The central bank sold 30,500, or 76 percent, of the 40,000 reverse currency swaps on offer in the auction for a financial value of about $1.5 billion. The contracts mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets.

In Peru, intervention efforts have failed to slow gains for the sol. The currency hit its strongest level in 15 years, advancing 0.11 percent to 2.673 per dollar despite the central bank's purchase of $118 million in the spot market, its third consecutive intervention this week.

Mexico's peso traded flat at 12.8321 per dollar. The currency trimmed early gains after banks gobbled up more than half a trillion euros of cheap three-year funds offered by the European Central Bank in an effort to stabilize the euro-zone financial system.

Stronger-than-expected U.S. fourth-quarter growth data bolstered an early firming of the currency. But comments by Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke, warning that the U.S. job market is far from normal, limited advances.

Bernanke told the U.S. Congress that unless growth accelerated, the unacceptably high U.S. unemployment rate would not keep dropping. But he stopped short of signaling further Fed bond purchases, tempering traders' hopes for monetary stimulus.

"Some see Bernanke's comments as an indication there will be no monetary stimulus in the short term," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with Forex Chile, a brokerage in Santiago.

Chile's peso weakened 0.65 percent to bid at 479.80 per dollar. Declining copper prices - Chile's main export - also contributed to the weakening of the peso.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  gains ahead of ECB cash boost
text:
(Updates prices, adds details)

* Brazil's real strengthens past key 1.70 level

* Mexico's peso firms 0.37 pct, Brazil gains 0.33 pct

By Rachel Uranga

MEXICO CITY, Feb 28 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies strengthened on Tuesday ahead of an expected flood of cheap cash from Europe that could keep Brazil's real beyond the key 1.70 level despite increased intervention by the country's central bank.

Europe's banks were expected to guzzle up another half a trillion euros of cheap three-year loans offered by the European Central Bank on Wednesday, according to a Reuters poll of money market traders.

Analysts said the rock-bottom interest rates on the loans would push banks to use the cash to buy higher-yielding, riskier assets. That is pushing speculators to make the same bets and it could fuel further demand for Latin American debt ahead.

"Yields will probably bump lower as a consequence of the liquidity that's being injected," said Enrique Alvarez, Latin America bond and currency analyst with IDEAglobal in New York.

Brazil's real f irmed 0.33 percent to bid at 1.6982 per dollar, breaking past the 1.70 level that market players think the central bank and authorities are defending.

A similar liquidity boost from the ECB in December helped fuel a sharp rally in riskier assets during January and currencies in Brazil, Colombia, Chile and Mexico were top gainers among the world's most traded currencies.

Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at Brazilian brokerage BGC Liquidez, said he expects the real to continue to strengthen if central banks and governments continue easing monetary policy.

The real has appreciated more than 9 percent so far this year, pushing the central bank to revive dollar purchases in the spot and derivatives markets to try to slow its advance.

"Authorities are very clear, it's a reflection of containment at this time," Alvarez said. "Changing the trend or equalizing the trend is very difficult."

After a nearly four-month hiatus Brazil began to buy dollars in the spot market earlier this month, in a bid to protect exporters from strong local currencies that undermine their competitiveness.

The Brazilian government said on Tuesday it could also use its sovereign wealth fund to buy dollars in the spot foreign-exchange market but it would hold off and not interfere in the central bank's policy.

Peru's sol is trading around a 15-year high despite the central bank's buying $76 million in the local spot market on Monday.

In Colombia, where the central bank last week extended its dollar buying program though August, the peso has strengthened 0.27 percent to 1767.15 per dollar.

The central bank has gone in the opposite direction to other regional banks raising its interest rates by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent last week in an effort to check inflationary expectations and curb an increase in consumer credit.

Mexico's central bank is not seen intervening any time soon. The peso appreciated 0.37 percent to 12.8525 per dollar .

Gains in the peso were limited by mixed U.S. data

in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

New orders for U.S. manufactured goods fell in January by the most in three years, suggesting the U.S. economy started the year on a weaker footing than expected.

Allaying worries, consumer confidence spiked to a one year high this month according to a private business research group.

Chile's peso strengthened 0.55 percent to 476.70 per dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real rises despite cenbank, rates jump
text:
(Updates with Brazil FX intervention, Mexico peso falling)

* Real gains despite 2 central bank auctions to buy dlrs

* Brazil neutral interest rates seen higher than expected

* Mexican peso weakens on euro-zone concerns

By José de Castro

Feb 24 (Reuters) - Brazil's real rose on Friday as persistent central bank intervention failed to fully absorb dollar inflows, while the country's interest-rate futures rose sharply after a survey suggested the economy needed tighter-than-expected monetary policy to grow without inflation.

Most Latin American currencies were supported by commodity gains, with expectations of higher interest rates further boosting the Colombian peso. However, worries about the euro-zone crisis weighed on the Mexican currency.

The Brazilian real trimmed some of its earlier gains but still traded 0.3 percent higher at 1.705 per dollar after two dollar-buying auctions launched by the central bank less than one hour apart.

The bank's action came one day after it offered to sell reverse currency swaps for the first time since August and also bought dollars in the spot market.

The real has gained more than 9 percent so far this year and the central bank's interventions in the foreign exchange market added to the perception that the government is drawing a line at 1.7 reais per dollar.

"The psychological level has inevitably shaped around the 1.7000 handle in spot, though clearly the central bank is struggling to absorb the large debt inflows related primarily to external corporate debt issuance and overall strong capital account inflows," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, currency strategist at RBS Securities.

At Friday's auctions, the central bank initially bought dollars at a cutoff price 1.7059 reais, and then at 1.7057 reais.

INTEREST RATES JUMP

Concerns about the pace of monetary policy easing in Brazil increased after the central bank released a survey showing economists estimate the economy can grow without inflationary pressures if real interest rates are about 5.5 percent - higher than the 4.5-5.0 percent expected by many traders.

Brazil's benchmark interest rate is now at 10.5 percent , after four, half-percentage-point rate cuts since August. Inflation for the 12 months ending Jan. 31 was 6.22 percent, giving Brazil a real interest rate of about 4.3 percent, more than a percentage point below the neutral rate survey estimate.

"There is this feeling that the central bank might be exaggerating and, just to be sure, markets raised the rates," said a trader in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's interest-rate contract for January 2013 rose to 9.270 percent from 9.220 percent in Thursday's adjusted close. The contract for January 2014 jumped to 9.750 percent from 9.670 percent.

COMMODITIES SUPPORT LATAM FX

Strong dollar inflows have provided powerful tailwinds to Latin American currencies this year, and analysts expect that trend to intensify as commodity prices rise and the European Central Bank floods the markets again with cheap money next week.

The Chilean peso rose as much as 0.7 percent during the session before ending broadly flat against the dollar, at 480.30 per dollar, as local dollar purchases offset a jump in prices of copper, the country's main export.

The Colombian peso gained 0.2 percent to 1,773.05 per greenback. Boosting the prospects for the Colombian currency, the country's central bank will likely increase the key interest rate for a second straight month at its meeting on Friday, in an attempt to ease economic growth and cool the pace of bank lending.

In Mexico, however, the peso weakened 0.4 percent to 12.876 per dollar. The currency has been unable to break past 12.65 per dollar, trading in a narrow range this week on persistent concerns over the future of the euro zone debt crisis.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's dollar purchases end real rally
text:
* Brazil's real reverses gains after intervention

* Central bank buys forwards first time this year

* Mexico, Chile pesos gain amid better global views

By Silvio Cascione and José de Castro

SAO PAULO, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real weakened for the first day in four on Friday, after the central bank intervened in the currency market for the first time this year to stem a rally that risks slowing an economic recovery.

The real fell 0.3 percent to 1.725 to the dollar in early afternoon trading after the central bank called an auction to buy U.S. dollar forwards. That reversed earlier gains of as much as 0.3 percent. By buying forwards, the central bank soaks up excess dollars in the currency market by capping future supply of the greenback.

"What's important here is that the central bank intervened, which signals that it won't permit the currency to rise too much," said Glauber Romano, a trader with Intercam Corretora de Cambio in Sao Paulo.

The bank's first attempt to arrest the real's 8.3 percent jump this year indicates worries among government policymakers over the size and impact of the rally on exports and economic growth. A stronger currency usually makes Brazilian-made goods less competitive in global markets, hampering export revenue.

The last time Brazil's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market was on Dec. 15, when it tried to sell dollars on the spot market after the currency weakened sharply on fears the global economy was slipping back into recession.

Some of the gains in the real stem from massive capital inflows from investors seeking high-yielding, riskier assets such as Latin American stocks, bonds and currencies. A record $7.1 billion flowed into the Brazilian stock market last month, according to data by BM&FBovespa, the exchange operator.

Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff is seeking to help local carmakers by hiking taxes on some foreign-made cars last year. She is also said to have ordered the end of a long-standing deal with Mexico for tariff-free bilateral trade in automobiles and parts.

Other major Latin American currencies kept strengthening on Friday after a surge in job creation in the United States added to market optimism that the global economy is improving.

Chile's peso was trading at a fresh 4-1/2 month high, boosted by rising prices for top export copper and better-than-expected U.S. jobs data. The peso was 0.35 percent stronger to bid at 478.20 pesos to the dollar.

Better job data in the United States also strengthened the Mexican peso, which was trading 0.65 percent firmer.

"As world volatility comes down investors are getting more constructive and you see a resumption of carry trade and a search for higher yields," said Igor Arsenin, an emerging market strategist with Credit Suisse. "Authorities in Brazil are very sensitive to the level of the currency. We are likely to see more interventions."

(Writing by Alonso Soto and Guillermo Parra-Bernal; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  rise to multimonth highs
text:
(Recasts throughout; updates to close)

* Mexico, Chile pesos hit 4-1/2-month highs

* Brazil's real hits 3-month high, intervention eyed

* Brazil real firms 0.67 pct, Mexico peso up 0.69 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Mexico's and Chile's peso firmed to their strongest in 4-1/2 months on Thursday, while Brazil's real hit a three-month high, as expectations of low U.S. interest rates fueled demand for higher-yielding assets.

Easing fears that Europe's debt crisis could spark another global financial debacle have driven global investors into Latin America, and the region's currencies have led gains among emerging market assets this year.

U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke defended low interest rate policies before Congress on Thursday, saying the economy of the United States still needs plenty of support.

Last week, the Fed said U.S. overnight interest rates would likely remain near zero through late 2014, pushing even more investors to pile into higher-yielding Latin American local-currency debt.

"The added impulse for yield hunting is starting to take the top seat among the different elements that are affecting the market and that is helping Latin America," said Enrique Alvarez, an analyst at IDEAglobal in New York.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.69 percent to 12.8010 per dollar while Chile's peso surged 1.42 percent stronger to 479.90 pesos after the cost of dollars in pesos fell below its 200-day simple moving average.

Brazil's real bid 0.67 percent stronger at 1.7218 per dollar.

Riskier assets around the world have gained as the European Central Bank calmed fears of a full-blown euro crisis by pumping 489 billion euros of cheap three-year loans into the banking system since December.

A Reuters poll showed on Thursday that further gains by Latin American currencies could be limited in the coming months, but its also indicated that Mexico's peso is best-placed to benefit from another asset-buying program by the Fed.

The Brazilian real is likely to fall back to 1.75 per dollar this month as investors fear another bout of strong official action to protect local manufacturers, which have struggled to sell abroad as the currency strengthened.

Traders are closely eyeing the 1.70 reais per dollar level that was seen spurring intervention in the past.

Further easing fears about Europe on Thursday, Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said China is "considering increasing its participation in the solution of the European debt crisis" through the region's bailout fund.

"Those comments from China have helped ease market worries," said Reginaldo Galhardo, exchange trade manager for Treviso Corretora in Sao Paulo. "This optimism is bringing investors back to emerging markets."

* Brazil real hits key 1.75/dlr level, triggers profit-taking

By Brad Haynes and Rachel Uranga

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Chile's peso led gains among Latin American currencies against the U.S. dollar on Monday on optimism that Greece can avoid a debt default that would drag on global growth.

The session's gains may be fleeting, however, as the region's markets closed before news that euro zone finance ministers had rejected an offer made by private bondholders to help restructure Greece's debts.

France's foreign minister earlier had said a deal between Greece and its creditors was "taking shape" ahead of a meeting to set the terms of a rescue package for Athens.

The Chilean peso firmed nearly 0.9 percent to 487.9 per U.S. dollar, hitting a four-month high as a rally pushed the currency's relative strength index to its most overbought levels seen in a year.

"The risk at these levels is profit-taking, but I would see that as a chance to reload," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a Latin American currency strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut.

She said investor flows into Latin America are driving the region's currency strength, as moderating concerns about Europe's debt woes drive investment into emerging markets seen benefitting from a global economic recovery.

Mexico's peso gained 0.23 percent to end at 13.1700 per dollar, gaining for the sixth straight day after economic data last week confirmed a brightening outlook in the United States, which accounts for nearly 80 percent of Mexican export earnings.

Francisco Diez, director of emerging market trading at RBC Capital Markets in New York, said the peso's rally could break 13 per dollar to set a four-month high. Betting on the stronger peso "plays on the strengths of the recovery in the U.S., and (Mexico's central) bank is very unlikely to intervene," said Diez.

In Brazil, where the central bank has a track record of aggressive currency interventions, the real weakened slightly more than 0.4 percent on Monday to trade at 1.7512 per dollar after its recent rise triggered concerns about a policy response.

"The 1.75-level has been historically significant for policy interventions, so local traders are talking up the risk of a (Brazilian) central bank move, which prompted some profit-taking," said RBS' Cattan-Naslausky.

She noted, however, that an intervention in Brazil seemed unlikely before the exchange rate approaches 1.70 per dollar. Brazilian companies' foreign financing needs and possible equity offerings are supporting the currency's recent rally, she added.

title: ANALYSIS-Peru's steady sol  currency  may defy emerging markets jinx
text:
* Peru currency strengthened most in Latin America in 2011

* Some say Peru's commodities mix makes it recession-proof

By Caroline Stauffer

LIMA, Jan 19 (Reuters) - Peru's sol may not repeat its 2011 performance as Latin America's star currency this year, but strong exports of crisis-proof gold, low currency volatility and growing confidence in the new president could make it a sound emerging market bet.

Local businesses and economists consulted by Reuters mostly see the sol, which gained 4 percent last year, holding stable or strengthening slightly despite the risk of lower commodity prices and fallout from Europe's financial mess.

Peru's currency has been the region's least volatile for years and low volatility makes currencies more attractive for investors looking for less risky bets.

The Mexican and Chilean pesos and the Brazilian real , in contrast, each lost about 10 percent in 2011, lashed in the second half of the year when Europe's debt woes drove risk-shy investors out of many emerging markets.

The sol outperformed mostly on high prices paid for the commodities it exports, including gold, and got a boost when President Ollanta Humala, a one-time radical leftist, pleasantly surprised investors by appointing conservatives to run economic and monetary policy after taking office in July .

"There's a flood of money coming in, both from abroad and internally," said Javier San Miguel, budget manager at Peru's largest consumer goods company Alicorp. "Exports are still quite good even though commodities prices have come down some. We see a favorable outlook."

"Everything Humala has done to date is in line with what the business sector wanted," he added.

San Miguel believes the sol will end 2012 up nearly 2 percent from 2011 at 2.65 per U.S. dollar. Alicorp imports basic food goods like wheat and soy in dollars and sells 75 percent of its finished products domestically in soles.

The sol has been trading around its strongest level in more than a decade so far this year, and is 0.15 percent stronger than its 2011 close of 2.96 per U.S. dollar.

RECESSION-PROOF?

While many economies in Latin America export commodities, Peru is unique. Unlike neighboring Chile, where copper is dominant and accounts for roughly 50 percent of monthly export revenue, Peru is the world's No. 2 copper and silver producer and Latin America's top gold producer.

The dollar value of Peru's monthly gold exports has been nearly equal to that of its copper sales abroad.

Ricardo V. Lago, a former World Bank economist, has said that Peru's role as a gold exporter could mean it is virtually recession-proof in a scenario when precious metals prices leap on safe-haven buying in a global economic meltdown.

Other economists say even though prices for copper and zinc Peru exports may be softer, prices for its gold and fishmeal are still high. It is the world's top fishmeal producer.

"There might be other countries in the region that export gold but it's not as important as in Peru," said Nomura analyst Benito Berber.

Peru, one of the region's most open economies, is also an emerging leader in niche agricultural products like asparagus and it has a growing manufacturing sector, mainly textiles. The government forecasts economic growth of around 5.4 percent in 2012, which could be one of the region's fastest rates.

"The sol doesn't just depend on commodities. Peru has been more successful in exporting value added goods than other countries in the region and is supported by strong macroeconomic fundamentals," said Mariel Koehler, a trader for Peruvian miner Volcan, the world's No. 4 zinc producer.

Koehler sees the currency gaining 3.5 percent in 2012 to end at 2.6 per dollar, barring unexpected global economic trauma.

$50 BILLION IN THE PIPELINE

Others say that while Peru will likely again have the least volatile currency in the region this year, it is not entirely risk free.

Some $50 billion in investment in mining and energy are lined up for the next few years, and some analysts fear the cash will only come through if Humala can avert protests against natural resource extraction in remote areas of the country.

U.S.-based Newmont's $4.8 billion copper and gold project has been on hold since locals started protests in northern Cajamarca, demanding the company stop work on the mine for fear it will disrupt scarce water supplies.

"The risk for the sol is basically a fall in investment if social conflicts break out in mining areas," said Pedro Tuesta, a Peruvian economist with the 4Cast consultancy, who sees the sol trading between 2.68 and 2.72 at year's end.

The sol will likely trade sideways at a time when the Mexican peso could rebound on stronger signs of recovery in the United States, Tuesta said. Barclays Capital says the Mexican peso and Brazil's real could both outperform the sol in 2012.+

But the sol's performance is not entirely determined by market factors. The central bank's ample reserves and frequent interventions have played a role in the sol having a lower volatility. Because Peru is a small market, central bank intervention is much more effective at curbing volatility than in Chile or Mexico.

The central bank intervenes frequently, purchasing $4.7 billion in 2011, because half of all bank accounts in Peru are held in dollars and exchange rate volatility hurts businesses and consumers, who often get paid in soles and owe debts in dollars.

Regardless of how Europe's debt crisis, Chinese demand for minerals and the economic recovery in the United States play out, the sol could well emerge relatively unscathed in 2012.

"It will again be the currency with the lowest volatility," said Nomura's Berber. "And in a scenario in which things continue to complicate in Europe towards mid-year, I see the (sol) depreciating, though less than many other currencies."

(Additional reporting by Ursula Scollo; Editing by Terry Wade and W Simon)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real slides on trade lines; Mexico level
text:
* Expiring trade lines, credit crunch pressure Brazil real

* Mexico intervention concern pushes Brazil real selling

Updates prices, adds Mexico peso comment)

By Jeb Blount and Rachel Uranga

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY , Dec 14 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped to a three-week low against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as investors sought greenbacks to pay trade-finance credit lines unlikely to be renewed as Europe's debt crisis prompts banks to limit lending.

Brazil's real led a general slide in Latin American currencies, shedding 1.24 percent to 1.8727 to the dollar. Earlier it weakened as much as 1.36 percent to 1.8750, its weakest intraday level since Nov. 25. Mexico's peso weakened 0.40 percent to 13.9202.

The real's declines were likely amplified as some investors used the Brazilian currency as a way to reduce their exposure to Latin American risk without causing Mexico's peso, the most-traded regional currency, from falling enough to trigger an intervention by the country's central bank, said Diego Donadio, Latin America currency strategist with BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

"Not only do you have trade lines maturing with the prospect of higher rates and lower availability, you have the Mexican factor," he said.

Because of Mexico's Virgin of Guadalupe holiday on Monday, Mexico's official peso fixing rate showed only a 1.06 percent slide on Tuesday from Friday's fix, the previous business day's official rate.

That loss was short of the 2 percent loss required for Mexico's central bank to enter and buy $400 million of pesos, an act that could have caused losses for those betting against the Mexican currency, Donadio said.

Meanwhile, the spot rate slipped more than 2 percent when Monday's offshore, nonlocal trading was included.

"In a climate where risk aversion is high, it made more sense to sell the real than to sell the peso," Donadio said. "If people had sold the peso as heavily as the real it would have rapidly hit the intervention limit."

Donadio expects all the region's currencies to slide in coming days as investors continue to buy the dollar and dollar-denominated assets instead of Latin American currencies and local-currency assets, which are considered riskier than dollars.

In addition to the need for companies and investors to pay down year- and month-end credit lines, many want to hold dollars to protect against the risks related to a European debt crisis that threatens to push the world economy into recession.

The real, Donadio said, is likely to slide to 1.90 or 1.91 in the coming days and weeks, levels that will then likely spark a response from Brazil's central bank, concerned that a weaker real could stoke inflation or make it difficult for some Brazilian companies to pay dollar debts.

"The market is going to test the central bank at around 1.90 because it believes the central bank has made it clear that it won't tolerate bigger weakening," he said.

Mexico's peso will likely find resistance near 14.10 to the dollar based on Fibonacci retracement measures, he said.

Cesar Elizalde, a currency trader at Banorte-IXE, believes the peso could easily pass the 14 per dollar mark, thanks to European concerns and the failure of the U.S. Federal Reserve to take stronger action to prevent Europe's problems from hurting the United States.

On Wednesday, Italian 10-year debt yields, a proxy for government long-term borrowing costs, rose to a record 7.3 percent.

"There is no clear definition to the problem of the crisis in Europe and there is worry about the Federal Reserve, so this is the principal problem, the environment and a bit of liquidity," Elizalde said.

Intervention by Mexico's central bank is unlikely, he said, as investors appear to be increasing their bets on a stronger peso in the futures markets.

Elsewhere in Latin America, Chile's peso weakened 1.19 percent to 521.20 to the dollar, its weakest since Nov. 30. Colombia's peso weakened 0.42 percent to 1,937.60.

(Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Mexico November Consumer Confidence 89.5 Versus 88.5 Year Ago
text:
MEXICO CITY -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's consumer confidence rose in November from a year earlier, but fell from the previous month in seasonally adjusted terms, the National Statistics Institute, or Inegi, said Monday.

Inegi said its consumer confidence index was 89.5 last month, up modestly from 88.5 in November 2010 but down 0.78% seasonally adjusted from October.

Compared with a year ago, consumers were less upbeat about the current economic situation and their ability to buy big-ticket items, while more confident about economic prospects for a year from now.

Banco Santander said in a report ahead of the release that confidence generated by jobs growth and credit expansion in Mexico has been offset by discouraging news on the international economic front, and particularly the peso's depreciation against the U.S. dollar.

In November, the peso fell to its weakest level since March 2009, trading above MXN14 to the dollar as a result of global risk aversion generated by uncertainty about the future of the euro. The peso has recovered ground in the past week after the Bank of Mexico and Finance Ministry announced plans to intervene to keep the currency from sharply declines.

The Bank of Mexico suspended its dollar purchases through monthly auctions of dollar put options and instead will sell up to $400 million on days when the peso is 2% weaker than the previous session.

The central bank shift from a buyer to a potential seller of dollars contributed to peso gains the past week. The currency was recently quoted in Mexico City at MXN13.4895 to the dollar, compared with MXN13.5925 at the close Friday.

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Flat On The Day, Up On The Week Vs Dollar
text:
--Mexican currency is now 4.6% stronger than it was a week ago

--Peso appreciates after Mexican authorities say they will intervene in forex markets

--The Bank of Mexico leaves interest rates unchanged at 4.5%


 
   By Juan Montes 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed nearly flat Friday against the U.S. dollar, concluding a positive week in which improved sentiment about the European debt situation, and planned intervention by the Bank of Mexico to curb sharp swings in the exchange rate, lent support to the currency.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN13.5925 to the dollar, compared with MXN13.60 Thursday and 4.6% stronger than it was a week ago.

Investor doubts about the future of the euro and prospects for some euro-zone countries have made the peso a lightning rod for risk aversion, since it is one of the most-traded emerging-market currencies. Investors also have been hedging their exposure to Mexican securities through the currency futures market, contributing to the peso's recent decline to its weakest level since March 2009.

On Tuesday, the country's foreign exchange commission announced that the central bank will sell up to $400 million on days the peso is 2% weaker than the previous session, and also said it would halt its monthly dollar put options, which it had conducted as a means of accumulating foreign reserves by buying dollars when the peso was appreciating.

"The exchange rate is continuing its downward trend ahead of a possible dollar selling period by the central bank," said brokerage Actinver in a note, adding that the support level is MXN13.50.

On Friday, the Bank of Mexico left its policy interest rate unchanged at 4.5%, in line with analyst expectations. The Mexican central bank said economic growth risks have deteriorated and a rate cut couldn't be dismissed in the future, but also highlighted that weakness and volatility in the peso remain a key risk for inflation.

"Consistent with Bank of Mexico not changing its tone, the market's reaction to the statement has been fairly muted," said Barclays Capital analysts. "The central bank continues to show a neutral stance, with no urgency to start easing."

title: Mexico Intervention  Kick-starts Peso Turnaround
text:
--Mexico's peso likely to see further gains in medium-term

--Central bank says it will intervene when peso falls 2% against the dollar on the day

--The currency is still susceptible to volatility inspired by risk aversion

By Erin McCarthy

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Mexico's surprise pledge to intervene in support of its currency should hasten the peso's long-awaited turnaround.

For the first time in three years, Mexico's typically conservative central bank took steps this week to steady its wildly swinging currency. Until its announcement on Tuesday, the Bank of Mexico had been one of a dwindling number of emerging-market central banks to stand by as its currency's value plunged. On Friday, the peso hit its weakest point against the dollar since March 2009, having fallen about 22% since August.

"It was a huge policy decision and it was a credible one because it was so not like them," said RBS strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky.

Analysts point to MXN14 against the dollar as a likely line in the sand for the central bank.

On Thursday, the peso traded at MXN13.5584 against the dollar, more than 2% stronger since the intervention announcement, according to CQG.

It looks like the start of a rally long anticipated by investors and analysts.

Before the announcement, trading in the peso had been a "one-way street down," said Michael Woolfolk, senior currency strategist at Bank of New York Mellon in New York.

The peso's a popular pick for investors looking to buy and sell emerging market currencies, due to its high trading volume and the ability to trade it freely throughout the global day.

But now investors who are short the peso may be more worried about intervention risks, and may want to protect their portfolios ahead of year-end, said Michael Lee, a portfolio manager at Wells Fargo Asset Management.

BNY Mellon's Woolfolk sees the peso ending the year around MXN13.50 to the dollar, and strengthening to MXN12.5 in mid-2012.

The peso's also got more room to gain, as it has lagged other emerging-market currencies this year. Some investors say the peso is undervalued by as much as 15%.

But investors and analysts warn that the peso could see some bumps along the way. A global economic downturn, or financial turmoil in Europe, could spur investors to sell the peso even in the face of any interventions.

"It doesn't mean that we're in a one-way directional trade, because we're still susceptible to the headline risks," said RBS's Cattan-Naslausky.

The Bank of Mexico said Tuesday it will sell as much as $400 million a day in the exchange market on days when the peso is 2% weaker against the dollar than the previous session, the country's foreign exchange commission said on Tuesday. It also cancelled its monthly auctions of dollar put options, which previously took advantage of peso appreciation to boost dollar reserves.

Mexico primarily wants to stem sharp swings in its currency, since sudden ups and downs can turn investors off of peso-denominated assets, such as local-currency bonds. A steep fall in the peso would also lead to an uptick in inflation.

The Bank of Mexico has plenty of firepower to stand behind the plan, with nearly $140 billion in foreign exchange reserves and a $73 billion flexible credit line with the International Monetary Fund.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com
