title: Bank Of  Mexico  Seen Holding Rates Despite  FX Intervention  Plan
text:
--Central bank seen keeping rate at 4.5% this week

--Measures to stabilize peso make room for future rate cut

--Peso's 16% slide vs dollar since July could impact inflation


 
  By Juan Montes 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Mexico is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged Friday, despite recent measures taken by local monetary and financial authorities to curb the depreciation of the Mexican peso.

Fifteen of the 17 analysts consulted by Dow Jones Newswires still think the central bank will leave its overnight lending rate target at 4.5%--where it has stood since July 2009--when it publishes its decision and monetary policy statement at 10 a.m. EST Friday.

A heavily depreciated peso was one of the reasons behind analysts' expectations for the bank to stay on hold at its last meeting of the year. This week, however, Mexico's foreign exchange commission announced an intervention measure to prevent the peso from charting sharp single-session losses.

The Bank of Mexico will sell as much as $400 million a day when the peso is 2% weaker than the previous session, the country's foreign exchange commission said on Tuesday. The peso rallied on the decision and now is trading at MXN13.6035, after trading above MXN14 Monday, its weakest level in 2 1/2 years.

"After the announcement, there have been some rumors among analysts and traders about an increasing possibility of a rate cut Friday, but we still think the Bank of Mexico won't act," said Sergio Martin, HSBC's chief economist for Mexico.

Martin explained the Mexican economy is still growing at a steady pace and inflation pressures are under control, so an interest rate movement wouldn't make sense right now even though the peso has recovered some ground after the exchange commission announcement.

The Mexican economy gained momentum in the third quarter, growing 4.5% versus the year-ago period, showing strong domestic demand that could offset a slowdown in industrial output.

JP Morgan's chief Mexico economist, Gabriel Casillas, said this week's peso appreciation could be short lived. "We do not believe the significant depreciation of the peso that we have observed in the past few months will be reverted in the next few days. Even if this happens, we do not believe Bank of Mexico members would react to short-term dynamics," he explained.

The peso remains about 16% weaker than its levels at the end of July, before the European debt crisis sparked a surge in global risk aversion.

"It is still early to assess the impact of the [Tuesday] announcement on the currency," added Credit Suisse analyst Alonso Cervera. "Probably the central bank will still want to get more clarity as to the unfolding European crisis."

Stepping away from the pack, Nomura analyst Benito Berber changed his call and now expects the Bank of Mexico to cut rates after Wednesday's coordinated action by the world's largest central banks to provide liquidity to the financial system.

Berber is expecting a 25 basis point cut Friday and perhaps one more in the first quarter of 2012.

"The door has been opened for the Mexican central bank to cut its policy rate. It looks like the decision to intervene [in Mexico] could be part of a broader strategy," Berber said in a report.

The Bank of Mexico has a reputation of being prudent and avoiding hasty policy decisions. In early November, Mexican central bank Governor Agustin Carstens suggested the central bank won't put peso stability at risk by cutting rates, as the exchange rate could impact inflation in the future.

-By Juan Montes, Dow Jones Newswires; (5255) 5980 5178, juan.montes@dowjones.com [ 01-12-11 1909GMT ]

title: WSJ: Mexico's  Central Bank  To Back Peso
text:
MEXICO CITY--Mexico's central bank will begin selling dollars to support the peso on days the currency comes under heavy pressure, a move that shows how Europe's financial crisis is forcing even the most orthodox central banks to become more active in the markets.

The Bank of Mexico will sell as much as $400 million a day in the exchange market on days when the peso is 2% weaker than the previous session, the country's foreign exchange commission said on Tuesday. The commission is made up of members of the Bank of Mexico and the Finance Ministry.

The decision to reinstate dollar sales, which hadn't been used here since the last global financial crisis in 2008-2009, comes after the peso recently fell to its weakest level against the U.S. dollar since March 2009, largely as a result of risk aversion brought on by the debt crisis in Europe.

The peso rallied on the news to 13.76 in late afternoon trade compared to 14.05 at the close Monday.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Mexico's central bank has a reputation as a very conservative institution that tends to shy away from signaling a price for the peso. Rather, it tends to let the markets set the price.

But the European debt crisis has forced investors to seek safer investments like the U.S. dollar rather than currencies like the peso, which has tumbled from 11.75 per dollar on Aug. 1. A depreciating currency adds to inflationary pressure by making imports more expensive.

While the Bank of Mexico doesn't want to tell markets where it wants to see the peso and risk having the market test the bank's resolve, it also risked taking too hands off an approach, some economists say.

"Trying to draw a line in the sand is a dangerous move and the market will test you. But being quite so out of the market and laissez faire will also cause the markets to test you, too," said Gray Newman, chief economist for Latin America at Morgan Stanley. "There are times you have to marry your economic principles with the way markets operate."

Newman said the move should help the central bank cut interest rates in the coming months without having to worry about a currency that is fast weakening.

For the past year and a half, the only mechanism the Bank of Mexico used to intervene in the markets was a system of dollar put options that took advantage of peso appreciation to boost dollar reserves.

Mexico's foreign reserves stood at $139.6 billion at the end of last week, close to record levels. Mexico also has an unused $72 billion flexible credit line with the International Monetary Fund.

On Tuesday, the exchange commission said that it would suspend the sale of dollar put options for the time being. That suggests that the crisis has forced the bank's priorities to change, from making sure the peso doesn't get too strong and undermine the competitive position of Mexican exports to making sure the currency doesn't get too weak and stoke inflation.

The news also helped the price of Mexican government debt. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds was down 15 basis points to 6.49%. Local bonds have been largely unscathed by the recent financial upheaval, with some investors hedging their risk through the currency instead.

The last time that the Bank of Mexico sold dollars in the exchange market was during the 2008-2009 global financial crisis. Between October 2008 and October 2009, the central bank sold more than $30 billion through direct auctions, conditional auctions with the 2% rule, and occasional unannounced direct interventions to curtail speculation. The conditional auctions were gradually lowered from $400 million to $250 million, and suspended in April 2010. [ 11-29-11 2019ET ]

title: UPDATE 4-Mexico  central bank  moves to defend peso
text:
* Mexico central bank steps up support for peso

* To offer $400 million on days of big peso drops

* Analysts say move could support later rate cut

(Adds quote from official, paragraphs 3-4)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Nov 29 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank moved to defend the peso on Tuesday as a slump in the currency risks fanning inflation and driving investors from the country's bond market.

In its most forceful move to protect the peso since the collapse of U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers during the 2008 financial crisis, the central bank said it would restart daily market intervention on days of huge peso losses.

"A volatile international environment can provoke major swings in the currency, more so than local conditions," said Mexico's deputy finance minister Gerardo Rodriguez, who sits on the foreign exchange commission that sets policy for the peso.

"These abrupt fluctuations are what we are trying to avoid with the measures taken by the commission," Rodriguez told local radio.

Analysts said the decision by perhaps Latin America's most orthodox supporters of free markets suggested policy-makers are concerned that Europe's debt crisis could explode into a global financial panic similar to 2008.

"They are being pre-emptive here, given how fluid the external situation remains," said Roberto Melzi, a currency strategist at Barclays in New York.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> surged nearly 1.5 percent on the news, rising to 13.8250 per dollar after trading past 14 per dollar earlier in the session.

Market players have been eyeing the potential for intervention from the central bank since the peso broke past 14 per dollar to a 2-1/2-year low last week.

For a CHRONOLOGY on peso interventions: [ID:nN1E7AS1O9]

For a FACTBOX on Mexico risk: [ID:nRISKMX]

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Mexico's last round of currency intervention was triggered in October 2008 when the peso dropped 6 percent in a single day to hit its lowest level in 16 years amid tight liquidity conditions.

Still, the current threat of action falls short of the nearly $11 billion the central bank auctioned up front in October 2008. Daily dollar auctions were only suspended in April last year.

The risk that a weak peso could drive up inflation pushed investors to call off bets of an interest-rate cut this Friday. All 19 analysts in a Reuters poll expect the central bank board to keep rates on hold on Friday. [ID:nWNA4305]

But JP Morgan economist Gabriel Casillas said if the intervention mechanism succeeded in stabilizing the peso, it could give the central bank cover to eventually cut its benchmark rate from the current 4.5 percent.

"This could set the conditions for a rate cut in the future," he said.

AUCTION MECHANISM

On days when the peso is buffeted by big market moves of more than 2 percent in a single session, the bank will offer up $400 million daily in a bid to shield the currency from global turmoil.

The peso has fallen 2 percent in a full day's trade about eight times since volatility spiked in August. While the $400 million is only a fraction of the amount traded daily in Latin America's most liquid currency, some analysts said the signal was key and suggested more intervention could follow.

The central bank also suspended a monthly sale of dollar put options aimed at preventing the peso from appreciating, a mechanism that has helped boost foreign currency reserves to $140 billion.

A slump of more than 16 percent in the peso since August has fanned concerns that higher import prices could feed into inflation, and the central bank has said this could be one hurdle in cutting interest rates to support a still weak economy.

"What is happening is that the exchange rate has depreciated a lot and very fast," said Deutsche Bank economist Fernando Losada. "The central bank wants to prevent a contamination of the exchange rate into domestic prices."

Other central banks have taken a more hands-on approach to sharp currency moves in the past, slapping on capital controls and directly intervening in markets.

But Banco de Mexico Governor Agustin Carstens is generally loath to intervene in markets, and analysts say he would probably not intervene at the central bank's discretion unless liquidity considerations deteriorated significantly. [ID:nN31220972]

The move to set the framework for limited intervention should offer bondholders some insurance against further losses that could push them to abandon Mexican debt. Foreign investors hold a record amount of longer-term Mexican debt, worth around $50 billion.

More currency losses could force investors to dump bonds, which would further hurt the peso, and push more investors to sell bonds in a deepening spiral of losses.

"If the currency were to exaggerate and overshoot, it would create huge deleveraging risk," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut. "The central bank has to intervene."

(Additional reporting by Lorena Segura, Noe Torres and Luis Rojas Mena in Mexico City and Walter Brandimarte in New York; Editing by Jan Paschal, Gary Hill)

title: UPDATE: Bank Of Mexico To Sell Dollars On Days Peso Weakens 2%
text:
--Bank of Mexico to sell as much as $400 million a day when peso is 2% weaker

--Monthly dollar put options suspended until further notice

--Peso, government bonds rally on decision

(Updates with details of previous auctions, level of foreign reserves, market reaction)

By Anthony Harrup

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's foreign-exchange commission said Tuesday that the Bank of Mexico will sell as much as $400 million a day in the exchange market on days when the peso is 2% weaker than the previous session, and that it will suspend its monthly auctions of dollar put options under which the bank had been buying dollars.

The decision to reinstate the conditional dollar sales, which were used in previous crises, comes after the peso recently fell to its weakest level against the U.S. dollar since March 2009, largely as a result of risk aversion brought on by the debt crisis in Europe.

The foreign-exchange commission, formed by the Bank of Mexico and the Finance Ministry, said in a statement that the sale of dollars is intended to maintain orderly functioning of the exchange market and provide liquidity when needed, given current conditions in the international financial markets.

Beginning Wednesday, the central bank will auction $400 million a day at a minimum price that is 2% above the previous day's exchange rate, so that dollars will only be sold when the peso is at least 2% weaker from the previous session.

The Bank of Mexico is also suspending the sale of dollar put options under which the central bank would buy up to $600 million a month. The put options, which were used to bolster foreign reserves, were exercisable on days when the peso was stronger against the dollar than its 20-day average. None of the $600 million in options for November have been exercised, and Wednesday's auction of options for December was canceled.

Mexico's foreign reserves stood at $139.6 billion at the end of last week, close to record levels. Mexico also has an unused $72 billion flexible credit line with the International Monetary Fund.

The peso rallied sharply on news of the planned central bank intervention, and was quoted in Mexico City at MXN13.7655 around 4 p.m. EST, according to Infosel, compared with MXN14.0530 at the close Monday.

Government bonds also gained, pushing yields lower. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds was down 15 basis points to 6.49%, and the yield on 20-year bonds was off 12 basis points at 7.59%. Local bonds have been largely unscathed by the recent bouts of global risk aversion, with several analysts saying that foreign investors, rather than selling, have been hedging the risk through currency futures, leading to net short peso positions in Chicago.

The last time that the Bank of Mexico sold dollars in the exchange market was during the 2008-2009 global financial crisis. Between October 2008 and October 2009, the central bank sold more than $30 billion through direct auctions, conditional auctions with the 2% rule, and occasional unannounced direct interventions to curtail speculation. The conditional auctions were gradually lowered from $400 million to $250 million, and suspended in April 2010.

title: INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1-Mexico official sees market volatility
text:
* Overall market liquidity has not been compromised

* Does not rule out action to support market functioning

(Adds details, quotes, background, byline)

By Luis Rojas and Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Mexico's markets may be volatile in coming days but so far investors have shown no sign of abandoning peso investments, Deputy Finance Minister Gerardo Rodriguez said on Wednesday.

In an interview with Reuters, Rodriguez said officials did not rule out taking necessary measures to stabilize markets, including currency market intervention.

With U.S. financial markets closed on Thursday for a holiday, there may be more volatility on Mexican markets in coming days due to lower volumes.

"Markets become a bit more sensitive in periods of less liquidity. I think that's what we can expect in the next few days," Rodriguez said.

He said officials were not interested in defending a particular level of the peso <MXN=><MXN=D2>, which hit a 2-1/2-year low against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday.

But asked about the possibility of currency intervention, Rodriguez said: "At this moment I don't think it's possible to rule any option out, what I would say is that we are always closely monitoring developments in the markets.

"We see that market integrity has not been compromised, but this does not imply that we are not watching intently."

Mexico's last round of currency intervention was triggered in October 2008 when the peso dropped 6 percent in a single day and hit its lowest level in 16 years amid tight liquidity conditions.

So far, there are few signs foreign investors are turning against Mexico, Latin America's second-largest economy. Bond positions have remained firm and shorter-term debt has bounced back after a sell-off.

"The reduction was very, very slight and has been quickly recouped," Rodriguez said. "It's one factor that we have to keep watching closely to make sure that markets keep operating normally."

As of Nov. 11, the latest data available from the central bank, foreign holdings of longer-term Mexican debt had dipped only 0.4 percent from a record high of 696.9 billion pesos ($49.2 billion) on Nov. 7.

NO WORSE THAN BEFORE

Rodriguez, who will play a key role in Mexico's presidency of the Group of 20 developed and emerging economies in 2012, said he did not see weakness in a bond sale in Germany on Wednesday as a sign of further deterioration in the euro zone economy.

"It's not about anything in particular, we are just seeing new manifestations of the same problems, which are sparking volatility," he said of the situation in Europe, where the euro <EUR=> hit a six-week low on Wednesday. [ID:nL5E7MN309]

The prospect of more International Monetary Fund help for the troubled euro zone was an issue to be addressed at the G20 level, he said.

IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde will visit Mexico next week as part of a regional tour, but Rodriguez said he did not expect any changes to the country's credit line.

The IMF extended its credit line to Mexico to more than $70 billion the last time its chief visited Mexico, but Rodriguez said it was not time to review the agreement yet.

He confirmed that Mexico had not yet tapped the credit line, which runs until 2013, and said it remained a precautionary measure.

Officials were not considering any particular contingency plans in case of wider fallout from the euro zone crisis, but were monitoring conditions closely.

Economic activity remained solid and Mexican banks had sound capital buffers, Rodriguez said. ($1 = 14.1690)

(Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle and Ana Isabel Martinez; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso hits 2-1/2 year low, real tumbles
text:
* Latin American commodities fall as China factories slow

* Weak German debt auction spurs fears of wider EU crisis

* Brazil real slumps 2.9 pct, Mexico peso off 1.7 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle and Jeb Blount

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso slumped to a 2-1/2 year low on Wednesday and Brazil's currency sank after weak Chinese factory data added to mounting concerns about Europe's debt troubles.

Brazil's real lost nearly 3 percent on concern a slowing Chinese economy will hit demand and prices for the country's iron ore, soybeans other commodity exports.

The weak Chinese data also weighed on Chile, as prices tumbled for copper, the country's top export.

Undermining demand for riskier assets around the world, a weak German bond sale sparked fears that Europe's debt crisis was beginning to threaten even Berlin. Leaders of France and Germany are still at odds over a longer-term structural solution. For details, see [ID:nL5E7MN1VS]

"Things are getting worse in Europe. The market has lost faith in the politicians coming up with a sound solution," said Clyde Wardle, a currency strategist at HSBC in New York.

Major global banks, especially those based in Europe, are facing deepening losses on their euro zone bonds. Their units in Latin America will likely cut back on loans to the region, which would drag down local growth, analysts said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MXN=D2> slumped 1.72 percent to 14.23 per dollar and hit its weakest level since April 2009.

The peso's sharp losses have raised concerns that Mexico's central bank could intervene to halt losses.

Mexican Deputy Finance Minister Gerardo Rodriguez told Reuters that officials were closely monitoring markets, but he said recent volatility had not compromised the integrity of the market for Mexican assets. [ID:nWNA4350]

Rodriguez also said officials were not interested in defending a particular level for the peso.

Mexico has the only freely traded currency in Latin America and analysts doubt authorities will follow Brazil's recent moves to defend its currency.

Moreover, the peso's weakness will help boost earnings from exports and make them more competitive abroad.

"Given the highly uncertain external environment, we believe authorities will be comfortable with a weak peso, which is helping the export sector," Wardle said.

The Mexican peso's slump back past the psychological 14-per-dollar level this week has pushed investors to call off bets that the central bank could cut interest rates on Dec. 2.

A Reuters poll showed 19 of 19 economists surveyed see Mexico holding its benchmark rate steady at 4.50 percent. [ID:nWNA4305]

The central bank is probably unwilling to cut interest rates when a prolonged bout of weakness in the peso since August could end up feeding into higher inflation through more expensive imports, analysts said.

"What is worrying the central bank is what is happening with the exchange rate. If it stays around 14, or above 14, there will be pressure on inflation," said Salvador Orozco, a debt strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

In Brazil, the real <BRBY> weakened 2.85 percent to 1.8578 to the dollar, its weakest close since Oct. 4 <BRLCLOSE=>.

The real has lost nearly 9 percent this month, putting it in a virtual tie with the New Zealand dollar <NZD=> as the biggest loser among the more than 150 currencies tracked by Thomson Reuters against the dollar.

Data on Wednesday showed factory activity in China shrank at its fastest pace in 32 months. [ID:nL4E7MN1HM]

China, the world's second-largest national economy, is Brazil's top trading partner.

"The data is showing a major contraction in China, which means that in addition to export volumes, prices are falling, too," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist with the Sao Paulo unit of WestLB, a German bank.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 1.2 percent weaker at 524.70, its weakest in nearly seven weeks as copper prices hit a one-month low. [ID:nL5E7MN0R3]

Chile gets about 55 percent of its export earnings from copper.

(Reporting by Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso approaches two year low
text:
* Peso weaker than 14 boosts outlook for c.bank action

* Peso erases losses to gain against U.S. dollar

* Weak Mexico peso, strong GDP raises inflation concern

* Latin America FX trades mixed on Europe debt, U.S. GDP

(Updates prices to close)

By Jeb Blount and Michael O'Boyle

RIO DE JANEIRO/MEXICO CITY, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Investors eyed the potential for central bank intervention and called off bets of an imminent interest-rate cut after Mexico's peso nearly hit its weakest point in two years.

The peso <MXN=D2> firmed 0.25 percent to 13.9850. Earlier it slipped 0.52 percent to 14.0928, just short of 14.1396, a September intraday price that is the weakest since April 2009.

A weaker peso, which has lost about 12 percent in the last three months during the European debt and banking crisis, makes imports more expensive and risks driving inflation higher, a result the central bank is charged with preventing.

"To short the peso beyond 14 right now you have to be very brave," said Alberto Bernal, head of research at Bulltick Capital Markets in Miami. "If the central bank comes in to protect the peso, they (investors) will get hammered."

As the peso has declined over the last three months - it is the seventh-worst performer among the 36 most-traded currencies against the dollar in the period - concern about inflation and currency intervention has risen.

That in turn has seen investors increase their bets that the central bank will not cut interest rates at its next meeting on Dec. 2.

Inflation concerns rose after a report on Tuesday showed the Mexican economy <MXGDPQ=ECI> grew a seasonally adjusted 1.3 percent in the third quarter, nearly two-thirds higher than the 0.8 percent estimate of 16 economists surveyed by Reuters. [ID:nN1E7AL0J3] and [ID:nN1E7AF22O]

Some said expectations of central bank intervention are overdone. The central bank is unlikely to intervene unless the world financial system seizes up, said Benito Berber, a currency analyst with Japan's Nomura Securities in New York.

Mexico's central bank intervened to support the peso in 2008 and 2009 as bank lending and financial system liquidity dried up after the U.S. mortgage and banking crisis.

"The bank will only intervene if there is no liquidity in the markets," Berber said.

Just such a situation, though, may be in the offing as investors seek protection from a potential European financial collapse by buying the dollar in favor of the peso and other Latin American currencies, which are considered riskier.

"If Europe falls apart, if the euro breaks up, the world financial system will collapse and there is nothing you can do to hedge your risk," Bernal said. "We are hostage to that situation in Mexico."

Elsewhere in Latin America, currencies traded mixed against the U.S. dollar as Europe's debt crisis worsened, the U.S. economy showed signs of life and investors moved to protect holdings ahead of a long holiday weekend in the United States.

Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 0.343 percent to 1.8058 after weakening as much as 0.88 percent. Chile's peso <CLP=CL> was unchanged from Monday at 518.40.

"This is a consolidation day, a day where people are closing up positions ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend and very little solid news," said Kathy Lien, a strategist with GFT Forex a New York currency brokerage. "We're not going to get a trend, until things in Europe settle down."

The region's currencies fluctuated as Spanish bond yields, a proxy for borrowing costs, rose to a 14-year high, raising concern that Spain may soon join Italy and Greece as countries facing unstable finances and rising default risk.

The United States, the world's largest economy, cut its estimate for third-quarter growth to 2 percent from 2.5 percent. The decline, though, was based on inventories, one of the most volatile parts of GDP figures. The data suggests that fourth-quarter growth could be greater than 3 percent, the highest in 18 months. [ID:nN1E7AL0E2]

"The GDP cut is not a sign of slowing," Lien said.

(Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: UPDATE 1-POLL-Mexico peso seen firming nearly 4 pct by year end
text:
* Mexican peso seen trading at 12.96/dlr by end 2011

* Stronger currency could back bets for a rate cut

* Cenbank seen intervening if peso weakens to 14.50/dlr

(Recasts; adds comments, background)

By Jean Luis Arce and Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso will firm nearly 4 percent by the end of the year, according to the median of a Reuters poll, which analysts said could give the central bank more room to cut interest rates.

Mexico's peso slumped about 11 percent in September in its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis.

Analysts said the peso would likely firm from current levels if Europe can contain fears about its debt crisis and if data suggests United States, Mexico's top trading partner, will skirt another recession.

The median expectation of 26 analysts surveyed by Reuters is for the peso <MXN=> to trade at 12.96 per dollar by the end of 2011, compared to current levels around 13.46.

Mexico's central bank signaled last Friday it was prepared to cut interest rates if the global economy worsens but a further fall in the peso could be a stumbling block, since higher import prices may stoke inflation. [ID:nN1E79C25Y]

"To the degree that the peso appreciates, the chance of a cut is going to be much higher," said Gabriel Casillas, an economist at JPMorgan in Mexico City.

Benchmark Mexican credit costs have been at 4.5 percent since mid-2009.

<^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Interactive graphic on economies in the Americas:

http://r.reuters.com/nem92s("http://r.reuters.com/nem92s")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

INTERVENTION AT 14.50/DLR

Mexican inflation is hovering just above the central bank's target rate of 3 percent but prolonged weakness in the peso could worry policymakers. [ID:nWNA1278]

Bets on Mexican interest rate swaps see a nearly two-in-three chance for a 25 basis point cut by the central bank in December and the market has fully priced in such a cut by January. <BOMWATCH2>

By the close of 2012, the currency is seen trading at 12.70 per dollar, or 6 percent stronger from current levels, according to the median of 22 analysts.

Mexico's central bank, led by perhaps the most orthodox supporters of free markets in Latin America, is seen intervening in markets to support the peso if it weakens to 14.50 per dollar, according to the median of 18 analysts.

However, many analysts refused to name a specific level for when authorities could intervene.

They said the central bank would only wade into markets to defend the peso in the case of an extremely quick depreciation that was accompanied by big outflows from the local bond market in conditions of distressed liquidity. [ID:nN1E79D130]

"It is all about the velocity of the depreciation and if there are outflows or not, not so much the level," said Salvador Orozco, a currency strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

The last round of currency intervention was triggered by a 6 percent drop in the peso in a single day to its lowest in 16 years, amid the market turmoil of October 2008.

(Additional reporting by Noe Torres; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: ANALYSIS-Mexico bondholders resist sell-off, shield economy
text:
* Mexican bondholders sit tight amid global panic

* More long-term investors seen, little hot money

* If bonds sell off, could trigger cenbank intervention

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Global investors in Mexican bonds sat tight through a brutal September for riskier assets, indicating a new resiliency among investors that will lend stability to Mexico's economy.

The amount of peso debt held by foreign investors tripled over the last two years to a record high of $70 billion last month as investors starved by ultra-low U.S. interest rates piled into emerging market debt.

Those huge inflows made the Mexican bond market look like a bubble ready to pop when volatility hit last month, but investors surprisingly stuck to their positions despite currency losses.

A sudden reversal of those flows could spur huge currency losses similar to 2008, when Mexico's peso tumbled by the most since the devastating 1994 Tequila Crisis.

"The magnitude of the foreign position is frightening," said Gabriel Casillas, an economist at JPMorgan in Mexico City. "But the investor base is broader. It is more long-term investors and less hot money."

When Mexico's peso <MXN=> slumped about 13 percent against the dollar in September to its weakest level since 2009, short-term foreign investors dumped nearly $3.3 billion in Mexican T-bills, or one-fifth of their holdings, according to central bank data.

But investors in longer-term notes sold only about $760 million, or 1.5 percent of holdings, and the notes still hover near a record high.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Mexican bond time bomb? http://link.reuters.com/hyq93s 

Foreigners sit tight: http://link.reuters.com/raq44s ("http://link.reuters.com/raq44s")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Had more bond investors sold, it would have deepened currency losses, which could trigger more bond sales, further weakening the currency in a vicious cycle.

A sell-off in bonds would push up market rates, dragging on growth, while a weaker peso could stoke inflation and make it harder for the central bank to cut benchmark credit costs.

READY TO RALLY?

Mexico, with Latin America's most freely traded currency and bonds, has been a magnet for investors fleeing crippled public finances and rock-bottom rates in major economies.

The recent sell-off in the peso tested the mettle of these new investors, and the resiliency of bond positions suggests they will not be spooked by another round of peso weakness.

"This has been a good, solid test," said Enrique Alvarez, a debt and currency analyst at IDEAglobal in New York.

If European leaders make good on a pledge to deliver a bold plan to contain the continent's debt crisis by the end of the month, "there could be a pretty large flow coming back into Mexico, Brazil and emerging markets," Alvarez said.

Data from fund-tracker EPFR shows that redemptions from local-currency EM bond funds scaled back to a relative trickle this week after spiking in September.

Fund managers stocked up on cash to prepare for even more redemptions, and now they may be ready to start buying bonds again, RBS Securities wrote in a note. A rally back by Mexican bonds has already begun.

The yield on Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> fell on Friday below its 50-day moving average, down more than 60 basis points since last week to 6.17 percent, suggesting yields could drop even more.

Moreover, the peso's tumble last month shook out speculators. Net futures contracts on the Chicago exchange wagering on a stronger peso plummeted since July, while bets on a weaker peso are hovering near a four-year high.

That means there would now be less of a scramble to dump the peso if global sentiment sours again.

"The risk of another violent sell-off in the peso is more contained since positioning has improved," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays.

Edwin Gutierrez, who helps manage $7 billion of emerging market debt at Aberdeen Asset Management in London, expects volatility to keep the peso on the ropes but doubts there will be a repeat of 2008's market slump.

"Emerging markets came back pretty quickly then, and we will come back even better than developed markets this time," he said.

Mexico's policy makers, perhaps the most orthodox supporters of free markets in Latin America, have so far refrained from intervening to halt the peso's precipitous slide.

But a sudden bond outflow could push Mexico to tap nearly $210 billion from a war chest of record currency reserves and a credit line with the International Monetary Fund.

"Mexico will have to show their hand in terms of intervention if they are tested again," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America debt strategy at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut. "There is no way you could adjust to that shock of a mass exodus."

(Reporting by Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Leslie Adler)

MARKETS-MEXICO/BONDS (ANALYSIS)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso up on Bernanke, Chile peso slumps
text:
* Bernanke keeps hopes alive of further Fed stimulus

* Euro-zone worries seen keeping pressure on Latam FX

* Chile's peso hits 14-month low on copper's rout

By Michael O'Boyle and Jean Luis Arce

MEXICO CITY, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso gained on Tuesday after the head of the U.S. Federal Reserve raised hopes of more economic stimulus, but Chile's peso slid to a 14-month low on a rout in copper prices.

Mexico's peso advanced and U.S. stocks cut losses after Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke said the central bank is prepared to act further to help the economy of the United States, which is Mexico's top trading partner. [ID:nW1E7KM007]

"The signal that the Fed could take more action down the line is what gave markets a bit of a boost," said Alejandro Padilla, an analyst at Banorte-Ixe in Mexico City.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MXN=D2> rose 0.77 percent to 13.96 per dollar. Four straight sessions of steep losses had taken it within striking distance of a more than two-year low.

But analysts said the peso and Latin American currencies would remain vulnerable to more losses. The euro zone's debt troubles will likely push investors to keep dumping riskier assets, such as emerging market currencies and debt, analysts said.

"In the medium term, the issue of Europe is going to keep weighing. There is clearly the worry about whether Greece will be able to meet its obligations," Padilla said.

European finance ministers are considering making banks take bigger losses on Greek debt and have postponed a vital aid payment to Athens until mid-November, setting up a moment of truth in the euro zone's sovereign debt crisis. [ID:nL5E7L419D]

Investors fear another financial crisis could further drag down global growth just as the U.S. and European economies are already slowing down.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.18 percent firmer at 1.8870 per dollar, helped by an auction of currency swap contracts that mimic the purchase of dollars in the futures market and provide investors with insurance against declines in the value of the real. [ID:nN1E7930UT]

Brazil's central bank has been intervening in its currency market to bolster the real, and some analysts think authorities could step up efforts to support the local currency if it breaks 1.90 per dollar.

Brazil's real has slumped about 18 percent since late July. The currency was undercut in August after the central bank made a surprise move to cut interest rates, curbing the appeal of the currency to yield-hungry investors.

Expectations that Brazil could further relax monetary policy are sapping support for the currency. The real had been a favorite bet for emerging market investors due to the country's high interest rates for much of the recovery from the 2008 financial crisis.

Meanwhile, Mexican authorities have recently suggested they will not intervene in the market to support the peso. Mexico's peso has shed around 16 percent since late July.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> shed 1.8 percent to bid at 534.70 per dollar as prices for copper, the country's main export, continued to slump, also trading near a 14-month low

"There is no recovery in copper, so there will be no respite for the peso," said Daniel Soto, an analyst at Forex Chile.

Chile's peso has lost 17 percent since late July.

(Additional reporting by Froilan Romero in Santiago; Editing by Jan Paschal)

title: Mexican Peso Stumbles On Greek Worries, Near 2.5-Year Low Again
text:
--MXN falls 0.9% against USD on Greece concerns

--Carstens downplays role of central bank interventions

--Remittances rise, but economists see Mexican economy cooling


 
    By Amy Guthrie 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--The Mexican peso fell against the U.S. dollar Monday, finishing the session on the cusp of its key MXN14 psychological level, as concerns resurfaced about Greece's ability to make debt payments.

Infosel quoted the peso closing at MXN13.9945 to the U.S. dollar, once again hovering near a 2 1/2-year low and 0.9% weaker than its close Friday of MXN13.8735.

The Greek government said Sunday that it will miss its deficit targets this year, splashing doubt onto whether the European Union will dispense aid in time and driving investors away from risky global assets.

In Mexico Monday, central bank governor Agustin Carstens downplayed the benefits of foreign exchange market interventions, saying that what will ultimately elevate the Mexican currency is solid economic fundamentals.

"The Bank of Mexico stopped intervening in pursuit of a certain exchange rate many years ago," Carstens said.

The "sporadic" interventions that the bank has undertaken, Carstens said, have occurred with one fundamental objective in common: to guarantee the orderly function of the market while avoiding illiquid conditions that could lead to "excessive volatility" in the exchange rate.

Carstens said he expects that Mexico's economic fundamentals will anchor the peso at stronger levels in the medium-term.

In local economic news, remittances from Mexicans living abroad rose 9.2% in August from the year-ago month, to $2.13 billion, bringing remittances for the first eight months of the year to $15.19 billion, a 4.9% increase.

Yet the peso's recent tumble led economists surveyed in September by the central bank to lower their year-end forecast to MXN12.62 from MXN12.12 in the August survey.

The average estimate for 2011 growth in gross domestic product was 3.8%, while the estimate for 2012 fell to 3.5% from 3.6% in August.

"Mexico's link with the U.S. has meant that the slowdown is well underway," Morgan Stanley wrote in a note, saying that evidence that the Mexican economy is cooling will likely motivate the central bank ease monetary policy by year-end.

title: Bank Of Mexico Governor Sees Stronger Peso In Medium Term
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexican central bank governor Agustin Carstens said Monday that the Mexican peso should strengthen in the medium-term, anchored by the country's "strong economic fundamentals."

Concerns about the global economy pushed the peso to a 2 1/2-year low in September of MXN14 to the U.S. dollar. The currency was trading around MXN13.8865 early Monday, off 17% from its strongest 2011 close, reached in April.

Mexico adopted a free-floating peso in 1994, which Carstens said has helped infuse the foreign exchange market with stability.

"The Bank of Mexico stopped intervening to maintain a certain exchange rate many years ago," Carstens said.

When the central bank opts to intervene, Carstens emphasized, it does so in a transparent manner so that market participants are not caught off guard.

The Bank of Mexico sold dollars in the market under several different mechanisms between October 2008 and October 2009 as a lack of liquidity in the market put pressure on the exchange rate. This time officials say there has been adequate liquidity, and have shown no signs they are planning to intervene.

In contrast to the flight to safety behind the peso's recent sharp depreciation, Carstens highlighted that the average maturity for Mexican government debt in pesos, at 7.4 years, now exceeds that of the U.S., at 5.2 years.

The willingness of investors to extend Mexico such long debt maturities is a reflection of confidence, Carstens said, reiterating the country's commitment to stable fiscal and macroeconomic policies.

Going forward, Carstens said that world economic policymakers require a clear and immediate response from the largest economies to the serious problems of indebtedness plaguing the U.S. and Europe, including a more committed strategy for the adjustment of their fiscal accounts.

title: Mexican Peso Ends Weaker As Risk Rout Hits Emerging  Currencies
text:
--Peso loses ground for third straight session

--Bank of Mexico sells $600 million in dollar put options

--Eventual central bank intervention remains a discussion point


 
   By Anthony Harrup 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed weaker against the U.S. dollar for a third consecutive session Friday, losing ground along with local stocks and bonds in another bout of global risk selling.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN13.8735 to the dollar, according to Infosel, compared with MXN13.69 Thursday, for a loss on the week, month and quarter.

Investor worries about euro zone debt troubles, and a slowdown in U.S. and global economic growth, have buffeted the peso the past two months. The currency is off 17% from its strongest close of the year in April, and near to its weakest level in 2 1/2 years.

Friday's U.S. economic data were mixed, with better-than-expected consumer confidence and Chicago factory readings offsetting a surprise dip in personal income, but participants appeared determined to focus on the negative such as a drop in German retail sales and a rise in euro-zone inflation that could keep the European Central Bank from cutting interest rates.

On the local front, the Bank of Mexico sold all $600 million of its monthly dollar put options for October, which will allow holders to sell dollars to the central bank if the peso appreciates next month. While demand for the options fell to $1.55 billion from $2.5 billion a month ago, the average premium rose to MXN65.32 per $1,000 from MXN61.72. Someone tested a bid for MXN1.01 per $1,000 for $10 million in options.

The September options expired without any being exercised as the peso depreciated for a second straight month.

With the continuing volatility in exchange markets, and worries about developed economies hitting emerging market assets, analysts are discussing the likelihood of eventual intervention by the Bank of Mexico.

Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch said it thinks Mexico and Chile are the two major Latin American countries least likely to see foreign exchange intervention, "unless there is a fast and disorderly move in those currencies."

Mexico's foreign exchange commission, made up of Finance Ministry and Bank of Mexico officials, is unlikely to intervene in the near term since officials see the peso weakness overdone as a result of risk aversion, and expect the peso to recover soon.

"In the recent past, interventions have only occurred when the market turned highly illiquid. And in that case, they were implemented in a transparent manner, with clear rules. Therefore, we do not expect any change in the intervention process in coming weeks in our central scenario," BofA said in a report.

Local stocks fell 0.6%, well off intraday lows, and government bonds lost ground, pushing yields higher. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds rose 10 basis points to 6.58%, and 20-year yields were up 6 basis points to 7.58%. The local debt market has seen only modest outflows despite the peso's weakness.

"In Mexico, positioning risk in fixed income is probably still quite high," RBS said in a report.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Mexico  FX  rebound on euro-zone hopes
text:
(Refiles with fresh headline)

 * Brazil real, Mexico peso gain in day of see-saw trading

 * Currencies rebound on expectation Europe to act on debt

 * Chile peso firms vs U.S. dollar; Colombia peso weakens

 * Peru's sol trades unchanged from Friday on intervention

 By Jeb Blount

 RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso and Brazil's real erased losses and gained against the U.S. dollar on Monday, on expectations that Europe will find a way to cut Greek debt and bolster its banks, preventing sovereign debt defaults from choking off global lending and growth.

 Euro-zone officials are seeking new ways to boost their means to fight a widening debt crisis, Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, an executive board member of the European Central Bank, said on Monday in New York. [ID:nLDE78P01H]

 The expectation that the euro zone and the ECB -- after months of ineffectual action -- will take stronger measures to prevent a Greek default from spreading to Portugal, Ireland, Spain and Italy helped markets rebound in late trading on Monday.

 "The market seems to have convinced itself that the Europeans will take stronger action," said Pedro Tuesta, Latin America currency and fixed-income analyst with 4Cast Inc. in Washington.

"I don't buy it, but a lot of people seem to, and they're the ones who've bid the market back up today," he added. "That's about the only way to explain today's gains. Nothing really fundamental has changed, Greece is still a mess and whatever happens will be painful."

 Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 0.88 percent to 1.8200 reais to the dollar. Earlier, it weakened as much as 1.55 percent and gained as much as 1.32 percent.

 Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> firmed 0.60 percent to 13.5019 to the dollar. Earlier, it firmed as much as 1.35 percent and weakened as much as 1.44 percent.

 HURT BY WEAK U.S. HOME SALES

 Early declines were fueled on Monday by concern about growth in the United States, which is responsible for nearly a quarter of world economic output and the source of about 80 percent of Mexican export earnings.

 Weak U.S. housing added to concern that the world's largest economy could slip back into recession.

 New single-family home sales fell in August to a six-month low, a sign the country's near-zero interest rates and expanded credit haven't been enough to boost consumer appetite for long-term investments. [ID:nS1E78P0CJ].

 In such situations, many global investors sell assets in Latin America and other markets considered risky, and buy assets denominated in dollars, the world's most negotiable, or liquid, currency.

 Weak U.S. growth and concern about European debt are the main causes for the Brazilian real's and Mexican peso's declines this month, the biggest in Latin America and among the worst in the world.

 Despite today's gains, the Mexican peso has still lost nearly 10 percent in September and the Brazilian real nearly 13 percent.

 Any doubt about Europe's ability or willingness to solve its debt problems is likely to start the slide again, Tuesta said.

 Chile's peso gained for a second day, firming 0.78 percent to 512.00.

 Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> weakened 0.16 percent to 1,907.00 to the dollar.

 Peru's sol <PEN=PE> closed trading unchanged from Friday at 2.7700 to the dollar after the central bank sold $186 million in the currency market and sold 100 million soles ($36 million) of dollar-linked Adjustable Certificates of Deposit (CDRs).

 The sale of the currency and notes drives up demand for soles, putting pressure on the currency to gain or limiting losses.

(Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by Andrew Hay and Jan Paschal)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains after  FX  swap; Latam rebounds
text:
* Brazil c. bank swap sale checks real slide, sets 'limit'

* Mexico, Chile pesos rebound from sharp Thursday declines

* Peru intervenes in currency market; sol erases loss

(Updates prices, adds Brazil, Peru, Colombia comment)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real reversed losses to gain more than 3 percent against the dollar on Friday -- its biggest one-day gain in almost 16 months -- after the central bank's move to bolster the currency a day earlier raised expectations it will act again to limit sharp falls.

Thursday's sale of $2.75 billion of currency swaps effectively put a limit on how far the bank will allow the real to slide, said Mario Battistel, head of trading at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage. For more see [ID:nS1E78L0PK].

Currency swaps mimic the sale of dollars and provide investors with insurance against future declines in the real.

The real has lost more than 15 percent of its value since the central bank unexpectedly cut its benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point to 12 percent on Aug. 31. The move was based on the bank's expectation that a world economic slowdown would push down Brazil's 7 percent inflation rate. [ID:nE5E7IM05G] and [ID:nL3E7KN1BZ]

"The central bank swap intervention was a pleasant surprise," Battistel said in a telephone interview. "They're clearly worried about inflation and exporters and our other clients weren't about to start moving their large dollar holdings back into Brazil until they had some idea of when the real's plunge would stop."

Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 3.19 percent to 1.8360 to the U.S. dollar, its first gain in six sessions and its biggest one-day gain since May 27, 2010.

The currency had lost more than 1 percent in early trade and still ended the week down about 5.75 percent against the dollar.

The government is ready to intervene more in the currency market to curb wide swings, or volatility, in the market, Finance Minster Guido Mantega told investors in Washington. [ID:nS1E78M134]

Brazil's central bank targets inflation of 4.5 percent plus or minus 2 percentage points and has long said that inflation, now outside the target range, will come under control soon.

A strong real helps control inflation by cutting the cost of dollar-denominated commodities such as food and the cost of essential imports such as machine-tools for Brazil's industry.

Battistel said the central bank, which as recently as August was working to prevent the real from gaining against the dollar, is signaling that it will act any time the real weakens beyond 1.90 to the dollar or strengthens beyond 1.60.

Other traders said the bank is targeting the first dollar futures contract <DOLc1> on the Sao Paulo BM&FBovespa exchange, moving to weaken the real when it firms beyond 2.01 to the dollar and to strengthen the real when it weakens beyond 1.78.

The real-dollar spot exchange rate's close link to the futures market, where bets can be ramped up using loans or "leverage" is one of the reasons the real lost so much in recent weeks, the government said Wednesday.

In first futures trading, which measure expectations for late September, the real shed 2.16 percent to 1.8585.

Bets on a strong real were a key component in the real's nearly 8 percent rise through late July.

Since then the real has reversed all those gains and is now about 9 percent weaker than it was at the end of 2010.

Elsewhere in Latin America currencies rebounded from steep Thursday declines on expectation losses related to concern about a potential Greek default may be overdone.

Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> jumped 3.63 percent to 13.5584 to the dollar, reversing some of Thursday's losses that took the peso beyond 14 to the dollar for the first time since April 2009. For the week the peso trimmed losses to 3.89 percent.

"I think the market has pushed the currency too far too fast and we may see a bit of retracement in the peso's favor," said Francisco Diez, director of emerging-market trading at RBC Capital Markets in New York.

The next point the peso will test if it begins weakening again is 14.25 to the dollar Diez said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> gained 0.93 percent to 516.00 to the dollar after plunging more than 5 percent on Thursday.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> gained 0.58 percent to 1,904.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> trimmed early losses to trade little changed from Thursday at 2.7700 after the country's central bank sold $21 million dollars for pesos, driving up demand for the local currency and helping it firm.

(Additional reporting by Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Raymond Colitt and Kenneth Barry)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Peru step in to halt  forex  plunge
text:
* Brazil sells swaps, Peru trades soles for dollar debt

* World growth outlook knocks commodities, LatAm currencies

* Brazil swap auction helps trim loss that reached 4.79 pct

(Updates prices)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's real trimmed some of its biggest losses since the 2009 world recession and Peru's sol backed away from three-month lows as the countries' central banks moved to bolster their currencies in the face of deteriorating prospects for world growth.

In the face of a nearly 5 percent plunge in the real, Brazil's central bank sold $2.75 billion in currency swaps, intervening in the futures market to support the currency <BRBY>. This reversed a tactic used as recently as August to use sell swaps to prevent the real from strengthening.

After the swap auction, the currency rebounded, eventually reversing losses. It closed spot market trading at 2 percent weaker than on Wednesday at 1.8946 the real's weakest close in more than two years. [ID:nS1E78L0PK]

"The market got the feeling that the central bank wants to put a range on the real," said Moacir Marcos Junior a currency trader at Interbolsa, a Sao Paulo brokerage. "It's like the bank saying, 'look, 1.60 to the dollar, I don't want, but I don't want 1.90 either and I won't let that happen.'"

Thursday's declines bring the Brazilian real's losses this month to more than 15 percent, turning what was a nearly 8 percent year-to-date gain in July to 1.52, a 12-year high, into a nearly 15 percent loss.

In Peru, after the sol <PEN=PE> fell more than 1 percent to 2.7910, a three-month low, the central bank sold 600 million soles ($216.2 million) of readjustable certificates of deposit, or CDRs.

In the operation, local banks trade soles with the central bank for dollar-denominated bonds a trade the mimics the sale of dollars and puts pressure on the sol to gain. The sol rebounded to 2.7690, trimming losses to 0.4 percent [ID:nS1E78L0U7]

The declines on Thursday came on increasing signs of slowdown in the U.S., Europe and China -- economies responsible for 60 percent of world output. That outlook caused the price of oil, coffee, copper, soybeans and other commodities, which form the bulk of Latin American exports, to fall too. For more information see: [ID:nS1E78L0M6] [ID:nL5E7KM1AQ] [IDnS1E78L0CR]

Adding to the gloom, a decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve late Wednesday to launch "Operation Twist" -- an attempt to cut long-term borrowing rates by shifting Fed holdings of U.S. Treasury debt into longer-term bonds -- was seen as too weak to boost the sluggish U.S. economy.

In Greece, a 24-hour anti-austerity strike raised doubts about passage of a plan to stave off a Greek debt default that could hobble international banks and cut-off credit and growth world-wide. [ID:nL5E7KM2H3]

"We are staring at a possible new global recession and that's pushing investors out of Latin American and other commodities-based currencies and into the dollar," Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

In times of economic stress investors frequently sell assets in currencies considered high risk, such as Brazil's real and Mexico's peso, and buy assets priced in dollars, the world's most "liquid" or widely negotiated currency.

Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> weakened 2.83 percent to 14.0701, breaking beyond 14 to the dollar for the first time since April 27, 2009. In contrast to Brazil and Peru, Mexico's finance minister Jose Antonio Meade said intervening to protect a level for the peso would unwise. [ID:nS1E78L1NN]

Now that it's weakened beyond 14.0200 to the dollar, it could fall to the 15.59 range, a level last seen at the height of the world recession in March 2009, said Win Thin, an emerging market currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

"Emerging markets are getting killed, and Mexico is going to get killed also," he said. COMMODITY PRICES FALL

Chile, the major regional economy most dependent on a single commodity, also saw its currency plunge. The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> weakened 3.91 percent to 520.80 to the dollar after falling as much as 5.06 percent to 527.20, its weakest level since July 21, 2010.

The world's largest copper producer earned more than half of export earnings from the base metal, an important component in electrical equipment and electronic goods.

Copper <CMCU3> which was already trading at its lowest levels since November after four days of losses plunged for a fifth day, losing 8.19 percent to $7,647.00 a tonne in London, its lowest in more than a year.

The Reuters Jefferies commodities index <.CRB>, a measure of 18 key Latin American energy and agricultural commodities such as oil and soybeans, fell 4.41 percent to 307.24, its lowest level since Dec. 1.

Colombia, a key producer of oil and coffee and a growing producer of coal, saw its peso <COP2=STFX> fall 2.19 percent to 1,916.05 to the dollar.

(Additional reporting by Rachel Uranga in Mexico City and Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Chizu Nomiyama)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed, Brazil real slumps on new tax
text:
* Derivatives tax knocks real from 12-year high

* Chile's peso hits 3-year high, more intervention eyed

* Real sheds 1.33 pct, Mexico's peso dips 0.16 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, July 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's government surprised the market with new capital controls on Wednesday, knocking the real off a 12-year high, but the measures are unlikely to keep the currency from regaining its strength.

Chile's peso hit a three-year high, raising concerns of more intervention there, while Mexico's peso weakened as investors grew increasingly nervous about the political stalemate over raising the U.S. debt limit.

Brazil's government imposed a 1 percent tax on currency derivatives, while allowing for a tax of up to 25 percent in the future. For details, see [ID:nN1E76Q01I]

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said the government stood ready to take further actions to curb the real's strength, which is hurting domestic industries by curbing export profits and cheapening rival imports.

"A lot of people thought the government was not going to take further measures," said Roberto Padovani, a strategist at West LB in Sao Paulo.

"The fact that this same rule allows for further tax hikes means that risk in the local foreign exchange market has dramatically increased," he added.

The real <BRBY> bid 1.33 percent weaker at 1.5585 per dollar, heading for its steepest one-day loss in nearly three months. The currency pared losses of nearly 2 percent.

The new rules are the latest in a series of measures that Brazil has taken to discourage banks and speculators from gaming the global financial system in the so-called "carry trade," in which investors borrow low-interest rate currencies and invest in higher-yielding ones.

Analysts said the new measures would likely end up reducing the yield that investors can earn on non-deliverable forward contracts <BRLNDFOR=>, which is a favored vehicle for foreign investors.

RBS Securities strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky said the measures would reduce liquidity in the local market, which may increase the effectiveness of the central bank's dollar purchases in taming the real's gains.

The market had shrugged off recent threats of new measures, pushing the real past 1.55 per dollar this week -- a level that many saw the government closely eyeing.

The country's capital controls and intervention strategy have occasionally spurred steep, short-term losses in the real. But the currency has maintained an appreciation trend since 2009 as investors are drawn to Brazil's double-digit interest rates and strong domestic growth.

"Ultimately, the new measures will not likely be very effective to stem the real's appreciation," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American fixed-income strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

"You have foreign direct investment flows and you have the overall global dollar weakness. People will still be looking to acquire Brazilian assets, but this will make it more complicated," he said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> firmed to a three-year high, bidding 0.24 percent stronger at 456.50 per dollar.

The Chilean peso has strengthened despite a pause in interest rate hikes this month after a string of increases took the benchmark rate to 5.25 percent. The peso's gains have raised concerns that the country's central bank could step up its dollar purchases, or try some other measure.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.16 percent to 11.6574 per dollar.

If U.S. politicians fail to raise the debt ceiling, U.S. interest rates could rise sharply and crimp the economic recovery in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

If the debt limit is raised without spending cuts, ratings agencies could still downgrade the United States' debt rating, which could also push up interest rates.

Also hurting the Mexican peso, a report from the U.S. Federal Reserve showed economic growth slowed in much of the United States in June and early July, which bodes poorly for Mexican exports. [ID:nN1E76Q1G2]

"The Fed's report and the impasse in the U.S. debt talks are hurting the peso," said a trader in Mexico City. "If there is no deal by Friday, the peso could weaken to 11.85 or 11.90."

(Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real hits 12-yr high, minister jawbones
text:
* Investors test Brazil's resolve to limit gains

* Finance minister threatens more intervention

* Brazil real firms 0.7 pct, Mexico peso off 0.1 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, July 25 (Reuters) - Brazil's real hit a more than 12-year high on Monday as investors tested the resolve of Brazilian authorities worried by its gains, while fears about the U.S. debt stalemate held back other Latin American currencies.

Brazil's real broke past the 1.55 level to trade at its strongest since the currency was freely floated in early 1999.

Local authorities have tried to undermine bets on the real with a range of intervention measures, from dollar purchases to taxes. The currency's strength is hurting local industries by cutting into export profits and making rival imports cheaper.

But the market is betting that authorities may allow further gains in the real to help keep import prices down and cool inflation, analysts said. Inflation expectations for 2012 crept up in a poll released on Monday. [ID:nN1E76O03S]

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Monday scoffed at the idea that the country uses its currency to fight inflation and said the government stood ready to take further intervention measures. [ID:nN1E76O18G]

But analysts doubt authorities are willing to turn to more draconian measures, such as higher taxes on stock market investments, that could spur sharp losses in the real and end up further fanning price pressures.

"There is very little the government can do unless they turn to less market-friendly measures," said Marianna Costa, chief economist with Link Investimentos, a Sao Paulo brokerage.

The real <BRBY> bid 0.71 percent stronger to close at 1.5427 per dollar. Some analysts expect the real to hit 1.50 per dollar this year.

RATE ALLURE

Costa said the central bank could step up its dollar purchases in the spot and futures markets, but that would do little more than slow a further appreciation of the real.

Last week, Brazil tightened borrowing costs for the fifth time this year to raise its benchmark rate to 12.50 percent, the highest of any major economy <0#PRIME=>.

The allure of Brazilian interest rates has spurred a tide of money flows into Latin America's top economy. Signs that slowing global growth will keep the United States, Europe and Japan rates down for the foreseeable future will fuel further demand for Brazilian assets, analysts said.

"With those rate hikes postponed, this only insures that the flows to Brazil could continue at the same pace," Costa said.

Moreover, continued concerns that the U.S. debt rating could be downgraded should weigh on the dollar, thereby supporting commodity prices and currencies linked to raw materials exports, such as the real.

A divided U.S. Congress on Monday pursued rival budget plans that appeared unlikely to win broad support, pushing the country closer to a debt default. Even if the debt limit is raised, the country may face a ratings downgrade if lawmakers cannot find a way to cut the deficit. [ID:nN1E76M0B0]

The currencies of Mexico and Colombia, the two Latin American economies with the closest trade ties to the United States, saw volatile trading. But their pesos pared losses as the market held to bets that politicians would manage to avert a U.S. default.

"I think everyone still has this hope that they will do something. They are playing politics as politicians do, but in the end, it will get done," said Ramses Villela, head of currency trading at Bulltick Capital Markets in Mexico City.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.11 to 11.6430 per dollar, but the currency erased steep losses that had pushed the cost of dollars in pesos up to just below its 50-day moving average at 11.7250.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> bid 0.44 percent weaker at 1,763.50 per dollar, but it recovered from an earlier 1.5 percent loss.

In a recent poll of analysts, all but one of the 25 analysts surveyed expected that Colombia's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 4.5 percent at its Friday meeting, marking the sixth straight rate increase since February. [ID:nN1E76O172]

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.24 percent weaker at 462.40 per dollar.

The currencies of Chile and Colombia remain near three-year highs and further strength could push their authorities to try further intervention measures, analysts said.

(Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City and Nelson Bocanegra in Bogota)

title: UPDATE: Bank Of Mexico Policy Could Tighten Without Rate Increase
text:
--Because of easing inflationary pressures, the Bank of Mexico may gradually see tighter monetary policy without hiking interest rates, says deputy governor

--The Mexican peso's strength helps curb inflationary pressures

--The euro-zone debt crisis and recent soft U.S. economic data remain concerns for Mexico's economy

(Adds more comments and background in paragraphs 5-6 and 10-13.)


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Tighter monetary policy in Mexico may be possible without raising interest rates, thanks to benign inflation, Bank of Mexico Deputy Gov. Manuel Sanchez said Thursday.

Since U.S. monetary policy is relatively accommodative, it makes Mexico's rate relatively more restrictive, which helps control inflation, Sanchez said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires. "We don't have to move because inflation is coming down, and actually, now our monetary policy stance may be gradually looking a little tighter because inflation is coming down without moving anything."

The Bank of Mexico left its overnight interest rate target unchanged at 4.5% last week. The bank has held the rate at that level for two years, and is widely expected to stay on hold until the second quarter of 2012.

This is primarily because inflationary pressures remain tame in Mexico, with consumer prices unchanged in June and annual inflation standing at 3.28%. Annual core inflation was at 3.18% last month.

One thing that could put pressure on noncore inflation is gasoline subsidies, Sanchez said. The government sets the retail price of gasoline, and has been raising prices gradually, but not at the same rate that international prices have been rising. As a result, state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos , which exports crude oil but imports gasoline, ends up subsidizing the fuel.

If the gap between domestic and international gasoline prices continues to widen, there is potential for sharper increases in Mexico, he said. The central bank is monitoring that carefully so inflation expectations aren't "contaminated" and don't move away from the bank's inflation target, Sanchez said.

The central bank maintains an inflation target of 3%, plus or minus one percentage point.

The Mexican peso's appreciation is also helping to keep inflation in check, Sanchez added. The peso has strengthened about 5% against the dollar since the beginning of 2011, according to CQG.

Though other regional central banks have taken steps to curb their currencies' appreciation, Mexico is known for a less interventionist policy. The central bank buys up to $600 million a month via a system of put options that can be exercised when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average. Under the options, the central bank takes advantage of currency strength to bolster foreign reserves.

Sanchez said he doesn't see concern about the peso's strength, especially because Mexican exports continue to perform well, although the economy faces several external risks, particularly the euro zone's debt crisis.

The central bank continues to monitor European and foreign banks in Mexico closely, though "we are pretty much confident that their operations are sound," he added.

Mexico has recently seen significant capital inflows, especially in its local currency government debt market, with foreign positioning in peso-denominated government debt at all-time highs. Sanchez expects capital inflows to continue, although an extreme external event could trigger a sudden reversal in flows.

Also, with Mexico's economy so closely linked to the U.S. "a weaker-than-expected U.S. economy is worrisome in the sense that it may induce a weaker-than-expected base of economic recovery in Mexico," Sanchez said.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

--Anthony Harrup contributed to this article. [ 07-14-11 1331ET ]

Under the options, the central bank takes advantage of currency strength to bolster foreign reserves.

Sanchez said he doesn't see concern about the peso's strength, especially because Mexican exports continue to perform well.

title: Mexico's Peso Ends Weaker At 11.6430 To The Dollar On Euro-Zone Worries
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--The Mexican peso weakened against the U.S. dollar Friday as euro-zone debt worries swayed investors away from high-yielding assets.

The peso was quoted closing at MXN11.6430 to the dollar in Mexico City versus MXN11.6250 at Thursday's close, according to Infosel.

U.S. stocks lost ground, while Mexico's local stock index eked out a 0.1% advance. The euro, which the peso frequently tracks, plunged against its major rivals Friday.

Given external dynamics such as E.U. periphery risk premiums and divergent monetary policies, analysts with BBVA said Friday that they expect the peso to trade within a wide range of MXN11.50-MXN11.80 in the near term.

They also believe that long peso positions have declined enough to make room for fresh bets on the currency.

"We believe USD/MXN now stands close to fair value and would expect it to stabilize over the medium and long-term so long as Banxico [Mexico's central bank] does not materially intervene and foreign inflows materialize as we expect them to," the BBVA team said, adding that they expect the peso to finish the year at MXN11.90.

Foreign investment in local currency-denominated Mexican debt instruments remains near an all-time high in spite of recent risk aversion-inspired selling.

Mexico's macroeconomic panorama is also encouraging. Mexico's National Statistics Institute reported Thursday that the economy grew by 4.6% on the year in the first three months of 2011, marking its seventh consecutive quarter of expansion. The figure fell short of market expectations as the economy showed signs of slowing from last year's 5.4% expansion.

Even so, the Mexican central bank predicts that the economy will grow an enviable 4% to 5% this year, and private sector predictions remain high.

"We trust that economic activity will rebound in the second half of the year amid improved domestic demand, based on the positive trajectory of various consumer and investment factors," said Eduardo Gonzalez, analyst with Citibank's Mexican unit, Banamex.

Gonzalez sees Mexico's gross domestic product growing 4.8% this year.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real shrugs off new tax; pesos mixed
text:
* Market shrugs off new Brazil tax on foreign borrowing

* Peru sol stable after worst slump in nearly two years

* Brazil real firms 0.48 pct, Mexico peso up 0.19 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 29 (Reuters) - Investors in Brazil tested the government's resolve to curb the appreciation of the real on Tuesday by driving the currency higher in the face of the latest measure meant to undermine its global appeal.

The real <BRBY> shrugged off the government's announcement of a new tax on foreign borrowing for loans of up to 360 days. [ID:nN29248075]

"The market was expecting something a bit more aggressive," said Diego Donadio, a strategist at BNP Paribas in Sao Paulo.

The real bid 0.48 percent stronger to 1.652 per dollar on the local spot market. That left it less than 0.6 percent from a 2-1/2 year high just past the 1.65 level that has been considered the finance ministry's unofficial limit.

Financial flows into Brazil have been tempted by the huge spread between interest rates in developed markets and Brazil's double-digit rates.

In October, Brazil tripled to 6 percent the so-called IOF tax it charges foreigners when they buy local bonds.

But analysts said the lack of a tax on locals was allowing domestic banks and companies to borrow abroad, invest in Brazil's high-yielding debt and pocket the difference between interest rates.

Analysts said market players would likely find ways around any new measures, short of a broad flat tax on all inflows.

"The impact of a strong measure would be severe and the government is not willing to take this risk," Donadio said. "The finance ministry could become more vocal, but it is hard to fight all this abundant liquidity from abroad," he added.

Barclays Capital noted much of current and future inflows would likely be related to equity investments, which are only taxed at a rate of 2 percent.

RBS strategists said demand for upcoming Brazilian stock offerings could boost demand for the real, opening up the chance for the currency to trade in the 1.60 to 1.65 range.

The real has firmed more than 5 percent from a November low despite increased government and central bank efforts.

STRONG SUPPORT

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.19 percent to 11.9525 per dollar, but the currency was tripped up at the key 11.95 per dollar level.

Mexico's currency hit its strongest in nearly 2-1/2 years this month on signs of recovery in the United States, which buys most of Mexico's exports.

Solid monthly U.S. payrolls data due this month could help push the peso toward new highs around 11.80 per dollar, traders said. The fact that Mexico is not stepping up its intervention efforts could also help it draw in more flows, analysts said.

"The lack of direct intervention in exchange policy ... and the fact that there are good economic data in Mexico, all this is providing strong support to the peso," said Rebeca Lizarraga, a strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.33 percent weaker to 481.90 per dollar. The currency has been hurt by recent weakness in the price of copper, the country's main export.

Peru's sol stabilized after its biggest slump in nearly two years in the previous session after polls showed the left-wing nationalist presidential candidate leading the race. [ID:nN28200405] and [ID:nPOLLSPE]

The sol <PEN=PE> bid a slight 0.04 percent weaker to 2.814 per dollar to notch its weakest close since December.
