title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  firm, conviction seen weak
text:
* Mexico peso firms 0.59 pct, Chile peso up 0.33 pct

* Investors seem to rule out deepening EU debt crisis

* Brazil real up 0.18 pct as intervention eyed

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 24 (Reuters) - Key Latin American currencies firmed on Thursday, supported by a weaker dollar and rising stock markets, but analysts noted a lack of conviction behind the gains amid a host of global risks.

Brazil's real hit a two-week high, while Mexico and Chile's pesos traded at their strongest in more than a week.

Demand for riskier assets like stocks and emerging market currencies rose despite worries about the ongoing violence in the oil-producing Middle East, fears that Portugal will need a bailout and concerns about Japan's nuclear crisis.

The cascade of the negative global events had slammed Latin American assets this month.

"The market took a breath over the last couple of weeks, the global backdrop deteriorated, but it hasn't changed significantly, so investors are willing to put some money to work," said David Beker, head Latin American

"But I wouldn't say these investors have a strong hand, people are willing to put on short-term positions, but not medium- or long-term positions," he added.

Japan's disasters could end up weighing down global growth, as could a sustained spike in oil prices or the expansion of Europe's debt crisis to a major economy like Spain.

Global investors have been taking advantage of recent declines in Latin American currencies on global jitters to place fresh bets on the region's high-yielding debt.

Latin American currencies could see support from high prices for local commodities, like Chile's copper and Brazil's iron and soy, while expectations of further interest rate hikes will tempt global investors with higher yields.

"Latin America has high commodity prices and these guys are more willing to hike interest rates," said Win Thin, an emerging markets strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

Mexico and Colombia are oil exporters while Brazil is energy self-sufficient, so they may be able to better weather higher oil prices than Asia, where most countries import, Thin said.

While intervention in Brazil could limit gains, Mexico and Chile may be poised to advance further.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> firmed 0.59 percent to 11.9480, edging past the psychological 11.95 level, which could open the field for a run toward its nearly 2-1/2 year high hit earlier this month at 11.8585.

Local banks exercised $200 million in dollar put options on Thursday, exhausting the last of the $600 million a month sold by the central bank.

Outstanding options can help contain the peso's gains, but with the monthly allotment used up, the currency will find less resistance to advance in the coming sessions.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.33 percent stronger to 479.70 per dollar.

Chile imports most of its crude, but strong copper prices can help offset the impact of higher oil costs, analysts said. Chile is the world's top copper producer.

Brazil's real <BRBY> firmed 0.18 percent to 1.656 per dollar, gaining ground for the fifth straight session and trading at its strongest since March 9.

The real is than 1 percent from a 2-1/2 year high hit earlier this month that stirred concerns of fresh moves by authorities to tame the real's strength, which is hurting local manufacturers.

Traders said the market was cautiously pushing the real stronger amid expectations that new measures could be announced.

title: Emerging Mkt Debt,  Currencies  Strengthen As Risk Aversion Eases
text:
-Moderation in risk aversion helps emerging market assets

-In Latin America, Brazilian real, debt gain strength


 
   By Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market debt strengthened and Latin American currencies gained ground as investors showed more willingness to take on risk as concerns about Japan's nuclear crisis abated temporarily.

The risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was 7 basis points tighter, to 303 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was up 0.08%. Latin American currencies also climbed against the U.S. dollar, with currencies like the Mexican peso and the Brazilian real making gains.

"Risk is back on today on less worry about Japan," said RBS strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky. Risky assets got beaten down early last week on worries about the potential for a global economic fallout from the earthquake in Japan.

In Latin America, the Mexican peso gained, with the dollar recently down 0.69%, to MXN11.9853. Cattan-Naslausky said the peso tends to benefit when oil is rising, as the country is a net oil exporter. Also, Mexico's policy of not intervening in forex makes the peso an outperformer when risk assets do well.

Helping risk assets on Monday was a temporary easing of concerns about the situation in Japan. On Monday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, said that the situation at the Japanese earthquake- and tsunami-battered Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant is steadily improving, but risks to the downside still remain.

Among emerging market assets, the Brazilian real also climbed, with the dollar down 0.38%, to BRL1.666. Brazil will cut an additional 500 million Brazilian reais ($300 million) in spending from its federal budget this year, the country's Planning Ministry said Monday. Brazil's credit was ten basis points tighter, to 175 basis points over Treasurys. In price term, Brazil's index was up 0.27% on the Embig.

Chile's peso ended barely stronger versus the dollar Monday on improved investor sentiment, but pared most of its early gains. The currency ended at CLP480.50 to the dollar, versus Friday's close of CLP480.80, while trading in a range of CLP479.30 to CLP481.80.

Some of the riskiest emerging market debt outperformed, with Argentina 12 basis points tighter, to 579 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index was up 1.21%. Goldman Sachs also revised its 2011 GDP growth forecast for Argentina to 6.8% from 5.6%, citing Friday's release of higher than expected real GDP figures for the fourth quarter of 2010. Venezuela was 22 basis points tighter to 1163 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms its index was up 1.01%.

Meanwhile, China's yuan rose to its highest level against the U.S. dollar under the current system late Monday in Asia after the central bank set a record-low dollar/yuan central parity following its latest bank reserve hike.

-By Anjali Cordeiro; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com [ 21-03-11 1936GMT ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso, Brazil real up; Chile peso slumps
text:
* Japan disaster keeps investors cautious

* Chile rate hikes seen backstopping peso losses

* Brazil seen preparing more intervention measures

* Brazil real firms 0.24 percent, Mexico peso 0.11 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 14 (Reuters) - Mexico peso and Brazil's real firmed on Monday as investors bet neither Japan's disaster nor oil prices will have a big enough impact on global growth to deter demand for Latin America's high-yielding debt.

Mexico's peso shook off losses to firm past 11.90 per dollar. The currency traded at its strongest level since October 2008 during the session.

The Mexican currency tracked a recovery from session lows in U.S. stocks markets as investors bet the broad impact on equities from Japan's disaster may be short-lived.

"People seem to be thinking the reaction to the Japan disaster was overdone," said Dirk Willer, head of Latin American local markets strategy at Citigroup in New York.

A catastrophe at one of Japan's nuclear power plants that was damaged in the earthquake could spur more losses, Willer said. "But if they get the reactors under control, the flooding and the earthquake itself will lead to a reconstruction boom, and that might, if anything, be seen as positive for global growth," he added.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.11 percent to 11.8950 per dollar while Brazil's real <BRBY> firmed 0.24 percent to 1.660 per dollar.

Brazil is offering some of the highest interest rates in the world, bolstering demand for its currency.

The market awaited news of more intervention measures from Brazilian authorities, who want to keep in check the real's gains that are hurting local manufacturers by cheapening imports.[ID:nN14145427]

However, any new measures may not be able to spur more than short-term losses in the currency, which has advanced more than 40 percent since 2009. Increasing intervention has slowed the currency's gains, but has not reversed its advance.

Unrest in North Africa and the Middle East has put pressure on oil prices, but analysts said that the cost of crude would have to rise much higher for a sustained period to take a major toll on global growth and derail the stability of the region's currencies.

Mexico's peso is seen getting further support from signs of an improving local economy that is tracking the recovery in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

Data showed Mexican industrial production rose at its fastest pace in 15 months as manufacturing output jumped and the construction sector posted a big increase. [ID:nN14143186].

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> lost 0.52 percent to 481 per dollar. Chile's local spot market closed before U.S. stocks pared losses.

Analysts said expectations of further interest rate hikes could limit losses in the Chilean peso this week.

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent this Thursday.

"Chile is still hiking and could hike more than what is priced in; you would have to have a very negative shock on the global growth outlook for this to change," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  sink on menace of Saudi unrest
text:
* Mexico peso bounces off key 12/dlr level

* Investors eye possible new intervention in Brazil

* Brazil real sheds 0.5 pct, Mexico peso 0.4 pct

* Chile peso slumps to weakest since early February

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 10 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened sharply on Thursday as reports of unrest in Saudi Arabia and sinking stock markets raised risks that the region's strong currencies could be hit by rising global uncertainty.

Brazil's real, already under pressure from concerns of more intervention, sank in international trade, while Mexico's peso managed to bounce off a key level, which may bode for a quick recovery if global tensions ease.

Reports of protest in Saudi Arabia, the top OPEC producer, revived concerns of further disruptions in oil supplies.

A sustained push higher in crude prices could weigh on global growth and push investors to dump riskier assets like emerging market currencies and retreat into safe-haven assets like U.S. Treasuries.

"The situation in the Middle East is far from being resolved and it will be the main driver. The question is if there will be a sustained pickup in risk aversion or not," said David Beker, head of Latin American debt and currency strategy at Bank of America-Merrill Lynch.

Fears drove the Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> down nearly 2 percent in its worst slump in seven months. [ID:nN10178483]

Brazil's real <BRL=> shed 0.51 percent to 1.6618 per dollar in international trade. Losses seemed more contained on the local spot market <BRBY>, with the real off 0.24 percent at 1.659 per dollar.

Investors remained leery of fresh intervention measures to keep the real's gains in check. Last week, the real closed at a 2-1/2 year high, stronger than what many see as the Finance Ministry's unofficial limit around 1.65 per dollar.

Brazil has steadily escalated its intervention in currency markets since 2009. But it has only slowed the ascent of the real, which has been buoyed by a tide of global investment that is drawn to its double-digit interest rates.

The real has firmed more than 40 percent since 2009.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> sank 0.8 percent to 481.50 per dollar, its weakest level since early February.

Chile's local spot market closed before news of the protest in Saudi Arabia, but the currency was hammered by falling prices for copper, Chile's main export, after a drop in Chinese import data cast doubt on demand from the world's top consumer of the metal.

Chile's central bank said on Thursday it would allow more foreigners to issue bonds in pesos in the domestic market. [ID:nN10144530]

A trader said the policy would not likely have a major impact on the currency, since local pension funds already buy foreign debt abroad.

Risk appetite had also been hurt during the session by renewed fears about Europe's debt after a rating agency downgrade of Spain.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> lost 0.38 percent to 11.9760 per dollar, paring steeper losses after bouncing off the key 12 per dollar level.

On Wednesday, Mexico's peso hit its strongest since October 2008, breaking past the 11.95 level that had marked a range since January. With that support for the dollar knocked out, traders said the currency could set out a new range between 11.80 and 12 per dollar.

As long as oil prices do not spike further and stay high, hitting U.S. demand, the peso should benefit from the economic recovery in the United States.

Moreover, the peso has lagged gains in other emerging market currencies, and policymakers have not threatened to fight the further gains, unlike Brazil and Chile.

"The peso will still trend stronger. You do not find any other country in the region where the central bank has given a green light to further FX appreciation," Beker said.

(Additional reporting by Jose de Castro in Sao Paulo; Editing by Dan Grebler)

* Euro bounce supports bids for emerging market currencies

* Market awaits possible intervention measures in Brazil

* Mexico peso up 0.23 pct, Chile peso firms 0.11 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean pesos firmed on Wednesday as a stronger euro backed bids for riskier assets, but further gains could be limited by uncertainty related to Europe's debt troubles and rising oil prices.

Meanwhile, investors awaited possible news of fresh government measures to tame gains in the Brazilian real when local markets reopen this afternoon following Carnival holidays.

The euro recovered from lows on Wednesday after Portugal successfully sold bonds, easing some concerns about European countries struggling with high debt burdens. [ID:nN09244748]

The euro is often a proxy for investor appetite for riskier assets such as emerging market currencies and the Mexican peso tracked the euro's bounce.

"We have seen a rebound in the euro, which has set a better tone for risky assets, so emerging markets are benefiting from that," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, a managing director at TD Securities in Toronto.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.23 percent to 11.9775 per dollar. The currency has struggled to definitively break past the 12 per dollar level since a rally stalled in late January.

"The peso does not have much more room to go, the outlook on Europe really is mixed," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones in Mexico City.

The cost of dollars in pesos would have to fall below a 2-1/2 year low hit in January at 11.9439 to open up the field for a significant break lower, Perez-Duarte said.

Worries about high oil prices could also begin to weigh on markets again and unravel peso gains, traders said.

Chile's currency <CLP=CL> firmed 0.11 percent to 474.50 per dollar on rising prices for copper, the country's main export.

However, higher oil prices could keep investors worried that inflationary pressures may hit economic growth and demand for copper.

Global markets are expected to remain jittery among concerns that political unrest in Egypt and Libya could spread to other oil states such as top producer Saudi Arabia.

PARTY'S OVER

With the end of Brazil's Carnival holiday, local authorities may move soon to try and sober up investors who pushed the real to a 2-1/2 year high last Friday, beyond what many see as the finance ministry's unofficial limit.

Brazil's financial markets reopen at 1 p.m. local time (1600 GMT). A Finance Ministry source told Reuters the government may announce a new round of measures this week. [ID:nN04241800]

The real closed at 1.645 per dollar on Friday in the local spot market, below the 1.65 per dollar level that has been seen as a trigger to intervention measures in the past.

Testing government resolve, the real bid stronger at 1.6443 in international trade <BRL=> on Wednesday.

Brazil has steadily escalated its intervention in currency markets since 2009 as a tide of global investment was drawn to its double-digit interest rates. The flows pumped up the real by more than 40 percent since the beginning of 2009.

The stronger real is hurting local manufacturers who have to compete with cheapening imports.

So far, Brazil's efforts to weaken the currency have slowed, but not deterred its advance.

Last October, the government tripled to 6 percent a tax on foreigners buying local bonds and trading in currency derivatives. The central bank, meanwhile, is buying dollars in the spot market as well as acting in the forward and swap markets.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso firms as data backs bigger rate hike
text:
* Chile data supports bets of 50 bps hike next week

* Higher oil prices contain gains

* Further intervention measures expected in Brazil

* Mexico peso firms 0.14 pct, Chile peso 0.23 pct

By Moises Avila and Michael O'Boyle

SANTIAGO/MEXICO CITY, March 7 (Reuters) - Strong economic growth data out of Chile on Monday boosted the peso as it backed bets of a steeper interest rate hike next week, while Mexico's peso nudged below the key 12-per-dollar level.

A broadly weaker U.S. dollar supported bids for the region's assets. Investors are betting the U.S. Federal Reserve will lag Europe in raising interest rates. Brazil and Chile are already hiking rates, pushing up yields on their debt.

Data showing Chile's economy grew 1.3 percent in January compared with December backed bets that the central bank could step up the pace of its recent interest rate hikes to 50 basis points in its next policy decision on March 17.

"The data was was better than expected, too much better," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile. "The data is clearly firming the peso," he added.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.23 percent stronger at 472.60 per dollar. The head of the central bank was seen taking a stronger tone in a speech last Friday in comments on the need to attack the threat of rising inflation.

Global investors are expected to keep pumping up Latin American currencies. Since U.S. interest rates are seen on hold until next year, market players can borrow in dollars, invest in Latin American debt, and pocket the difference between interest rates.

Tricio warned that a push higher by oil prices could erode support for the Chilean peso. Chile imports most of its oil and demand for copper, the country's main export, could be damaged if higher crude prices weigh down global economic growth.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.14 percent to 11.9880 per dollar. The peso has struggled since late January to definitively break past the 12 per dollar level.

Investors worry that rising oil prices could hit the U.S. consumer, who buys most of Mexico's exports. Those fears derailed a peso rally that began last November, leaving the currency to trade in a range.

Brent crude rose to $118 a barrel and U.S. oil hit the highest since September 2008 on Monday as fighting in Libya disrupted its supplies and renewed concern of wider disruptions in the Middle East.

"Conflicts will have to subside to see the currency advance toward 11.90/11.92," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at brokerage Vector in Monterrey.

The local spot market in Brazil was closed for Carnival, but in international trade the real rebounded <BRL=> from a 2-1/2 year high hit on Friday.

A source at the Finance Ministry told Reuters the government could introduce new measures later this week to stem the currency's gains, which are hurting local exporters. [ID:nN04241800]

In international trade, the real was 0.7 percent weaker from its close on the local spot market, trading around 1.6547 per dollar.

Brazil has used a barrage of measures to curb the real, considered one of the world's most overvalued currencies.

The country offers interest rates that are among the world's highest, and last week policymakers raised their benchmark rate to 11.75 percent with further increases expected.

(Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: WRAPUP 1-Inflation needs decisive attack: Chile cbank chief
text:
* De Gregorio says must attack inflationary pressures

* Chile peso back near pre-intervention levels

* Mexico seen holding rate later on Friday

* Brazil raised interest rates on Wednesday

By Daniel Flynn and Brad Haynes

PARIS/SANTIAGO, March 4 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank must attack inflation to mitigate risks from higher oil and food prices, bank president Jose De Gregorio said on Friday, seen as a signal the bank could opt for steeper interest rate hikes.

De Gregorio's comments in a speech in Paris contrasted with minutes from the central bank's February rate-setting meeting released earlier on Friday, in which board members cautioned against "overreacting" to inflationary expectations, noting core inflation was limited.

The minutes appeared to rule out accelerating the pace of raising its interest rates, saying that it could send the wrong signal about inflation expectations and suggesting more steady, gradual rate hikes like February's unanimous 25 basis point increase are to come.

Several of the board's five members preferred in the minutes from the Feb. 17 rate-setting meeting to be "prudent" and not overreact to rising inflation expectations in light of muted underlying, or core, inflation.

However one unidentified board member said if inflation expectations increased persistently, steeper interest rate increases may be necessary.

Speaking at a global central bankers meeting in Paris, De Gregorio said not acting on inflationary pressures could hit credibility and the ability to rein in prices.

"The risk of propagation towards prices in the wider economy must be mitigated, in particular in economies like Chile's, which are producing close to their potential," De Gregorio said in the speech, a copy of which was released in Santiago.

"Not attacking inflationary pressures could affect credibility, which would have negative consequences for the future capacity to achieve stable inflation with low costs in terms of activity," he added.

The comments were viewed by some as suggesting steeper interest rate increases.

"It (De Gregorio's comments) suggests they're contemplating 


a 50 basis point increase at the next meeting... This points
clearly to the possibility of   steeper rate hikes ahead." said


Matias Madrid, chief economist Banco Penta in Santiago.

Brazil and Chile are among a slew of emerging market countries from India to Israel that tightened monetary policy this year to fight inflation fueled by higher global prices for food and commodities. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ > For full coverage of economy [ID:nN30113748] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Chile's central bank has repeatedly voiced concern about rising prices and signaled at February's monetary policy meeting more rate hikes would follow. [ID:nN23137413]

The board only considered a 25 basis point increase last month, according to the minutes. A decision to hold rates in January was the first pause since the central bank started raising rates last June.

"Several board members said that while inflation expectations had risen ... it did not seem prudent to overreact at this moment, especially because effective inflation, and in particular core inflation, were limited," the bank said in a statement.

"Accelerating the pace of rate normalization after a pause in January could be confusing because it could be interpreted as an abrupt change in the central bank's inflation forecasts, which is not the case," it added.

Chile's central bank resumed its cycle of rate hikes despite the fact the local peso <CLP=CL> has bounced back to levels that prompted a $12 billion currency intervention in January, hurting exporters and raising questions about what additional steps the bank and government could take. [ID:nN17130996]

Chile's central bank was seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent at its March monetary policy meeting, a fortnightly central bank poll of traders showed last month. [ID:nN23137413]

The bank is seen raising its benchmark rate to 5 percent in six months time', meaning the market is betting on steady interest rate increases.

Inflation quickened in Brazil and Chile in January on rising food and transport costs, putting more pressure on central bankers to push interest rates higher.

Chile releases February inflation data on March 8.

Chilean consumer prices are seen rising 0.2 percent in February after a 0.3 percent increase in January, according to a Reuters poll. Core inflation rose 0.1 percent in January.

With prices for main export copper near life highs and the dollar weak internationally, the peso is firming on factors beyond Chile's control.

Brazil raised its interest rates on Wednesday for the second time in three months, opting for an increase in line with market expectations despite mounting concerns about the pace of inflation. [ID:nN01145534]

Brazilian central bank policymakers voted unanimously to lift the benchmark Selic rate to 11.75 percent from 11.25 percent, even though some economists had recently changed their forecasts for a rise to 12 percent on worsening inflation expectations.

text:
10:51 (Dow Jones) Mexico's central bank will likely continue its non-interventionist approach to peso strength, Brown Brothers Harriman says, adding that currency appreciation will help contain inflation pressures. (anthony.harrup@dowjones.com)

10:41 (Dow Jones) Liberty Media reports 4Q subscriber gains at its premium cable movie network, Starz (LSTZA), that exceeded expectations. The performance provides ammunition for the company to use against critics who claim its streaming video deal with Netflix (NFLX) could lead pay-TV customers to drop their cable subscriptions for premium channels like Starz, HBO and Showtime. Starz's subscriber tally increased 800,000 during 4Q to 18.2M. The gain comes as HBO lost subscribers in 2010--a setback the company attributed to economic weakness and a lack of promotional efforts from satellite-TV providers. LSTZA up 4.1% to $71.67. (nat.worden@dowjones.com)

10:36 (Dow Jones) AES is seeing stronger-than-expected economic and power-demand growth in Latin America and Asia, which CEO Paul Hanrahan says is helping offset deteriorating conditions in North America. Weak natural gas prices and high coal costs continue to erode profitability in the region, which is eclipsed revenuewise by Latin America. Those woes have been impacting US power producers the past several years. AES up 1.7% at $12.47 even as 4Q EPS missed analysts' expectations. (naureen.malik@dowjones.com)

10:35 (Dow Jones) Barclays Capital upgrades the financial sector to what it calls a "small overweight," noting a recovery in returns on equity might finally be under way. "Despite all of the risks and the long-term effects of higher regulatory capital, we believe that the sector is approaching the point in the recovery process when return on equity can begin to climb back towards potential," firm says. Barclays thinks that in the not-so-distant future large banks might trade at 1.3 times to 1.5 times book value. "This won't necessarily happen in 2011," but outlook warrants an upgrade to marketweight plus from marketweight. (matthias.rieker@dowjones.com)

10:31 (Dow Jones) Sandler O'Neill cuts Jefferies (JEF) F1Q EPS estimate to 41c from 48c, reduces 2011 forecast to $1.60 from $1.65, as firm thinks JEF's likely to report lower-than-expected capital markets activity. While high-yield debt and equity trading volumes rebounded from December slowdown, firm says magnitude of improvement is "less than we had hoped for." Says investment-banking revenue should be resilient as equity underwriting will likely be up on strong volume, but fixed-income underwriting likely to decline, though by less than league tables would suggest. Advisory revenue likely down 5% sequentially, Sandler says, but helped by more attractive blend of reported deals. JEF down a fraction at $24.24. (brett.philbin@dowjones.com)

10:30 (Dow Jones) Citi stock strategist Tobias Levkovich says not to head to the inflation bunker on a misremembering of the 1970s. Higher oil-and-gas prices don't necessarily result in inflation, though one X-factor is labor costs. During the '60s and '70s, nearly a third of the private sector was unionized, and cost-of-living wage adjustments that were built into contracts caused "a massive change in inflation expectations." Levkovich contends thinned-out unions are one reason the huge jump in crude prices from $9/barrel in 1998 to $147 in 2008 didn't bring an accompanying surge in CPI. (christopher.dieterich@dowjones.com)

10:24 (Dow Jones) Boston Federal Reserve President Eric Rosengren says it is assumed--perhaps incorrectly--that state and local finances won't be disruptive to the national economy. While most of the states having problems are wealthier ones and have the economic capacity to deal with their problems, the question is "will the politicians have the wherewithal to actually find a solution that won't be disruptive?" Rosengren also says in a speech, "While I expect these issues will be resolved without widespread or cascading problems, we should consider what scenarios could emerge if political impasses result in more disruptive outcomes." (bradley.davis@dowjones.com)

10:21 (Dow Jones) Amid being pressured by interest-rate expectations in Europe, the dollar could remain so as the week progresses with Bernanke addressing Capitol Hill starting Tuesday. Traders will be hanging on any dovish remarks, says Kathy Lien of GFT Forex, contending if the Fed chief suggests staying in an accomodative mindset "is even a small possibility," the dolalr "could head even lower." The euro was recently at $1.3824, up from 1.3754 late Friday, according to EBS via CQG. (andrewj.johnson@dowjones.com)

10:14 (Dow Jones) The turmoil in Libya could cause the country's oil-and-gas output to be shuttered for "months," says Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch. It estimates up to 1.2M barrels of daily oil output has been lost following production halts by the country's largest oil producers. The investment bank says the disruption "could well be the 9th largest supply shock since 1950." Other OPEC countries, including Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, have signaled they will make up for any shortfall in crude supplies due to the revolt in Libya. April crude on Nymex trades down 75c at $97.13 while Brent falls 27c to $111.87. (dan.strumpf@dowjones.com)

10:08 (Dow Jones) Long-dated Treasurys are edging slightly lower as US stocks gain more ground. Pending home sales are basically in line with forecast, so that's not a mover for markets. The 10-year note is 2/32 lower to yield 3.424%. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

10:06 (Dow Jones) The US economy is far from facing a stagflationary economic environment, but if inflation were to surge at a time of low growth, monetary policy wouldn't be easy or comfortable, says New York Fed President William Dudley. If price-pressure gains prove persistent "that would make the monetary policy more complicated because on one hand we'd be far away from our employment objective, but we'd have inflation above what we were seeking," he argues. But fortunately, "right now we are not in that circumstance," and "as long as we keep inflation expectations well anchored...I don't think we are going to have that problem." (michael.derby@dowjones.com)

10:04 (Dow Jones) Current softening in spot iron ore prices from recent record highs will be short-lived and won't hit Brazilian miner Vale's "very strong earnings momentum for 1H11," Barclays Capital says. Credit Suisse notes iron ore demand strength, from China and elsewhere, should push prices up again in 2Q as March-May typically the global steel industry's seasonal strong period, driven by construction. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed; Chile peso hits 6-week high
text:
* Chile peso hits 6-week high after rate hike

* Brazil real contained by intervention

* Bets on Mexican peso hit highest since April 2010 (Rewrites throughout)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Chile's peso jumped to a six-week high on Friday as the market bet on more interest rate hikes and doubted authorities would step up intervention efforts, while Mexico and Brazil's currencies lost steam.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.26 percent stronger to 468.50 per dollar after the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent, adding to the appeal of the currency. For details, see [ID:nN17302923]

A string of comments from Chilean officials also eased concerns that authorities will expand their efforts to contain the peso's gains after introducing a $50-million-a-day dollar purchase program at the beginning of January.

"There is a clear commitment to continue to fight inflation and we have heard from central bank board members that they will pay more attention to the inflation target than the exchange rate," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist at Roubini Global Economics in New York.

The Chilean peso racked up a 0.79 percent gain for the week, despite a sharp drop in the price of copper -- the country's main export -- which hurt the currency early in the week.

The currency would likely firm toward a nearly three-year high around 450 per dollar, "as long as nothing happens to the price of copper," Delgado said.

Brazil's currency, the real <BRBY>, slipped 0.06 percent to 1.662 per dollar as central bank intervention kept the currency within a narrow range.

Brazil's central bank held a forward auction and a reverse swap auction, both of which can weigh on the currency. Policymakers were apparently reacting to a jump in the previous session, when the real posted sharp gains.

The lower house of Brazil's Congress shook off pressure from labor unions and approved the new administration's proposal for a small increase in the minimum wage late Wednesday, boosting confidence in the new government's clout.

The real has been trading in increasingly narrow ranges in recent weeks, slowed by the central bank's intervention, but still steadily firming as investors are drawn to Brazil's interest rates, among the highest in the world.

The real gained 0.18 percent in the last week.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.12 percent on Friday to close at 12.023 per dollar, notching 0.08 percent gain for the week.

The peso ran into a brick wall at the psychologically key 12-per dollar after sharp gains on Thursday. Local companies have been heavy buyers of dollars around the 12 level.

Many local companies fixed their budgets for the year with expectations of a peso at 12.50 per dollar during 2011, making the 12-per-dollar level hard to resist.

The Mexican peso has been a favorite bet since last November, gaining more than 4 percent on an improving outlook for the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

Delgado said the peso would need surprisingly strong data in the United States to break below 12 per dollar in the short term, but he said the peso would eventually firm toward 11.50.

Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in Chicago showed on Friday that the net amount of bets in favor of the Mexican peso rose to their highest level since April 2010, according to Win Thin, a currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

"Everyone is really long and that makes me nervous," Thin said, noting the peso could be hit by any increase in global jitters related to political unrest in the Middle East or Europe's debt troubles. A spike in worries about Europe hammered the peso down from a high in May 2010.

The Mexican peso has the most bets in its favor of the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. [ID:nN18104672]

While that backs up the fundamental backdrop boding for futher gains, it also makes it vulnerable to any global shocks that could send speculators running for the door.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Mexico  peso sinks;  intervention  fears hit Chile
text:
* Chile currency hurt by concerns of further intervention

* Mexican currency slumps, heavy positioning weighs

* Mexico peso slumps 1 pct, Brazil real 0.06 pct

By Michael O'Boyle and Froilan Romero

MEXICO CITY/SANTIAGO, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Chile's peso slumped by the most in six weeks on Tuesday on falling copper prices and bets authorities may try to limit speculative inflows, while Mexico's peso sank to a two-week low.

Chile's peso slipped back from a six-week high as prices for copper, the country's main export, retreated from a record high. Rising inflation in top copper consumer China raised concerns that tighter borrowing costs there that could hit global demand. [ID:nLDE71E21N]

Traders also cited growing speculation that the government could try again to contain the peso's gains, which are hurting local exporters.

"Banks are taking long-dollar positions to protect themselves from an eventual announcement of measures to brake the peso's gains, this time it could come from the finance ministry," said a trader in Santiago.

The peso <CLP=CL> shed 0.6 percent to 472.30 pesos.

The peso lost ground for the first time in five sessions after surging on bets that Chile's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate this week.[ID:nN14110508]

Expectations of higher interest rates had helped the currency firm back close to a nearly three-year high and erase most of its losses since the central bank unveiled an intervention program at the beginning of January.

The central bank is not expected to boost its daily dollar purchase program, but the finance ministry could move to tax foreign inflows or it could change regulations governing the market operations of local pension funds, traders said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> sank 1 percent to 12.17 per dollar, on track to post its biggest one-day loss since violent protests in Egypt rattled global markets at the end of January.

The peso began to weaken after a report on January U.S. retail sales showed they grew less than expected. Mexico sends most of its exports to the United States and it is depending on U.S. demand to fuel economic growth this year.

The Mexican peso weakened past its 20-day moving average, pushing some traders to dump the currency, which then pushed it through other investors' stop-loss levels, deepening the peso's slide.

"There is a complete lack of conviction out there, some people are taking risk off the table and Mexico is vulnerable because everyone is so long," said Paul Biszko, a senior emerging markets strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

The Mexican peso has by far the most speculative bets in its favor - or long positions - among the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. [ID:nN11301566]

Before Tuesday's losses, the Mexican peso gained more than 4 percent since November on the back of a better outlook for the economy of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

But the heavy bias in favor of the peso can end up hurting the currency when unforeseen losses, such as Tuesday's, push speculators to run for the door.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.06 percent weaker at 1.668 per dollar, likely supported by IPO-related flows into the markets, Biszko noted.

The real's strength would probably be limited by continued central bank intervention in the market, traders said, as Latin America's top economy seeks to limit currency gains that make its exports less competitive.

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures contracts <0#DIJ:> edged lower after local retail sales volumes stayed unexpectedly flat in December and investors pared their bets for a cycle of interest rate hikes. Brazil's retail sales were expected to rise 0.6 percent, according to Reuters poll. (Additional reporting by Moises Avila in Santiago, Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso hits 6-wk high, Brazil yields jump
text:
* Chile peso boosted by copper prices, rate hike bets

* Brazil yields rise after jump in inflation expectations

* Brazil real dips 0.12 pct, Mexico peso 0.15 pct (Updates prices, adds comments)

By Moises Avila and Silvio Cascione

SANTIAGO/SAO PAULO, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Chile's peso hit a six-week high on Monday amid higher copper prices and bets of an interest rate hike this week, while yields on Brazilian rate futures shot up on rising inflation expectations.

Prices for copper, Chile's main export, rallied to a fresh record high on Monday following data showing a surge in China's copper imports. For details, see [ID:nLDE71D0PP]

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark rate to 3.50 percent this week, resuming hikes after a pause last month partly to avoid further appreciation in the peso.

Moreover, the market has ruled out an increase in the central bank's $50 million-a-day intervention program for the time being after the head of the central bank suggested last week that inflation concerns will drive monetary policy, not concerns about the exchange rate.

"Besides the increase in copper prices, the market continues to bet on a stronger peso after central bank chief Jose De Gregorio said the bank will focus more on controlling inflationary pressures," said Bci analyst Osvaldo Cruz.

"The market is also betting on the bank increasing its benchmark rate and that could affect the (exchange) rate."

Chile's peso <CLP=> firmed 0.6 percent to 469.40 per dollar, strengthening below the key resistance level of 470. It is now within striking distance of the 465.50 per dollar level that triggered the launch of the currency intervention program last month to protect exporters from the currency's strong gains. [ID:nN30113748]

Traders see the peso's next resistance level at 468 per dollar.

BRAZIL RATES

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> shot up after economists jacked up inflation expectations for 2011, despite government promises last week for a $30 billion budget cut meant to ease price pressures. [ID:nN14119393]

Brazil's central bank is struggling to keep the economy from overheating. Some investors are betting that policymakers are not taking strong enough action to control inflation. In January, the central bank hiked its benchmark lending rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent.

"We suspect it will take bolder policy action before inflation expectations improve much," BNP Paribas analysts said in a research note.

The yield on the rate contract due January 2012 <DIJF2> rose from 12.33 percent to 12.43 percent after the inflation survey.

Brazil's real <BRBY> was bid 0.12 percent weaker to 1.667 in the local spot market, continuing its recent tendency to trade in a narrow range. The central bank bought dollars at two auctions in a bid to contain its strength

Government and central bank efforts to curb the real's strength have put a cap on gains below 1.65 reais per dollar, for the time being, but flows continue to seek out investments in local bonds, which offer among the world's highest interest rates.

"There are still investments entering Brazil," said Marcos Marcos Trabbold, a trader at brokerage B&T Corretora de Cambio. "But without a doubt, the central bank interventions are keeping the dollar in a range," he added.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> weakened 0.15 percent to 12.05 per dollar. Mexico's peso has been unable to definitively break past the 12-per-dollar level since firming below the key benchmark last month for the first time since October 2008.

Analysts said renewed speculation that the government could boost the amount of dollar put options it is selling every month to accumulate reserves is helping keep the peso in check.

Mexico's dollar option auctions are seen as a less aggressive form of intervention being used by other central banks in the region like Chile and Brazil.

title: MW Mexico unlikely to follow LatAm  currency  controls
text:
By Carla Mozee, MarketWatch

LOS ANGELES (MarketWatch) -- With a newly lowered inflation forecast, and increasing growth in its economy, Mexico is unlike to follow its Latin American neighbors' moves to hike interest rates and impose capital controls, analysts say.

The Mexican peso has begun to test levels not seen since the height of the global financial crisis and recently broke through the psychologically key level of 12 pesos per U.S. dollar for the first time since late October 2008.

Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero has said the country is keeping tabs on the currency's appreciation but has pointedly said Mexico isn't interested in imposing capital controls.

Mexican authorities appear to be content with the peso's rise, according to Marc Chandler, global head of currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman "And why shouldn't they be? A small, gradual increase in their currency is slow enough so that they can build up their reserves...and by having a stronger currency, it limits their inflation."

With the slow-growth U.S. as its largest trading partner, Mexico stands in contrast to the rapidly expanding Brazilian economy, Latin America's largest.

Brazil this year extended its battle against currency appreciation by issuing a reserve requirement for local banks and initiating intervention in the futures market, as well as continuing daily auctions to purchase dollars on the spot market. In 2009 Brazil raised taxes on certain foreign investments to cool capital inflows.

"Mexico has maintained a desire to have a free floating exchange rate for many years," said Clyde Wardle, an emerging-market currency strategist at HSBC.

Mexico's only recent intervention was when it sold dollars during the peak of the credit crisis to protest the peso and the economy from certain stresses. "They've indicated that it doesn't make sense to counter one perceived distortion in the market...perhaps the U.S.'s [second quantitative-easing program]...with another distortion such a capital control," said Wardle.

Even with the peso's gains, its advance still lags behind those in other Latin American currencies. Since hitting an all-time low in early March 2009, the peso has risen roughly 20% against the U.S. dollar, trailing the Brazilian real's gain of about 30% during the same period.

Chile's peso also outpaced Mexico's over most of the period. The central bank in Santiago this year adopted its first intervention plan since April 2008, extending through March 8 its plan to make dollar purchases of $50 million a day and the peso has pulled back since the intervention program was launched last month.

While Chile has said it's not looking to implement capital controls the market "sees a non-negligible chance of the government taking further steps to curb peso appreciation," Citigroup analyst Maria Belen Olaiz said in a note to clients this week. However, historically high copper prices will likely make it difficult for the Chilean government to avoid further peso strengthening, she said.

Alfredo Coutino, Moody's Economy.com's director of Latin American research said Mexico's current low-inflation environment puts its policy makers at an advantage over regional counterparts who are facing the prospect that interest-rate hikes to combat inflation will further fuel currency appreciation.

"Mexican authorities have really not been overly defensive in the media with regard to peso appreciation," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin American fixed-income research at IDEAGlobal in New York.

He expects the central bank will likely act in a "moderate form" and become "increasingly rhetorically defensive," to hedge against the risk of a quick currency rise if the peso breaks below the 11.80 level.

HSBC's call is for the peso to reach 11.80 by the third quarter of this year, said Wardle.

Coutino also said the country can take a more relaxed stance compared with its regional competitors partially because Mexico has "lower attractiveness to hot money," stemming in part from its ties to slow growth in the U.S. as well as the low level of speculative returns offered by domestic bonds.

Brazil's benchmark interest rate stands at 11.25%, and Argentina's is above 10%. Mexico's benchmark has remained at 4.5% since July of 2009. Coutino said in real terms, the highest return is offered by Brazil, followed by Peru and Chile, and "Mexico at the end."

Mexico has tried "almost all kind of capital controls in the past, with very poor results and extremely high costs for the whole economy," Coutino said. "Policy makers know that the short-term benefits of capital controls are not worth enough to compensate for the sacrifice in the future."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso firms to over 1-mo high, Brazil dips
text:
* Chile bets backed by rate view, lower intervention risks

* Real slumps from more than one-month high

* Mexican finance minister rules out intervention

* Brazil real slumps 0.6 pct, Mexico peso flat

By Michael O'Boyle and Ana Nicolaci da Costa

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO (Reuters) - Chile's peso hit its strongest level in more than a month Thursday after a poll backed bets of higher interest rates and intervention risks were seen receding, while Brazil's currency slumped.

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.50 percent next week, according to a poll.

Chilean policymakers held borrowing costs steady last month to try to discourage yield-hungry investors from pouring into its assets. The pause complemented a currency intervention program introduced at the beginning of the year.

But the move spooked bond investors, who fear the central bank is not doing enough to tame rising inflation. Now policymakers appear to be changing course.

The central bank held back from expanding the intervention program this week despite solid gains in the peso.

"People feel more comfortable that they will tolerate a stronger peso, because they need to worry about inflation," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American debt strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

Seven straight rate hikes last year drove the Chilean peso to a nearly three-year high, pushing the central bank to buy $50 million a day to help protect local exporters.

Chile's peso bid 0.57 percent stronger to 473.50 per dollar, its strongest since early January. The peso has clawed back more than 5 percent from a 7 percent loss spurred by news of the intervention in early January.

Brazil's real shed 0.6 percent to 1.669 per dollar, pulling back sharply after the currency hit a more than one-month high in the previous session.

A broadly stronger dollar and a slump in the euro, a key proxy for gauging demand for riskier assets like emerging market currencies, weighed on the real and Mexico's peso.

NO MEXICAN MEDDLING

Brazil's government unveiled budget cuts of about $30 billion Wednesday in a bid to regain credibility among investors worried that overspending is driving inflation higher and beyond the control of the central bank.

"Yesterday we had a positive economic context here, especially with the announcement of the budget cuts, it makes Brazil seem more trustworthy ... so the day after it is normal that you have an adjustment," said Andre Sacconato, economist at Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

Brazil has been waging an even more intense battle than Chile to contain the strength of the real, which is considered one of the most overvalued currencies in the world.

Brazil offers among the highest interest rates available, and a relentless flow of funds from global investors continues to bode further strength despite heavy intervention.

The central bank held a reserve currency swap auction Thursday, though the real did not react noticeably to the news.

The Mexican peso reversed steep early losses to trade flat at 12.0765 per dollar after Mexico's finance minister said the country will not intervene in foreign exchange markets, brushing off complaints from exporters who want a weaker peso.

Mexico's peso has lagged the gains in other emerging markets currencies, giving policymakers more room to stay on the sidelines.

But some had begun to bet Mexico could follow suit with greater intervention after the peso gained around 4 percent since November to hit a nearly 2-1/2 year high last month. (Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: UPDATE 2- Mexico  finance minister rules out  FX intervention
text:
* Mexico respects rules of free-floating currency regime

* Peso hasn't risen as much as some Latam currencies

* Mexico's export strength doesn't require weaker peso

* Finance Ministry could revise up Mexico 2011 growth view (Adds details on growth forecast, background)

By Walter Brandimarte

NEW YORK, Feb 10 (Reuters) - Mexico will not intervene in foreign exchange markets to curb the appreciation of its currency, Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero said on Thursday, brushing off complaints from exporters who want a weaker peso.

Unlike other emerging market countries, Mexico has seen only modest currency gains in the past few months, Cordero told a housing conference in New York. He noted that the peso is still weaker than pre-crisis levels.

"In Mexico, we respect the rules of the foreign exchange market. We do not intervene in it and we will remain like that," he told reporters after a presentation to investors.

"It's very difficult to determine the equilibrium price of a currency," Cordero said.

The Mexican central bank has been on the sidelines of the so-called currency war that has pushed many emerging market countries to intervene in foreign exchange markets in order to protect their exports from local currency appreciation.

Cordero dismissed complaints from some Mexican exporters, who want a weaker peso to better compete with Chinese products in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

"Mexico's exporting strength does not depend on our currency. It depends on the human capital that we have, our geographic position, lower costs of transport and our logistic platform," he said.

Cordero also said inflation is under control in Mexico even as growth accelerates. He said the Finance Ministry will likely revise its current 2011 growth forecast of 4.0 percent, which he called "conservative."

"Probably the same story that happened in 2010 is going to repeat and we'll be improving that forecast in Mexico," he added.

title: HIGHLIGHTS-Mexico sees lower inflation, strong growth
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 9 (Reuters) - Mexico's inflation rate will be lower in 2011 than last year and the country's economy is likely to show strong growth this year and next, central bank chief Agustin Carstens said on Wednesday. [nN09172638]

Below are highlights of his comments at the presentation of the central bank's quarterly inflation report.

FX INTERVENTION

"You can't depend on exchange rate intervention, firstly because the Bank of Mexico cannot intervene for its own pleasure."

"The message to the country's business leaders is that the Bank of Mexico will continue with its prime mandate of beating inflation ... and that medium- to long-term competitiveness can only be gained through greater public and private spending."

NO LABOR PRESSURES

"The salary base is growing, but from the point of view of inflation ... we don't see pressures."

CAPITAL FLOWS

"We cannot rule out more forex volatility due to a reversal in capital flows."

MEXICAN INFLATION

"Our objective is 3 percent and our margin does not reflect a comfort zone."

"For 2011 ... we expect to see levels below the inflation we saw in 2010."

"Looking at inflation expectations to the close of 2011, they are again quite well behaved, I reiterate, above 3 percent."

PESO STRENGTH

"The national currency's strength has cushioned the impact of rising prices abroad."

ECONOMIC GROWTH

"We've got to be very clear ... Mexico's economic fundamentals remain solid."

"Exports continue to be an important growth factor." (Reporting by Mexico Newsroom)

title: MARKET TALK: Indonesia's Jan CPI Likely +6.81% On-Year - Poll
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

2300 GMT [Dow Jones] PREVIEW: Indonesia's inflation is expected to slow in January thanks to easing food prices, giving the central bank further room to hold off raising rates. The median forecast of 11 regional economists in a Dow Jones poll is for CPI to rise 6.81% on-year, vs +6.96% in December; on-month, the index is expected to rise a milder 0.63% in January vs +0.92% in December, according to nine economists polled; the data are due around 0400 GMT. The market is closely watching the upcoming data for indications when the first rate hike this year will be; eight economists polled expect no hike at the next rate-setting meeting Friday; while three expect a 25 bp increase. She says the current weakness in activity was, however, expected to be temporary. (lucy.craymer@dowjones.com)

2225 GMT [Dow Jones] Foreign exchange volume in London and New York, the world's two biggest trading centers, surged to new records in October, marking another milestone in the global financial system's recovery. (james.glynn@dowjones.com)

(robert.flint@dowjones.com)

text:
30 Jan 2011 04:01 EDT *DJ  Mexico's Carstens: Exports Growing Very Fast

30 Jan 2011 04:01 EDT *DJ  Mexico's Carstens: Exports To Continue To Support Growth

30 Jan 2011 04:01 EDT *DJ  Mexico's Carstens: Floating FX Regime Working Well

30 Jan 2011 04:02 EDT *DJ  Mexico's Carstens: Watching Others' FX Measures Very Closely

30 Jan 2011 04:44 EDT =DJ  INTERVIEW: Mexico Carstens: To Adjust Rates On Monetary Factors

By Natasha Brereton

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

KYOTO, Japan (Dow Jones)--Mexico's central bank will adjust interest rates based primarily on monetary policy conditions, but it is closely monitoring action by others in the region to address capital inflows, its governor said Sunday.

Speaking to Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of meetings in Kyoto, Agustin Carstens said that exports were growing very strongly, despite appreciation in the Mexican peso, and that he expected them to continue to support output growth in future.

Interfering with market forces isn't very effective and introduces distortions, he said, adding that so far Mexico's anti-intervention policy has worked well. But the central bank has to constantly evaluate its stance, he noted.

"We are watching very closely what others (in the region) are doing and actions on capital flows," he said.

Policymakers across the globe have been spurred to take measures to limit capital inflows into fast-growing parts of Africa, Latin America and Asia--a trend which has been amplified by super-loose monetary policy in sluggish developed economies.

-By Natasha Brereton, Dow Jones Newswires, +65-6415-4044, natasha.brereton@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE: INTERVIEW: Mexico Carstens: Adjust Rates On Monetary Factors
text:
-- To set interest rates based on monetary considerations

-- Monitoring steps against inflows by others in region

-- Exports growing very strongly, to remain robust

(Adds more comments, context)

By Natasha Brereton

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

KYOTO, Japan (Dow Jones)--Mexico's central bank will adjust interest rates based chiefly on monetary-policy considerations, but it is closely monitoring action by others in the region to address capital inflows, its governor said Sunday.

Speaking to Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of meetings in Kyoto, Agustin Carstens said that exports were growing very strongly, despite appreciation in the Mexican peso, and that he expected them to continue to support output growth in the future.

Interfering with market forces isn't very effective and introduces distortions, he said, adding that "so far" Mexico's anticurrency-intervention policy has worked well. But the central bank has to "constantly" evaluate its stance, he noted.

"We are watching very closely what others [in the region] are doing and actions on capital flows," he said, when quizzed whether he was concerned that the central bank's hard-line attitude could encourage additional inflows.

Asked if rate cuts would be preferable to other measures to curb peso appreciation, Carstens said: "We will adjust the policy rate based primarily on monetary policy considerations."

Policy makers have been spurred to take measures to limit capital inflows into fast-growing parts of Africa, Latin America and Asia--a trend which has been amplified by super-loose monetary policy in sluggish developed economies.

Faced with appreciating currencies, Brazil, Argentina and Chile have all intervened in the foreign exchange market.

Carstens shrugged off the suggestion that the strength of the peso was hurting Mexico's international competitiveness.

"Right now, exports are growing very fast and are making an important contribution to growth, because the export sector has been developing other comparative advantages," Carstens said.

"I expect it to continue to provide support to growth."

Asked whether the cost of sterilizing foreign-exchange reserves was a deterrent to continuing to accumulate them, Carstens said that the central bank had a very clear mandate to bring inflation under control and provide financial stability.

"We have to guide our actions accordingly," he said.

-By Natasha Brereton, Dow Jones Newswires, +65-6415-4044, natasha.brereton@dowjones.com [ 30-01-11 1440GMT ]

title: WEEKAHEAD-View from editors in the Americas
text:
NEW YORK, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Following is the view from editors in the Americas on the top stories for the week ahead:

HIGHLIGHTS:

* ECONOMIC DATA: U.S payroll report

* MARKETS: Jitters on Egypt unrest

* EARNINGS: Oil, pharma, media reports

Watch the Weekahead on Reuters Insider:

http://bit.ly/ekIvJ5("http://bit.ly/ekIvJ5")

ECONOMIC DATA

The U.S. Labor Department has made a habit of disappointing Wall Street lately. In three of the last four monthly employment reports, the jobs tally fell short of economists' expectations. Friday's data for January offers an opportunity for redemption. A preliminary Reuters poll of economists shows they are looking for a gain of 150,000 jobs in January, which would be an improvement over the 103,000 reported in December. As for that December number, watch for any revisions. The Labor Department revised up its job count for five consecutive months starting in July. ADP's private payrolls data comes two days earlier. This is its first monthly report since wrong-footing markets by reporting a huge December jobs gain that looked nothing like the Labor Department's. Also on tap are personal income data on Monday, which includes the Federal Reserve's favorite inflation gauge. Tuesday brings January manufacturing sector data, followed by the much-larger services sector on Thursday.

MARKETS

Turmoil in Egypt is unlikely to be quelled quickly, so markets will open Monday with fresh reaction to events over the weekend. Equities, particularly energy shares, may face pressure again while safe havens, including Treasuries and the dollar, could see renewed vigor. Emerging markets currencies, commodity currencies and the euro will still be under pressure. The stock market will wade through a further slew of earnings and Friday's payroll report, if solid, should help stocks. In the municipal market, eyes will be on New York's budget to see how lawmakers plan to close an approximate $10 billion gap.

OIL/ENERGY RESULTS

Exxon Mobil, the world's largest listed company, leads the quarterly updates from the energy sector, following news of stronger profits from the likes of Chevron, ConocoPhillips and Occidental. (See story at [ID: nN28275236]). Exxon is expected to say it scored massive quarterly profits lifted by the strength in oil prices, but it will have to convince investors that its big bet on North American natural gas will pay off in the years to come. Other energy giants including Marathon Oil Corp, Anadarko Petroleum and coal producer Massey Energy will also report, as will the largest U.S. maker of chemicals, Dow Chemical.

BERNANKE FACES REPORTERS

U.S. Federal Reserve officials hit the speech circuit after their latest decision to stay the course with their $600 billion bond-buying plan. Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke stages a rare question and answer session with journalists after a speech on Thursday, which will be closely parsed for clues on how patient the central bank will be as the economy builds its strength. The Fed has been mulling holding regular news conferences: could this be a warm up? On Friday, Dallas Fed chief Richard Fisher, an inflation hawk who rotated into a voting seat on the Fed's policy panel this year, will explain why he defied type and backed QE2. Minneapolis Fed's Narayana Kocherlakota, a centrist, speaks on Thursday.

MEDIA/PHARMA EARNINGS

The media sector reporting season cranks up with News Corp and Time Warner on Wednesday and Viacom on Thursday. All face questions about advertising's fate as video streaming grows. Merck on Tuesday and Pfizer a day later top the list of "Big Pharma" names detailing quarterly results. For them, the big issue is likely to be price pressure as it was in Johnson & Johnson's results this past week. In finance, Visa and MasterCard - both furiously lobbying for an easing in the Fed rules on interchange fees - will report on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively. Finally, United Parcel Service, the world's largest package delivery company, will provide a snapshot on Tuesday of fourth-quarter economic activity.

MEXICAN PESO

Mexico's central bank will begin publishing minutes from its monetary policy meetings on Friday, raising questions about whether the more transparent approach will affect volatility in Mexican assets. Investors will be watching for any signs of concern about the strength of the peso although President Felipe Calderon has said no intervention is planned, setting Mexico apart from many other countries in Latin America which are trying an array of measures to curb their currencies.

CANADA

In Canada, Friday's employment data is expected to show the economy added just 16,000 jobs in January, down from a revised 30,400 in December. Further confirmation the recovery is intact but sluggish should also be found in Monday's monthly GDP data for November, which is forecast to rise 0.3 percent from a month earlier. title: Mexico's Carstens sees peso as undervalued -papers
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank governor Agustin Carstens said the peso remains undervalued despite a recent rise to 2-1/2 year peaks, local newspapers reported on Friday.

Carstens was reported to have made the comments at a meeting on Thursday with members of the Business Coordinating Council, the newspapers said, citing people present at the discussion.

"Rather than being over-valued, the peso is under-valued, according to the Bank of Mexico," council president Mario Sanchez told daily Excelsior after the meeting.

Mexico has so far refrained from steps to limit capital inflows which have driven up currencies around the region and prompted intervention from regional peers, but markets have nervous that Mexico could join the fray.

El Economista said some business leaders raised concerns about the risk that the peso <MXN=> would keep rising and crimp exports, which have been driving the country's recovery from recession.

But Carstens said the peso was weak compared to other currencies.

The central bank confirmed the comments were accurately reported.

Mexico has so far refrained from steps to limit capital inflows which have driven up currencies around the region and prompted intervention from regional peers.

Mexican President Felipe Calderon warned in an interview with the Wall Street Journal on Thursday that state intervention in currency markets could become dangerous.

title: FACTBOX-Steps countries are taking to counter hot money
text:
Jan 27 (Reuters) - More governments around the world are moving to keep their currencies from strengthening or control the flow of money into their economies as investors pour money into higher-yielding markets, turning their backs on low interest rates in developed economies.

Below are recent cases of direct or indirect government intervention in the currency markets, compiled by Reuters:

ISRAEL SEEKS TO ANNUL TAX EXEMPTION ON SHORT-TERM DEBT

* Israel's Finance Ministry says on Jan. 27 it is acting to annul a tax exemption for foreign investors on profit from investments in short-term government bonds and short-term Bank of Israel bills called makams.

* The Bank of Israel says on Jan. 20 it will impose a 10 percent reserve requirement for foreign exchange swaps and forwards trades conducted by non-residents, effective Jan. 27.

* On Jan. 19, the central bank announces it will require Israelis and foreigners to report on transactions in foreign exchange swaps and forwards of more than $10 million in one day.

* Non-residents who perform transactions in short-term Bank of Israel bills known as makams and short-term government bonds of more than 10 million shekels in one day will be required to report details of the transactions and their balance of holdings of such assets.

-- Story links: [ID:nLDE70Q1HO] [ID:nLDE70J19Z] [ID:nLDE70I0EK]

BRAZIL ACTS IN FUTURES MARKET, TARGETS BANKS' POSITIONS AND INFLOWS

* The central bank on Jan. 14 sells $988 million in reverse currency swaps, a derivative that effectively allows the bank to buy U.S. dollars on the futures market.

* New reserve requirements on banks' short positions on U.S. dollars aim to reduce speculative trade.

* Aggressive measures promised by incoming President Rousseff on Dec. 31, including targeted tariff increases and tax breaks to address effects of strong real <BRBY>.

* Raises bank reserve requirements on Dec. 4 to cool a credit boom and ease the currency situation.

* Sovereign wealth fund authorized to buy dollars on spot market.

* Government triples tax on foreign purchases of bonds to 6 percent on Oct. 18 to curb inflows into fixed income market.

* Government increases tax on derivatives margins to dissuade short-term investors.

-- Story links: [ID:nN14137379] [ID:nLDE7050Z6] [ID:nN30113578]

CHILE LAUNCHES FOREX INTERVENTION, HALTS RATE HIKES

* Central bank holds benchmark interest rate steady on Jan. 13 after raising it for seven consecutive months, in a move widely seen complementing its currency intervention.

* Central bank begins a record $12 billion in dollar purchases during 2011, warning against intervention "addiction".

* Chilean President Sebastian Pinera says he has no plans for capital controls.

* Central bank lifts limits on pension funds' overseas investment.

-- Story links: [ID:nN13283103] [ID:nN04206531] [ID:nN04221079]

PERU BUYS DOLLARS, ENCOURAGES INVESTMENT ABROAD

* On Dec. 31 government trims average tariff on imports to 3.4 percent from 5 percent, possibly resulting in increased imports and less appreciation pressure on the sol <PEN=PE>.

* Central bank buys about $9 billion dollars on the spot market in 2010, equivalent to around 6 percent of GDP. The treasury also bought around $500 million.

* On Nov. 26 banking regulator SBS says drawing up rule to curb use of short-term derivatives called non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) to limit pressure on the sol.

* Central bank raises deposit requirements on bank accounts, especially those tied to foreign loans, in a bid to limit speculation on the sol.

-- Story links: [ID:nN26131354] [ID:Nn31130618]

TAIWAN TIGHTENS FOREX RULES

* Financial Supervisory Commission says on Dec. 30 it will investigate bank trading to see whether foreign capital involved in speculation.

* On Dec. 27 the central bank caps trading in non-deliverable forwards at one fifth of a bank's total foreign exchange trading.

* Tightened reserve requirements ratio for Taiwan dollar passbook deposits held by foreign investors.

-- Story links [ID:nTOE6BR007] [ID:nTOE6BT02Q] [ID:nTOE6B200N]

SOUTH KOREA SET TO IMPOSE BANK LEVY, WITHHOLDING TAX

* Announces on Dec. 20 a proposal to levy banks' foreign currency debt from late 2011, expected to be at a level less than 0.5 percent.

* Government expected to reinstate withholding tax on local bond holdings by foreign investors' later this year, expected to be set at 14 percent.

* In June, sets ceilings on foreign exchange derivatives that banks can hold of 250 percent of equity capital for foreign bank branches and 50 percent for domestic banks. Says at end of December that these will be cut further to 200 and 40 percent respectively.

-- Story links: [ID:nTOE702015] [ID:nTOE6B6021] [ID:nSUL000219]

TURKEY RAISES RESERVE RATIOS ON LIRA DEPOSITS

* Central bank on Jan. 24 raises reserve requirements on one-month lira deposits by 200 basis points to 10 percent of the amount deposited, at the top end of analysts' expectations.

* Central bank on Jan. 20 cuts its one-week repo policy rate by 25 bps in a surprise move.

* Central bank says on Dec. 21 it will use all tools in its policy arsenal to cap speculative inflows.

* Increases reserve requirements for banks' short-term lira deposits, to prevent lira strengthening.

* Signals may also lift requirement for foreign-exchange deposits.

* Says not actively considering Tobin tax on hot money.

-- Story links: [ID:nLDE70N12F] [ID:nLDE70J19K] [ID:nLDE6BK0TQ]

SOUTH AFRICA EASES EXCHANGE CONTROLS

* South Africa eases exchange controls on Dec. 14, allowing local institutions to invest more money abroad

* Government says it will build up foreign currency reserves to curb rand <ZAR=> appreciation.

* But analysts doubt it has financial muscle to force down rand; finance minister says international cooperation needed.

--Story links: [ID:nL3E6NE0FH] [ID:nLDE68F1ER]

INDONESIA SAYS TO CONTROL BANKS' FOREIGN CURRENCY HOLDINGS

* Central bank signals on Dec. 3 it will impose new measures to control inflows, including management of commercial banks' minimum reserve ratios in foreign currency bank accounts and rupiah-denominated giro accounts held by foreigners with local banks.

* The central bank introduced a minimum holding period of one month for its bills in June this year in a move to channel strong capital inflows away from short-term investments.

-- Story links: [ID:nL3E6N30LR][ID:nL3E6NA0BJ]

PHILIPPINES RELAXES FOREX RULES IN RESPONSE TO INFLOWS

* On Nov. 17 the central bank says it will use measures such as building up foreign exchange reserves and additional bank regulations to deal with foreign inflows.

* Approves six measures in late October, involving higher ceilings for residents' foreign exchange purchases and outward investments, and encouraging foreign debt prepayments by the private sector -- moves aimed at encouraging outflows of capital and dampening a peso currency <PHP=PDSP> that has reached 2-year highs.

* Bank to stay active in market as peso <PHP=> rises.

-- Story links: [ID:nSGE6AG058][ID:nSGE69R0EK] [ID:nSGE69R0I4]

COLOMBIA INTRODUCES DOLLAR PURCHASES, STRUCTURAL MEASURES

* Finance ministry says on Nov. 17 it will only use external financing in 2011 to meet outside obligations to ease pressure on peso <COP=>.

* Central bank says on Oct. 29 it is buying at least $20 million daily until at least March 15.

* Government kept $1.5 billion abroad last year, which included $1.4 billion in government dividends from state oil firm Ecopetrol.

* Plans to possibly hedge up to $3.7 billion in external debt service payments in 2011.

-- Story links: [ID:nN29291838] [ID:nN16108112] [ID:nN02213742]

THAILAND TAXES FOREIGN BOND INVESTORS

* Thailand imposes 15 percent withholding tax on interest and capital gains earned by foreign investors on Thai bonds from Oct. 13, 2010.

* Central bank says on Nov. 24 would consider further measures including a Tobin-style tax on international transactions.

-- Story links: [ID:nL3E6MO0SA] [ID:nSGE69B0A6] [ID:nSGE6970DX]

MEXICO ESCHEWS INTERVENTION, PESO SET TO OUTPERFORM

* Central bank buying $600 million per month by selling dollar put options as a means to build up its reserves.

* Says capital controls do not work.

* Mexican peso <MXN=> lagged gains in other markets, yet to firm back to pre-crisis levels.

* Strategists see intervention measures across Latin America boosting attraction of free-floating Mexican peso.
