title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real up on minutes,  intervention  eyed
text:
* Brazil's real adds 0.2 pct after central bank minutes

* Bank seen stepping up intervention via swaps, forwards

* Chilean peso up 0.4 pct, Mexican peso flat

By Samantha Pearson

SAO PAULO, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's currency, the real, pushed higher on Thursday after minutes from the country's latest central bank meeting indicated further interest rate hikes in the months ahead.

Rising prices are likely to force Brazil to keep increasing its benchmark interest rate, which would attract more foreign investment and boost the already overvalued local currency.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.24 percent stronger at 1.665 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market in early trading, getting closer to the 1.65-per-dollar level which could prompt more aggressive intervention in the market.

Meanwhile, higher copper prices pushed up the Chilean peso but Mexico's currency struggled to break free of the key 12-per-dollar level.

"The minutes (from Brazil's central bank meeting) showed even more interest rate hikes. The long end of the interest rate futures curve is continuing to rise, which shows the market is beginning to prepare for a longer tightening cycle," said Andre Ferreira, director of the Futura Corretora brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"That will end up bringing more dollars to the market," he added.

In the minutes from last week's rate-setting meeting, Brazil's central bank said it would require "prompt corrections" to bring inflation back on target. [ID:nN27240799]

At that meeting, policy-makers raised Brazil's benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent and indicated further hikes were to come.

But the real's gains could force the authorities to take even more aggressive action in the market to curb the currency's appreciation and protect local manufacturers.

"We'll see two auctions today for sure," said Futura's Ferreira, referring to the central bank's daily purchases of dollars in the spot market.

The central bank may also later announce another reverse swap auction, which has the same effect as buying dollars in the futures market, or even call its first forwards auction. [ID:nN25294325]

COPPER RISE BOOSTS PESO

The Chilean peso <CLP=>, which has also become a source of concern for the country's authorities, firmed 0.43 percent to 486.7 per dollar.

The currency was boosted as the price of copper, the country's main export and economic lifeline, rose on supply worries. [ID:nLDE70Q1B6]

Earlier this month, Chile announced a record $12 billion in dollar purchases during 2011. The government has said it will also invest its military copper funds abroad and look to increase local financing of foreign businesses in an effort to ease pressure on the peso. [ID:nN26126403]

The Mexican currency <MXN=> was flat at 11.99 per dollar in early trading, struggling to definitively break the 12-per-dollar level.

Mexico's non-interventionist stance has made the peso a relatively attractive bet in the region but the 12-per-dollar level has proved to be a strong barrier of resistance. ( Editing by W Simon )

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real flat; Fed pledge supports region
text:
* Brazil real flat after latest intervention move

* Mexico peso firms 0.79 pct, Chile peso adds 0.8 pct (Adds comments, updates prices; changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Samantha Pearson and Walter Brandimarte

SAO PAULO/NEW YORK, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real shook off the latest intervention measures deployed by local authorities to end unchanged on Wednesday, while Mexico's and Chile's peso currencies were supported by solid U.S. housing data.

Latin American currencies received further support from a pledge by the U.S. Federal Reserve that it would keep up its bond-buying program, which has boosted higher-risk assets around the world. For details, see [ID:nN25283937]

By underpinning demand for the U.S. bond market to keep yields down, the Fed is pushing investors to seek higher returns in other assets.

"We will continue to have a very large overhang of liquidity," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York. "That continues to point to currency appreciation in Latin America."

The pledge from the Fed after its first meeting of the year was largely anticipated by markets.

Low interest rates in the United States and across the industrialized world have boosted demand for Latin American assets, driving currencies to multiyear highs. Regional policymakers have waded into foreign exchange markets to weaken their respective currencies in an effort to protect the competitiveness of local manufacturers.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid unchanged at 1.669 per dollar on the local spot market, although it firmed in international trade <BRL=> after the Fed's statement.

Brazil's central bank said late on Tuesday that it could for the first time ever offer currency forwards at auction, adding to its growing toolbox of market mechanisms aimed at cooling the real's gains. [ID:nN25294325]

CLOSING LOOPHOLES

The lack of market reaction to the announcement was blamed on uncertainty about the frequency of such auctions as well as their aim, since the forwards market is tiny compared to Brazil's spot and futures markets.

Analysts said this latest measure is likely an attempt to keep speculators from trying to get around previous measures.

"The decision looks like an effort to close a loophole to capture all sides of the market," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York, in a research note.

Brazil has the highest yields in the region as it hikes interest rates to keep its strong economy from overheating.

The real is expected to keep strengthening until authorities introduce more drastic measures such as widespread quarantines or capital controls, analysts said.

"The next instrument (to be announced) could be some type of restriction on a specific inflow, something like the quarantine," said Jorge Lima, a consultant at Previbank DTVM in Sao Paulo. "But Brazil can't shut itself off from long-term investment, so it would have to be a very specific restriction on speculative transactions."

The Mexican and Chilean pesos both firmed on Wednesday, helped by data showing U.S. single-family home sales in December rose to their highest in eight months.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.79 percent to 12.0025 per dollar.

"The outlook for the U.S. housing sector could be improving, and that is a good sign for the economy. (The United States) is our biggest trading partner and so this is having a good influence on the peso," said Mario Copca, an analyst at the Vanguardia brokerage in Mexico City.

In Chile, the peso <CLP=CL> firmed 0.8 percent to 489.90 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, was supported by the U.S. economic data.

The Chilean peso closed at its strongest close since the country's central bank announced a $12 billion currency intervention Jan. 3 aimed at keeping the currency in check.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico's peso dips on official's  currency  talk
text:
* Mexico finance minister says govt is eyeing peso gains

* Comments increase market bets on more intervention

* Analysts doubt any Mexican action is imminent

* Mexico peso down 0.24 pct, Chile peso dips 0.2 pct (Updates prices, adds background)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso weakened on Tuesday after the country's finance minister said the government was eyeing the peso's recent ascent, raising concerns in the market that Mexican authorities could increase intervention.

Analysts doubted Mexico was on the verge of wading deeper into the so-called currency war that has drawn an increasing number of economies to intervene or enact capital controls as they seek to protect their exporters from surging currencies.

Mexican Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero said on Tuesday that the government was "paying a lot of attention" to the peso currency's appreciation but he did not think controls on capital inflows would be appropriate for Mexico. [ID:nLDE70O1KC]

Traders and analysts have been speculating that Mexico's central bank could increase the $600 million in dollar put options it is selling every month.

"Businessmen are complaining the strong peso could affect competitiveness, and authorities could start buying more dollars to break the appreciation a bit," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones in Mexico City.

The options program is a less aggressive measure than those that have been taken by other emerging economies to fight strong currencies that have been inflated by flows from yield-hungry foreign investors.

Still, a move to increase the program could spur temporary losses in the peso, analysts said.

But many analysts think the peso will have to mount even stronger gains before authorities could decide to take action.

The currency has gained around 4 percent from a November intraday low, helped by an improving outlook for the closely-linked U.S. and Mexican economies.

WHAT, ME WORRY?

Even if exporters are grumbling about getting less pesos for their exports, the government is not feeling the pressure as a surge in oil prices is generating a windfall in government revenue from crude oil sales sales, analysts said.

"We have surplus peso revenue due to the level of oil prices, despite the exchange rate," said Salvador Orozco, a currency and debt strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

Mexico gets about one-third of its revenue from oil sales by the state-run monopoly. Congress set the 2011 budget with a $65.40 per barrel estimate for Mexican crude prices, but the market the price for the country's blend <MEX-OSP> has climbed to just below $84 per barrel.

"I do not think the government will worry if (the peso) gets to 11.80 (per dollar) ... If it goes to 11 (per dollar), maybe there would be distortions," Orozco added.

Chile's peso <CLP=> bid 0.2 percent weaker at 492.70 as investors worried that rising interest rates in emerging economies like China would dampen demand demand for copper, the countries top export.

Brazil's local market was closed for a holiday, but the real <BRL=> bid almost flat, edging 0.03 percent firmer in international trade at 1.6708 per dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  narrowly mixed; Brazil real flat
text:
* Brazil real up 0.06 pct after interest rate hike

* Chile peso slumps 0.45 pct as copper price falls

* Mexico peso rises 0.15 pct on U.S. housing data (Adds comments and context, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Moises Avila

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Brazil's real edged firmer on Thursday after the country raised interest rates as expected for the first time since July, but investors were cautious of further intervention to crimp the currency.

Meanwhile, Mexico's peso firmed after U.S. housing data beat expectations and Chile's currency slumped on concerns China could tighten borrowing costs and hit demand for copper, the country's main export.

Brazil's central bank increased its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent late on Wednesday. For details, see [ID:nN19215154]

Although economists say higher borrowing costs are necessary to curb a worrying surge in inflation, the move is likely to attract even more investors to Brazil chasing higher yields and push the local currency to fresh highs.

"People think interest rates could go up even more," said Carlos Gandolfo, a partner at Sao Paulo's Pioneer brokerage.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.670 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

Brazil has been using an array of measures to tame a rally in the real, which has gained about 13 percent since last May. The central bank said it would call a reverse currency swap auction on Friday, its latest mechanism to reel in the currency. [ID:nN20147163]

The central bank also said it would take other measures beside interest rate hikes to try to cool inflation, such as a recent increase in bank reserve requirements.

"The tightening cycle will be smaller than the market was imagining," Andre Perfeito, an economist with Gradual Investimentos in Sao Paulo, said in a research note.

Investors pared back bets on the size of future interest rate hikes, pushing down yields on short-dated interest rate futures contracts <0#DIJ:>.

MEXICO UP, CHILE DOWN

The Mexican currency <MXN=> firmed 0.15 percent to 12.0675 per dollar, helped by data that showed U.S. existing home sales rose more than expected in December.

"The home sales data came out very strong ... this indicates that the United States (economy) is doing better than expected. This is helping us," said Omar Martin del Campo, a trader at Ve por Mas, a bank in Mexico City.

Mexico's currency this week hit its strongest level in more than two years and it has gained more than 4 percent since a November low on the improving economic outlook for the United States, which buys most of Mexico's exports.

The Mexican currency pulled back from early losses that took it to its weakest in five sessions on fears that China could tighten monetary policy also crimp global growth.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.45 percent weaker at 494.20 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, fell sharply.

A slowing of the Chinese economy could reduce its demand for raw materials, hurting the economies of commodity-producing Latin American countries. [ID:nTOE70J02S]

"What is weighing most are the declines by European stocks and the negative effect of lower commodity prices, such as copper," said a currency trader in Santiago.

Mining stocks dragged European markets down, on the assumption that demand for basic resources would fall if China's growth is reined in. [ID:nLDE70J0E3]

title: ANALYSIS-Latin America  FX intervention  may be here to stay
text:
* Commodity prices, Chinese demand to pressure currencies

* Brazil real would be 10 pct firmer without intervention

* Measures more acceptable because of Chile, China

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 19 (Reuters) - Intervention to tame Latin America's currencies could be here to stay as strong Chinese demand for commodities and rising inflation make governments reluctant to cede control over their markets.

Brazil, Peru, Colombia and even Chile's conservative authorities have aggressively intervened over recent months, surprising nerve-racked investors with an arsenal of measures.

Politicians such as Brazil's finance minister have blamed the rallies on the developed world, slamming the United States for keeping interest rates low and the dollar weak through its quantitative easing policy.

But rising Chinese demand for many of Latin America's key exports is likely to support commodity prices even as the dollar recovers, pushing the region's currencies to new highs and maintaining the need for intervention.

"There's a long-term case for Chinese demand as a fundamental element underpinning Latin American currencies," says Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin American research at IDEAglobal in New York.

"This has become one of the major driving forces for Latin American economies, especially those that export traditional commodity-based materials such as Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia -- just about the entire gamut of Latin American countries."

China's trade with Latin America grew ten-fold between 2000 and 2007, according to the U.S. Congressional Research Service, and in 2009 the Asian giant overtook the United States to become Brazil's top trading partner. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Factbox on regional intervention [ID:nLDE70514E]

Graphic on Brazil's measures http://r.reuters.com/mez94r 

Graphic on region's FXhttp://r.reuters.com/cat64r ("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Higher inflation, partly as a result of a global surge in commodity prices and food costs, is also likely to force policymakers to raise interest rates across the region, boosting currencies further.

Brazil's central bank is expected to hike its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 11.25 percent later on Wednesday to curb inflation, currently at a six-year high.

Chile is also set to raise lending costs in coming months.

"As the central bank keeps raising its benchmark rate and attracting foreign investment, it's likely that we'll see additional (currency) measures," said Alejandro Puente, an economist with BBVA Chile in Santiago.

INTERVENTION: THE NEW NORM?

Although countries such as Brazil are working on long-term solutions to bring down interest rates and relieve pressure on their currencies, intervention is likely to remain a popular and necessary option in the meantime.

Without such measures, the Brazilian real and the Chilean peso would now be trading around 10 percent stronger at 1.50 and 450 per dollar respectively, analysts say.

"Lock-up" periods on foreign capital could be imposed in Brazil while countries such as Colombia may choose to extend dollar purchases. [ID:nN10257143]

"Oh intervention does work! It may not change the theoretical value of where the currency should be but in the short-term it absolutely does have an impact on markets," says Michael Woolfolk, senior currency strategist at BNY Mellon in New York.

The difficulty of exiting intervention policies is amplified by their beggar-thy-neighbor nature.

Many currency speculators make money via regional cross trades (buying one Latin American currency against another), which means whichever country ditches intervention first risks luring the wave of cash washing around the continent.

Before Chile's central bank shocked investors earlier this month with a $12 billion dollar-buying plan, many banks were advising buying the peso against the Brazilian real. Those same banks then advised clients to buy the Mexican peso against Chile's currency, driving Mexico's peso to a two-year high this week. Now speculation is rising Mexico may also have to intervene to match its neighbors' aggressive efforts.

The proliferation of such policies has also made them more acceptable among investors, giving countries little incentive to ditch them prematurely.

"Chile gave intervention more respectability because its central bank has long held the view that intervention is not successful in the medium term and that the (19)90s capital controls had limited impact at best," says Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at 4Cast Inc in Washington.

China's growing economic clout, achieved despite its fixed-rate foreign exchange policy, could also be changing the rules of the game globally, says Paul Biszko, senior strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

"There is the view that: China is doing it, the United States is doing it indirectly, why can't we do it?!" (Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real firms, helped by rate hike bets
text:
* Mexican peso retreats after break below 12/dlr

* Easing euro zone worries support region's currencies

* Brazil's real up 0.3 pct, Chile's peso up 0.2 pct (Updates to afternoon)

By Samantha Pearson and Sean Mattson

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 18 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed on Tuesday ahead of an expected interest rate hike, while Mexico's peso retreated after breaking the psychological 12 per dollar barrier for the first time since late 2008.

Expectations that Brazil's central bank will have to raise interest rates on Wednesday helped the real to outperform the region. For more, see: [ID:nSPG003198]

Brazil has been reluctant to raise its already high borrowing costs for fear of attracting even more short-term, speculative money. The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.3 percent stronger at 1.676 per dollar on the local spot market.

Rising inflation has made an interest rate hike seem inevitable. While the consensus among economists and market participants is for a 50-basis-point rise, the market has also partially priced in a 75-basis-point increase.

"(A) recent surge in food commodity prices ... could aggravate the situation further and could further deteriorate inflation expectations," Zeina Latif, chief Brazil economist at RBS in Sao Paulo, said in a research note.

Rising investor sentiment in Germany and signs that policymakers will eventually firm up plans to ease the euro zone's debt crisis helped support riskier assets worldwide and weakened the dollar. [ID:nLDE70H0UU] [ID:nLDE70H0DQ]

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> also firmed 0.2 percent to 490.20 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, rose because of the weak dollar. [ID:nLDE70H0DP]

PESO PULLBACK

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.51 percent to 12.0325 per dollar as investors took profits after the peso broke below the key 12-per-dollar level on Monday for the first time since a steep devaluation in October 2008.

The Mexican peso, which has lagged the gains in other emerging market currencies, strengthened more than 5 percent from a November intraday low to Tuesday's session high boosted by an improving outlook for U.S. and Mexican growth.

"It looks like a good opportunity to lock in some of the gains," said Marjorie Hernandez, an analyst at HSBC in New York, who expected the peso to firm back toward 11.80 per dollar.

"The underlying story hasn't changed. It's still a great macro call for the year, people believe the U.S. is going to recover, it's still cheap, and they still aren't intervening," she added.

The Mexican currency has also been supported by flows from investors looking for a haven from intervention tactics of other central banks.

Mexico's peso is barely clawing back toward its pre-crisis levels, but analysts say Mexico's central bank could move to increase a program under which it is selling $600 million of dollar put options every month to local banks.

Luis Flores, an analyst at brokerage IXE in Mexico City, said a bigger options program would still be seen "as a more patient and subtle" reaction compared with intervention mechanisms in Chile, Brazil and Turkey. The shock of the announcement could derail peso gains, but "only for a matter of days," he said.

"Fundamentally it will not remove the favorable tendency for the peso," Flores said.

The options allow local banks to sell dollars to the central bank at a slightly preferential rate when the peso has been on a winning streak and is below a 20-day moving average. By sucking up dollars directly from banks, policymakers can keep some dollar off the open market.

Gabriel Casillas, an analyst at JP Morgan in Mexico City, said the central bank could take a bolder move to begin daily dollar purchases if further peso gains take the currency quickly and significantly below 12 per dollar.

"This would still be a market-friendly mechanism -- relative to capital control measures that other countries have recently adopted -- and could reduce the speed of appreciation of the peso," Casillas wrote in a report. (Writing by Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Weaker; USD/MXN Back Above 12
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed weaker Tuesday as participants took some profits following the currency's first close below MXN12 to the U.S. dollar since October 2008.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.0330, according to Infosel, compared with MXN11.9945 at the close Monday. The move back above MXN12, seen as an important psychological level for the peso, came as the dollar ceded ground against other majors.

RBC Capital Markets lowered the stop on its recommendation to buy pesos against a 65% dollar/35% euro basket. "By most metrics, MXN continues to stand out as fair-to-slightly undervalued at a time when many other [emerging market] currencies appear significantly over-valued," RBC said in a report.

At the same time, RBC sees little likelihood of intervention to weaken the peso as "Mexican policy makers seem willing to accept gradual currency appreciation and reject implementing taxes/controls on capital."

Bank of America/Merrill Lynch echoed that view in a report, citing commitment to a free-floating regime, a still competitive exchange rate reflected in narrowing external deficits, and tolerance for some currency strength among authorities.

While Mexico's inclusion in Citigroup's World Government Bond Index makes capital controls highly unlikely, other intervention options would also be of dubious effect, BofA/Merrill said in a report.

With the size of the peso market--globally $50 billion a day according to the 2010 Bank of International Settlements survey--a dollar-buying program would have to be large to affect the exchange rate, and include discretionary intervention, BofA/Merrrill said. Currently, the Bank of Mexico buys up to $600 million a month under a system of put options that can be exercised when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average.

BofA/Merrill said a cut in the Bank of Mexico's overnight interest rate target from the current 4.5%, which has been among points of speculation, could even be counterproductive and encourage more investment flows. "Yields in short-term bills (Cetes) and implied yields in currency forwards are already trading below the 4.5% policy rate given excess local liquidity, and this has yet to discourage investors," the investment bank said.

The yield on benchmark 28-day Cetes fell by seven basis points at the central bank's primary auction Tuesday to 4.13%.

Rodrigo Barros Reyes, the Finance Ministry's director of public policy analysis, said at a U.N. press event that the government doesn't see the peso's appreciation as a threat to Mexico's 2011 economic growth outlook, which has been revised upward by a number of economists in recent weeks.

"The central scenario is that the economy will see good growth rates in 2011, even incorporating the trend of capital inflows that has led the currency to slightly stronger levels," Barros said.

title: Mexico's Peso Ends Stronger Vs Dollar, Teases Key MXN12 Level
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed stronger against the U.S. dollar Friday, toying with a key dollar support level following positive U.S. industrial production numbers that bode well for Mexican economic growth.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.0390, according to Infosel, stronger than Thursday's MXN12.1425 close and its best level since early October 2008.

A local trader said the peso several times approached, then shied away from, the psychologically important level of MXN12 to the dollar, which the currency hasn't touched since the start of the 2008 global financial crisis.

Other local markets weren't particularly supportive--stocks closed modestly lower despite U.S. gains, and local government bonds were mixed. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds slipped two basis points to 7.03%, and the yield on 20-year bonds was flat at 7.8%.

Many analysts see a break below MXN12 to the dollar as just a matter of time. With Brazil and other Latin American governments and central banks acting to keep their currencies from appreciating further, a number of investors have turned their attention to the Mexican peso given what is seen as a low risk of intervention.

The Bank of Mexico buys up to $600 million a month under a system of put options, where banks can sell dollars to the central bank when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average. The central bank bought about $4.6 billion under the options in 2010 and has bought all $600 million under the options for January. Oil dollars are the main source of Mexico's foreign reserves, which were a record $116.9 billion last week.

In a report Friday, Bank of America/Merrill Lynch said it expects the main Latin American countries, and especially Brazil, to slow their rate of reserve accumulation in 2011. Colombia may accelerate its accumulation, while reserve building should "decelerate somewhat" in Mexico and Peru.

"In Mexico, the renewal of the IMF's [flexible credit line] for $72 billion probably reduced the desire to increase reserves, but the recent appreciation of the MXN adds some upside risks to our FX accumulation forecast," BofA/Merrill Lynch said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile's peso up on rate move, Mexican peso dips
text:
* Brazil's real and Chilean peso both gain 0.5 pct

* Mexican peso dips 0.2 pct after U.S. jobs data

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Chile's currency firmed on Thursday, helped by bets the central bank would hike interest rates, drawing in yield-hungry investors even as policymakers intervene to weaken the currency.

Chile and Brazil's currencies were also supported by successful bond auctions in Spain and Italy that helped to ease euro zone fiscal concerns, while Mexico's peso dipped on a rise in U.S. jobless claims.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.47 percent to 488.20 per dollar as some investors in a divided market bet that Chile's central bank will hike its benchmark interest rate for the eighth consecutive time later on Thursday. [ID:nN13261867c]

"There should be an increase of 25 points," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago. "And we should keep seeing increases from here onward, especially because of the inflation pressures," he added.

Others think policymakers will leave borrowing costs steady so as not to lure even more hot money to the country and undermine the $12 billion intervention plan launched last week that knocked the peso off a nearly three year high.

Broadly supporting bids for riskier assets, Spain sold 3 billion euros of five-year bonds, raising the maximum amount targeted. Italy's auction of 5- and 15-year government bonds also went well. [ID:nLDE70C0IA].

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.48 percent stronger at 1.667 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The worries over Europe are diminishing a little... I'm not seeing any real difference to yesterday, we're continuing on the same track," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

However, investors were reluctant to push the currency much higher in case it triggered more aggressive government intervention in the market, he said.

MEXICAN PESO RETREATS FROM 2-YR HIGH

The Mexican currency <MXN=> slipped 0.21 percent to 12.0965 per dollar after jobless claims in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner, jumped to their highest level since October. [ID:nN13271305]

The news helped weaken the peso after the currency hit its strongest level since Oct. 2008 in the previous session. But overall, U.S. data was mixed, with higher producer prices and a jump in U.S. exports.

"The fact that there was inflation in the United States tells you the economy is recovering and it is not all bad," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones.

The peso has won favor among investors since it is one of the few currencies in the region which is not at risk from intervention.

However, Mexico's free-market orthodoxy has not been challenged too much with the peso barely clawing back from pre-crisis levels.

If the peso reaches 11.50 per dollar, the Mexican central bank could take measures similar to Chile's dollar-buying plan, said Benito Berber, an economist at Nomura in New York.

title: ANALYSIS- Mexico  peso seen rising as  intervention  eschewed
text:
* Improving U.S. outlook also seen boosting peso

* Peso may soon test levels close to 11.80/dollar

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso, trading at a more than two-year high, could strengthen further on bets of improved U.S. demand for its exports and enhanced by the rising tide of currency intervention in other emerging markets.

Forecasts for 2011 economic growth in Mexico, which sends most of its exports to the United States, are edging up, which could help the peso as Americans buy more Mexican cars, televisions and refrigerators.

Mexico's free-floating peso has an added luster as central banks from Brazil and Chile to Turkey and Taiwan intervene in markets to slow gains in their currencies driven by yield-hungry investors seeking to beat returns in developed countries like the United States.

As a devout supporter of open financial markets, Mexico is the only major country in Latin America that has stayed on the sidelines of the battle between speculators and central banks.

"Mexico is the last holdout," said Clyde Wardle, a strategist at HSBC in New York. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ For a factbox on intervention risks: [ID:nSGE69503F] Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r ("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Investors are betting Mexico's peso will outperform other emerging market currencies where authorities are intervening, like Turkey's lira or Chile's peso, analysts said.

"The probability that speculators will pile onto the appreciative momentum of the peso is high, and that could quickly push the currency below 12 per dollar," said Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura in New York.

Last year, the Mexican peso was hurt by fears the United States could slip back into recession, but surprisingly strong U.S. and Mexican data, as well as the decision to not raise taxes in the United States, pushed analysts to revise up growth forecasts for 2011, helping the peso gain more than 4 percent from a November low.

While other emerging market currencies have been trading at multi-year highs, Mexico's peso is only beginning to catch up from its sharp devaluation during the 2008 financial crisis.

GAINS COULD ACCELERATE

On Thursday, the peso hit its highest level since mid-October 2008, trading around 12.07 per dollar <MXN=>.

And gains below 12 could trigger stop losses from investors who have been betting on a stronger dollar and further accelerate the peso gains towards 11.80 per dollar, said Nomura's Berber.

Citigroup technical analysts noted that a close this week below 12.05 per dollar, the 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the peso's August 2008 to March 2009 devaluation, would suggest the currency could firm to as much as 11.21 per dollar, with good support in the 11.50 to 11.70 range.

Mexico's peso traded between 10 and 11 per dollar in the years running up to the financial crisis, and a break past 12 per dollar may not immediately spur concerns from local authorities, said Gabriel Casillas, an economist at JPMorgan.

In a meeting with analysts in New York in December, central bank chief Agustin Carstens suggested authorities would welcome the boost to sluggish domestic demand that a stronger peso could provide, HSBC's Wardle said.

While Mexico has eschewed the direct intervention of other central banks, it did start conducting monthly auctions of dollar put options early last year, but these are viewed as less aggressive.

JP Morgan's Casillas said a quick jump to levels below 11.80 per dollar could spur policymakers to increase the its options auction. "Even then, it is very moderate," he said. (Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: FACTBOX-Steps countries are taking to counter hot money
text:
Jan 10 (Reuters) - More governments around the world are moving to keep their currencies from strengthening or control the flow of money into their economies as investors pour money into higher-yielding markets, turning their backs on low interest rates in developed economies.

Below are recent cases of direct or indirect government intervention in the currency markets, compiled by Reuters:

BRAZIL TARGETS SHORT-SELLERS, HOPING TO WEAKEN REAL

* Brazil made its boldest move so far to curb gains in the national currency, imposing on Thursday reserve requirements on banks' short positions on U.S. dollars in a bid to reduce speculative trade that has pushed the real near two-year highs.

* The surprise move will make it more expensive for banks to bet against the dollar. Short positions on dollars, a bet the real will strengthen against the greenback, surged to the highest on record at the end of December.

* Chilean President Sebastian Pinera says no plans for capital controls.

* Central bank lifts limits on pension funds' overseas investment.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latin American  currencies  dip on Portugal woes
text:
* Fears over intervention in futures market weigh on real

* Brazil's real loses 0.12 pct, Chile's peso dips 0.2 pct

* Mexico's peso firms 0.14, aided by less intervention risk

(Adds comments and updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, (Reuters) - Chile's peso and Brazil's real slipped Monday after concerns that Portugal may be the next European state to seek a bailout pushed investors to sell riskier assets.

Pressure grew Monday on Portugal to follow in the footsteps of Greece and Ireland by seeking financial help from the European Union and International Monetary Fund. Some investors fear a widening debt crisis in Europe could weigh down global growth.

Latin American currencies were largely tracking the euro, a key barometer used by investors to gauge overall risk appetite, traders said. Regional currencies pared losses after the euro bounced off a four-month low.

Brazil's real also suffered from concerns that the government could take further steps to control its recent appreciation.

The country's sovereign wealth fund was formally authorized Monday to operate in the foreign exchange market while speculation about action in the futures market intensified.

The Brazilian real was bid 0.12 percent weaker at 1.686 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The expectation that the central bank could act in (the) derivatives (futures market) is reinforcing the global move. It's a mix of global moves and local noise," said Roberto Padovani, chief Brazil economist with WestLB bank in Sao Paulo.

MEXICAN PESO ON SIDELINES

The Chilean peso sank to a four-month low past the key 500-per-dollar level early Monday but snapped back to bid only 0.2 percent weaker at 498.50 per dollar.

"The 500-level is a level that a number of clients have mentioned where they would find the peso as attractive," said Rafael de la Fuente, an economist at UBS in New York. "The economy is doing very well, it is fundamentally strong."

Chile's peso was hammered down about 6 percent last week from a near three-year high after the central bank said it would buy $12 billion this year in the foreign exchange market to weaken its currency, whose strength is hurting exporters.

The market is divided about whether Chile's central bank could hike interest rates Thursday to cool rising inflation or if it could leave borrowing costs steady so as not to boost the attraction of its debt to yield-hungry investors.

The country's central bank chief Monday said the intervention plan was working and that policymakers felt "independent" to move its benchmark rate according to the bank's inflation objectives.

"It is an interesting comment. I think they will hike, precisely because even though they have introduced foreign exchange intervention, the risks to inflation are skewed to the upside," de la Fuente said.

The Mexican currency firmed 0.14 percent to 12.2180 per dollar, backed by bets of stronger exports and less risk of intervention.

Mexico's peso has yet to recover its strength since before the 2008 crisis and policymakers are not threatening to take any action.

"Currencies on the sidelines of this currency war, like the Mexican peso, will be attractive in 2011," Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE, wrote in a report.

The Mexican currency is also supported by an improving outlook for the economy in the United States, its top trading partner, as well as rising oil prices as Mexico's export blend trades around its highest price since Oct. 2008. (Additonal reporting by Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso slumps on  intervention ;real recovers
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Chile's peso closes down 4.5 pct at 9-week low

* Brazilian real pares losses after press conference

* Finance Minister Guido Mantega announces no new measures

* Mexico eschews intervention, benefiting peso (Adds comments from Mexico, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Chile's peso suffered its biggest daily drop in more than 25 years on Tuesday on tough new intervention plans while the Brazilian real recovered after Brasilia stopped short of introducing further measures.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> slumped as much as 4.9 percent to 489.60 per dollar. It later closed 4.5 percent down at a 9-week low of 487.60 -- its biggest daily loss since February 1985, according to daily central bank data.

Brazil's real <BRBY> also weakened sharply after the government announced it would hold a news conference in the afternoon to tackle foreign exchange issues, prompting speculation fresh measures could be announced.

But Finance Minister Guido Mantega said very little and only reiterated that the government was ready to act, causing the real immediately to pare losses.

Chile has taken one of the most hands-off approaches in Latin America to its foreign exchange market. But it surprised investors late on Monday with a massive dollar-buying plan.

The central bank announced it will buy $12 billion to tame the peso, which has appreciated more than 17 percent against the greenback since the end of June. For details, see [ID:nN03137860].

Like many attractive emerging economies across Latin America and Asia, Chile has struggled with currency appreciation that has made its exports more difficult to sell abroad and flooded the country with cheap imports. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Chile's surprise move added to existing concerns about intervention across the region as it could give countries such as Brazil an excuse to implement more currency measures.

"If the pretty conservative Chilean central bank intervenes, what can you expect of the Brazilian central bank!" said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington.

However, others played down a possible regional impact.

"Chile is just the last domino to fall into intervention. I don't think it changes others' attitudes as they are already intervening," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging markets research for the Americas at Nomura in New York.

BRAZIL: KING OF INTERVENTION

The Brazilian real pared its losses to close 0.79 percent weaker at 1.662 per dollar on the local spot market, after closing at its strongest level since Sept. 1 2008 in the previous session.

Brazil's trade and industry minister said on Monday the country would not remain "passive" while the real continues to strengthen.

Latin America's biggest economy has already taken the lead in the region when it comes to intervention, buying vast amounts of dollars on a daily basis and raising taxes on inflows. But investors worry the government could increase those levies even further and take other measures, such as intervening in the futures market. For possible measures, see [ID:nN01117570].

Mexico is now the only major Latin American country that is not heavily intervening in its currency market, partly because the peso is fully convertible and thus more widely traded and harder to control.

The country has also suffered more from the financial crisis, which means it has not seen the flood of currency-boosting investment experienced by Chile and Brazil.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> gained 0.14 percent to 12.2318 per dollar, even as U.S. stocks were mixed.

"If you believe that intervention in Mexico is pretty moderate and subtle, then the peso become more attractive in the eyes of investors," said Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE in Mexico City. (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico's peso posts 6 pct gain in 2010
text:
* Mexican peso firms almost 6 percent in 2010

* Slower growth seen cooling Mexico gain in 2011

* Intervention threatens other Latam currencies

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso firmed on Friday as the currency notched a nearly 6 percent gain for the year, boosted by a strong recovery in exports to top trading partner the United States.

The peso <MXN=> firmed to 12.3650 per U.S. dollar on Friday. Local markets in other major economies were closed for the New Year's eve holiday.

Analysts expect much weaker gains seen in currencies across Latin America against the dollar in the coming year as growth slows in Mexico and southern economies step up intervention to weaken their currencies.

"Investors should not extrapolate the Mexican peso's outperformance in 2010 to 2011," said Jimena Zuniga, an analyst at Barclays Capital in New York.

Stronger than expected data and the extension of tax cuts in the United States pushed some analysts to revise up their forecasts for U.S. growth in 2010, but Zuniga points out that Mexico's economy will see slower growth next year compared to 2010, when it likely grew around 5 percent.

"Both the U.S. and Mexican economies had a lot of slack in 2010 to support growth, but the slack has diminished a lot in Mexico even if not so much in the United States," Zuniga said.

Low interest rates in major economies, which are trying to spur growth and underpin a recovery from the 2008 financial crisis, spurred high demand for Latin American debt and currencies in 2010, helping drive solid gains across the region. For details see [ID:nN30121533].

While yield-hungry investors starved by low U.S. rates will likely continue to pile into Latin American assets early in 2010, some analysts believe faster than expected growth in the United States could awaken expectations of a rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve toward the end of 2011.

"This could deter flow from foreign investors toward emerging markets, and we could even see outflows," wrote analysts at Santander, which expects the Mexican peso to weaken more than 2 percent to 12.70 per dollar by the end of 2011.

Other currencies in the region could also see gains crimped by increasing intervention by officials who are concerned that strong currencies are hurting local exporters and that foreign flows could be inflating bubbles in the region's assets.

Brazil and Colombia have mounted significant dollar buying programs by their central banks to contain gains in their currencies, while Chile could soon join the fray if its peso gains much more ground, said Barclays' Zuniga.

"We envision more of this type of war between flows that are attracted to the market's fundamentals and the policy response by authorities," she said.

Chile's currency closed 2011 at a 31-month high as the domestic economy roared back from the devastation of an earthquake early in the year. [ID:nN30111514]

But slowing growth may lead the country's central bank to halt a string of rate hikes in January, which could portend that policymakers are willing to pump up inflation by weakening the peso, Zuniga said. [ID:nN30111514]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil rates dip, Latam  FX  firms on US data
text:
* Investors pare Brazil rate hike bets after retail data

* Chile invokes intervention as peso hits 30-mo high

* Brazil's real firms 0.35 pct, Mexico peso adds 0.13 pct (Adds comments, changes byline, updates prices)

By Jose de Castro and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures fell on Tuesday after weaker than expected retail sales prompted bets the central bank will be under less pressure to raise borrowing costs.

Brazilian retail sales rose only 0.4 percent in October from the prior month, which pushed market players to rethink widely-held expectations that Brazil's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate - called the Selic - early next year to cool inflation pressures. For details, see [ID:nN14196422]

"Now there is some doubt over if, in fact, the Selic will go up and, if it goes up, by how much." said Jason Vieira, an analyst at the Cruzeiro do Sul brokerage.

The yield on the interest rate contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily-traded of the session, fell 5 basis points to 11.85 percent.

A head trader at a bank in New York noted that the drop in rates on Tuesday showed the market is now pricing in a rate hike of only about 30 basis points at the central bank's next meeting in January. Last week, the market had been betting on a 50-basis-point increase.

Currencies across Latin America firmed after surprisingly strong November U.S. retail sales boosted optimism about consumer spending in one of the region's top trading partners.

Brazil's currency <BRBY> bid 0.35 percent stronger at 1.693 per dollar. Traders were buying up the currency after the real pierced the key 1.70 level without without prompting additional intervention measures, traders said.

CHILE JAWBONES

Chile's peso surged to a 30-month high on the back of record prices for the country's main export, copper, and despite warnings from officials that they could intervene in the market.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.44 percent to 472.70 per dollar even after the country's central bank chief said policymakers were continuing to evaluate the possibility of intervening to slow the peso's gains. [ID:nN14274122]

Mexico's peso initially firmed the U.S. retail sales data, which boosted the outlook for Mexican exports to its top trading partner.

But the Mexican currency gave up gains late in the session after the U.S. Federal Reserve showed no signs of curtailing its economic stimulus measures, raising the prospect of accelerating U.S. economic growth and also inflation.

The Fed's statement sparked steep losses in the price of U.S. bonds, driving up yields.

That pushed investors to dump riskier Mexican debt in favor of the rising yields on safer U.S. bonds, undermining the peso currency as investors bought dollars to sink into U.S. government debt.

The yield on the government's 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> jumped 13 basis points to bid at 7.17 percent.

"People are expecting a possible boom now in the U.S. economy, and with that pushing up returns on U.S. bonds, it is more attractive to be in Treasuries," said an analyst at a foreign bank in Mexico who does not have permission to speak to media. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real slips,  Mexico  peso firms slightly
text:
* Brazil's real hurt by intervention expectations

* Higher copper price helps support Chilean peso

* China rate hike fears, EU debt woes may weigh next week

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Friday, hurt by expectations of intervention by the local authorities to curb the currencies gains, while the Mexican peso edged up, helped by stronger than expected U.S. data.

The real closed 0.35 percent weaker at 1.713 on the local spot market <BRBY>, recording a 1.64 percent loss for the week.

Traders pointed to comments from Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega on Thursday that authorities could step up efforts to contain the real's gains, which are hurting exporters.

"After Mantega spoke yesterday, people became even more alert to the possibility that the government could act with more force in the currency market," said Jose Carlos Amado, a currency trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's central bank (BCB) has recently started calling two auctions a day, instead of just one, to buy U.S. dollars.

"With the USDBRL now close to 1.71, the BCB resumed intervening once during the day, reinforcing our thesis that BCB becomes more aggressive below 1.70," wrote analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed to a fresh 30-month high in early trading but was later flat at 475.80 per dollar. The price of copper, the country's main export, pared early gains.

Chinese imports, including copper, soared in November while bank lending topped forecasts, suggesting the booming Chinese economy will continue to gobble up Latin American commodities such as Chilean copper and Brazilian soybeans.

Chile's currency gained 0.86 percent during the week.

CHINA, EUROPE LOOM

The Mexican currency <MXN=> firmed 0.21 percent to 12.4505 per dollar after U.S. data consumer confidence to its highest level in six months and trade data showed that imports from Mexico rose to a record high in October. [ID:nN10163525]

Mexico sends around 80 percent of its exports to the United States and Latin America's No. 2 economy is counting on a firm recovery north of the border to support its own rebound from a deep recession.

The Mexican peso was on track to post a weekly loss of around 1 percent.

Analysts said Latin American currencies could be hurt by signs that China could soon move to hike interest rates. Chinese data on Saturday that is expected to show another pick-up in inflation.

"The intensity of the depreciation will depend on the comments that are made in China and the measures they take to keep the economy from overheating," said Mario Copca, an analyst at brokerage Vanguardia in Mexico City.

Further signs of trouble in Europe's debt crisis could also weigh next week.

EU heads of state and government meet on Dec. 16-17 to discuss the region's spreading debt crisis. Expectations of meaningful progress are low after Germany and France on Friday rejected calls for an increase in the bloc's rescue fund and joint sovereign bonds. [ID:nLDE6B90K3]

"There is going to be more noise from Europe ... the big risk is that Italy gets downgraded," Copca said. (Additional reporting by Jose de Castro in Sao Paulo and Lorena Segura in Mexico City; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile and Mexico's  currencies  firm on US data
text:
* Strong U.S. data raises hopes about export demand

* Brazil's real weakens as dollar recovers worldwide

* Mexican peso adds 0.3 pct, Chilean peso up 0.5 pct

* Colombia's central bank warns of "big" interventions (Adds comments about Colombia and Mexico, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The currencies of Chile and Mexico firmed on Friday after strong U.S. jobs data raised hopes about demand for both countries' exports.

But Brazil's real edged lower as the dollar recovered from sharp losses in the wake of U.S. stimulus measures.

Data showing the United States added more jobs than expected in October lifted hopes about the global recovery, boosting the price of many industrial metals. [ID:nN0528209]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> gained 0.51 percent to 477.3 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, hit a two-year high. For details, see [ID:nSGE6A4055]

Like many other Latin American currencies, Chile's peso has soared in recent months, putting pressure on the country's exporters.

After soaring as much as 2.1 percent on Thursday, the peso recorded a weekly gain of 2.5 percent, its biggest since May this year.

The peso barely budged after the country's central bank on Thursday announced fresh measures to encourage outflows and ease the peso's recent rally. [ID:nN04221079]

The central bank raised the foreign investment limit for pension funds -- a measure analysts at Standard Chartered said should have little impact. "Tax breaks to encourage outbound investment may be required to sweeten the deal," they wrote in a note on Friday. [ID:nN04221079]

"The Chilean peso still appears to be one of the strongest currency plays in Latin America," they said.

The Mexican peso currency <MXN=> also fared slightly better thanks to improved U.S. jobs data. The United States buys about 80 percent of Mexico's exports. The peso is very sensitive to the changing outlook for the U.S. economy.

The peso firmed 0.25 percent to 12.2015 per dollar and was heading for a weekly gain of 1.15 percent.

Analysts believe Mexico's hands-off approach to its currency market will help boost the peso over coming weeks.

"The central bank will be willing to take the appreciation as long as it's not in a very disordered fashion," said Italo Lombardi, a Latin American economist and strategist with BNP Paribas in New York.

COLOMBIA GETS TOUGH

Meanwhile, Colombia and Brazil have taken much more aggressive measures to slow their currencies' rallies.

Colombia's central bank chief Jose Dario Uribe said on Friday that the bank is not ruling out the possibility of "big" interventions in the foreign exchange market. [ID:nN05292894]

The Andean country has already extended dollar purchases in the market but some fear the country may resort to capital controls.

Brazil's real struggled on Friday, but largely because of the dollar's recovery rather than intervention fears.

The dollar had plummeted on Thursday following the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to pump $600 billion into the economy, boosting Brazil's real to a two-week high and giving Chile's peso its biggest one-day gain in more than a year.

On Brazil's local spot market, the bid quote for the real <BRBY> traded flat for most of Friday, closing 0.12 percent weaker at 1.678 against the dollar. The U.S. data had less direct impact on Brazil, which counts China as its top trading partner.

But the currency still firmed 1.37 percent over the week thanks to the post-Fed boost, its biggest weekly gain in five weeks.

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Stronger As US Fed Unveils Stimulus Plan
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed Wednesday at its strongest level against the dollar since late April as the U.S. Federal Reserve unveiled plans to buy Treasurys in support of the U.S. economic recovery.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.2510 to the dollar, compared with MXN12.3450 at the close Monday. Local markets were closed Tuesday for the All Souls Day holiday.

The decision by the Federal Open Market Committee to buy $600 billion in Treasurys by the end of June, and reinvest an additional $250 billion to $300 billion in proceeds from mortgage holdings, was broadly in line with expectations.

The implications for the peso of Fed support for the U.S. economy are twofold, as increased global liquidity prompts inflows into emerging markets, and the peso benefits from growth in the U.S. economy, which receives around 80% of Mexico's exports.

"The peso has responded more strongly to expectations of a possible second round of quantitative easing in the U.S.," BBVA Research said in a report. "This increased sensitivity, combined with the outlook on foreign flows, favors a positive short-term trend in the currency."

With the Bank of Mexico showing little willingness to intervene to keep the peso from strengthening, measures such as Brazil's tax on fixed-income operations could encourage a preference for Mexican assets and invite more capital inflows in the short term, BBVA said, adding that it expects the peso could move toward MXN12 to the dollar in the remainder of the year.

Mexico's economy is more closely tied to the U.S. than those of Brazil and other South American countries, and the slowdown in the U.S. recovery is expected to take some of the steam out of the export manufacturing-led rebound in Mexico. Gross domestic product grew 5.9% in the first half of the year, and is estimated to have grown 5% in the third quarter. Mexican officials are expecting domestic demand to take up some of the slack from a slowdown ahead in the pace of export growth.

RBC Capital Markets said in a report that at a meeting with investors, Bank of Mexico Governor Agustin Carstens indicated some gradual strengthening of the peso would be welcome as it would have a positive impact on consumer perceptions. "Gov. Carstens was very clear, stating they oppose FX policy actions which could have a damaging long-lasting impact on markets, specifically highlighting capital controls and tax measures as undesirable [although he did mention that under very extreme circumstances these could be necessary]," RBC said.

The Bank of Mexico buys up to $600 million a month under a system of put options that give holders the right to sell dollars to the central bank when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average. At last week's options auction, banks paid the highest premium yet for the options, an indication that further peso gains are expected.

The central bank uses the options to accumulate additional foreign reserves against future bouts of global market volatility. The central bank reported Wednesday that reserves were a record $110.66 billion on Oct. 29, up $19.82 from the end of 2009. The main source of the reserves is crude oil, as the central bank changes dollars for state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos.

-By Anthony Harrup, Dow Jones Newswires; 5255-5980-5176, anthony.harrup@dowjones.com [ 03-11-10 2020GMT ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  seesaw on Fed,  intervention
text:
* Uncertainty grows over scale of U.S. stimulus package

* Brazil's real adds 0.1 pct, Mexican peso loses 0.5 pct

* Chile peso weakens 0.6 pct, intervention eyed

* Argentina's risk spread narrows after Kirchner's death

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies seesawed on Wednesday on uncertainty over the extent of likely stimulus measures to revive the U.S. economy, which are expected to boost the region's bond market.

The U.S. Federal Reserve is expected next week to unveil a program of U.S. Treasury bond purchases worth a few hundred billion dollars over several months, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday. That rattled some investors who had envisioned a bigger and more immediate stimulus package.

Such measures are likely to keep U.S. yields low, encouraging more investors to pump cash into Latin America's higher-yielding bonds.

Brazil is a prime target because its benchmark interest rate of 10.75 percent is one of the highest in the world.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> opened weaker but was later bid 0.12 percent stronger at 1.702 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"There is some uncertainty over the Fed's policy next week so the market is 'on the fence' today," said Carlos Gandolfo, a partner at Sao Paulo's Pioneer brokerage.

But traders were also looking to get back into the market after recent losses. The currency has underperformed the region over the past few days because of tough action by the government to curb the real's recent rally, which is hurting exporters and widening the current account deficit.

The central bank has recently stepped up its dollar purchases in the spot market. The government also this month tripled its tax on foreign bond purchases to 6 percent and raised a tax on the collateral investors must put down to trade in the futures market. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on intervention: http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p("http://r.reuters.com/kuv79p")

Analysis on Brazil's forex reform: [ID:nN26120199] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

But such measures may only have a short-term effect on the real, some analysts say.

Higher commodity prices and stimulus measures abroad are likely to overshadow intervention, causing the real to keep appreciating, analysts at Citigroup said in a research note.

"Our skepticism regarding the impacts of those measures on medium- and long-term horizons led us to reduce our year-end 2010 and 2011 USD/BRL forecasts to 1.65 (from 1.72) and to 1.70 (from 1.80), respectively," they said.

EXPORTERS IN FOCUS

The Mexican currency <MXN=> weakened 0.51 percent to 12.468 per dollar after trading at multi-month highs earlier this week.

The peso has rallied about 6 percent since the end of August. But Mexico is not losing export competitiveness because of these currency gains, the finance minister said on Wednesday. [ID:nN27223162]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 0.58 percent to 494.10 per dollar, hitting its weakest level in about a month.

The currency has come under pressure from the threat of intervention. Unlike Mexico, Chile has faced growing pressure from its exporters to take action.

President Sebastian Pinera said on Monday his government is working to open capital accounts and relax limits on investments abroad to battle the currency's rally.

Traders are concerned that more aggressive measures are on their way, such as a return to dollar purchases.

Elsewhere in the region, the risk spread on Argentina's bonds narrowed to 511 basis points following the death of former President Nestor Kirchner. [ID:nN27249576]

The policies of Kirchner, who was expected to run for president in 2011, have caused great concern among investors. (Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Little Changed After Breaching 12.30 Mark
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed little changed against the U.S. dollar Monday in a volatile session in which the rate dipped briefly below the key 12.30 level.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN12.3505, compared with MXN12.3490 at the close Friday. The currency gave back early gains, which were prompted by a weekend agreement by Group of 20 developed and developing nations to avoid competitive devaluations of currencies, encouraging investors to move into emerging markets.

The concern for a number of Latin American countries, and particularly Brazil, has been the appreciation of their currencies as portfolio investors pour money into their markets seeking more attractive yields.

The Mexican peso has appreciated less than most of its regional peers, and Mexico is seen among the least likely to intervene directly or impose capital controls.

"We do not expect the MXN to join the 'currency wars,'" Citigroup Banamex said in a report. Given the three usual options in the face of strong inflows--to allow the currency to appreciate, intervene in the local foreign exchange market, or slash local interest rates--"we think the first option is the most likely in the case of Mexico," Banamex added.

The Bank of Mexico buys up to $600 million a month under put options that can be exercised by banks when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average. On the rates front, the central bank has held the benchmark overnight rate at 4.5% since July 2009 and is expected to leave it unchanged until the third quarter of 2011.

The recent gains in the peso, Banamex said, are probably a response to an attractive carry trade, where investors sell currencies with low interest and buy currencies offering higher yields.

The brief move below 12.30, and prospects of continued dollar weakness, prompted RBC Capital Markets to again move the target on its long peso recomendation to 12 to the dollar from 12.30, and to tighten the stop loss to 12.45 from 12.55.

ING Mexico said in a report that markets are likely to continue responding to increased appetite for risk with a weak dollar as a counterpart, and to uncertainty over how the U.S. Federal Reserve will go about quantitative easing.

"The external context remains favorable for local assets and we anticipate further appreciation of the peso toward our target of 12.25," ING said.

Mexico's stocks rose modestly Monday, but enough for another record-high close, while government bonds gained ground, pushing yields down. The yield on benchmark 10-year bonds fell two basis points to 6.11%, and the yield on 20-year bonds slipped one basis point to 6.81%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real suffers from gov't pressure
text:
* Intervention concerns push Brazil's real down 1 pct

* Mexican peso adds 0.1 pct, U.S. jobs data helps

* Chile's peso dips 0.1 pct after new gov't measure

By Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's real underperformed the region's currencies on Thursday as moves by the government to curb the real's recent rally unsettled investors.

Late on Wednesday the country's authorities closed some loopholes in one of their most recent measures: a tax on the money investors have to put up to trade Brazilian derivatives.

The authorities blocked local banks from lending, swapping, or renting out securities to foreigners for use as collateral. It also forbid the exchange from accepting letters of credit as collateral. Shares of Brazil's BM&FBovespa exchange operator led declines on the country's stock market on Thursday.

"The persistent change to the rules of the game generates unwelcome uncertainty, giving the message that foreigners are not welcome in the domestic fixed-income market," wrote analysts at HSBC.

Brazil has taken aggressive action to curb the recent rally in the real, which is making exporters' goods more expensive abroad and worsening the current account deficit.

The real <BRBY> fell 1 percent to 1.690 on the local market in intraday trading on Thursday, recoiling further from the 2-year high it hit earlier this month.

The real's losses were largely due to these new minor rule changes, said Rodrigo Nassar, head of trading at brokerage Hencorp Commcor in Sao Paulo. "This has ended up making the market uncomfortable" and is "causing more discontent," he said.

Growing expectations the U.S central bank will launch a new round of asset buying, known as quantitative easing, to kick-start the economy have boosted Latin America's currencies to multi-month highs.

Such easing is likely to keep yields on U.S. Treasuries close to record lows, encouraging investors to flock to higher-yielding debt in Latin America.

CHILE'S PESO GETS FIRST TASTE OF FX MEASURES

Chile announced on Thursday it would cut red tape on customs to help exporters hit by a strong peso as one measure to ease the effects of the local currency's rapid appreciation. The government also threatened that other tools could be on their way. [ID:nN21292275]

But the measure was relatively mild compared to the activities of other countries in the region and the Chilean peso <CLP=> only lost 0.05 percent to 484.65 per dollar. In the last couple of weeks, analysts have started to talk more about the possibility of government measures to tame the peso, which is trading around a 29-month high against the dollar.

Other potential announcements could include changes to pension fund regulations, analysts said.

As an openly traded currency, Mexico's peso does not present the same intervention risk for investors.

On the other hand, the country's close trade links with the United States has been the main concern, causing volatility in the market as the outlook for the U.S. economy constantly changes.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> crept up 0.06 percent to 12.3878 per dollar on Thursday after data showed U.S. claims for unemployment benefits fell more than expected last week, pointing to some improvement in the labor market. title: =DJ  FOREX  VIEW: Mexico Likely To Stay Neutral In  Currency  Battles
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Latin American countries fighting what some governments see as a currency war aren't likely to find an ally in Mexico.

Amid global tensions over exchange rates, Brazil has raised a tax on certain financial operations in an effort to discourage the heavy foreign capital inflows that are boosting its real, while Thailand this week removed a tax break on foreign investment in its government bonds in an attempt to slow the baht's rise, and the U.S. Federal Reserve appears poised for another round of quantitative easing that could weaken the dollar.

The Mexican peso still has room to recover from the beating it took in 2008 and 2009, despite its own recent appreciation. The peso is trading around MXN12.40 to the dollar, up 6.5% year-to-date and 26% from its all-time low in March 2009, but still nearly 20% weaker from before the 2008 crisis. Brazil's real, meanwhile, is up 5% year-to-date but 41% stronger from the end of 2008.

Mexican policy makers appear loathe to intervene to weaken the peso and give Mexican exports a competitive advantage.

During a weekend visit to Washington, Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero said his country "believes and trusts" in a free-floating currency, which has allowed Mexico to absorb external shocks in the past. Cordero said countries need to be careful when implementing "easy fixes" such as capital controls, noting that the Brazilian real continues to appreciate despite such measures. Exchange policy shouldn't be a trade policy tool, he added.

Cordero described Mexico's currency circumstance as "fortunately different" than that of some other Latin American countries, alluding to recent export gains in the U.S. market. Mexican products now represent 13% of U.S. imports compared with 10% just three years ago, Cordero said, attributing the advance to structural advantages that Mexico boasts over other countries--its geographical location, border trade infrastructure, and improving labor productivity--rather than relying on foreign exchange advantages.

"It's evident that Mexico is a stand-alone case compared with South American countries because of its greater exposure to the U.S. trade balance. We have seen that when the risk premium rises due to uncertainty about the U.S. recovery, the peso is the currency that most suffers," said Moises Junca, chief Latin America foreign exchange strategist with BBVA Securities.

Yet some see Mexico's export gains as a crutch.

"The Mexican peso has been a laggard among the region's appreciating currencies for a reason: whereas other countries can rely on some degree of domestic demand strength to cushion their economies against currency strength, the Mexican recovery remains externally driven," Luis Arcentales, an economist with Morgan Stanley, wrote in a Monday research note. "And with export-oriented industry already decelerating, Mexico seems to be the economy that can least afford significant currency strength."

Gross domestic product expanded 5.9% in the first half of the year and is expected to slow in the second half for full-year growth between 4% and 5%. Below-capacity output and low inflation have allowed the central bank to hold its benchmark overnight lending rate at 4.5% since July 2009, with no signs that it's contemplating a rate increase before the second half of 2011. Brazil's benchmark selic rate is 10.75% and expected to rise early next year.

The rebound in exports after a trade slump in 2009, rising crude prices, and remittances from Mexicans living in the U.S. are all sources of peso strength. Also this year, Mexico's Oct. 1 inclusion in Citibank's World Government Bond Index is seen attracting as much as $16 billion in fresh foreign investment, much of which has presumably already arrived.

While policy makers in countries like Brazil, Colombia and Peru are intervening to limit currency appreciation, Mexico has adhered to a comparatively subtle mechanism of selling $600 million in dollar put options each month. The Bank of Mexico uses the options to build foreign reserves when the peso is appreciating; commercial banks can exercise the options when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average.

Recent peso gains have led to some discussion on whether the central bank might opt to raise the dollar amount of the options it sells each month. RBC Capital Markets thinks that's a possibility, but adds that "the MXN is one of the least vulnerable emerging market currencies to foreign exchange intervention."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains despite threats; peso firms
text:
* Brazil's real gains despite intervention warnings

* Mexico peso firms 0.2 percent on Fed hopes

* Chile's peso strengthens for fourth straight session

(Adds comments about Brazil's real, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/BRAZIL, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's real strengthened on Monday despite fresh efforts by the government to talk down the currency and protect the country's struggling exporters.

Brazil's finance minister said the country still has an arsenal of measures to stop the real strengthening during an "international currency war" in which governments are manipulating currencies to boost export competitiveness. See[ID:nN27256208]

But traders have gradually become used to hearing such threats, which have yet to be followed up by concrete action.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.06 percent stronger at 1.708 reais on the local spot market after the warnings.

A record-breaking stock sale from state oil company Petrobras has prompted investors to pour money into Brazil over the past few weeks.

Since buyers must hand over their cash for the shares on Wednesday this week, Monday is the last day when foreign investors will bring their dollars into the country because it takes about 48 hours to make a currency transaction in Brazil.

It's possible Mantega's comments were just "a conditional threat he hopes not to have to act upon," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging market research for the Americas at Nomura Securities.

Even if the government does take further measures, it is likely they are "waiting for both the Petrobras transaction to close and next Sunday's presidential election to pass before acting," he said.

Mexico's peso extended gains on Monday, also boosted by the weaker dollar which sent investors looking for higher-yielding assets in Latin America.

The peso <MXN=><MEX01> strengthened 0.19 percent to 12.526 per dollar. The currency is poised to record its largest gains in the month of September in 28 years according to Mexican bank Banamex.

EYES ON FED

Investors are betting the U.S. central bank will boost money supply to aid economic recovery in the United States, Mexico's most important trading partner.

Investors expect the Fed will keep interest rates near zero through 2011 and could even increase its purchases of U.S. bonds, which would also help keep yields down on Treasuries.

The expectation of lower yields on U.S. Treasuries has prompted a rally in higher-yielding Latin American assets.

Still, traders said the peso's rapid acceleration could slow later in the session as U.S. stock markets edged lower.

"Last week's gains were helped by a strong performance in the stock markets, but the peso's acceleration is going to pause a bit as markets are a bit sluggish on renewed concerns about the health of European banks," said Ramon Cordova, a trader at brokerage BASE in Monterrey, Mexico. .

The euro earlier dipped after ratings firm Moody's cut Anglo Irish Bank's lower-grade debt and kept it on review for a downgrade, a move that highlighted concerns over the euro zone banking sector. [ID:nN27338134]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed for the fourth straight session, gaining 0.25 percent to 485.3 per dollar and closing at its strongest level since June 2008. A weaker dollar, booming growth, and strong demand for Chile's copper exports have boosted the currency over recent months.

Lower yields in the United States have also prompted investors to venture into some of the most inhospitable parts of Latin America's capital markets, such as Venezuelan debt.

Prices for Venezuela's benchmark bonds due in 2027 <VENGLB27=RR> were boosted further on Monday as investors bet that opposition gains in Sunday's parliamentary elections might temper the behavior of President Hugo Chavez. [ID:nN27245671]
