title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed; Brazil real puts focus on cbank
text:
* U.S. jobs, housing and manufacturing data boosts region

* Brazil's real firms 0.9 pct, Mexican peso adds 0.2 pct

* U.S. payrolls report could determine Brazil c.bank moves (Updates closing levels)

By Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real extended its rally on Thursday after the government confirmed a long-awaited oil fundraising plan which should lure a huge amount of money to Brazil.

The gains put more pressure on the central bank to step up its intervention in the currency market to protect exporters, whose goods have become increasingly expensive abroad as a result of the real's rally.

Optimism over the U.S. economic recovery after a rush of strong employment, manufacturing and housing data over the past two days, also boosted the rest of Latin America's currencies.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.86 percent stronger at 1.730 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market -- the third straight day of gains, taking the real to a fresh four-month high.

After weeks of speculation, Brazil's government finally set the price it will charge state-owned oil company Petrobras for crude reserves to be used in a $43 billion oil-for-shares swap. [ID:nN01187399]

The announcement put an end to recent uncertainty and boosted the currency.

"For the currency, the biggest effect really is the confirmation of the capitalization. This is what is giving most support to the real, even though it's now under this support level of 1.75 (reais per dollar)," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for the CM Capital Markets brokerage in Sao Paulo.

INTERVENTION THREAT

If Brazil's currency remains stronger than 1.75 reais against the dollar for an extended period, the central bank could try to intervene in the market, analysts had said.

But now some believe the central bank could only take new measures once the 1.70 real-per-dollar level is broken.

Verbal warnings, bigger or multiple U.S. dollar purchases and intervention in the futures market via so-called reverse swaps are the most likely options. [ID:nN23213114]

"It is a near-term risk; either that they buy dollars more aggressively or possibly resume those FX reverse swap auctions as we approach 1.70," said Paul Biszko, a strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

If Friday's key U.S. monthly payrolls report comes out better than expected, prompting the currency to rally further, the central bank may well step up its intervention, he said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> edged 0.2 percent higher to 13.0364 per dollar following the strong U.S. data which raised hopes about the recovery of Mexico's top trading partner.

However, investors were cautious ahead of the payrolls report.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 0.14 percent to 497.20 per dollar after hitting its strongest level in more than seven months, as the price of copper, the country's main export, rose. [ID:nLDE6810SN]

Traders in Santiago said banks took advantage of the early rally to buy dollars at a relatively cheap level.

YIELDS FALL AFTER BRAZIL RATE HELD

Yields fell on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> after the country's central bank held the benchmark interest rate at 10.75 percent late on Wednesday.

Although the decision had been widely expected, the bank also signaled that there was little chance of further rate hikes in the months ahead. [ID:nN01111893]

"We retain our view of protracted pause of the monetary policy as long as commodities prices remain well behaved," said analysts at RBS Securities.

However, they said yields were also falling after sharp gains on Wednesday following strong manufacturing data from China and the United States.

The interest rate futures market in Brazil tends to react just as much to the changing outlook for global growth as it does to national interest rate expectations, they noted.

The yield on the contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily traded contracts of the early session, fell to 11.31 percent from 11.37 percent. (Additional reporting by Froilan Romero and Molly Rosbach in Santiago; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso sinks, Colombia unit firms
text:
* Mexico peso hit by weak retail, bomb threat scare

* Colombia central bank holds trigger on intervention

* Mexico peso weakens 1.24 pct, Colombia unit adds 0.43

* Brazil's real slips 0.4 pct, tracking U.S. markets (Recasts, changes byline and dateline, updates prices)

By Jean Luis Arce and Nelson Bocanegra

MEXICO CITY/BOGOTA Aug 23 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso sank to a one-month low on Monday, hurt by surprisingly weak June retail sales data while Colombia's peso firmed in relief the central bank did not begin intervening in the currency market.

Mexico's June retail sales report undermined hopes that consumer demand will offset slowing growth in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner. [ID:nN23157622]

June retail sales fell 0.77 percent compared with May, and only grew 1.5 percent year-on-year, compared with expectations of a 4.1 percent rise.

"That's a sharp slowdown and doesn't help for consumers and it doesn't tell us a good story in terms of consumption, which is what we expect to recover in the coming months," said Italo Lombardi, a strategist at BNP Paribas in New York.

The Mexican currency extended already steep losses on reports of a bomb threat to the stock exchange in Mexico City, which officials later said was a false alarm. [ID:nN23212566]

Rising violence related to the government's battle against drug cartels has made the peso more sensitive to news related to security concerns.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> sunk to its weakest since July 20 against the dollar, losing 1.2 percent to 12.9075 per dollar.

INTERVENTION RELIEF

Colombia's peso firmed on Monday, outperforming the region's currencies, after the country's central bank surprised investors late Friday by not announcing measures to curb the peso's recent rally.

Investment in Colombia's booming oil and mining sectors has caused the peso to strengthen about 13 percent this year, putting huge pressure on the country's exporters.

The peso <COP=STFX> bid 0.43 percent stronger to 1,813.40 per dollar.

However, traders and analysts were still cautious and expected the central bank could move to intervene if the dollar-peso exchange rate fell much below 1,800 per dollar.

"The trend is moderate, since traders still expect an announcement from the central bank in the coming days," said Banco de Bogota in a report.

Venezuela's announcement late last week that it would pay Colombian companies $200 million to compensate after a trade dispute also lifted the peso, said Karen Alfonso, head of economic research at the Afin brokerage in Bogota. [ID:nN20166203]

The Chilean peso, which has also been under pressure due to intervention threats, bid down a slight 0.1 percent at 504.50 per dollar.

Analysts doubt Chile will implement major dollar purchases to keep its currency from appreciating. However, the government could slow the pace at which it repatriates dollars from copper sales.

Brazil's real <BRBY> shed 0.4 percent to bid at 1.765 per dollar.

Traders in Sao Paulo said the currency was taking its lead from Wall Street due to the absence of key U.S. economic data -- firming in the morning as U.S. stocks gained but trading weaker in the afternoon when the major U.S. equity indexes turned negative.

However, the real was trading at its strongest level against the Mexican peso <BRLMXN=R> in over a month. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson and in Sao Paulo and Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Mexico  currencies  gain
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Chilean peso surges 1 pct in week on rate hike

* Intervention talk knocks Colombian peso down 1.1 pct

* Mexico peso dips 0.31 pct on growth fears

* Brazil real sheds 0.7 pct

* Mexican bonds rally after Fed maintains low rates

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso and Brazil's real edged up on Friday after being battered through the week by concerns about slowing growth in the United States even as losses were contained by flows into the region's bonds.

Chile's peso brushed off global concerns to surge about 1 percent this week as the central back hiked interest rates for the third month in a row. But Colombia's peso sank more than 1 percent since the previous Friday amid the threat of government intervention in the exchange market.

The U.S. Federal Reserve expressed deeper concerns about U.S. growth this week that rattled stock and currency markets. Some investors are betting the U.S. economy could slip back into recession after recovering from a deep slump last year.

"There is real uncertainty about the economic activity in the United States, and this will keep affecting the foreign exchange market," said Salvador Orozco, a currency and debt strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

But investors sitting on cash were drawn to Latin American bonds. Local debt offers higher yields than the meager returns on government bonds in major developed markets, where policymakers have pledged to keep interest rates low to support growth.

More prudent fiscal management in Latin America during the past decade has put the shine on local debt amid Europe's debt troubles.

Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> shed 25 basis points this week to bid at a record low of 6.29 percent on Friday.

"We never thought we would see such low yields, but it is a function of the foreigners' liquidity," Orozco said.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> edged up 0.07 to 12.7225 per dollar on Friday after data showed rising, but still tepid, U.S. August consumer confidence and July retail sales. The peso shed 0.31 percent for the week.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.11 percent stronger at 1.770 per dollar in the local spot market. In international trade, the real <BRL=> shed about 0.7 percent for the week.

JAWBONING GAINS

Colombia's peso sank for a second straight session due to concerns local authorities will intervene in the foreign exchange markets to cool sharp currency gains that are hurting local exporters.

Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> shed 0.47 percent to 1,834.90 per dollar, racking up a 1.1 percent loss for the week.

Before sharp losses in the last two sessions, the Colombian currency had gained about 12 percent since early May, boosted by investment flows into the country's oil and mining industries, which also drew speculative traders.

Analysts think Colombia could reinstate daily dollar purchases that expired in June, but that would do little more than slow the pace of gains.

Chile's peso closed at a five-month high on Friday, a day after the country's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 2 percent, in line with expectations, as the economy bounces back from a devastating earthquake. For more, see [ID:nN12145806]

Chile's peso's <CLP=CL> edged up 0.02 percent to 509.40 per dollar, posting a 1 percent gain for the week.

The country's currency has firmed about 7 percent since the end of June. Chilean President Sebastian Pinera hinted Thursday the government could cash in less dollar revenue from copper sales to offset the flows into Chilean assets. [ID:nN12124343]

But analysts looked for the currency to firm further on expectations of more interest rate hikes by the central bank, which is seen taking its benchmark rate to 3.75 percent by year-end. [ID:nN12129420] (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  dip on U.S. consumer mood
text:
* Brazil Finance Minister tips possible intervention

* Brazil real loses 0.41 pct, Mexico peso slides 0.15 pct

* Chiles peso knocked off three-month high

(New throughout, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, July 27 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies slipped on Tuesday, hurt by a drop in U.S. consumer confidence, and Brazil's real lost ground after the country's finance minister backed further central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso hit its highest level in over a month early in the session and Chile's peso traded at a three-month high before lackluster stock markets pushed investors to cash in on recent gains in the region's currencies.

Confidence among American consumers dropped in July to the lowest level since February on worries about the job market, the Conference Board reported on Tuesday.

"There are a lot of mixed signals out there, such as talk of deflationary pressures but then you see good earnings reports," said Jorge Perez-Duarte, managing director of emerging markets at TD Securities in Toronto.

"We have seen a good rally in the last few days, so it is a bit of a technical rebound as people take some profits," Perez-Duarte said.

Mexico's peso has advanced 3 percent from a low on July 2, while the real has gained more than 2 percent since June 29.

Concerns have eased about a financial crisis in Europe following stress tests of banks, while solid revenue outlooks from some bellwether companies like FedEx have offset fears the U.S. economy is slowing.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> slipped 0.15 percent to 12.6895 per U.S. dollar while the Brazilian real <BRL=> bid 0.41 percent weaker in international trade to 1.7688 per dollar. Chile's peso <CLP=CL> shed 0.19 percent to 519.70 per dollar.

BRAZIL JAWBONING

Brazil's finance minister Guido Mantega on Tuesday voiced his support for central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets. [ID:nN2798713]

Speculation is mounting that the central bank could step up measures to contain the real's strength, which is hurting exporters. The bank itself informally sounded out demand for reverse currency swaps last week.

But analysts were skeptical that new measures would have much more success than a capital inflow tax and daily dollar purchases.

"I do not think verbal intervention will be enough, because even actual intervention has not been enough," Perez-Duarte said.

Investors will continue to demand Brazilian assets due to the country's prospects for growth and some of the highest yields among investment-grade emerging markets, analysts said.

Brazil launched $750 million worth of reopened 2021 global bonds on Tuesday, more than the $500 million initially offered, as the deal found strong demand among investors, Thomson Reuters' IFR reported. [ID:nN27184714]

Yield spreads between emerging market bonds and U.S. Treasuries, a key gauge of risk aversion, narrowed 10 basis points to 273 basis points on Tuesday, according to the JPMorgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ>.

The country risk spread on Brazilian bonds fell 7 basis points to 198 basis points, trading at its narrowest since the middle of May. (Editing by Eric Walsh)

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm  currencies  firm on US housing data
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Surge in U.S. home sales eases concerns of "double dip"

* Mexican peso firms 0.47 pct, Brazil's real up 0.61

* Colombia peso at 9-month high, Chile's at 3-month peak (Updates prices, adds comments)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, July 26 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Monday after data showing a surge in sales of new homes during June in the United States restored some confidence in the recovery of the world's biggest economy.

Brazil's local spot market was kept on edge by concerns the central bank could shift the method its uses to intervene in the market to limit the real's appreciation.

Mexico's peso <MXN=>, which is closely linked to its northern neighbor and top trading partner, rose to its strongest in more than a week. Colombia's peso hit a nine-month high and Chile's currency headed toward its strongest close in almost three months.

A surprising 23.6 percent jump in new home sales in June from May countered some disappointing data in recent weeks that heightened concerns the economy may slip back into recession.

"The U.S. housing market is not as a bad as it was thought previously. There is a very high improbability of a double dip and that is helping currencies around the world," said Kathryn Rooney, an analyst covering Latin America at Bulltick Capital Markets in Miami.

Fears over a fresh slowdown in U.S. growth have hit Mexico particularly hard since the country sends about 80 percent of its exports to the United States.

The Mexican currency firmed 0.47 percent to 12.67 per dollar, according to Reuters data, while Chile's peso <CLP=CL><CLP=> gained 0.25 percent. Brazil's real <BRL=> gained 0.61 percent to 1.7618 per U.S. dollar in international trade.

Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> strengthened 0.47 percent to 1859.35 per U.S. dollar.

Colombia's currency has been boosted by higher expectations for oil revenue, as well as bets the country's president-elect will pass fiscal reforms that will win the country an investment grade from Wall Street ratings agencies.

"Colombia is taking a right step and we expect a ratings upgrade in the near future," wrote Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch strategists in a note to clients.

The bank's analysts last Friday raised their target for the Colombian peso to 1850 per dollar for the end of the third quarter.

Gains for the Mexican peso were limited during most of the session as local banks exercised $571 million in dollar options. The central bank began selling $600 million in dollar put options every month earlier this year to accumulate reserves.

The exercise of the options can limit the peso's appreciation in the spot market as local banks sell dollars to the central bank, rather than dumping them into the spot market.

With the amount exercised on Monday, no more options contracts remain for the rest for July.

On Brazil's local spot market, the real <BRBY> was 0.4 percent weaker, closing at 1.765. Concerns about intervention by the central bank hit the real in international trade late on Friday after the local market had closed.

Traders cited chatter that the central bank could move to sell reverse swaps instead of, or as well as, buying U.S. dollars in the spot market.

Reverse swaps are a form of derivative that would allow the central bank to take a long position in the U.S. dollar futures market in exchange for a short position in the interest rate markets.

Selling reverse swaps would be a way to reduce the arbitrage opportunities in the market, which have arisen due to the huge reserves the central bank has amassed through daily U.S. dollar auctions used to slow the real's appreciation. (Editing by Dan Grebler)

* IMF raises LatAm growth forecast for 2010, 2011

* Mexico peso up as cenbank says recent gains not excessive

* Brazil markets closed due to national holiday

By Walter Brandimarte

NEW YORK, April 20 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies gained on Wednesday, with the Chilean peso rebounding sharply and the Mexican peso supported by comments from the country's central bank chief.

News that the International Monetary Fund revised up its growth forecasts for the Latin America supported the view that policymakers will soon raise rates to curb accelerating inflation, drawing more dollars to the region.

Latin American stocks ended slightly lower, however, as a Wall Street rally ran out of steam and Brazilian financial markets were closed due to a national holiday.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.4 percent to 12.1682 per dollar after Banco de Mexico Governor Agustin Carstens was quoted by the El Economista newspaper as saying a recent surge in the value of the currency was not excessive. For details see [ID:nN21183915]

"This undermines the idea that the Bank of Mexico could intervene in a more aggressive way," said Daniela Blancas, a currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City.

The Mexican currency has gained more than 7 percent this year and that has stoked speculation that the central bank could become more active in the market with measures such as the daily auctions to buy dollars seen in Brazil and Colombia.

In Chile, the peso <CLP=CL> rallied 1.04 percent to 521.80 per dollar after six consecutive sessions of losses took the exchange rate to a three-week low.

Traders said investors decided to take profits after the currency found strong support at around 528 pesos per dollar.

Also boosting currencies were the IMF's new growth forecast for the region this year, which was revised up to 4 percent from 3.7 percent. [ID:nWEQ003880]

The fund said monetary policy in the region should move from highly accommodative to more neutral levels once the recovery has gathered momentum, adding that Brazil appears to be close to that turning point.

Despite the optimism in the foreign exchange market, Latin American stocks edged lower, with the MSCI stock index for the region <.MILA00000PUS> dipping 0.11 percent.

Mexico's IPC stock index <.MXX> lost 0.88 percent, while Chile's blue-chip IPSA index <.IPSA> finished near flat.

title: Mexico peso firms, bond yields fall to 1-year low
text:
* Peso firms 0.4 pct, helped by central banker's comments

* 10-year bond yields hit lowest since early May 2009

* IPC stock index falls 0.88 pct as America Movil drags (Adds closing stock prices, background on peso strength)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, April 21 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso firmed on Wednesday after comments from the country's central bank chief cooled speculation that policymakers could intervene in markets to curb the currency's recent surge.

The country's currency was also supported by flows into local peso bonds as investors bet Mexico's economic prospects were better than those of some countries in Europe, driving yields down to their lowest in almost a year.

The peso <MXN=> <MEX01> strengthened 0.4 percent to 12.1682 per U.S. dollar.

The IPC stock index <.MXX> closed down 0.88 percent to 33,517.18, hurt by a 1.34 percent loss in shares of index heavyweight wireless provider America Movil .

Central Bank Governor Agustin Carstens said a recent surge in the peso's value was not excessive, according to a newspaper interview. For details see [ID:nN21183915].

"This undermines the idea that the Bank of Mexico could intervene in a more aggressive way," said Daniela Blancas, a currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City.

Some market players have been speculating that the peso's more than 7 percent gain this year has been making policymakers uncomfortable. A strong currency makes exports more expensive and may crimp Mexico's rebound from a deep recession in 2009.

Some analysts expect the central bank will raise the amount of dollars it buys from the market each month through a program of dollar option sales it implemented to build up reserves.

But others have speculated the bank could take even more aggressive measures such as the daily dollar auctions seen in Brazil and Colombia.

On Wednesday, the central bank said option holders had sold $5 million to the central bank, the last of $600 million in options sold at the end of last month.

The option program has helped the central bank lift reserves to a record 97.4 billion as of the end of last week.

The yield on the government's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> bid down 10 basis points to 7.45 percent, its lowest since May 7, 2009, according to Reuters data.

Spreads between Greek and German bond yields hit a 12-year high on Wednesday, highlighting uncertainty about how Athens would resolve its debt crisis and boosting the appeal of Latin American countries with comparatively better debt profiles.

"There is a greater stability in terms of managing debt in the region of Latin America," said Alejandro Martinez, a debt and currency strategist at HSBC in Mexico City.

The stronger peso has also helped reduce inflationary pressures by cheapening imports and analysts have been paring back expectations on when Mexico will hike interest rates.

Brokerage IXE this week said policymakers will wait until early next year before tightening borrowing costs.

title: Mexico peso sinks on Greece woes, stocks fall
text:
* Peso falls by most in 2 weeks, IPC slips from record

* Greece debt worries hit global markets

* Speculation on more cenbank intervention also weigh (Recasts throughout, adds comments, closing stock prices)

MEXICO CITY, April 7 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso sank by the most in two weeks on Wednesday as concerns over Greece's debt problems sapped appetite for riskier assets and pushed investors to take profits on recent gains.

The peso <MXN=><MEX01> lost 0.52 percent to 12.2881 per U.S. dollar while the IPC stock index <.MXX> fell 0.5 percent from a record peak to 33,632.35.

Greece's borrowing costs hit a new high on Wednesday as the government said the country's banks sought increased support and euro-zone states argued about conditions of potential bailout loans. For details see [ID:nLDE636138]

"There is nervousness in currencies due to Greece," said Carlos Gomez, an analyst at Invex brokerage in Mexico City.

Concerns of a debt default in Greece have weighed on emerging market currencies in recent months, as riskier assets could sell off if Europe's debt troubles spur a larger financial crisis.

The peso fell by its biggest one-day percentage drop since March 24, when concerns of Portugal's downgrade hit global markets.

Despite the peso's losses, traders noted it outperformed other emerging market currencies and argued the peso's appreciation trend will continue.

"The market is taking a little breather," said Daniela Blancas, a currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City. "This does'nt imply a change in tendency," she added.

The peso has gained more than 7 percent this year, before today's losses, helped by signs of an economic rebound in Mexico and its top trading partner the United States.

Some analysts pointed to bets that the central bank could soon step up its dollar purchase program, which could hurt the peso as the bank buys up dollars through option contracts. For details see [ID:nN06583990]

The peso was hurt by "speculation that Banxico could slow the recent appreciation of the Mexican currency by increasing its current mechanism to accumulate reserves," wrote Gabriela Siller, and analyst at brokerage BASE in Monterrey.

title: Mexico's Stocks Chalk Up Second Straight Record-High Close
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexican stocks rose to a second consecutive record-high close Tuesday as investors continued to bet on the economic recovery and the peso reached its strongest level against in the dollar in 18 months.

The stock market's IPC index of leading shares closed up 0.5% at 33801 points. Volume was a moderate 162 million shares worth 4.94 billion pesos ($404 million).

After setting an all-time intraday high of 33,822, the IPC ceded some ground as the Dow Jones Industrials slipped back into the red and ended about flat.

Positive U.S. economic data this week, as well as last Friday's U.S. employment report for March, gave additional fuel to the local market as investors expect the U.S. economic recovery to be reflected in Mexico and in company earnings.

The Monex brokerage said in a report that the IPC could move above 34000 points.

"Most of the price patterns of the different stocks that make up the IPC show highly positive movements," Monex said.

Mining and railways company Grupo Mexico (GMEXICO.MX) B shares led the charge, rising 4.7% to MXN35.80 after UBS initiated coverage of the stock with a buy recommendation.

UBS cited "near-term expectations for $4 copper" and a potential separate listing of Grupo Mexico's railways business support expectations for share-price gains. UBS set its price target at MXN44.

IPC heavyweight America Movil (AMX) L shares rose 0.1% to MXN31.66, and cement and building materials company Cemex (CX) CPO shares rose 0.5% to MXN13.36, adding to the previous day's gains.

The peso appreciated for a seventh straight session against the U.S. dollar, closing in Mexico City at MXN12.2160. It was the strongest close early October, 2008, just before the Bank of Mexico embarked on a year-long series of interventions in the market selling dollars at the height of the global financial crisis.

Now the Bank of Mexico is buying dollars to bolster the country's foreign reserves against future market debacles via a series of monthly put options for $600 million under which banks can sell dollars to the central bank when the peso is appreciating.

On Monday banks exercised $501 million of the $600 million for April.

Mexico's foreign reserves rose by $1.2 billion last week to a record $95.68 billion, mostly from the central bank changing dollars for state oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos. Oil remains the biggest source of Mexican foreign reserves, and rising crude prices also contribute to peso strength.

The recent market rally hasn't been without voices of caution, as liquidity from fiscal and monetary stimulus in developed countries has contributed to emerging market gains, and will eventually be withdrawn.

ING Mexico said in a report that it considers peso positions to be "saturated in the near term," and that the currency is vulnerable to a correction in equities.

title: ANALYSIS-Emerging market  currencies  show short-term cracks
text:
NEW YORK, March 30 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies have been all the rage the past year given their robust economies, but it seems these assets have become less appealing to some investors at least in the short term.

After out-sized gains in 2009, these currencies, including the Brazilian real, the Chilean peso, and others in Asia, have slipped against the U.S. dollar in 2010, and strategists say these assets are showing some vulnerability as their yields have started to fall.

Most fund managers, though, are still gung-ho on EM currencies in the medium to long term, but some say it has become harder to extract gains in the short term for these normally buoyant units.

Many investors made a fortune using carry trades -- borrowing in a low-interest currency like the dollar and lending in a high-interest one such as the real, and pocketing the rate difference. But these trades no longer seem to be sure-fire money-makers.

"Risk-adjusted carry in emerging markets by historical standards is not attractive at the moment," said Ron Leven, executive director for currency research at Morgan Stanley in New York. "And it's due to a combination of the compression of rates and rising currency volatility."

Leven cited the case of the Brazilian real, which has a risk-adjusted carry of 45 percent, based on Morgan Stanley estimates, which means its carry rates had been better than current levels 55 percent of the time the last five years.

"Historically, 45 percent is just average -- not terrible, but not great," Leven said.

Brazil's capital controls, instituted in October last year to slow the real's appreciation, have pressured the currency's rate in the forward market, analysts said, reducing its carry yield against, say, the U.S. dollar and euro.

The Brazilian real <BRL=> has struggled against the dollar this year, falling nearly 3 percent, after rising 33 percent versus the U.S. dollar in 2009. Yet it remains the darling of the currency world.

EM NO LONGER CHEAP

"Certainly emerging market currencies in the short term are not as attractive as they were when they got crushed during the Lehman collapse. Brazil, for one, isn't particularly cheap at the current level," said David Gerstenhaber, president of New York-based macro hedge fund Argonaut Capital Management.

Gerstenhaber manages assets totaling $900 million.

Mike Moran, senior emerging market strategist at Standard Chartered in New York, thinks much of the cyclical rally in emerging market currencies is finished, which should make 2010 a tougher year.

"It's going to be less directional. We're going to see increased volatility," Moran said.

Carry trades thrive in an environment of low volatility, a period when there is diminished risk aversion and the global economy is in the midst of an expansion.

Analysts also say given the global downturn, some countries have engaged in currency intervention and that complicates investing in emerging markets.

This is part of what makes Brazil a little less alluring despite strong economic fundamentals, analysts said. Its central bank intervenes to stem currency gains, a move aimed at preserving its export competitiveness.

Intervention is also a threat in Mexico, Southeast Asia, and specifically China. Beijing has kept its currency artificially weak against the dollar, prompting U.S. legislators to threaten tariff sanctions if China doesn't revalue the yuan.

MOST EM PORTFOLIOS UNHEDGED

Despite these challenges, most emerging market portfolios remained largely unhedged, suggesting a belief that growth will remain strong in the region.

"There's certainly a positive correlation between equities and currencies," said Gavin Francis, head of client management at Pareto Investment Management in London. Pareto is one of the world's largest FX managers, with assets totaling $45 billion.

"You certainly remove that correlation and you're giving up the gain when you hedge. This whole question of hedging comes down to whether the return is paying you enough for the extra fear that you face in the long term," he added.

Standard Chartered's Moran believes it's impractical to be completely exposed to the vagaries of emerging market investing. "My sense is that 2010 is still a tremendous unknown in terms of policy and the global economy and putting no hedges on your EM portfolios is a punchy move."

Overall, the outlook for emerging markets remains strong and hedge funds have kept their faith in their currencies.

The prospect for growth is a lot stronger in some of these countries, said Aston Chan, portfolio manager at GLC, a London-based macro hedge fund with assets under management of about $2 billion.

In that instance, high growth may once again increase the yield advantage of these markets. "The rate-hiking cycle in Brazil and Mexico is going to be much earlier than in G10 countries, except Australia, and this is going increase these currencies' carry advantage," Chan said. (Reporting by Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss; Editing by Kenneth Barry)

title: Mexico's Foreign Reserves End 2009 At Near-Record $90.84B
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's foreign reserves dipped slightly last week to $90.84 billion, ending 2009 sharply higher than they began after the government cashed in on a major oil hedging program and the local currency posted steady gains in recent months.

The Bank of Mexico said Tuesday that international reserves slipped by $93 million last week due to mostly unspecified operations.

Reserves were $5.4 billion higher than at the end of 2008, however, and finished 2009 just shy of their historic record of $90.93 billion set Dec. 24.

The recent accumulation of foreign currency in the central bank's coffers was possible, in part, thanks to the steady appreciation of Mexico's peso during the past six months.

Increasing stability in the peso after a volatile first half of the year allowed the Bank of Mexico, at the end of September, to suspend its daily interventions in the exchange market selling dollars.

Between October 2008 and September 2009, the bank auctioned off about $31 billion in the market. Foreign reserves bottomed out at $72.6 billion in August.

But with the peso recovering to around MXN13 per dollar at the end of the year from an all-time low of MXN15.60 in March, and oil prices recovering, Mexico's reserves began to be replenished.

The central bank continues to offer $250 million on days when the peso is 2% weaker against the dollar, but in the last three months it has sold only $511 million.

Also boosting reserves was the federal government's deposit of about $5 billion last month as the Finance Ministry cashed in on put options purchased in 2008 to protect the budget from fluctuations in the price of Mexican oil.

The government hedged much of 2009's oil exports at $70 a barrel when prices soared to record levels during 2008. The government netted about $3.5 billion through the hedges.

Mexico's peso appeared set to continue its New Year rally against the dollar Tuesday. The currency was recently quoted in Mexico City trading at MXN12.8085 to the dollar, compared with MXN12.8885 at Monday's close.

-By Paul Kiernan, Dow Jones Newswires; (5255)5980-5178, paul.kiernan@dowjones.com [ 05-01-10 1607GMT ]

title: Mexico's Foreign Reserves Up $3.86B To $90.93B As Of Dec 24

title: Fitch Downgrades Mexico's Foreign  Currency  Rating to 'BBB'; Outlook Stable
text:
NEW YORK - (BUSINESS WIRE) - Fitch Ratings today downgraded Mexico's foreign currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) to 'BBB' from 'BBB+' and local currency IDR to 'BBB+' from 'A-'. The Rating Outlook is Stable. In addition, the country ceiling was downgraded to 'A-' from 'A'. The short-term rating was affirmed at 'F2'.

Fitch downgraded Mexico's ratings as the global economic and financial crisis and falling oil production have accentuated weaknesses in the sovereign's fiscal profile, including the high oil dependence of public sector revenues, a narrow non-oil tax base and a limited fiscal cushion. These weaknesses limit Mexico's fiscal maneuverability in the face of future oil income shocks. Mexico's limited ability to implement a credible counter-cyclical fiscal policy this year (in contrast to that observed in some of its rating peers) also highlights the underlying structural fiscal weaknesses.

Mexico's general government debt is expected to reach 37% of GDP in 2009, which is above the 'BBB' median, while the debt to revenue ratio is significantly above the peer median highlighting the narrowness of its revenue base. Mexico's less dynamic growth performance and outlook relative to similarly rated peers (sovereigns rated 'BBB+', 'BBB' and 'BBB-') suggest fiscal income pressures could continue, especially if oil production continues its secular decline. Finally, Mexico's external buffers are also limited compared with peers to deal with potential external shocks in the future.

Oil income, which constitutes over 35% of the public sector revenues, has been adversely impacted by the fall in oil prices from their peak and oil production. Oil production declined from a peak of 3.4 million b/d in 2004 to 2.6 million currently, with the rate of the decline accelerating to 9% in 2008 representing a structural shock to public finances. In Fitch's view, the 2008 energy reform does not provide sufficient confidence that oil production will not continue to decline over the medium term. While Pemex could announce incentive-based contracts to attract private investment next year, it is difficult to ascertain the timing and pace of such investments.

'Recently approved tax measures are a step in the right direction, but more is required to materially address structural weaknesses of public finances especially in the context of continued uncertainty over the outlook for oil production. Prospects for future revenue-enhancing tax reforms are not bright as the opposition party controls the Lower House of Congress and going forward political dynamics will be heavily influenced by the 2012 presidential elections,' said Shelly Shetty, Senior Director in Fitch's Sovereign group.

Despite the recent tax increase measures, oil related revenues will still account for over 30% of total revenues, while the non-oil tax/GDP ratio will rise only modestly to 11% by 2012, and the federal government's Oil Stabilization Fund will be almost depleted this year. In contrast, the 'BBB' median general government revenue/GDP ratio stood at 36% in 2008 (compared with Mexico's 18%), while investment-grade sovereigns with significant oil dependence have lower debt burdens and larger fiscal cushions to deal with shocks to oil income.

Mexico's economic performance has been less dynamic than its rating peers, with its five-year average GDP growth of 3.4% compared with 5.5% for the 'BBB' median. The Mexican economy is likely to contract by close to 7% this year, a larger contraction than the 'BBB' median of 3%, and grow by 3% in 2010.

'Further progress on structural reforms is needed to enhance Mexico's growth potential, which in turn would also be favorable for expanding the non-oil tax base and improving public debt dynamics' added Shetty. The liquidation of the Luz y Fuerza de Centro (one of the state-owned electricity companies), the potential auctioning of fiber-optic networks and greater infrastructure spending could help support growth but deeper structural reforms may still be needed to materially enhance medium-term growth prospects.

Mexico's relatively healthy banking sector, resilient external accounts, the sovereign's manageable external debt amortization profile, as well as its ability to tap the IMF Flexible Credit Line (FCL) in case of a significant worsening of external financial conditions support Mexico's 'BBB' rating and Stable Outlook. However, the scale of foreign exchange intervention by the Central Bank of Mexico in response to distress in the corporate sector in the months following the intensification of the global financial crisis underscored the necessity of increasing international reserve assets.

Going forward, Fitch would view positively increases in non-oil income and fiscal buffers as well as faster-than-expected improvement in public debt dynamics. Structural reforms that enhance competitiveness and evidence of higher growth prospects would support creditworthiness, as would improvement in the international liquidity position that strengthens Mexico's external resilience. On the other hand, significant fiscal deterioration or sustained economic weakness that undermine debt dynamics would be viewed negatively.

title: Reuters Summit-UPDATE 1-Mexico could keep shrinking until 2010
text:
(For other news from the Reuters Latin American Investment Summit, click on http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment09?PID=500("http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment09?PID=500"))  (Adds Carstens quotes, background)

 By Jason Lange

 MEXICO CITY, May 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's economy will shrink in the third quarter from a year earlier and might not grow again until the first quarter of 2010, Finance Minister Agustin Carstens told Reuters on Friday.

 Speaking at the Reuters Latin American Investment Summit in Mexico City, Carstens said Mexico's recession was extending longer than previously expected. The country's economy is in freefall because exports to the United States have collapsed.

 "The two hardest quarters will be the first and second of this year and afterward the GDP will continue to be negative in annual terms," Carstens said. He added that there will be no growth "until the fourth (quarter of this year) or maybe the first quarter of next year."

 Carstens also said the exchange market for Mexico's peso currency is working "rather well" since the government and central bank began selling dollars from the country's currency reserves in daily auctions and intervening more directly.

 "The truth is I think the market is working quite well," Carstens said. "What we are interested in is having orderly markets where there's volume and liquidity."

 The minister, who sits on a commission that decides on interventions, declined to say whether Mexico would halt its daily dollar sales to boost the peso.

 The Mexican currency plunged last year as the economy slipped and investors retreated from emerging markets. But it has strengthened to nearly 13 to the dollar in recent days.

 Mexico's economy, which relies heavily on U.S. demand, contracted 1.6 percent in the first quarter from a year earlier and a much steeper drop is expected in the period between April and June.

 The swine flu outbreak that killed dozens of people in Mexico and shut down the economy for five days is expected to shave up to half a percentage point from gross domestic product in 2009.

title: Mexico's Peso Gains Ground Vs Dollar; Strongest Since Jan
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso gained against the U.S. dollar for a fifth straight session Tuesday, closing at its strongest level since January as U.S. stocks surged on continued optimism about the financial sector.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN14.0450 to the dollar, compared with MXN14.5150 at the close last Friday. Local markets were closed Monday for a holiday.

Joel Virgen, an analyst at Citigroup Inc. (C) unit Banamex, said the peso's recent bounce-back from record lows just over a week ago came amid a broad recovery in emerging market currencies, but with greater volatility because of Mexico's close ties to the U.S.

"Just as the peso did especially badly, this time it did especially well," he said.

The peso had sunk to an all-time low MXN15.60 to the dollar in after-hours trading March 9.

Banamex said the peso's rebound was helped by changes in the Bank of Mexico's foreign exchange market interventions and news that local pension fund managers will invest only in local assets for a year to help the economy.

The exchange rate dipped briefly below MXN14 during Tuesday's session, as it had Monday in foreign trading with local participants absent.

The current exchange rate is "closer to levels that could be considered justified by fundamentals," Virgen said.

Solid gains in U.S. stocks, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising 2.5%, also contributed to the peso's strength.

The Bank of Mexico began last week auctioning $100 million a day at market rates, and $300 million at a minimum exchange rate 2% above the previous session's "fix." Before that, the bank was auctioning $400 million at the minimum rate.

title: ANALYSIS-Mexico plays defense as economy,  currency  slip
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 13 (Reuters) - Pummeled by a plunging currency and shrinking economy, Mexican authorities are reacting with the caution of an outmatched boxer who can't land a solid punch and can only try to avoid a severe beating.

Mexico's economy is one of the most tightly linked in the world to the United States, where a deep recession is choking off demand for Mexican exports.

Analysts think Mexican output will contract about 2 percent this year, and hundreds of thousands of Mexicans have lost their jobs in recent months. Unemployment spiked to 5.0 percent in January, the highest level since 1996.

The weak economy and a retreat by Wall Street investors from emerging markets have pushed the peso to record lows against the dollar despite the central bank's efforts to prop it up by selling $20 billion from dollar reserves.

Even Mexico's president, Felipe Calderon, acknowledges that his government simply lacks the firepower to compensate for America's economic freefall -- where Mexico ships about 80 percent of its exports.

"We're too close to the earthquake's epicenter," Calderon told a conference on Thursday.

Mexico became an export powerhouse after it entered the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, with the United States and Canada in 1994. Exports are now collapsing, and fell 32 percent in January from a year earlier.

Calderon is running up a modest budget deficit this year to stimulate the economy but the Finance Ministry says it does not plan to ask for more deficit spending beyond what Congress authorized in October, which is equivalent to 1.8 percent of gross domestic product.

Further complicating matters, the peso's rapid devaluation -- down by about a third since August -- is fueling inflation by making imports more expensive.

High inflation, in turn, has led the central bank to take some of the punch out of its own efforts to boost the economy.

After slashing its benchmark overnight rate by 50 basis points in January, the bank cut the rate by just 25 basis points in February after data showed the peso's losses were helping to keep inflation near a seven-year high.

And while authorities stepped up efforts this week to boost the peso, they have signaled they will put tight limits on how much they will dip into the country's $80 billion in dollar reserves.

Put together, the different policy responses are seen more as a series of defensive parries than an all-out counterattack.

"They're trying not to get knocked flat," said economist Enrique Alvarez at IDEAglobal in New York.

GHOSTS OF CRISES PAST

Mexico's caution stands in contrast to Chile's more aggressive interest rate cuts and Russia's more forceful currency interventions.

But Mexico is loathe to abandon its hard-earned principles of budgetary restraint, a free-floating currency and a commitment to low inflation -- all adopted in the wake of the mid-1990s financial meltdown known as the Tequila Crisis.

Going too far with fiscal, monetary or currency policies could make things worse, analysts say, stirring memories of the 6.2 percent economic contraction of 1995.

So policymakers have told markets they won't go to war for the currency in 2009, saying last week that Mexico will only sell the dollars it expects to accrue from 2009's oil exports -- about $19 billion over the whole year.

If authorities were to challenge currency traders by setting a limit on the peso's losses, as they did in the early 1990s, the risk is that they could quickly run out of dollars, triggering a collapse in the currency.

"If the market goes against you they're going to try to test the central bank's resolve," said currency strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky at RBS in Greenwich, Connecticut.

The bank this week began selling $100 million daily into exchange markets, though that is just a fraction of the $3 billion to $5 billion in daily peso trading volumes, according to central bank data.

The peso <MXN=> <MEX01> rose 1 percent on Friday to 14.59 per dollar, helped by growing confidence in the recovery of the U.S. banking system. The peso has posted gains this week, helped by rebounding global equities and the dollar sales.

Finance Minister Agustin Carstens last week compared the U.S. recession to a tsunami crashing into Mexico. Nevertheless, Carstens has no plans of asking Congress to increase this year's planned budget deficit, said ministry spokesman Rodrigo Brand.

Mexico has run high deficits in the past, but a pile of debt can make lenders charge higher interest rates for both the government and private borrowers, putting the government in a precarious position and hurting the wider economy.

"You could boost spending right now, but you have to be careful that the financing of that debt is sustainable over time," said Brand.

Instead, the Finance Ministry will focus on pushing reforms for key sectors like telecommunications to improve the economy's long-term growth potential, Brand said. (Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: Mexico peso, stocks fall on GM bankruptcy warning
text:

MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Mexico's peso currency weakened sharply and stocks fell Thursday as worries about the U.S. economy grew after auditors warned General Motors could face bankruptcy, a situation that could pose huge risks for Mexico's export-dependent industries.

The peso lost 0.94 percent to trade at 15.3450 per dollar as of the central bank's 1:30 p.m. reference, despite news the central bank plans to buy a $100 million worth of pesos per day.

The benchmark IPC index fell 2.58 percent to close at 17,365.02 points as most major shares lost ground.

GM's auditors said Thursday there was "substantial doubt" the company could continue operating amid continued huge losses. A bankruptcy of the giant automaker would have huge repercussions for the U.S. economy and would hit Mexico's export-dependent industries hard. Mexico sends about 80 percent of its exports to the United States.

GM also operates four assembly plants and a regional engineering center in Mexico.

Shares in cement maker Cemex, a top supplier of the U.S. construction industry, plunged 15.44 percent to 7.01 pesos. Dominant cell phone operator America Movil fell 2.37 percent to 18.91 pesos.

The central bank said it will begin daily auctions of $100 million on Monday aimed at boosting liquidity in the foreign exchange market.

The auction mechanism in place since October will also continue to be used, offering dollars in daily auctions at 2 percent below the rate they fetched the previous day. The amount offered daily will be reduced to $300 million from $400 million.

"We are sceptical the Banco de Mexico's new foreign exchange intervention approach will be very successful," RBC said in a note to clients.

The yield on Mexico's benchmark 10-year government bond was down two basis points to 8.75 percent.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm falls as US GDP fans recession fears
text:
* LatAm stocks fall as U.S. GDP suggests deeper recession

* Mexico central bank intervenes, peso weakens past 15/dlr

* Colombian central bank cuts rates by 100 bps

* Brazil Bovespa briefly erases 2009 gains, closes flat

By Walter Brandimarte

NEW YORK, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Latin American financial markets fell on Friday after a worse-than-expected U.S. GDP report stoked fears of a deeper and longer global recession that could choke the region's already weakening economic performance.

Mexico's markets were among the most hurt due to their heavy reliance on the U.S. economy. While Mexican stocks sank to four-month lows, the peso closed above 15 per dollar for the first time, despite a central bank intervention.

The MSCI stock index for Latin America <.MILA00000PUS> fell 1.27 percent to its lowest level in nearly three months. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 <.SPX> closed at 12-year lows, also pressured by news that the U.S. government is taking a large stake in Citigroup's common shares, and possibly in other banks.

"This is contaminating investor sentiment, even as emerging economies still post a better economic performance," said Ricardo Tadeu Martins, a research analyst with Planner brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's benchmark Bovespa index <.BVSP> erased all of its 2009 gains in the worst moment of the session, but bargain hunters cushioned the market's fall, causing the index to close flat.

Mexico's IPC <.MXX> lost 1.63 percent, while Chile's blue-chip IPSA index <.IPSA> slid 1.92 percent.

Latin American currencies also weakened on worries that a prolonged world recession may further reduce the dollar inflows from exports.

The Mexican peso <MXN=><MEX01> lost 1.12 percent to 15.099 per dollar at the government's 1:30 p.m. (1930GMT) final reference rate, even after the central bank intervened with direct sales of dollars to banks. The currency sank further to 15.25 later on the day.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened 1.1 percent to 2.37 per dollar while the Chilean peso <CLP=CL> ended 0.18 percent lower at 596.80.

On the other hand, the Colombian peso <COP=RR> strengthened 0.21 percent to 2,554.0 per dollar before the central decision to cut interest rates by 100 basis points, larger than the 50 basis points expected by most economists.

The decision could be supportive for the peso next week, as it may be seen as a sign that the central bank is acting to protect the economy, Goldman Sachs' senior economist Alberto Ramos wrote in a report.

"Admittedly, the current financial conditions are extremely tight for the very weak cyclical position of the economy and that is perhaps one of the key drivers for the recent weakness of the Colombian peso," he said.

U.S. government data on Friday showed the recession in the United States worsened in the fourth quarter even more than initially estimated, with the economy suffering its deepest contraction since early 1982.

That bodes ill for Mexico, which sends around 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

"There will be a similar drop during the first quarter, reflecting the deterioration of dollar flows to this country," including tourism and exports," said Mario Copca, an analyst at MetAnalisis consultancy in Mexico City.

Also weighing was news that the U.S. government is boosting its equity stake in Citigroup Inc , which raised worries about which other U.S. banks might see similar actions.

By Peter Millard

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed at a record low on Thursday as concerns about the length of the global downturn hurt the local currency.

In Mexico City the peso was quoted as closing at 14.96 to the U.S. dollar, sharply weaker than Wednesday's close of MXN14.87. Strong demand from corporate clients who need to make payments to foreign suppliers or pay down foreign debt before the end of the month put pressure on the peso.

On its Web site, the Bank of Mexico said the peso hit an intraday record low of 14.9975 to the dollar on Thursday before recovering some ground ahead of the close. One currency trader said there were some trades on Thursday that broke the MXN15.00 psychological barrier before recovering slightly.

"If it stays at this level or weakens more on Friday we could see the central bank intervene," said the trader.

The Bank of Mexico didn't intervene in the market with dollar sales to shore up the currency on Thursday. The Bank of Mexico started using discretionary dollar sales earlier this month to combat volatility in the exchange market and curtail speculation against the local currency.

The central bank sold $555 million last week in the exchange market to fight volatility. Mexico's foreign reserves have fallen around $4.5 billion since end-2008, partly due to heavy intervention in the currency market.

Analysts have mentioned the drop in foreign reserves as a source of concern.

Bank of Mexico Deputy Gov. Guillermo Guemez said Thursday that he expects the country's foreign reserves to end the year at levels similar to those observed now. The Bank of Mexico has spent about $18.5 billion in reserves since last October to support the peso during periods of high volatility.

The gloomy outlook for the U.S. economy has hurt Mexican financial markets because Mexico's economy is heavily dependent on exports to the U.S.

Mexico's economic activity fell 2.4% in December from the year-ago month, with declines in industry and services offset by higher agricultural production.

Mexican Deputy Finance Minister Alejandro Werner said Thursday the government expects the economy to contract this year due to the global financial crisis that has eroded demand for Mexican exports, slowed foreign investments and eroded remittances from Mexicans working abroad.

"All of this will result in a decrease in economic activity," he said.

title: ANALYSIS-Bets rise on Mexico debt downgrade
text:
MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Traders in Mexican debt are increasingly betting the country may be downgraded by credit ratings agencies, worsening already tight financing conditions as the economy stumbles into a recession.

The cost of insuring Mexico's sovereign debt against default has surged by a third this month and is now more expensive than insuring Brazilian bonds -- which enjoy a lower credit rating.

A slumping economy as well as falling oil exports, which fund a third of Mexico's government spending, are making the country's investment-grade debt less attractive to investors as they look toward future government budgets.

"People are expressing a negative view when it comes to Mexico. There are a lot of challenges and headwinds Mexico has to face right now," said Nick Chamie, global head of emerging market research at RBC in Toronto.

Even a war between rival drug gangs that killed 6,000 people last year is seen as weighing against Mexico.

In November, credit rating agency Fitch Ratings revised its sovereign credit rating outlooks for Mexico to negative from stable, warning about the deepening U.S. recession, tight liquidity in financial markets and falling crude prices.

Mexico's economy is expected to shrink more than 1.0 percent this year as U.S. demand for the country's manufactured exports dries up.

Mexican oil production fell 9.2 percent in January to its lowest level since November 1995 as output from the aging Cantarell oil field dwindled.

Analysts are skeptical that state oil company Pemex can reach production targets this year.

"The recession, political risk -- it's more than oil, but I think oil is an important part of the story," said Alonso Cervera, an economist at Credit Suisse in New York.

LINE IN THE SAND

Raising concerns about Mexico's foreign reserve stockpile, the central bank has intervened directly in the market to buy pesos this month after a mechanism of regular auctions established in October failed to stem losses in the currency.

Experts have questioned how far the bank might be willing to go to defend the peso, hurt by global risk aversion and the economic downturn, and whether its war chest of $82 billion in foreign reserves is enough to fight a prolonged campaign.

The cost of insuring $10 million of Mexico's five-year dollar bonds for a year Wednesday was $452,000, higher than investors were paying to insure similar Brazilian debt, according to Markit data service. At the end of last year, it was slightly cheaper to ensure Mexican debt than Brazilian.

"The fact that the price has gone up tells you about the perception of eventual default risk, but the levels we're talking about are still quite low," said Cervera.

Lower ratings on Mexican debt, even if still within the investment-grade range, would likely make it more expensive for the government to issue bonds.

A sharp rise in violence as Mexican soldiers battle drug cartels is also weighing on sentiment for Mexican assets.

"There is an increasing awareness of public security issues in Mexico. That is certainly being picked up in some circles and is being added to the list of reasons to sell Mexico," Chamie said.

Mexico is rated "BBB+" by both Standard & Poor's and Fitch Ratings and "Baa1" by Moody's Investors Service. All of the ratings are three notches above the minimum investment grade credit rating.

Fitch and Standard & Poor's rate Brazil's foreign-currency debt at "BBB-" but Moody's Investors Service still rates Brazil's sovereign bonds below investment grade.

ROOM TO RUN

Mexico has hedged its oil exports this year at $70 a barrel, in line with its budget and far higher than current prices of around $36 for the country's blend of crude.

But ongoing low oil prices and production could force the government to cut spending or accept a deficit in its 2010 budget.

A decade of conservative fiscal policy have given President Felipe Calderon room to run a small deficit for 2009 to boost spending on infrastructure investment as well as health and education as part of its plan to bolster the economy.

JP Morgan estimated in a report that a continued weak exchange rate could help boost revenues in pesos from oil sales next year, helping limit the government's revenue shortfall to around 1.0 percent. (Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: Mexico Peso Rebounds On Equity Gains After Record Low
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso strengthened Tuesday after closing at a record low versus the dollar in the previous session, as large gains in local stocks and higher oil prices supported a relief rally.

The peso was quoted in Mexico City closing at MXN14.8255 to the dollar, compared with MXN14.8620 in morning trading and MXN14.95 at Monday's close.

Ramses Villela, a senior foreign exchange trader at Bulltick Capital Markets in Mexico City, said the gains will probably be short-lived.

"In technical terms, we're still in a bull market," Villela said, adding the peso would have to strengthen to MXN14.35 to mark a change in tendency and that the currency is still pushing to break the MXN15 level.

Opinions among analysts vary as to whether the peso's recent depreciation - to its current value from MXN10 to the dollar a little more than six months ago - is based on Mexico's economic fundamentals or the broader market's aversion to risk and shortage of liquidity.

The Bank of Mexico said Tuesday it sold $155 million through direct interventions in the exchange market last week, in addition to the $1.06 billion it sold earlier this month, to curtail the peso's recent volatility.

While the central bank and Finance Ministry deny having a target for the exchange rate, concerns are growing that currency weakness may be feeding local inflation in addition to weighing on the balance sheets of local companies with dollar-denominated debt.

The Bank of Mexico reported Tuesday the country's inflation was higher than anticipated in the first half of February, with the consumer price index rising 0.17%, compared with economists' expectations of 0.14%.

Core inflation, which excludes the cost of energy and fresh produce, rose 0.29% in the first two weeks of the month, above the market's forecast of a 0.22% rise. The annual core inflation rate increased to 5.81% from 5.76% at the end of January.

"Merchandise goods other than processed foods are clearly suffering from the pass-through of the currency," BNP Paribas economist Rafael de la Fuente said in a note.

The peso was hammered by uncertainty about U.S. government efforts to shore up beleaguered banks, which pushed investors to dump risky assets like equities and emerging markets currencies. Mexican stocks sank to a four-month low.

Earlier this month, Mexico's central bank began a series of direct interventions in currency markets for the first time in more than a decade to prop up the local currency.

Earlier on Monday, investors initially welcomed reports the government could convert an earlier investment in Citigroup into a big common stock holding, but enthusiasm faded as investors worried U.S. banks would need even more aid.

title: Emerging Mkt Debt Slumps As Morning Gains Lost To Gloom

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market bonds slumped Monday as early morning risk tolerance gave way to far darker thoughts on the global economy.

Risk premiums, as measured by JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, were five basis points wider on the day, at 690 basis points over U.S. Treasurys, with returns -0.26%.

The benchmark Brazil 2040 Global was bid 3/4 lower at 122 7/16, according to Reuters.

"In the aftermath of President Chavez's victory in last Sunday's referendum, the coast is now much clearer politically for the government to make a long-overdue macroeconomic adjustment to address the reality of lower oil prices," JPMorgan said.

Despite ongoing fundamental deterioration, the market pricing of Venezuela at near-default levels is exaggerated, it said. "Investors seem to agree with this view, as the reduction of Venezuela underweights was one of the most salient trends of our February client survey," it said.

Mexico's central bank again intervened in the exchange market Monday as the peso approached a record low close against the dollar and neared the psychological barrier of MXN15.

Currency traders in Mexico said the central bank stepped in late in the session to sell an unspecified amount of dollars directly to trading desks.

Chile's Finance Ministry will transfer $3 billion in assets from one of its sovereign wealth funds to finance part of its $4 billion fiscal stimulus package, the ministry said Monday. title: Mexico's Stocks Fall On US Losses; Peso Closes At Record Low
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexican stocks fell for a fifth consecutive session to their lowest close since October, bonds were hammered and the peso closed at a record low against the dollar Monday as a tailspin in U.S. markets fed risk aversion.

The local stock market's benchmark IPC index of most-traded issues fell 2%, or 367.83 points, to 17,956.40. Volume was light, with 167.7 million shares traded for a value of 2.87 billion pesos ($192.4 million).

Carlos Gonzalez, an equity analyst at Mexico City's Ixe brokerage, said that although the local market's fundamentals have deteriorated, its recent losses reflect more uncertainty than anything else.

"I don't see a massive exit from the market; it's just that people aren't buying," Gonzalez said, adding that the trend probably won't change until more is known about the U.S. government's plan to rescue that country's banks.

The U.S. government said Monday it will remain "firmly behind the banking system during this period of financial strain." The statement came amid reports that struggling banking giant Citigroup is in talks with federal officials that could result in the federal government expanding its ownership of the bank.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which the IPC has been closely following, ended 3.4% lower.

Wireless operator and IPC heavyweight America Movil (AMX) L shares plunged 4.1% to MXN19.05, retailer Wal-Mart de Mexico (WMMVY) V shares slipped 1.3% to MXN29.10, copper miner Grupo Mexico (GMEXICO.MX) B shares fell 0.3% to MXN8.87, and fixed-line phone company Telmex (TMX) L shares ended 0.9% lower at MXN10.63.

Cement maker Cemex (CX) CPO shares slid 4.9% to MXN8.50 after Fitch Ratings further downgraded the company's credit ratings, citing concerns about its high level of debt in the ongoing economic downturn.

Prices also fell sharply in the secondary market for local government debt, pushing the yield on 10-year bonds due 2017 up 27 basis points to 8.57% and the yield on 20-year bonds due 2024 up 40 basis points to 9.07%.

Bonds came under pressure last week after the Bank of Mexico cut the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 7.5%, when most market participants were expecting a 50-basis-point cut.

Mexico's peso, meanwhile, closed at a record low against the dollar as weak local stocks and global risk aversion pushed the currency nearer to the psychological barrier of MXN15 to the dollar and prompting the Bank of Mexico to sell dollars directly in the market.

The peso was quoted in Mexico City closing at MXN14.95 to the dollar, compared with MXN14.7645 at the close Friday.

A local currency trader said the peso appears ready to break the MXN15 mark, as direct interventions in the exchange market by the Bank of Mexico in the past two sessions have done little to curb its depreciation.

"The outlook is nothing positive," the trader said, adding that odds are "remote" that the peso could reverse its weakening trend seen in recent weeks.

The central bank sold an undisclosed amount of dollars into the exchange market Monday afternoon, the trader said, temporarily causing the peso to strengthen to MXN14.83 from MXN14.93 - gains it quickly gave up.

"Given the market's reaction, I don't feel like there was a large amount (of dollars) involved," the trader said.

The Bank of Mexico started using discretionary dollar sales earlier this month to combat volatility in the exchange market and curtail speculation against the local currency.

It discloses the amount of dollars it sells in a weekly report on foreign reserves, published each Tuesday. The central bank also sold dollars directly in the market last Friday, in addition to $400 million sold in its scheduled daily auctions.

title: WRAPUP 1-Mexico economy contracts,  central bank  cuts rates
text:
* Mexico economy shrinks at 1.6 percent clip in Q4

* Central bank cuts rates by 25 basis points

* Peso falls again, bank intervenes to sell dollars

By Jason Lange

MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Mexico's economy contracted late last year as the U.S. recession tore into demand for exports, data showed Friday, and the central bank disappointed investors by cutting interest rates less than expected.

The peso fell sharply following the rate decision and on comments by the central bank that it was worried about a tumble in the currency, which has lost about 30 percent of its value since last August due to the world economic crisis.

The economy shrank at a 1.6 percent annual clip in the fourth quarter, meaning Mexico is firmly on the path toward recession. The government expects the economy will also contract during the first and second quarters of this year, and some private sector analysts are more pessimistic.

The U.S. recession, triggered by a collapse in the American housing market, has choked off orders for everything from cars to refrigerators made in Mexico.

Mexico's central bank cut its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 7.50 percent to try to soften the blow of an economic downturn unseen in the country since the Tequila Crisis of the mid-1990s.

Most analysts expected a 50 basis point reduction.

The bank warned it was increasingly concerned about the recent deterioration of the peso which could fuel inflation.

"Strong financial turbulence seen recently represents a risk for inflation expectations," the bank said in its monthly statement.

Markets jumped on that comment, as well as the size of the rate cut which was seen as timid, sending the peso downward.

"It has raised the specter in the market of whether they are trying to defend a range. That is very dangerous because it invites attacks," said Morgan Stanley economist Gray Newman.

The peso's depreciation prompted the bank to sell dollars directly to dealers again on Friday to prop up the currency. It was the latest of a series of measures to defend the peso that have had little success.

"The central bank is contributing to the very volatility that they are trying to avoid," Newman said.

Mexico's currency <MXN=> <MEX01> was down 1.22 percent to 14.80 per dollar on Friday afternoon.

A weak currency means many imports will become more expensive, raising fears of an inflation bump.

Mexico's economy grew a tepid 1.3 percent in 2008, slowing sharply at the end of the year.

The central bank eased monetary policy last month for the first time in nearly three years, cutting its benchmark rate by 50 basis points. Investors see it trimming its key rate to as low as 6.0 percent this year to boost growth. (Additional reporting by Noel Randewich, Luis Rojas Mena and Michael O'Boyle; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: Mexico Peso Closes At New Record Low Vs Dlr After Rate Cut
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed at a record low versus the U.S. dollar Friday, as investors reacted negatively to a lower-than-expected interest-rate cut by the central bank.

The peso was quoted in Mexico City closing at MXN14.7645 to the dollar, compared to an intraday low of MXN14.9850, and Thursday's close of MXN14.6100.

The peso weakened after the Bank of Mexico announced its decision at 10:00 a.m. EST to cut the benchmark overnight rate by 25 basis points to 7.5%. The market had expected a 50-basis-point cut to boost Mexico's sputtering economy.

The peso's slide prompted the central bank to sell $400 million at two scheduled auctions Friday and to sell an undisclosed amount of dollars directly to trading desks.

"We view this weakness as indicative of concern over recession in Mexico and the economy's links to the contracting U.S. economy; sentiment on Mexico is uniformly negative. We doubt that the prospect of sharply lower Mexican interest rates has been a key driver of peso weakness," Citigroup said in a report.

While recognizing that the downside risks to the economy have worsened, the Bank of Mexico said in its communique Friday that it is concerned recent volatility in financial markets could jeopardize the bank's inflation target.

The Bank of Mexico has forecast the annual inflation rate ending the year under 4%, and reaching its 3% target by the end of 2010.

The peso has fallen 6.4% against the dollar this year, after dropping 21% during 2008, as investors fear Mexico will join the U.S. in a deep recession. A weak currency threatens to feed inflation, which is still more than double the target.

"If indeed policy is now being driven by foreign exchange concerns, then Bank of Mexico will need to show resolve to stabilize the currency. If market perception in regards to Mexican risk does not improve, this cannot be done without substantial use of reserves. The market may well test Bank of Mexico's resolve," RBS Greenwich Capital said in a report.

Prior to Friday, the central bank had spent nearly $17.92 billion in foreign reserves, which stood at $81.56 billion on Feb. 13, since last October to support the peso.

Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz said last week that interventions will continue if needed to curtail volatility, but that the central bank isn't targeting a specific exchange rate.

In other local markets, Mexican government bonds were hit by selling, pushing yields sharply higher. The yield on 10-year bonds due 2017 rose 32 basis points to 8.25%, while the yield on 20-year bonds due 2027 spiked 43 basis points to 8.65%.

The benchmark IPC stock index was down 1.8% less than an hour from the close, tracking losses on Wall Street as investors fretted over the possibility the U.S. government might be forced to nationalize some of the country's biggest banks.
