title: ANALYSIS-Latin America cenbanks need to cut rates faster
text:
SANTIAGO, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Latin America's central banks are cutting interest rates to save their economies from recession, but some are not moving quickly enough and risk being overwhelmed as the global crisis bites deep.

Central banks across the region started cutting benchmark lending rates this year as economic activity, industrial output and retail sales sank.

Mexico, Chile and Peru have also expanded government spending, hoping that fiscal stimulus plans, combined with cheaper credit for consumers and businesses, will do the trick.

Chile has led the charge on monetary policy, slashing 2.5 percentage points off its monetary policy rate earlier this month.

But Brazil and Mexico have less room to maneuver and their central bankers are famously cautious, determined to prevent a return to the hyperinflation that triggered a string of financial crises in the late 20th century.

Inflation is above target in both countries, so policymakers worry sharp rate declines could further weaken their currencies against the dollar, causing new inflationary pressures.

Still, they are drawing criticism from some analysts who say the region's two biggest economies need a dramatic jolt now rather than gradual relief.

"It is useless to distribute the monetary relaxation along the whole year when the strongest effect from the external recession is going to be felt in the first three months of the year," said Alfredo Coutino, senior Latin America economist for Moody's Economy.com.

"You have to be aggressive," he said. "You need to apply the antibiotic immediately. You don't need to dosify over 12 months like some banks are thinking in the case of Mexico ... I don't know why they are waiting. What for?"

Mexico's central bank was widely expected to cut rates by a further half a percentage point on Friday, but it was more cautious, lowering the benchmark rate by just one-quarter of a point.

Central banks have room for further rate cuts because inflationary pressures will likely continue to ease, given steep falls in international commodity, food and fuel prices and sagging consumer demand.

"All the major central banks in the region will ultimately be cutting rates, just because the disinflationary implication of the downturn will dominate the short-run inflationary effect of the depreciation of their currencies," said Rodrigo Valdes, chief Latin America economist for Barclays Capital Research in New York.

RECESSION

Mexico's economy is falling into recession and inflationary pressures have begun to ease but the central bank also has to contend with the impact of the falling peso currency.

Pummeled since late last year by worries about deepening recession in the United States, which buys around 80 percent of Mexico's exports, the peso <.MXN><MEX01> hit record lows on Friday despite repeated central bank interventions to prop it up.

While Mexico's government has turned to budget deficit spending and loan guarantees for corporate borrowers to counter a credit crunch and economic slowdown, it has limited room for more fiscal stimulus.

Brazil is also in a tight corner and has had to put a temporary freeze on a quarter of its 2009 budget as the economy slows, tax revenues fall and companies lay off workers. The unemployment rate jumped to 8.2 percent in January as hundreds of thousands of people lost their jobs.

"Probably in a couple of countries we may see more (fiscal stimulus), but the problem is there is not much financing to do more fiscal packages," Valdes said.

"So more likely what we will see is some countries will have to probably be more careful with their spending because their fiscal deficit will be larger -- including Brazil, Colombia, Mexico most likely."

Chile, long touted as Latin America's most stable economy for its fiscal prudence, has cut its benchmark rate, which was at a 10-year high last year of 8.25 percent by 3.5 percentage points so far this year, hand in hand with a $4 billion government fiscal stimulus plan.

But while a clutch of Chilean banks have started to pass on some of those cuts to customers, others are lagging and many consumers won't feel the benefits for months.

Brazil's central bank's benchmark Selic lending rate is still at a whopping 12.75 percent even after a 100 basis point cut last month that was its first reduction in 16 months.

The central bank is signaling there will be more cuts ahead, as Brazil's growth has slowed sharply since the global credit crunch bit deep in September, hammering output and prompting layoffs.

"The authorities in Chile and Brazil have realized that, contrary to their original expectations, this is a very serious global economic meltdown," said Sebastian Edwards, professor of international economics at the University of California, Los Angeles' Anderson School of Management.

"Both Brazil and Chile had very high interest rates at the onset of the crisis. Bringing them down aggressively is the appropriate thing to do, and will help better weather the crisis by providing additional liquidity." (With reporting by Ariel Miranda in Santiago; Editing by Kieran Murray and Kenneth Barry)

title: ANALYSIS- Mexico 's peso to keep slipping despite  intervention
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 12 (Reuters) - A landmark intervention by the Mexican central bank to defend the battered peso is slowing its decline, but the currency is seen weakening further as Mexico slides into recession.

The bank startled markets last week by making direct U.S. dollar sales to brokers for the first time in more than a decade to prop up the sickly peso <MXN> <MEX01> after it hit a historic low of 14.70 to the dollar.

The bank has ample reserves to play with but market players see the peso weakening even further, testing the bank's resolve over how low it is willing to see it go.

Worries that U.S. efforts to stabilize the economy and shore up banks may not work knocked the peso back down this week to near its record lows.

With Mexico's exports in a tailspin, migrants in the United States sending home less cash, and state coffers hurting from declining oil output and depressed crude prices, analysts see little to support the currency in the coming months.

"All the factors that justify a depreciation of the peso are operating," said JP Morgan's chief Mexico economist Alfredo Thorne, who expects the peso to soon break past 15 per dollar.

Last week's $1-billion intervention helped pull the peso back by more than 50 centavos from 14.70 per dollar, its weakest since new pesos were introduced in 1993 and well off its 11-per-dollar level of the last few years. But nerves over the U.S. bank bailout sent it back above 14.60 by Thursday.

Central Bank's Gov. Guillermo Ortiz said on Wednesday he expected more intervention as markets remain volatile.

Policymakers are sitting on a hard-earned war chest of $82 billion in foreign reserves built up from oil exports. Analysts say that is plenty, for now, to keep up the fight to at least make sure the peso's slide is less volatile.

"The mystery is at what level the central bank will be comfortable with the exchange rate," said Daniela Blancas, a currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City.

AGAINST THE WALL

Besides its reserves, Mexico has access to a $30 billion swap line with the Federal Reserve.

It should also be able to replenish reserves with around $12 billion, according to analysts, from an oil price hedge that guarantees at least $70 per barrel for local crude. Mexico can also tap big credit lines from multilateral institutions.

Mexico's central bank has worked hard to establish its global credibility as a prudent and transparent monetary authority since the so-called "Tequila Crisis" devasted the country's finances in the mid-1990s.

But the peso's loss of a quarter of its value since October, has put the bank against a wall as it fields pressure to slash borrowing costs to boost the economy.

While President Felipe Calderon and Mexican companies want lower interest rates, policymakers worry the peso's freefall is pushing up import costs and fueling already high inflation.

Cutting borrowing costs could further undermine the peso as lower interest rates would make Mexico's debt less attractive.

To stabilize the peso the bank turned to interventions after regular dollar auctions started in October failed to stem the rout and invited speculation due to their predictability.

Some see the peso catching a break if U.S. stimulus plans work. BBVA Bancomer sees it rebounding to as strong as 12.50 per dollar by the end of 2009 if a U.S. rebound emboldens investors to return to Mexican debt.

Others say hopes for a quick U.S. recovery are unfounded and a deep downturn could hobble Mexico through 2010. Moreover, Mexico's oil price hedge will be exhausted by then and it may be still grappling with low crude prices and declining output.

"If the world does not recover by the second part of the year, that is what will really make the market nervous," said Salvador Orozco, Santander's currency strategist in Mexico.

title: UPDATE: Bank Of  Mexico : Will Continue To  Intervene  In  FX  Mkt
text:
(Recasts lead, adds further comments from central bank governor)

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz said Wednesday the central bank "will continue to intervene in the forex market if there is excessive volatility" but isn't targeting a specific exchange rate.

"We are not looking for a certain level of exchange rate. We certainly maintain our belief in the benefits of a floating exchange rate," he told reporters at a news conference.

Ortiz said the depreciation of emerging market currencies against the U.S. dollar has become pronounced around the world.

"The peso is no exception and the volatility has increased," he said.

He added that trying to predict the future path of a currency is a very complicated matter.

"My own view is that the fundamentals in Mexico are solid," he said, citing the banking system and debt indicators.

The peso has been under pressure in recent weeks, affected by falling expectations for economic growth, lower crude oil prices and the beginning of a monetary easing cycle.

Ortiz also said Mexico is projecting a current account deficit of 2.4% of gross domestic product for 2009, and expects January industrial production output to fall by 30% to 40%.

"In Mexico, we are expecting in January a fall of around 30%-40%," Ortiz said.

Late last month, the Bank of Mexico said it expects the nation's economy to contract between 0.8% and 1.8% this year due to the recession in the U.S. Mexico's economy grew an estimated 1.5% in 2008. The central bank previously forecast growth of 0.5%-1.5% for 2009.

Ortiz said the country's international reserves will be substantially higher at the year-end, while inflation should remain within expectations.

The central bank earlier said consumer-price inflation would end the year below 4%.

The Bank of Mexico now sees annual inflation averaging 5.75% to 6.25% in the first quarter, up from its previous forecast of 5.25% to 5.75%. In the second quarter, annual inflation will average 5.25% to 5.75%, up from 4.5% to 5.0%.

Asked if the central bank will cut interest rates further, Ortiz reiterated that monetary actions will depend on many factors.

Ortiz earlier said future monetary policy actions hinge on "inflation following the trajectory" forecast by the Bank of Mexico.

On Jan. 16, the central bank slashed its overnight rate to 7.75% from 8.25% and more cuts are expected.

The Bank of Mexico is expected to cut the overnight rate to 6.25% by the end of the year, according to the latest market survey by Citigroup Inc. (C) unit Banamex, published in late January.

title: INTERVIEW- Mexico FX intervention  not necessarily negative-S&P
text:
NEW YORK, Feb 10 (Reuters) - Mexico's new policy of direct interventions in the currency market is not necessarily negative for its credit-worthiness, as long as the central bank does not target a specific exchange rate, according to a Standard and Poor's analyst.

  Lisa Schineller, a director at S&P's sovereign ratings group, said it made sense for the Mexican central bank to use its foreign reserves to "smooth" currency swings at times of thin market liquidity, but not to support a naturally weakening peso.

 "The fact that they are intervening is not a credit negative per se," Schineller told Reuters in an interview late on Monday.

 "You had an accumulation of international reserves over a number of years to provide a buffer, to be able to intervene in moments of stress such as this," she said.

Mexico's central bank surprised investors last week by directly selling dollars to banks at undisclosed rates -- the first move of that type in more than a decade. Until then, Mexico had been selling dollars only through predictable and transparent auctions.

 In a separate interview, Fitch analyst Shelly Shetty said the ratings agency is carefully monitoring Mexico's new currency interventions as part of a broader analysis to decide whether to downgrade its ratings. The comments added pressure to the peso earlier in the day.

 Fitch placed Mexico's sovereign rating on negative outlook in November as it worried about the magnitude of the country's economic contraction and the performance of its fiscal and current accounts.

 S&P, on the other hand, maintains a stable outlook on the rating, assuming the government will cut expenditures to make up for an expected decline in revenues, just as it has adjusted to adverse conditions in the past.

 Both agencies rate Mexico at "BBB+," or three notches into investment-grade territory.

 GOVERNMENT COMMITMENT

 S&P's Schineller said, however, that currency interventions "cannot reverse the reality of the global environment," in which the Mexican peso is expected to weaken as a result of external shocks.

 "Clearly the Mexican economy is one of the more strongly hit because of oil, because of the link to the United States," she said.

 "But it does not necessarily mean pressure on the rating. We're assuming a proactive and prudent policy response, in line with the government long track record of doing so."

 Government commitment to prudent fiscal and macroeconomic policies, Schineller stressed, is the key for Mexico to keep its ratings amid a global financial crisis.

 The analyst said S&P would review Mexico's ratings if there was a reversal in the government's prudent policies, or a negative surprise in the private sector forcing the government to take over significant liabilities.   (Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

In his presentation to the investors, Carstens reiterated the Finance Ministry's call for flat 2009 gross domestic product for Mexico or a contraction of 1%. That contrasts with Banxico's current forecast of a contraction between 0.8% and 1.8%.

Growth remains "a main challenge" for Mexico, Carstens said. "The Mexican economy will not be spared this world tsunami."

But Mexico's economy will decline at a slower pace than the U.S., he added. In addition, the country is better prepared to weather the crisis, with no "financing problems in sight," Carstens said.

Carstens quipped that exactly one year ago he predicted that Mexico would only catch a "small cold" from the crisis brewing in the U.S.

A year later, Mexico is still doing better than the U.S., but as the richer neighbor "caught something worse, what we've got was worse," he said. "As much as we want to move forward it will take some time" for the U.S. to resolve its problems. Compounding Mexico's trouble is the decrease in the price of oil and other commodities, he said.

Carstens also said remittances - money that Mexicans abroad send home - will likely be lower even in real terms, taking into consideration the peso's devaluation.

What is happening in the U.S. is "of the essence" for Mexico, he said. But unlike past crisis, there's a silver lining, Carstens said.

"Mexico is facing this situation from a relative position of health and strength," he said. "We are close to the epicenter geographically but we have not created the crisis."

Carstens boasted of Mexico's healthy banking system and public finances, pointing out Mexico's public debt has decreased in GDP terms.

The minister said he expects Banxico to keep cutting interest rates. "In 2009 we will see lower interest rates providing support for the economy," he said.

He added the government also continues to be committed to the housing sector. "Housing is not only an essential need" but a high employment-creation industry, he said.

text:
(Recasts, adds quote from Carstens, background)

NEW YORK, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Mexico, in a bid to stabilize the peso, will continue intervening in the foreign exchange market with dollar auctions and a surprising new policy of direct currency sales to banks, Finance Minister Agustin Carstens said on Friday.

The Mexican central bank has been selling dollars directly to banks since Wednesday to stop certain market participants from "destabilizing the market," Carstens said.

He said some investors were trying to utilize the predictability of the dollar auction mechanism to generate profits.

"Therefore, to try to basically guarantee a more orderly working of the currency market, that's why the foreign exchange committee decided to slightly modify its intervention," he told investors at a Mexican housing conference in New York.

The central bank surprised investors on Wednesday by selling dollars directly to banks for the first time in more than 10 years as fears the U.S. downturn is driving Mexico into recession sent the peso tumbling to its weakest level since 1993, when "new" pesos were introduced.

The peso has weakened about 25 percent against the dollar since mid-September, when emerging markets were engulfed by a credit crisis that sharply widened following the collapse of Lehman Brothers.

Carstens said the central bank will continue to auction $400 million when the dollar appreciates more than 2 percent against the peso on a single session. But it will "reserve the right" to directly intervene when necessary.

He said that, unlike a decade ago, Mexico is currently not the epicenter of a global financial crisis. He said the recent strength of the dollar is "strange" because the United States is the center of the crisis.

Mexico spun into a deep recession in the 1990s after a sudden currency devaluation triggered financial upheaval in the country and across Latin America in what was called the "Tequila crisis."

The Mexican government will do everything in its means to support the economy, Carstens said, including increasing public expenditures and further loosening monetary policy. The central bank cut interest rates by 50 basis points last month.

"We expect that in the coming months we will see more of this," the minister said.

He also said Mexico is in a position of strength with a healthy financial system, solid public finances and a far better sovereign debt profile than in the past. (Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: Mexico's Peso Ends Stronger At 14.1970/Dlr On Ctrl Bank Move
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso gained against the U.S. dollar for a third straight day Friday, thanks to direct intervention by a central bank unhappy with recent pressure on the currency.

The peso was quoted closing in Mexico City at MXN14.1970 to the dollar, stronger than its MXN14.2830 close on Thursday but weaker from an earlier level of MXN14.15. The currency remains down 2.7% year-to-date after a 21% depreciation in 2008.

The Bank of Mexico stepped into the market Wednesday as the peso reached an all-time low MXN14.70, selling dollars directly to banks and without disclosing the amounts being sold.

The interventions, which continued Thursday and Friday, were seen as a way of discouraging bets against the peso.

The exchange commission, formed by Bank of Mexico and Finance Ministry officials, confirmed the interventions and said the amounts will be reflected in weekly reports on foreign reserves.

Finance Minister Agustin Carstens said in New York Friday that the interventions were necessary as some market participants were seeking to make profits on the weaker peso, and authorities will continue to intervene whenever necessary to maintain an orderly market.

The direct sales are in addition to the $400 million the central bank auctions each day at a minimum exchange rate 2% above the previous session, and estimates have varied on how much the central bank might have sold.

The Royal Bank of Scotland described it as a "tricky strategy."

While relatively small amounts could discourage speculation by introducing two-way risk in the market, if the recent depreciation is the result of rising risk aversion, "the risk is that Banxico will need to intervene more aggressively to hold the peso," RBS said in a report Thursday.

Citigroup unit Banamex said the decision to intervene directly suggests authorities took the view that the weakening was market-driven.

In a report, Banamex rejected as a justification for the recent extent of the depreciation the notion that Mexico's external accounts will suffer if the economy follows the U.S. into recession.

"Mexican exports are undoubtedly affected by weaker U.S. demand. However, due to the nature of the North American economic integration, Mexican exports are import-intensive," Banamex said.

The bank noted a 91% correlation between imports and exports since Nafta went into effect in 1994, compared with 40% in the previous decade-and-a-half.

"In terms of the peso scenario, that means that the argument that associates a weaker currency with a wider trade deficit should be clarified," Banamex said.

Banamex said it sees no problem with Mexico meeting its 2009 financing needs and said the widening of spreads on the country's credit default swaps to 386 basis points from 292 basis points at the end of 2008 wasn't justified by fundamentals.

Barclays Capital attributed the peso weakening largely to a rapid deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook.

"Technicals and financial variables only partially explain observed depreciation year-to-date, suggesting largely fundamentals-driven price action," Barclays said in a mid-week report.

The Bank of Mexico, meanwhile, is considered to have abundant ammunition to maintain a defense of the peso. In additional to $84 billion in foreign reserves, the central bank this week extended to Oct. 30 its $30 billion currency swap facility with the U.S. Federal Reserve, which gives it another channel of access to dollars.

NEW YORK, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies and stocks gained ground in tandem with rising U.S. equities on Thursday as investors took an optimistic view that a U.S. accounting rule change would be implemented.

The change, a relaxation of an accounting requirement on the recognition of losses that has resulted in billions of losses for banks, is potentially part of the Obama administration's plans to shore up the shattered U.S. financial system.

MEXICO CITY, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bankintervened in the foreign exchange market for a second straight day on Thursday, boosting the peso currency after it was hammered to a record low this week amid fears the local economy is heading into recession.

 The peso <MEX01> <MXN=> firmed 1.44 percent to close at 14.265 per U.S. dollar as the central bank sold greenbacks directly to banks, market sources said.

 The central bank and Finance Ministry later confirmed the intervention in a statement issued after the local market's close.

 "Basically, it said it will not allow further speculation against the exchange rate," a trader in Mexico City said.

 The central bank surprised investors by intervening on Wednesday after fears the U.S. downturn is driving Mexico into recession sent the peso tumbling to its weakest level since new pesos were introduced in 1993.

 The currency has lost about a quarter of its value against the dollar in the past five months, making it the worst performer among major currencies since the global economic crisis deepened late last year.

 This week's surprise move was Mexico's most direct intervention since 1998, although the bank has been auctioning dollars in recent months to soften the peso's fall.

 Oil-exporting Mexico has a cushion of around $80 billion in foreign reserves and can tap up to $30 billion from the U.S. Federal Reserve under a global liquidity program.

 "At this stage, the (Mexican) central bank has plenty of ammunition to intervene; admittedly, not to defend an unrealistic level for the peso, but certainly to prevent sharp disorderly adjustments," Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos said in a research note.

 MEXICO EYES RECESSION

 Mexico's economy, which relies heavily on exports to the United States, is seen shrinking as much as 1.8 percent this year, according to the central bank.

 Investors have been worried that a weak currency will push up the price of imports, fuel higher inflation and keep policy-makers from being able to cut interest rates to boost the slowing economy.

 In debt trading, bonds gained amid expectations the Banco de Mexico's intervention will help stabilize the peso.

 The government's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> rose 0.566 of a point in price, pushing its yield down 9 basis points to 7.89 percent.

 Kathryn Rooney, a strategist at Bulltick Capital Markets in Miami, said the steep downturn threatening Mexico's economy could push credit ratings agencies to downgrade the country's peso-denominated debt.

 "The bottom line is we are coming to a new equilibrium, a new stabilization of Mexico's peso," Rooney said.

Barclays analyst Roberto Melzi wrote in a note to clients that given the likely depth of Mexico's recession, he saw the peso fairly valued at around 15 per dollar.

 To limit steep losses in the currency, the central bank established regular dollar auctions in October, when the currency saw its steepest depreciation in more than a decade.

 But that program has failed to stabilize the unit.

 This week's intervention is different from the auctions because it is arbitrary and the central bank has not disclosed the amount of dollars it has sold.

 A UBS bank report said Mexico's central bank could have sold as much as $1.5 billion on Wednesday.

 "If it was that much, it is going to be difficult for the central bank to maintain this level of intervention," said Bulltick's Rooney.

 The cental bank and Finance Ministry did not disclose the amount of dollars sold to the market on Thursday, but said the figure would be apparent when the central bank reports its reserves data next week.

 In stock trading, the IPC benchmark index <.MXX> rose 0.58 percent to end at 19,736.96 points, led by gains in cellphone operator America Movil  ahead of its fourth-quarter earnings report.

NEW YORK, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Latin American stocks, currencies and bonds ended mostly lower on Thursday as persistent economic fears offset some Wall Street gains and a rebound in the price of oil.

U.S. crude oil prices settled 1.63 percent higher and rallied as much as 4 percent in after-hours trading, but other commodities fell, with investors still worried that an expected global economic recession will hurt exports and emerging countries.

"The slowdown in the G7 will hurt emerging markets through a broad range of channels, some of them self-reinforcing," RBC Capital Markets' analysts wrote in a research note, citing prospects of falling commodity prices, declining import demand, lower foreign direct investment, and restricted foreign financing.

As credit conditions continue to tighten in emerging markets, investors fear some companies might have refinancing problems. Banks are also on investors' radar, since a decline in lending activity might affect their profitability.

Bank shares led the Brazilian benchmark Bovespa index <.BVSP> 3.57 percent lower, while Mexico's IPC index <.MXX> lost 5.26 percent. Overall, Latin American shares fell 1.54 percent according to the MSCI stock index for the region <.MILA00000PUS>.

But Argentina's MerVal <.MERV> bucked the regional trend, gaining 2.43 percent in a technical correction that followed losses of more than 10 percent on Wednesday, after a government plan to take over the country's private pension funds unnerved investors.

Most Latin American currencies also weakened on economic fears, but the Brazilian real <BRBY> ended 3.3 percent higher after the central bank heavily sold dollars on the spot foreign exchange market. The bank also unveiled a program to sell up to $50 billion in currency swaps to support the currency.

"The central bank is trying to show it has the means to support the currency. That puts speculators on alert and shows that, if needed, the central bank will make use of all the weapons it has," said Vanderlei Arruda, currency trader at Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The Mexican central bank also sold $1 billion on the foreign exchange market on Thursday but that did not stop its currency <MXN=><MEX01> from weakening 0.7 percent. The peso has lost 6.7 percent of its value in four consecutive sessions of losses.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> weakened 1.4 percent to close at its weakest level in four years, hurt by a further decline in the price of copper, the country's main export.

Emerging-market sovereign bonds remained under pressure, with yield spreads over U.S. Treasuries widening an additional 27 basis points to 829 points, according to the JP Morgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ>.

IMF READYING AID FACILITIES

Outside of Latin America, other emerging-market governments were also struggling to contain the fallout of the global credit crisis.

Russia's central bank raised its main deposit rate by 0.5 percentage point to fight against capital outflows, while data showed the country's foreign reserves fell by $15 billion last week as Moscow tries to defend the ruble.

Countries without significant foreign reserves such as Iceland, Hungary, Ukraine, Serbia, Turkey and Belarus are reaching out to the International Monetary Fund for financial aid.

The IMF also said it is hurrying to approve by early November a liquidity swap facility that would provide liquidity to a select group of well-run emerging economies. For details, see [ID:nN23526514].

The facility would allow governments to swap their domestic currencies for U.S. dollars. Opening swap lines usually gives central banks more ability to lend to their local commercial banks, easing credit strains.

In other news, Standard & Poor's placed Bulgaria's "BBB+" sovereign credit rating on "CreditWatch negative" on concerns over the country's heightened external vulnerabilities. S&P said it will decide on Bulgaria's ratings by the end of the month, depending on the government response to the crisis [ID:nLN737475]. title: UPDATE:Emerging Mkt Bonds Fall As Crisis Deepens; Stks Rally
text:
(Updates with comments, fresh levels) 
 

By Giada Cardoletti Litner

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market debt came under intense pressure again Thursday, while developing country stocks traded in the U.S. closed flat following a highly volatile session.

The intervention of the governments of Brazil and Mexico to prop up the value of their falling currencies, and news that the International Monetary Fund is in discussions with a number of countries about possible loan packages, helped to pare the losses.

Both the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso, which have been pounded of late, benefited from central bank interventions. The peso closed in Mexico City at MXN13.3940, compared with Wednesday's close of MXN13.8550, while the real ended at BRL2.3050 to the dollar, markedly stronger than Wednesday's close at BRL2.3795.

With 10 minutes to go before the closing bell, ADRs pared losses from a session that featured several momentum reversals, as investors went into a buying frenzy.

The Bank of New York Emerging Markets American Depositary Receipt index closed up 0.02% at 174 points after hitting a low of 159 points earlier in the day. The Latin American ADR index climbed 0.93% and the Asian ADR index gained 0.23%.

The reversal tracked the U.S. market where the Dow Jones Industrial Average, in another roller-coaster session, closed up 2%, led by a big bounce in energy companies.

The exodus from emerging markets external debt, however, found no relief, as a combination of fear and deleveraging drove spreads sharply upward.

The spread on JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Global Diversified increased by 31 basis pointsto 850 basis points over Treasurys, its widest this year.

"Equities underperformed external debt and credit default swaps earlier this year (following U.S. equities), so now it's somewhat of a catch-up," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research for RBC Dominion Securities in Toronto.

"This global credit crisis is having a significant impact on global banking systems and capital flows, so this is much more than about equity valuations. It's about unwinding of a massive credit bubble that eventually raises the overall level of risk," he added.

In Central and Eastern Europe, where worries are mounting about current account deficits and large external debts in several countries, credit spreads were at all-time highs. Five-year credit-default swaps on Hungary were trading around 650 basis points, up more than 100 basis points on the day and 202 basis points on the week.

Pakistan, Ukraine, Belarus and Hungary are among the countries with which the IMF has said it's discussing potential loan packages.

The cost of insuring sovereign debt against default for five years rose across the board Thursday, regardless of the credit quality of the sovereign.

Brazil, the emerging markets' credit heavyweight, saw the cost of insuring its debt against default for five years jump 66 basis points to 610 basis points over Treasurys.

Even China, which sits on the world's largest foreign reserves cushion and is believed to be better shielded than other developing economies from the global financial crisis, saw its five-year CDS spread climb 23 basis points to 255 basis points over Treasurys, according to Markit.

"Right now fundamentals are put on the sidelines," said Roberto Sanchez-Dahl, who manages $600 million in emerging markets debt with Federated Investors. "It's all about technicals and the large liquidity needs that put pressure on prices. People are selling whatever they can, anticipating redemption and lower prices... it's like a vicious cycle."

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Stronger At 12.4160/Dlr; Stocks Gain
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's peso closed stronger Monday as demand for dollars from foreign investors eased as the local stock market rallied.

In Mexico City, the peso was quoted as closing at 12.4160 to the dollar, slightly weaker than MXN12.29 at the open but stronger than MXN13.0525 at Friday's close.

One Mexico City-based trader said foreign investors have stopped selling stocks and then buying dollars, a practice that contributed to a dive in the peso last week and prompted the central bank to sell over $8.9 billion in reserves to prop up the local currency.

The IPC stock index was trading up 9.2% at 19,905.2 points.

On Monday there were no takers at dollar auctions by the central bank that had been set up to contain recent exchange market volatility.

The bank has set up daily dollar auctions in which it offers $400 million at a rate 2% higher than the previous day's "fix." But the peso's rally Monday removed the need for the central bank to intervene.

The minimum price for Monday's auctions was MXN13.3484, while the peso was quoted on the market at MXN12.3990 at 2:40 p.m. EDT, when the auction took place. The minimum price for Tuesday's auctions will be MXN12.6218.

Market watchers expect the peso to continue firming.

"It's hard to forecast what levels the peso will be at in coming days, however, we think that with the interventions and the Bank of Mexico's experience in this kind of situation, the exchange rate could settle around MXN12 for several weeks before beginning to come down," the Mexican Institute of Finance Executives said in a report.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks in relentless sell-off, bonds sink
text:
* Emerging market stocks down over 50 percent this year

* Latin American central banks intervene, stocks drop

* Sovereign debt yield spreads widest in 5-1/2 years

* Investors looking to IMF meeting for answers (Updates with IMF/G7 details, closing prices, comment)

By Daniel Bases

NEW YORK, Oct 10 (Reuters) - The relentless slide in global markets swept emerging market assets to fresh multi-year lows on Friday with investors succumbing to panic selling while credit markets remain frozen.

In Washington, Group of Seven finance ministers struggled to agree on a unified approach to cure the crisis that threatens to trigger a deep global recession. (For more, click on [ID:nN10398960].)

Ministers of the Group of 24 developing nations called for a comprehensive response to the crisis and said the balance of risks is shifting to slower growth as inflation recedes. (For more, click on [ID:nWBT009978].)

A handful of emerging market bourses were shut down on Friday rather than risk further declines.

U.S. President George W. Bush implored Americans to remain confident on Friday and promised to restore stability. (For more, click on [ID:nN10363000] and [ID:nG7G8].)

The MSCI emerging markets stock index fell to a three-year low, dropping 4.75 percent, or 29.40 points to 589.50. The index is down 20 percent this week and nearly 53 percent for the year <.MSCIEF>.

In Latin America the picture was similar. The MSCI Latin American stock index tumbled 7.97 percent or 173.41 points to 2001.71. The index is down nearly 29 percent this week and 54 percent for the year <.MILA00000PUS>.

"There is tremendous uncertainty about the future path of the world economy and with more and more converging consensus that we will have a synchronized global recession," said George Hoguet, portfolio manager and emerging markets investment strategist at State Street Global Advisors.

"If that is the case, commodity prices will continue to fall and earnings estimates for emerging market companies will continue to be downgraded," he said,

According to Hoguet, emerging market corporate earnings valuations are reasonable, based on forward earnings forecasts of 7.5 percent to 8.0 percent.

But there is little confidence in the accuracy of estimates "and of course, emerging currencies have been weakening and the Treasury/eurodollar spreads continue to rise," he said.

On a year-to-date basis, the MSCI emerging markets index has lost $1.82 trillion in market value while the Latin American index is down $376.6 billion, according to Reuters EcoWin data.

For perspective, MSCI's main world index has suffered a $13.5 trillion loss of value -- with more than half of that since Lehman Brothers declared bankruptcy on Sept. 15.

Among the major bourses in Latin America, Brazil's Bovespa index <.BVSP> was off 3.97 percent and Mexico's IPC index <.MXX> fell 1.99 percent on Friday.

BOND SPREADS WIDEST IN FIVE YEARS

Emerging market sovereign bonds were trounced on Friday, pushing spreads wider by 56 basis points to 602 bps over weaker U.S. Treasuries. At one point the spread widened to 610 basis points, its worst level since April 11, 2003.

Year to date, the JPMorgan EMBI+ index is down 18.44 percent <11EMJ>. In 2007, the index returned 6.452 percent.

One illustration of the carnage in emerging market sovereign bonds is the plunge in market capitalization versus a minor drop in the face amount of bonds outstanding.

Until this wholesale sell-off of assets with even a whiff of risk, emerging market economies had held up relatively well given rising foreign currency reserves.

At the end of last year, the market capitalization for these bonds stood at $210 billion, according JPMorgan, while the outstanding face amount was $182 billion. Year to date, the market cap has plummeted to $170 billion while the face amount stands relatively unchanged.

That means $40 billion in market value has been wiped away, as of Thursday's close.

On Friday, Brazil's 2040 Global bond <BRAGLB40=RR> fell 4.63 points in price to bid 109, yielding 9.192 percent. At one point, the yield hit 10.168 percent, a four-year high.

Turkey's 2030 global bond <TRGLB30=RR> fell 12.94 points in price to bid 121.313, yielding 9.516 percent. In early New York trade, the bond fell 16.25 points in price, driving the yield to a better than four-year high of 9.836 percent.

INTERVENTIONS

Mexico defended the peso again on Friday with the sale of $6.4 billion on Friday, pulling the currency back from 14.075 per dollar, the weakest point since "new pesos" were introduced in 1993.

In midday New York trade, the peso was still down 3.877 percent at 13.05 per dollar. For the year, the peso is down over 15 percent against the greenback. <MX01><MXN=>.

Mexico's central bank has sold $8.9 billion to defend the peso this week, more than 10 percent of the $84 billion the bank reported holding as of Oct. 3.

Brazil's real fell 5.3 percent <BRBY> to 2.326 per dollar on Friday. Brazil's central bank flooded the spot foreign exchange market with three auctions of U.S. dollars.

Argentina's central bank sold over $500 million to support the local currency, foreign exchange traders told Reuters.

In formal trade between banks <ARS=RASL>, where the central bank intervenes, the peso closed 0.31 percent firmer at 3.22/3.2225 per dollar. In informal trade between foreign exchange houses, as measured by Reuters, the peso closed down 1.2 percent at 3.36/3.37 per U.S. dollar <ARSB=>. The peso is at its weakest level since a 2002 currency devaluation.

Peru's central bank offered to sell U.S. dollars in an attempt to keep its currency, the sol, from falling. The sol <PEN=PE> slid 0.6 percent to 3.105 per dollar.

Late on Thursday, Colombia's central bank said it eliminated a deposit requirement on foreign debt. (For more, click on [ID:nN09339141].)

"Some individual corporates are going through stress but as a sector, EM is not going belly up, we're not talking about a sovereign that is struggling or about extremely leveraged economies having to unwind," Drausio Giacomelli, head of emerging markets strategy at Deutsche Bank in New York.

"It does look like the EM of the past, but when you look more closely, the problems are concentrated in some smaller countries and specific markets. Systemically the regions will have to suffer through the adjustment because of the magnitude of the shock coming from the developed world has been massive. Therefore I wouldn't say we're back to a domino environment of the 1990's or early 2000's, but you may see some casualties."

Euroclear Bank, Europe's largest securities settlement firm, said on Friday it had resumed cash settlements in Icelandic crowns, but that the currency remained suspended for settlement of securities transactions.

Iceland's crown <ISK=><EURISK=> plunged in value this week after the Icelandic government was forced to take over three major banks, and remains volatile on foreign exchange markets. (For more, click on [ID:nLA616407].)

BOURSES SHUT

Russia's stock market remained shut on Friday but authorities planned to reopen on Monday. The government pledged 350 billion roubles to support stocks. (For more, click on [ID:nLA314643].)

Russia was among a handful that either didn't open or shut down after steep losses.

Ukraine's PFTS bourse was also closed. President Viktor Yushchenko, who called for a snap election in December, asked for funds to organize the polls from Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko. The two could not keep their ruling coalition together. (For more, click on [ID:nLA624975].)

Peru's stock exchange indefinitely suspended trade on Friday after the IGRA index <.IGRA> plummetted over 11 percent to 7,606, its largest drop ever.

In Washington, the White House dismissed suggestions that U.S. markets would be suspended so international financial rules could be rewritten. (Additional reporting by Manuela Badawy and Dan Burns in New York; Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Jorge Otaola and Walter Bianchi in Buenos Aires; Jean Luis Arce in Lima)

title: Mexico's Stocks Down On US Drop; Peso Weakens Vs Dollar
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Mexico's stocks accelerated their losses and the peso weakened against the dollar Thursday as U.S. stocks entered a late-session drop amid persistent worries about the global credit situation.

The local stock market's IPC index of leading issues closed down 1.8% or 368.77 points to 20,310.20. Volume was 288.6 million shares worth 5.52 billion pesos ($420 million).

The late drop in stocks was brought on by a dive in U.S. equities, where the Dow Jones Industrials fell 7.3%.

"As long as international markets are weak, we will perform in a similar way," said a Mexico City-based equities analyst.

The peso lost ground in late trading against the dollar, and was quoted in Mexico City at MXN13.15 around 4:10 p.m. EDT.

The peso weakened following a central bank dollar auction in which it sold $1.502 billion at an average exchange rate of MXN12.0794. Demand was $6.29 billion.

The depreciation wasn't enough to trigger dollar sales at subsequent auctions for $400 million, which are offered at a minimum rate of 2% above the previous day's "fix" - or MXN13.30.

The "fix" Thursday was MXN12.4433, putting the minimum exchange rate for Friday's $400 million auction at MXN12.6922.

The daily auctions for $400 million will be conducted until further notice.

A Mexico City currency trader said the central bank interventions, which began Wednesday, will take time to settle the market, although Thursday's session was a lot less volatile that the previous one.

Leading the decline in stocks were the CPO shares of cement giant Cemex (CX), which fell 15% to MXN10.52 after Citigroup cut the stock to "hold" from "buy," saying it should have done so four months ago. Homebuilder Homex (HXM) shares fell 10% to MXN43.37.

At the close, Cemex joined other companies that have issued statements on their financial conditions, given recent investor jitters over credit. Cemex said recent market volatility has led to a negative $500 million mark-to-market value in its derivatives position, compared with a positive $100 million at the end of September.

"We continue to have cash on hand to meet all of our operational and financial requirements," Cemex said.

IPC heavyweight America Movil (AMX) L shares held out for a 1.7% gain to MXN21.20, and debt-free retailer Wal-Mart de Mexico (WMMVY) V shares rose 1.2% to MXN31.01.

Government bonds were steadier than stocks and currency. The yield on 10-year bonds was flat at 8.54%, and the yield on 20-year bonds rose 3 basis points to 8.7%.

The Bank of Mexico began intervening in the exchange market after the peso weakened beyond MXN14 to the dollar Wednesday, its lowest ever level, causing the market to seize up.

The central bank offered $2.5 billion but placed only $998 million, with the rest sold Thursday morning.

Analysts widely praised the decision by the exchange commission, which includes central bank and finance ministry officials, to dip into the country's $84 billion foreign reserves to shore up the peso.

"We're convinced that fundamental variables don't concur with the depreciation of the peso," Citigroup (C) unit Banamex said in a report.

title: UPDATE 3-Mexico  central bank  steps in to boost troubled peso
text:
(Adds new auction Thursday, quotes)

MEXICO CITY, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank stepped in on Wednesday to halt the peso's worst slide since the Tequila Crisis of the mid-1990s, stopping the currency from collapsing due to the world financial crisis.

Breaking with its long-held aversion to intervening in currency markets, the bank offered to auction $2.5 billion and said it was setting up a daily dollar sales mechanism.

"The peso has become the whipping boy for emerging markets today," said Gray Newman, senior Latin American economist at Morgan Stanley, prior to the central bank intervention.

The credit crunch has thrashed currencies around the world but the peso was particularly hard hit, partly because it is easier to trade than many other emerging market currencies, Newman said. It fell almost 15 percent in a few hours on Wednesday.

The fall was compounded by Mexican companies rushing to buy dollars to cover debt payments in foreign currencies after supermarket firm Comercial Mexicana <COMEUBC.MX> warned it faced problems paying its debt, becoming the first major Mexican company in serious trouble from the credit crunch.

The peso crashed as low as 14.32 to the dollar, its weakest level since the early 1990s.

"The exchange movements today were exaggerated and not sustained by fundamentals," Finance Minister Agustin Carstens said.

The bank announced it would put $2.5 billion in dollars in the market but managed only to sell $998 million in two auctions. It will hold another auction on Thursday morning.

INFLATION

Central Bank Gov. Guillermo Ortiz said the peso's fall would not affect Mexico's inflation badly. Lower currency can often mean higher prices for imports, thus pushing inflation up.

Mexico's central bankers have often cited a bungled intervention that helped trigger the mid-1990s Tequila Crisis economic meltdown as an example of why authorities should keep their hands out of currency markets.

Mexico took years to recover from the crisis. The country ran out of foreign reserves and the peso plunged, sending millions into bankruptcy and poverty.

The central bank also moved to curb wide fluctuations in the exchange rate by announcing a separate dollar sales program that will kick in when the currency falls by more than 2 percent in one day.

Starting Thursday, it will offer to sell $400 million at a minimum 2 percent above the previous day's exchange rate every trading day until further notice.

"Consequently, the (daily $400 million) auction will not result in any foreign exchange sales except when the exchange rate has fallen by more than 2 percent," the bank said. (Additional reporting by Noel Randewich, Michael O'Boyle, Robert Campbell and Alistair Bell; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: Mexico peso plunges 6 percent on global crisis
text:

MEXICO CITY, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso plunged more than 6 percent against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as investors, shocked by a burgeoning world credit crisis, fled to safer securities such as U.S. Treasuries.

The peso <MEX01> <MXN=> traded at 12.97 per dollar, having earlier lost almost 13 percent.

Mexico's currency was also pressured by soaring demand from local investors and companies in need of dollars to meet foreign currency-denominated payments, traders said.

Central banks around the world, not including Mexico, cut interest rates in unison on Wednesday to try to limit economic damage from the worst financial crisis in 80 years.

In an unscheduled announcement made as New York traders were reaching their offices, the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its key federal funds rate to 1.5 percent from 2 percent.

In Mexico, where banks have largely weathered the credit crunch, some traders speculated the central bank could intervene to support the peso.

A further economic slowdown in Mexico would not be surprising because of the country's strong trade links with the United States, International Monetary Fund chief economist Olivier Blanchard warned in Washington on Wednesday. title: Emerging Markets-LatAm markets roiled, central banks  intervene
text:
* Selling of currencies met by central.bank interventions

* Global coordinated rate cuts give only temporary boost

* Sovereign debt spreads widen

* Russia and Ukraine halt stock market trading

* Iceland credit rating cut 3 notches by Moody's (Recasts, new throughout)

By Daniel Bases

NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Bouts of panic selling whipsawed Latin American currencies on Wednesday forcing central banks to uncork intervention measures that pushed the Mexican and Brazilian currencies back up from multi-year lows.

The interventions however did not help allay investor fears completely. Emerging market credit default swap spreads widened, indicating investor risk appetite continues to evaporate, although regional stock indexes recovered some ground from their lows.

Sovereign debt issues fell sharply and pushed yields on the benchmark Brazil 2040 bond, considered a proxy for the sector, to a three-year high of 7.802 percent on a flight-to-safety move <BRAGLB40=RR>.

The yield spread on the benchmark JP Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus <11EMJ><.JPMEMBIPLUS> widened by 13 basis points to 516 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. Earlier the spread hit 525, its worst level since May 20, 2004.

Latin America's distinct interest rate yield advantage was made more glaring by the coordinated interest rate cut by developed markets. The first coordinated central bank rate cut since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks was largely dismissed by the investors concerned authorities don't yet have a grip on the global credit crisis. (For related story click on [ID:nHKG77476].)

"It is completely panic selling. It is illiquidity compounded by fears of lower growth," said Benito Berber, Latin American strategist at RBS in Stamford, Connecticut.

"The coordinated rate cut should have made a difference but emerging market currencies are extremely susceptible to growth concerns and are extremely, extremely illiquid, so that allows the currencies to adjust very quickly and that prompted actions of central banks," he said.

CENTRAL BANKS

Mexico's central bank intervened in the market following the currency's sharp slide to a 16-year low of more than 14 per dollar earlier in the session.

Brazil's central bank intervened four times on Wednesday in order to prop up the real, which at one point fell more than 6.0 percent in value to its weakest point since August 2005 against the greenback.

"It seems that global investors had recently been using the dollar/peso as hedging vehicle, especially today when dollar/real trading was halted in the BM&F after it rose 6.0 percent," wrote Roberto Melzi of Barclays Capital.

"The announcement of U.S. dollar sales by the Brazilian central bank calmed the market and permitted dollar/peso to recover from the 14.05 unprecedented intra-day high."

For a time on Wednesday trading of dollar/real futures contracts froze on Brazil's Commodities and Futures Exchange (BM&F) when levels hit limits established by the exchange.

After the interventions the currency regained its footing, rising 0.74 percent to 2.294 per U.S. dollar <BRBY>.

The Mexican peso plunged more than 6.0 percent against the U.S. dollar as investors fled to the relative safety of U.S. Treasuries, which were themselves lower on the day.

The Mexican peso <MEX01><MXN=> traded down 7.71 percent at 13.16 per dollar, having earlier lost more than 15 percent which brought it to its weakest level in more than a decade of 14.32. (For related stories click on [ID:nN082099] and [ID:nN081356])

"The peso has become the whipping boy for emerging markets today," said Gray Newman, senior Latin American economist at Morgan Stanley in New York.

STOCK MARKET TURBULENCE

After an initial sharp downturn in Latin American stocks, losses were trimmed but still left benchmark indices at their weakest points in over two years.

"The (interest rate cuts) announced today give you the impression that governments are a little desperate. Monetary policy has only a limited effect, because we have a confidence crisis," said Roberto Padovani, Sao Paulo-based chief economist with WestLB.

A surprise increase in pending U.S. home sales for August helped buoy sentiment in U.S. markets, although volatile trade left them down on the day. (For related stories, click on [ID:nN08520388] and [ID:nN08184853])

Initially, the MSCI Latin American stock index plunged more than 14 percent to its lowest point since June 2006. By day's end the loss was cut to 5.43 percent <.MILA00000PUS>.

Brazil's Bovespa stock index <.BVSP> ended down 3.85 percnt at 38,593.4, while Mexico's IPC stock index <.MXX> ended down just 0.98 percent at 20,678.

MSCI's global emerging market stock index <.MSCIEF> fell to a three-year low before recovering slightly to end with a better than 7.0 percent decline on the day.

Latin America's central banks did not participate in the global central bank rate cuts and in recent months have been raising interest rates to fight rising inflation.

The direction for rates in the region could change given global recession fears and the fall in commodity prices which has lowered inflation concerns.

ICELAND MELTS, UKRAINE DISOLVES

In European emerging markets, Iceland's currency collapsed after the central bank abandoned efforts to defend the crown, allowing it to plunge from a two-day attempt to hold it at 131 per euro.

Currency dealers outside Iceland have been using Reuters matching system, traders said as the local market has stopped functioning smoothly.

The system was showing that the Icelandic crown dealt at 340 per euro <EURISK=D3> versus 245 per euro on Tuesday.

Moody's Investors Service cut Iceland's sovereign credit rating three notches to "A1" from "Aa1" while Fitch Ratings chopped its rating three notches to "BBB-" from "A-".

Ukraine's credit default swap spreads, a measure of risk sentiment, deteriorated on Wednesday moving to 1,015 from 899 on Tuesday, according to date provider Markit <UAGV5YUSAC=MP>.

In Kiev, Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko dissolved parliament, blaming Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, his estranged ally from the 2004 "Orange Revolution", for the collapse of the coalition government that emerged from that pro-Western upheaval which swept him from power.

Trading on Ukraine's PFTS stock exchange <.PFTSI><0#.PFTSI> remained suspended for a second day while Russia, one of the four biggest component economies in the MSCI emerging markets stock index, suspended share trading after steep declines in the first minutes of the session.

London-listed Russian shares however recovered to outperform global markets. The FTSE Russia index <.FTRIOB>, down 17 percent in earlier trade, closed off 2.93 percent.

title: ANALYSIS- Mexico  cenbank seen reticent to  intervene  on peso
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank is seen trying to avoid propping up the plunging peso amid the world financial crisis after years of opposition to currency market intervention, analysts said on Monday.

But the central bank might have to step in if the peso plummets further and puts Mexico's hard-won economic stability at risk.

The peso nosedived 6.43 percent to 11.98 against the dollar on Monday as investors agonized over a deepening global credit crisis and prospects of less economic growth worldwide.

It was the currency's worst single day since 1995, when Mexico was embroiled in an economic meltdown known as the Tequila Crisis.

Mexico's central bankers have often cited that crisis, when the economy tanked following an ultimately failed attempt by the government to prop up the currency, as an example of why authorities should keep their hands out of currency markets.

"In Mexico they don't do that," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist at IDEAglobal.

"But if things really deteriorate far worse than we are experiencing ... they will do something and everyone will understand that."

Delgado and other analysts speculated that if the central bank decided it had to protect the peso it could reinstate daily dollar auctions of international reserves that it suspended in July. Under that practice, the bank each day diverted a chunk of dollars from oil sales into currency markets.

TOUGH CALL

Dramatic changes in the value of a currency can wreak havoc in a country's economy.

The instability, which makes it harder to plan for the future, can dissuade investment. Rapid depreciation makes imports more expensive, stoking inflation, though a country's exports become cheaper abroad and therefore more competitive.

But a move to boost the peso's value could have big consequences because markets could put the central bank's will to the test by aggressively betting against the peso, analysts said.

That could put a big drain on Mexico's international reserves of $83 billion should authorities make a big effort to boost the peso.

"Those reserves ... would only last for a couple of days," said RBS Greenwich Capital economist Benito Berber.

During the Tequila Crisis, Mexico's peso-propping government eventually ran so low on reserves that it had to float the currency, triggering a massive devaluation overnight.

"It's a very tough call for a central bank," said UBS economist Gabriel Casillas. "I don't think the central bank will intervene directly. They have a tradition of non-intervention." (Writing by Jason Lange, Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: Mexico could step in to weaken peso - UBS
text:
MEXICO CITY, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Mexico could intervene in the foreign exchange market to weaken the peso currency, which has surged more than 10 percent this year and threatens to hurt the country's competitiveness, UBS said on Monday.

The finance ministry and central bank, which share responsibility for Mexico's foreign exchange policy, could announce a peso sale program as soon as this week, UBS economist Gabriel Casillas said in a report.

The government and central bank had no immediate comment.

Mexico's peso <MEX01> <MXN=> has soared in recent months as high interest rates have attracted foreign investors looking to beat paltry yields on U.S. Treasuries.

Mexican Central Bank Gov. Guillermo Ortiz warned last week the expensive peso could hurt Mexican exporters.

Also last week, Ortiz, asked by a reporter whether he might intervene in the foreign exchange market, said central banks cannot vow never to use any tool available.

"He was clearly saying, 'You know what? I have no problem intervening if I need to,'" Casillas said.

Mexico's central bank recently said it was suspending a daily sale of dollar foreign reserves, ballooning because of oil exports, that has strengthened the peso in recent years.

That is expected to reduce slightly demand for the peso, which gained to fewer than 10 to the dollar on Friday for the first time in more than five years.

The central bank said the dollar sale was being suspended after the government bought $8 billion to cover foreign exchange requirements for the coming months. But traders speculated the bank wanted to stem the peso's gain.

HSBC said in a report on Monday it does not expect the central bank to start selling pesos.

From 1996 to 2001, Mexico sold banks options to sell up to $250 million dollars a month to Banco de Mexico, a program that could easily be revived, Casillas said.

Intervention in foreign exchange markets by central banks can become expensive, economists warn.

"It would be unwise to take any move that could be read by the markets as trying to draw a line in the sand or defend a particular level," said Gray Newman, an economist at Morgan Stanley in New York. (Reporting by Noel Randewich; Editing by Dan Grebler) (Additional reporting by Luis Rojas)

title: UPDATE 1-Mexico central bankers flag peso risk, some see pre-Fed hike
text:

MEXICO CITY, May 19 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank board is worried global financial volatility could spur a deeper slump in the peso, and some of its members think it might need to hike interest rates before the U.S. Federal Reserve, according to the minutes of their last policy meeting.

Policymakers voted 5 to 0 to keep their benchmark rate at 3.75 percent at their May 5 meeting, according to the minutes released on Thursday.

The central bank had surprised markets with a 50 basis point hike in February.

According to the minutes of the last meeting, some board members thought Mexico may need to raise interest rates again independently of any move by the U.S. Federal Reserve to tighten borrowing costs due to the risks to inflation.

The peso has weakened sharply since late 2014, but inflation so far has been surprisingly cool.

One member thought there was enough slack in the economy to raise rates without hitting growth.

Most members thought that annual inflation would end the year around its 3 percent target, but the majority worried about the risk that global volatility could spark a "disorderly" drop in the peso that could have a bigger impact on inflation.

A sharp drop in the peso during February pushed Mexico's central bank to directly intervene in currency markets for the first time since 2009 and to unexpectedly raise interest rates after an unannounced meeting.

Since the bank's policy announcement early this month, the peso tumbled again, hitting a fresh three-month low on Thursday.

The speed of the peso's recent tumble has sparked speculation the central bank could soon intervene to try and cushion the currency's fall with direct dollar sales.

title: Mexico  peso hits 3-month low, market expects more  intervention
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 18 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso slumped to a three-month low on Wednesday, with the speed of its recent tumble sparking speculation the central bank could soon intervene to try and cushion the currency's fall.

The peso sank as much as 0.9 percent to 18.4510 per dollar, its weakest since February. The peso has lost nearly 7 percent this month, making it the second worst performer among the world's 36 most-traded currencies, behind the South African rand.

A prominent group of Mexican economists on Tuesday said the peso was under a speculative attack, and analysts said the country's central bank could soon sell dollars directly to the market, as it did in February.

"They are willing to use their firepower," said Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York.

"You need to anchor the currency at some point, if the peso goes to 19 or 20 (to the dollar) that could change the inflation outlook and the central bank is very mindful of that," Ramos said.

By midday Wednesday, the peso had pared losses to trade 0.45 percent lower at 18.3625.

A sharp peso drop in February pushed Mexico's central bank to directly intervene in currency markets for the first time since 2009 and to unexpectedly raise interest rates after an unannounced meeting.

Then, Mexican policymakers said the peso was being targeted by electronic trading programs and that its losses did not match with the relatively sound position of the economy.

On Tuesday, Deputy Central Bank Governor Javier Guzman said the bank may need to raise interest rates if global events hit the peso enough to affect inflation expectations. So far, inflation has been slower than expected.

Emerging market currencies have been slammed by renewed expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve could tighten borrowing costs, which could sap demand for higher-yielding but riskier assets.

The Mexican peso is one of world's most liquid currencies and unlike many other emerging markets there are no capital controls on its trade. That makes it easier to bet against the peso when global sentiment on risky assets turns sour.

"It's a cheap proxy for expressing a negative view on emerging markets," said UBS strategist Manik Narain.

Mexico's peso bonds are among the most widely held debt among those issued in emerging market currencies.

Foreign investors hold over 2 trillion pesos ($109 billion) in peso debt, and many need to hedge their positions when the peso slumps, further driving volatility, Narain said.

title: Mexico  cenbank may  intervene  to deter attack on peso -economists
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 17 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso is under a speculative attack and the country's central bank could soon intervene in foreign exchange markets, an influential group of Mexican economists said on Tuesday.

Hedge funds are testing the central bank through an attack on the peso, according to economists at the Mexican Institute for Finance Executives (IMEF), a trade group of local chief financial officers.

"The way to fight an exchange rate problem is with foreign exchange policy, not monetary policy, as in this case, with the sale of foreign reserves," Gabriel Casillas, the IMEF's vice president of economic studies, said at a conference in Mexico City.

Casillas, who is also chief economist at Mexican bank Banorte, said he believed the peso was under a "speculative attack."

Mexico's peso has shed more than 6 percent this month, making it the second worst performer in May among the world's 36 most-traded currencies, behind the South African rand.

In February, Mexico's central bankintervened directly in currency markets for the first time since 2009 and unexpectedly raised its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 3.75 percent.

At the time, the central bank said it acted after the peso experience losses that were not in line with the fundamentals of the Mexican economy, blaming electronic trading programs for attacking the peso.

"We think that at this time, given the current conditions, (Mexico's foreign exchange commission) could turn to an intervention to calm markets a bit," IMEF president Joaquin Gandara said.

Other economists think the central bank could use a combination of an interest rate hike and additional intervention to support the peso.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS- Mexico 's surprise  intervention  missed chance to nail speculators
text:
(Repeats Thursday story with no changes to text)

By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss and Michael O'Boyle

NEW YORK/MEXICO CITY, Feb 18 (Reuters) - The Banco de Mexico's surprise interest rate hike and intervention in the peso market has halted the slump in the currency for now, but the bank appears to have missed a chance to inflict maximum damage to speculators.

The central bank on Wednesday sold dollars directly to the market for the first time since 2009, abandoning a rules-based auction regime that Mexican authorities said had become predictable and exploited by market players.

The bank launched its assault about a week after some of the most aggressive bets against the peso in U.S.-based currency derivatives markets came off the board, data from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission shows.

The net short position by hedge funds and other big speculators in peso futures and options traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange dropped last week by the most in four months.

The pullback, a net drop of more than 32,000 contracts worth around $850 million (16 billion pesos), reduced the net short position among speculators from around a six-month high.

But while the intervention may not have hurt speculators as much as it could have, Mexico's shift to a new discretionary policy may yet prove a greater deterrent to peso shorts.

The currency has been a popular target for speculators since late September 2014, when it snapped a period of relative stability against the dollar and began grinding ever lower.

Hedge funds in the trade briefly pared back those bets last fall but piled back in over the last three months, building into the fifth-largest net short position on record valued at $2.1 billion (39.2 billion pesos) until last week's reversal, the CFTC data shows.

The reduction in short positions also coincides with last week's series of record lows for the peso against the greenback.

"One way bets like that can become self-fulfilling and get overextended, in particular as momentum traders and correlation (proxy hedging) trades starts kicking in," said Jeppe Ladekarl, a partner at global asset manager First Quadrant with assets of $20.3 billion.

Another analyst said the position was becoming very pricey to maintain as peso volatility rose in its relentless drop to a record low.

"Probably the hedge got too expensive due to volatility and it was just profit taking given that the peso had reached a historical level," said Marco Oviedo, an economist at Barclays in Mexico City.

On Wednesday, the liquid front-month peso future expiring in mid-March saw record volume of more than 128,000 contracts, some three standard deviations above the norm.

Open interest dropped by nearly 6,500 contracts, the most in a month and an indication of traders closing out positions.

The March peso contract gained more than 2.8 percent in Wednesday's session, the biggest gain in more than four years, and was up another 0.3 percent on Thursday.

To be sure, speculative bets against the peso appear far from fully flushed out, despite the turn around.

CFTC data from last week showed a net short position of more than 46,000 contracts, valued at about $1.2 billion (about 23 billion pesos) was then remaining in play. That compares with an average net long position among speculators over the last decade of nearly 34,000 contracts.

Still, Kenneth Lam, a strategist at Citi in New York, said the introduction of a system where the Banco de Mexico can enter currency markets at any time would deter some moves against the peso, which he expects to keep gaining ground in the near term.

title: UPDATE 1-Mexico  central bank  discussed possible interest rate rise in early Feb

(Adds detail, background)

MEXICO CITY, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Mexican central bank policymakers were unanimous in their Feb 4 decision to leave interest rates on hold, according to the minutes of the meeting reported on Thursday, but most added it was important to signal they could move at any time, as they subsequently did on Wednesday this week with a surprise rate hike.

At their early February meeting, policymakers voted 5 to 0 to keep their benchmark interest rate at 3.25 percent but a majority said monetary policy was in a complicated situation.

The minutes of the Feb. 4 meeting were published on Thursday, a day after the central bank surprised markets by delivering a 50 basis point interest rate rise to shore up Mexico's peso which had fallen by about 30 percent against the U.S. dollar in the past year. Mexico's peso ended up nearly 3.0 percent on Wednesday after the rate hike.

The central bank on Wednesday also suspended daily auctions to support the currency in favor of extraordinary interventions during moments of high volatility.

Mexico's peso hit a fresh record low last week on tumbling crude oil prices. Mexico is the world's tenth largest oil producer and oil revenues account for about 10 percent of its exports and about one third of government spending, according to the U.S. Energy Information Agency. Crude oil prices have fallen more than 70 percent in the past two years.

In the Feb 4 decision, some members said they would need to hike interest rates if the recent volatility in global markets worsened and said they should move on rates whether pressures came from the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy changes or any other source.

Laying the groundwork for Thursday's surprise interest rate rise in the minutes of the Feb 4 meeting, the majority thought it was important to send the message that the bank could act with "flexibility" to adjust monetary policy at the right pace.

The majority also highlighted worsening risks to growth and inflation in the short term.

Mexico's annual inflation rose faster than expected in January from a record low, partly reflecting the slump in the peso.

Inflation in the 12 months through January rose to 2.61 percent, up from a 2.13 percent rate in December. Prior to Wednesday's rate rise, Mexico's central bank had raised interest rates in December. (Reporting by Michael O'Boyle and Alexandra Alper; Editing by Simon Gardner and Clive McKeef)
