title: POLL-Scant room for more rate cuts in Latin America this year
text:
* For Latin America poll data click on

* GDP forecasts broadly unchanged from Jan poll

* Economists see growth divide between Pacific and Atlantic

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, April 11 (Reuters) - Latin American central banks will probably leave interest rates unchanged for now after relatively low inflation allowed them to give their economies an extra boost earlier this year, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.

The clear exception is Brazil, where inflation has pierced the official target ceiling and will probably force the central bank to raise interest rates soon.

The poll of 95 economists and analysts worldwide also underscored that economic growth is not at peril in most of Latin America, with forecasts broadly unchanged for most of the countries from a similar poll conducted three months ago.

In the latest regional Reuters poll in January, economists presaged correctly that there would be a window of opportunity to trim interest rates after a surprise slowdown in inflation. While prices have not become a threat in most of the region, economists now see scant room for further rate cuts.

Mexico's central bank trimmed its benchmark lending rate to a record low of 4 percent last month. It will probably leave it at that level through end-2014, according to the median of 18 forecasts in the poll.

Colombian policymakers took more aggressive action and chopped interest rates to 3.25 percent, the lowest in the region, as inflation hovered below the bottom end of the inflation target band. Now they will probably leave rates unchanged for the rest of the year, hiking them back to 4.25 percent only in 2014, the poll showed.

The possibility of further easing should not be ruled out, though, as a tool to fight massive capital inflows triggered by easy monetary policies in countries like Japan.

"If the Mexican peso continues to appreciate fast, the central bank might consider further rate cuts," wrote HSBC's economists led by Sergio Martin in a research note.

In Chile, authorities have considered raising rates to prevent the economy from overheating.

Economists say no action will be taken until the fourth quarter of this year as forecasts for inflation remain comfortably within the government's target.

Concerns about excessive currency gains should also affect monetary policy in Peru, where borrowing costs should be unchanged at 4.25 percent through the end of 2014, at least.

GROWTH DIVIDE

Despite an overall healthy outlook for economic growth in Latin America, economists notice a gap between fast-growing Pacific countries like Peru and Chile, and slower Atlantic economies such as Brazil and Argentina - where heavy government intervention has scared off foreign investors.

"Mexico is likely to outperform Brazil over the next few years. And while near-term growth in Peru and Chile should hold up fairly well, we expect Venezuela and Argentina to flirt with recession for the foreseeable future," wrote economists at Capital Economics in a note.

Mexico and Colombia, where interest rates dropped recently, will both grow between 3.5 and 4.5 percent in 2013 and 2014, and Peru will continue to expand by more than 6 percent annually - one of the best performances in the world.

Among the Latin American countries with inflation-targeting regimes, Brazil is the clear exception.

The central bank, which shocked markets by slashing interest rates 10 straight times in the past two years, is expected to raise borrowing costs from May on to push inflation back to the target bank.

The poll also showed that the political uncertainty in Venezuela after the death of President Hugo Chavez has taken a toll on forecasts for economic growth. The oil exporter will probably grow just 1.0 percent this year, down from a previous estimate of 2.0 percent, the median of 11 forecasts showed.

title: DJ Mexican Peso, Korean Won Rally Further
text:
The Mexican peso and the South Korean won led the continued rally in emerging-market currencies Thursday though the pace was much more muted.

The dollar hit a 20-month low to the peso, stirring some concerns that the central bank may be contemplating ways to decelerate the gains.

The Mexican peso's March rally ramped up even more after the Bank of Japan last week announced further monetary easing to stimulate its economy. Since then, higher-yielding assets, including emerging-market currencies, have seen sharp gains.

The dollar dropped to a fresh low of MXN12.0372, down 0.54% on the day, on the back of fresh inflows from investment managers and speculative money accounts. Analysts say that the peso has appreciated strongly not only versus the dollar but also against other majors like the yen and the euro.

This, they say, strengthens the argument for an intervention, or at least a counter measure from the central bank that could slow the pace of appreciation.

"We may be days or weeks from an intervention announcement in Mexico," said Benito Berber,

This may not be unusual, given other central banks such as Turkey and Chile had indicated that they would not be indifferent to currency appreciation. Mr. Berber expects the Mexican central bank to come up with a mechanism that would cushion the currency's volatility.

It is unclear what the trigger would be for such a move. One possibility could be when the dollar dips below MXN12.

South Korea's central bank surprised market participants by keeping its policy rates unchanged. But analysts expect the bank to ease in the coming months after it potentially revises its economic forecast lower.

The Korean won, however, got a lift after the unexpected move. The dollar fell to KRW1129.5, down 0.5% on the day.

In Brazil, expectations that the central bank may be forced to raise rates by at least 25 basis points at its rate-setting meeting next week, especially after comments by President Dilma Rousseff led to the rally in the real stalling. The dollar remained steady at BRL1.9736, according to CQG data

Market participants also expect the central bank to act given Brazil's accelerating inflation.

Meanwhile, emerging-market issuers continued their hectic pace of debt offerings.

On Thursday, the Dominican Republic and Lebanon were in the market with benchmark-sized deals. The Dominican Republic was in the market with a $1 billion, 10-year bond that is also expected to be priced later in the day.

Sovereigns and companies have been in the market this week tapping investors renewed quest for higher-yielding emerging-market assets. Many of these dollar bonds sell at much lower yields than the cost to borrow in their own countries.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso rallies to 19-month high, Brazil real flat
text:
* Optimism about upcoming U.S. jobs data encourages risk taking

* Investors alert for possible Brazil cenbank intervention

* Mexico peso jumps 0.8 pct; Brazil real unchanged

By Michael O'Boyle and Bruno Federowski

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, April 2 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso hit a 19-month high on Tuesday as a rally on Wall Street encouraged investors to take on riskier emerging market assets, but the Brazilian real ended nearly unchanged for the second consecutive session on fears of a central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso jumped 0.8 percent to 12.2720 per dollar, its strongest level since early September 2011, as major U.S. stock indexes rose to record levels.

Investors were growing optimistic that key U.S. jobs data on Friday will show the U.S. economy is on solid footing, increasing prospects for Mexican exports. The United States is Mexico's main trading partner.

"The peso could reach 12.15 per dollar with a good U.S. jobs data on Friday, but people should start buying dollars then," said Mario Copca, an analyst with CI brokerage in Mexico City.

The peso has rallied more than 6 percent from a December low, helped by bets the new government will push through major economic reforms.

But the surge may be petering out. Technical momentum indicators show the peso in "overbought" territory, and the currency's moving-average convergence divergence (MACD) indicator was on the verge of flashing a "sell" sign.

In Brazil, the real ended practically unchanged at 2.0201 per dollar, with investors wary of a possible central bank intervention.

Many analysts believe the Brazilian central bank wants the real to remain within a tight range of 1.95 reais to around 2 reais per dollar - slightly stronger than it was at the end of 2012 - to avoid inflation passthrough.

"There is no reason for bigger changes in the exchange rate. If you are going to test the currency band, you want to do it carefully or as the central bank can suddenly dump dollars on the market," said Mario Battistel, a manager at Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazilian policymakers last intervened in the market last Wednesday, when the real neared the level of 2.03 per dollar. On Tuesday, central bank president Alexandre Tombini reiterated that the bank is always ready to intervene to make sure the foreign exchange market is working properly.

text:
* EU gives Cyprus ultimatum to raise money or face bankruptcy

* Brazil real crosses 2/dlr mark for 1st time since Jan 30

* Mexico says any FX intervention would be rules-based

* Brazil real drops 0.6 pct, Mexico peso 0.5 pct lower

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 21 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real and the Mexican peso slid on Thursday as fears of a financial meltdown in Cyprus, combined with signs of economic weakness in Europe, drove investors to the safety of the dollar.

The Brazilian real dropped 0.6 percent, crossing the 2-per-dollar mark that many analysts considered a boundary of an informal trading band imposed by policymakers.

It was the first time since Jan. 30 that the real traded weaker than 2 per dollar, leaving investors on guard for a possible central bank intervention in the currency market.

"We have to see if the central bank will act now that the real has weakened past 2 per dollar," said Jaime Ferreira, a currency trader with Intercam brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"I believe it is too early for an intervention but, if this lasts till Friday, the central bank may very well do something."

Analysts believe the Brazilian central bank wants the real to remain within 1.95-2.0 per dollar, slightly stronger than it was at the end of 2012, to help lower the price of imported goods and anchor inflation expectations.

The Mexican peso lost 0.5 percent as investors feared an escalation of the euro zone crisis if Cyprus' banking system is allowed to collapse in the next few days.

On Friday, the European Union gave the island an ultimatum to raise the billions of euros it needs to secure an international bailout before the European Central Bank cuts off liquidity to Cypriot banks.

"People are worried about Cyprus. Either it accepts the EU conditions or it goes bankrupt," said Reginaldo Galhardo, a currency manager with Treviso brokerage.

Investor concerns were also fueled by purchasing managers' data showing French businesses had their worst performance in four years in March, likely pushing the euro zone's second-largest economy into recession, while Germany also seemed to be running out of steam.

The Mexican currency had hit its strongest level in more than 1-1/2 years on Wednesday, leaving some investors wondering whether the government was growing uncomfortable with the strength of the peso.

But on Thursday Finance Minister Luis Videgaray said Mexico will continue with its flexible exchange rate and that any intervention in the currency market would be based on rules.

text:

MEXICO CITY, March 21 (Reuters) - Mexican Finance Minister Luis Videgaray on Thursday said his country will continue with its flexible exchange rate and that any intervention would be rules-based.

Mexico's peso hit its strongest levels in more than 1-1/2 years this week, but Latin America's No. 2 economy has avoided using the direct intervention and capital controls that other emerging-market countries have used to tame currency gains.

 The peso's strong gains have fueled speculation that Mexico could reinstate a rules-based mechanism of auctioning dollar "put" options, which could show authorities are growing uncomfortable with the pace of peso gains. 

 "We will continue with a free-float exchange rate policy," Videgaray said at an event hosted by U.S. news agency Bloomberg in Mexico City.

 Deputy Finance Minister Fernando Aportela told Reuters on Saturday that Mexico's currency commission, made up of members of the central bank and the finance ministry, had not discussed any new measures to try to slow the peso's advance.

 "The currency committee's intervention will be as it has been until now: with rules that are made known previously and that aim to moderate abrupt variations," Videgaray said in response to a question.

 Mexico's peso has surged more than 3 percent this month, backed by growing optimism about the government's ability to push long-stalled economic reforms through a divided Congress.

 The central bank cut its benchmark interest rate to a record low of 4 percent on March 8 in what market players read as a bid to curb the appeal of the currency to yield-hungry investors.

 While lower rates could deter some speculators, analysts expect the peso to keep gaining ground due to euphoria about the chance for reforms and potential credit-ratings upgrades. 

 The peso has yet to recover to the levels seen before late 2008, and the currency's relative cheapness has boosted Mexican exports amid sluggish global growth.

 The Banco de Mexico warned on March 8 that heavy inflows could lead to an 'unnecessary' tightening in monetary conditions. A stronger peso could create drag on growth by crimping exporters' profits.

 Economy Minister Ildefonso Guarjardo said at the same event on Thursday that any loss to Mexico's competitiveness would be offset by gains from the series of planned economic reforms, including key energy and tax bills due later this year. 

 Mexican lawmakers were set to vote on Thursday on a  sweeping telecommunications bill that would threaten dominant companies with tougher regulation.

title: INTERVIEW-Mexico has learned to stick with flexible peso-Aportela
text:
* Authorities have not discussed reactivating dollar put auctions

 * No other intervention measures have been discussed 

 By Michael O'Boyle

 PANAMA CITY, March 16 (Reuters) - Mexico is committed to maintaining its freely floating exchange rate and is not currently contemplating any new mechanism to slow strong gains in the peso, deputy finance minister Fernando Aportela said on Saturday.

 The peso hit a 18-month high against the dollar last week, boosted by growing confidence in a reform drive by the new government and potential credit-rating upgrades, sparking speculation that authorities could take measures to slow the currency's advance.

 Aportela said Mexico's currency commission, made up of members of the central bank and the finance ministry, had not discussed any new measures to try and slow the peso's advance.

 "Mexico has learned that the sound macroeconomic policy of having a well-administered flexible exchange rate pays off in the end," Aportela told Reuters at an Inter-American Development Bank meeting in Panama City. 

Mexico has eschewed the direct intervention and capital controls that other emerging-market countries have deployed in recent years to tame local currency gains resulting from a flood of liquidity from developed markets seeking higher returns.

 Investors are watching to see if Mexico will reinstate a more market-friendly mechanism of auctioning dollar "put" options, which could indicate authorities are growing uncomfortable with the pace of peso gains. 

 The options, which the central bank used to accumulate reserves and slow peso gains in 2010 and 2011, give investors the right to sell dollars to the central bank at a better rate than the spot rate when the cost of dollars in pesos falls below its 20-day moving average.

 Aportela said policymakers had not discussed reinstating the auctions and they were not looking at any other tools either. "The set of instruments we have are what they are," he said. 

 Mexico's peso, one of the world's most liquid emerging-market currencies, has oscillated wildly since the financial crisis, tracking the ups and downs of riskier global assets.

 The currency has yet to recover to the levels seen before  late 2008, which has helped boost the competitiveness of Mexican exports amid sluggish global growth.

 "The exchange rate has shown itself to be effective in absorbing this type of external volatility," Aportela said.

 Market players read a 50 basis point cut to Mexico's benchmark rate to a record low of 4 percent on March 8 as a bid by the central bank to try and curb the appeal of local-currency fixed-income assets to speculators.

 The Banco de Mexico warned that heavy inflows could lead to an 'unnecessary' tightening in monetary conditions. A stronger peso could create drag on growth by crimping exporters' profits.

title: ANALYSIS-Mexico peso rise tests  central bank 's hands-off stance
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 14 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso is scaling new highs amid confidence in the country's reform push, a likely credit ratings upgrade and profit taking after last week's interest rate cut, sparking speculation about how far it will rise before authorities act.

The peso has gained 2.6 percent since the start of the month, the best performance of the 152 currencies tracked by Thomson Reuters, and broken through key levels of 12.50 per dollar for the first time in 18 months.

The rise has come despite a 50 basis point cut in benchmark interest rates to a record low 4 percent on Friday, which only served to fuel investor optimism about the outlook for Latin America's No. 2 economy.

A signal from ratings agency Standard and Poor's that it might upgrade Mexico's credit rating and the announcement of plans to introduce more competition into the communications sector have also boosted Mexico's standing.

"As an investor, this is positive ... and will attract more capital to Mexico," said Rudy Amoresano, founder of boutique fund manager Caerus Management, of the reform plan.

More capital is the last thing the central bank wants. The Banco de Mexico warned that heavy inflows could lead to an 'unnecessary' tightening in monetary conditions, as a stronger peso would drag on growth.

"The market is testing to see how far the central bank will allow the peso to appreciate without taking any kind of action,"

said Enrique Alvarez, Latin America strategist at IDEAglobal.

Even though the rate cut has not dissuaded investors in the short term, the famously non-interventionistBanco de Mexico has more options up its sleeve.

It could officially drop a mechanism triggering an automatic offer of dollars if the peso weakens sharply, introduced when the currency was going through a weak patch in late 2011.

Banorte-Ixe economist Gabriel Casillas said this could be a first step, possibly followed by reinstating a monthly auction of dollar "put" options. This would build up Mexico's foreign reserves cushion and also pour pesos into the market, helping to curb gains. The central bank did this in 2010 and 2011.

"It's an ingenious thing where actually the market intervenes and the central bank does not," said CIBC World Markets Latin America strategist John Welch.

Under the program, the Banco de Mexico auctions the right to sell dollars back to the central bank. If the peso appreciates strongly, a bank may exercise its option and it will get more pesos for its dollars than it would on the floating peso market.

SPECULATION COOLS

Welch said some of the recent peso gains could also be explained by an unwinding of hedge positions put on by investors during a recent rally in Mexican bonds before the rate cut.

"A lot of people hedge their rate exposure and their bond exposure by shorting the peso and buying dollars, so once they got the fact of the cut, many of them took profits and they would unwind the hedge, which is they would sell dollar-MX instead of buying it," he said.

One welcome sign for the central bank, which has publicly sworn off any involvement in the 'currency wars' of competitive devaluations, is that speculators are backing off from record bets on further peso appreciation.

Speculative net long positions are down more than 35 percent from mid-January, when the peso reached a 10-month high and the central bank first warned of lower rates ahead, according to data from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Net bets on a stronger peso were the weakest in three months for the week of March 5. The current week's data, due for release on Friday, will show if that trend has accelerated.

But Bank of America Latin America strategist Ezequiel Aguirre said the reduction in the positions was a signal for some traders to get back in.

"The position was cleaned out, so now you have a lot of investors getting together to push the peso," he said.

Another way to dampen upward pressure on the peso would be to give incentives to accelerate capital outflows, perhaps via Mexican pension funds, or Afores, which hold 1.9 trillion pesos ($153.51 billion) in assets.

Peru has raised the foreign investment limit for its pension funds to help stem currency appreciation, although Mexico's funds do not even hold the maximum in offshore assets allowed.

Data from regulator CONSAR show the funds hold 15.7 percent of their assets offshore, below the 20 percent limit, but up from the 11.9 percent they invested two years ago.

Barclays Capital economist Marco Oviedo said one reason the peso was not already at the 10.5 per dollar levels seen before the financial crisis was private capital outflows by Mexican residents, including the Afores.

Although foreigners pumped a record $80 billion into Mexican stocks and bonds last year, Mexicans sent $7 billion out of the country to invest in markets overseas, and another $26 billion in direct investments - double the level of 2011.

But if Mexico gains momentum on reforms, passing the telco changes and pushing ahead with proposals to shake up the tax system and energy sector, foreign capital inflows could push the peso to 12.20 by October, Oviedo said. ($1 = 12.3982 Mexican pesos)

Other Latin American currencies posted more modest gains, supported by rising metal prices, but the Brazilian real slipped for a second day following a Monday intervention by the central bank that halted its appreciation trend.

In Brazil, on the other hand, the real weakened 0.4 percent to 1.9632 per dollar, one day after the central bank intervened to keep the currency weaker than 1.95 per dollar - a mark many analysts consider as a boundary of an informal trading band imposed by policymakers.

"In a certain way the central bank indicated it is working with a 1.95 real floor to the currency. We are likely to see the exchange rate hovering between 1.95 and 2.0 units per dollar," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist with WestLB bank in Brazil.

The real had pierced the 1.95-per-dollar level for the first time in 10 months on Friday, after higher-than-expected inflation data increased bets that the central bank would soon raise interest rates, adding to the appeal of real-denominated assets.

title: PREVIEW-Mexico may cut interest rates for first time since crisis
text:
* Policymakers may cut borrowing costs to record low

* Inflation uptick could postpone decision to cut

* Worries about foreign flows could drive big move

* Decision due Friday 0900 local (1500 GMT

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 7 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank may brush off a recent uptick in consumer prices and make its boldest move in four years by cutting borrowing costs on Friday as policymakers claim they are winning the battle against inflation.

Sixteen of 21 analysts polled last week expect the Banco de Mexico to hold its benchmark interest rate at 4.50 percent on Friday, but the other five are calling for a cut of at least 50 basis points to a record low of 4 percent.

Since January, policymakers have been arguing that prudent monetary policy in the last decade has helped drag inflation steadily down toward the bank's 3 percent target, making room for a one-off adjustment to interest rates.

"This is the time to cut. Inflation behavior has been great," said Gabriel Casillas, an economist at Banorte-IXE who expects a 50 basis point to 75 basis point cut on Friday.

Mexico's central bank has clung to orthodox inflation-fighting policies since a devastating financial crisis in the 1990s. The bank now seems set on cashing in on that discipline to lock in lower borrowing costs for the economy and bring Mexican rates in line with easy money policies around the world.

While policymakers are loath to discuss the exchange rate as a major factor in their decisions, cutting the interest rate could slow big inflows and keep the peso from becoming too expensive.

Strong currencies can hurt local manufacturers by making imports cheaper. Mexico, a proponent of free markets, has eschewed the direct intervention and capital controls used by other emerging markets such as Brazil to try to deter flows.

Still, central bank chief Agustin Carstens last month warned that lower interest rates were not a "done deal" for Latin America's second-largest economy. In January, the bank's board said a recent drop in inflation from a 2-1/2-year high in September would need to be "consolidated" before cutting rates.

Inflation accelerated in February to 3.55 percent and Carstens warned it will tick higher through April - a hump which could keep policymakers from cutting now.

"The bank is in no hurry to implement the cut," said Marco Oviedo, an analyst at Barclays Capital in Mexico City.

However, the prospect of inflation back above 4 percent by the next meeting in April may leave policymakers thinking they have a narrow window to act. "If they do not do it now, inflation could become a problem again," said Salvador Orozco, a strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

Investors are betting on slightly less than even odds for a 25 basis point cut on Friday and are tilting toward 50 basis points in April or June, in line with the majority in the Reuters poll.

The last time Banco de Mexico (Banxico) slashed borrowing costs was in the first half of 2009 as the country slumped into a deep recession. The bank cut rates from 8.25 percent to 4.5 percent by July, leaving the main rate lower than the inflation rate at the time.

A decline in inflation since then means policy is tighter now than it was in mid-2009. Policymakers could also argue that growth risks justify easier credit after a sharp drop in exports and retail sales at the start of the year.

Mexico's growth is seen slowing this year to 3.5 percent expansion from a 3.9 percent expansion in 2012.

ONE LONELY HAWK

Carstens has been seen as aching to lower interest rates since his appointment in 2010, and his view may be aided by a new board member.

Jose Sidaoui, one of the board members most worried about inflation, was replaced by Javier Guzman, a Yale-trained economist who is seen as favoring loose policy. That leaves Manuel Sanchez as the only inflation "hawk."

The last two times the central bank leaned toward lower rates, in 2010 and 2012, global market turmoil hammered the peso and threatened to fan inflation through higher import prices, and the bank backtracked.

Now, the peso is trading stronger than the 13-per-dollar level that previously stayed policymakers' hands.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil yields rise on rate hike bets, real slips
text:
* Mantega says rates, not FX, are right tool to fight inflation

* Mexico yields flat after investors tame rate cut bets

* Brazil real weakens 0.38 pct as central bank intervenes

(Adds comments, updates prices)

MEXICO CITY, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazil's interest-rate futures soared on Friday after the country's finance minister suggested policymakers could raise interest rates to fight rising inflation.

Brazil's real currency, meanwhile, weakened after the central bank intervened to stop it from strengthening past 1.95 per dollar.

In Moscow for a meeting of the G20 group, Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega said that a rise in inflation above the government's target raises a yellow flag and that monetary policy, not the exchange rate, is the right tool to control prices.

Nomura analyst Tony Volpon said the central bank was likely to tweak its language in its March decision and remove a pledge to keep its benchmark interest rate at a record low of 7.50 percent for a "prolonged period."

"The Brazilian central bank has put its finger on the trigger," Volpon wrote in a note to clients.

Yields on interest-rate contracts jumped to price in a strong chance that the central bank will lift the base Selic rate as soon as in May.

Interest-rate contracts maturing in January 2014, among the most traded, jumped about 21 basis points to bid at 7.62 percent, closing at their highest level in four months.

Concerns about inflation have driven the real to strengthen 4 percent so far this year as investors bet policymakers would favor a stronger currency to cheapen the price of imported goods, but would still be forced to raise the Selic later.

Brazilian policymakers have intervened heavily in the currency market in recent years, acting to weaken the real against the dollar when they are concerned the exchange rate is hurting local manufacturers, but also moving to strengthen the currency when inflation becomes a worry.

The real briefly strengthened past the level of 1.95 per dollar for the first time in nine months early in the session. The central bank intervened with an auction of reverse currency swaps - derivative contracts that are designed to weaken the real against the dollar.

The real last bid down 0.38 percent at 1.9645 per dollar.

On Thursday, a source on President Dilma Rousseff's economic team said policymakers are more worried about curbing volatility in the foreign exchange market, indicating the real could strengthen past the level of 1.95 per dollar as long as the appreciation is gradual.

Meanwhile, Mexican interest rate swaps and bonds posted little change after a volatile week as the market gauges when the central bank of Latin America's second biggest economy could cut its 4.50 percent benchmark rate.

The interest rate swap market trimmed bets on the chance of a 25 basis point rate cut in March this week after Mexico's central bank chief Agustin Carstens on Wednesday warned that lower interest rates are not a "done deal."

Investors have priced in a 25 bps cut by April and some economists are eyeing the chance for a 50 bps or 75 bps point cut this year.

Mexico's peso traded little changed, edging 0.04 percent stronger to 12.6845 per dollar. Mexico's peso has pulled back from a 10-month high hit in January after the central bank signaled it could cut interest rates if inflation keeps cooling.

Lower interest rates could curb the attraction of the peso to global investors.

title: UPDATE 3-Mexico Dec industrial output slumps most since 2009
text:
* December industrial output falls 2.1 percent vs November

* Manufacturing dips, construction falls sharply

* Data backs expectations of interest rate cut

(Adds peso reaction)

MEXICO CITY, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Mexican industrial production in December posted its biggest monthly loss since a deep recession four years ago as factories and builders slowed, bolstering bets that the central bank could cut interest rates.

Industrial output fell 2.1 percent in December compared to the previous month, its biggest drop since May 2009, when Mexican factories were dragged down by a U.S. recession. Mexico sends most of its exports to its northern neighbor.

Mexico's central bank has said it could lower borrowing costs if inflation continues to cool and growth slows in Latin America's second biggest economy.

"The central bank could use this as an incentive to lower rates," said Alejandro Cervantes, an analyst at Banorte-IXE, who is expecting a 50 basis point to 75 basis point cut in March to Mexico's benchmark 4.50 percent rate.

December's seasonally adjusted output data was below a 0.2 percent rate of growth seen in a Reuters poll and the upwardly revised 1.28 percent month-on-month rate posted in November.

Yields on short term interest rate swaps edged lower as the market increased bets on the chance of a 25 basis point cut by March 8 to around 30 percent. The swaps market has fully priced in a cut by April.

The surprise drop in the data briefly drove the Mexican peso

to a one-month low before the currency pared its losses. Lower benchmark interest rates could curb the appeal of the peso to yield-hungry investors.

Among industrial components, manufacturing contracted 1.07 percent in December from the previous month. Analysts said that a drop in automobile production at the end of last year would likely be compensated by a surge in January's output.

Construction slid for its third month in a row, down 2.67 percent compared with November.

President Enrique Pena Nieto took office in December and the end of infrastructure projects from the previous administration could have hit building, Marco Oviedo, an analyst at Barclays Capital, wrote in a note to clients.

Economists are divided about the chance of an interest rate cut. About two out of five analysts now expect the central bank's next move will be a cut - the same amount who think the next move will be a hike, a survey by Banamex showed last week.

Solid U.S. demand has helped support Mexican factories amid sluggish global growth. Mexico's economy is seen slowing from an around 4 percent annual rate in 2012 to 3.5 percent in 2013.

"The manufacturing sector will see less demand in the first part of the year, and the appreciation of the peso could further limit exports," Banorte-IXE's Cervantes said.

Mexico's peso is trading more than 12 percent stronger from a 2-1/2 year low hit in the middle of last year. The peso's relative weakness since the 2008-09 financial crisis has helped boost shipments by Mexican exporters.

Some analysts think the central bank would like to try and curb peso strength by lowering the yield on Mexican debt.

Starved by low interest rates in developed economies, foreign investors have piled up record holdings of Mexican peso-denominated debt and flows are expected to continue this year.

Mexico has eschewed the types of direct market intervention and capital controls that other emerging markets have used to protect their exporters from strong local currencies.

Compared with December 2011, overall industrial output dropped 1.1 percent, missing expectations for a 2.0 percent rise and worse than November's upwardly revised 2.9 percent expansion.

title: POLL-Latam  FX  to keep governments under pressure
text:
* For poll data see

* Colombia, Peru, Mexico currencies to extend gains

* Chile peso seen weakening, but intervention not ruled out

* Brazil to keep currency in tight range

By Silvio Cascione

SAO PAULO, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Latin American governments will probably have a tough time trying to curb currency gains this year as improving market conditions boost dollar inflows, a Reuters poll showed.

After failing to foresee a surge in many Latin American currencies in the past few months, economists and strategists revised their forecasts to predict another leg of currency appreciation in Mexico, Peru and Colombia.

Such an outlook means that investors should remain wary for further government intervention - not only in those countries but also in Brazil, the birthplace of the latest "currency wars", and in Chile, where prospects of a weaker peso did not eliminate chances of increased dollar purchases.

"There's a good chance that in the current 'risk on' environment the Chilean peso will continue to appreciate towards 460 per dollar," said Michael Henderson, an economist with Capital Economics. "We think if it approaches 460 that might provoke the central bank into announcing measures such as foreign exchange purchases to weaken the peso."

The Chilean peso should remain at the current 472 per dollar this month, weakening to 480.00 in six months and to 486.59 in 12 months on prospects of feeble copper prices, according to the median of 13 forecasts.

Dollar purchases - the classic government tool - have already been used in Colombia, with little success so far. After increasing the daily amount of dollars purchased to $30 million from $20 million, Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said the government is planning to take on less external debt.

Six out of seven analysts who replied to an extra question on the Reuters poll said they expect additional government measures to curb the Colombian peso's gains in the next six months. The most cited was the extension of the dollar purchase program from May to the end of the year.

Even so, the Colombian peso is seen gaining ground to 1,780 per dollar in one month, 1,772.50 in six months and 1,770 in 12 months, according to the median of 14 forecasts. It last traded at 1,790.10 per dollar on Wednesday.

Peru has been more aggressive than Chile and Colombia in protecting its currency. Not only has it bought dollars, the government also announced it would prepay up to $1.5 billion in debt this year and flirted with capital controls by tightening reserve requirements on bank accounts denominated in dollars.

Analysts still expect Peru's currency, the nuevo sol , to strengthen this year, though.

It should trade at 2.560 per dollar in one month, 2.530 per dollar in six months and 2.520 per dollar in twelve months. It was at 2.5775 on Wednesday.

All the five top Latin American currencies gained between about 1.5 and 7 percent since mid-November. In the latest Reuters poll, in October, analysts said that currencies had little room to strengthen as government intervention was expected to yield better results.

The strongest intervention so far has been seen in Brazil, where the central bank has been keeping its currency, the real, trading within a narrow band between 1.98 and 2.05 per dollar through dollar purchases and currency swap auctions.

Mexico is the country less likely to intervene in currency markets. However, a rate cut could help stem further gains in its currency, analysts said.

title: POLL-Mexican peso seen advancing in 2013 on reform hopes
text:
* For poll data see

* Peso seen gaining in 2013 on economic reform hopes

* Possible interest rate cut could limit gains in short term

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Feb 6 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso is seen advancing in 2013, backed by expectations that the new government will push through key economic reforms this year, but the risk of an interest rate cut could limit gains in the coming months.

The peso is seen firming about 1 percent from Tuesday's close to 12.50 per dollar by next January, according to the median of 15 analysts surveyed by Reuters.

Investors are optimistic that new President Enrique Pena Nieto will be able to win support in a divided Congress to approve energy reform that will allow greater private investment in the state-run industry.

Investors are also expecting progress on a long-stalled tax reform this year.

"The political environment has a better outlook," said Marco Oviedo, an analyst at Barclays Capital in Mexico City who expects the peso to firm to 12.20 per dollar in 12 months.

"The president has political capital that he can take advantage of," Oviedo said, adding that progress on energy and fiscal reforms could spur credit ratings agencies to upgrade Mexico's sovereign debt.

Solid U.S. demand for Mexican exports is also expected to keep supporting the peso. Mexico's economy grew about 4 percent in 2012, compared to 2011, and it is seen slowing to a 3.5 percent rate in 2013, according to a Reuters poll.

RATE CUT EYED

Analysts said gains in the Mexican peso could be limited in the short-term due to expectations the central bank may cut its benchmark interest rate, currently at 4.50 percent, in the coming months.

By April, the median target of the Reuters poll puts the peso little changed at 12.61.

Last month, Mexico's central bank surprised analysts and the market by hinting it might lower borrowing costs if inflation continues to cool.

Analysts at Banorte-IXE are expecting the central bank to cut its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 75 basis points at its March meeting. The interest rate swaps market is pricing in at least a 25 basis point cut by June.

"Even if this will not reduce the flows coming to our country, since it still looks attractive, on the margin it should be a factor that will moderate them," said Juan Alderete, a strategist at Banorte-IXE in Mexico City.

Foreign holdings of peso-denominated debt surged more than 60 percent in 2012 to 1.571 trillion Mexican pesos ($124.42 billion). Some analysts think Mexican policymakers could be seeking to use the threat of an interest rate cut to curb inflows from yield-hungry investors.

Mexico has eschewed the ad hoc market interventions and capital controls used by other emerging markets to keep their currencies from gaining too much and hurting exporters.

But Mexican policymakers are clearly worried that further flows could eventually become dangerous.

Mexico's central bank governor Agustin Carstens said on Tuesday warned that emerging markets may face an exodus of capital when major economies begin to reverse accommodative monetary policy. ($1 = 12.6261 Mexican pesos)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico yields see-saw ahead of cenbank minutes
text:
* Mexico minutes could reinforce views on rate cut possibility

 * Peru, Costa Rica move to limit hot money flows 

 By Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Jan 30 (Reuters) - Mexican yields were little changed on Thursday ahead of the release of central bank minutes that could either deepen or undermine bets that policymakers could soon cut interest rates.

 Mexican bond yields recently hit record lows, and interest rate swaps are pricing in a 25 basis point cut to the country's benchmark rate of 4.50 percent by September.

 In a policy U-turn at its January meeting, the central bank moved from warning of a potential rate hike to saying it could cut borrowing costs if inflation keeps cooling. Minutes from the meeting are due Friday at 0900 local time.

 The minutes "may show that there was no consensus, at least one director will highlight that it is not yet the time to (cut) and that we need these trends to consolidate," said Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York.

 One reason to cut might be to discourage flows of hot money into the economy this year that could strengthen the peso currency to the point where it makes exports less competitive and crimps growth.

 The yield on Mexico's benchmark 10-year bond  fell 1 basis point to 5.03 percent after bidding up earlier in the session. The yield is trading just above record lows below 5 percent.

 The Mexican peso firmed 0.13 percent to 12.7105 per dollar. The peso has shed 1.2 percent since the central bank signaled it could cut rates. 

 Foreign investors have been piling into Mexican bonds;  foreign holdings of peso debt jumped 60 percent last year and are still rising. 

 "There is a element of preemptiveness to get ahead of the curve, with the steady flows into bonds," Ramos said. "They do not have an exchange rate problem yet, but they could have one down the road."

  An easing in the euro zone's debt crisis and new economic stimulus measures in Japan are seen fueling bumper investment flows into Latin America and other emerging markets in 2013 and policymakers are trying to ward off unwanted currency strength.

Mexico has eschewed the types of direct intervention and capital controls that other countries have used.

 Peru's sol currency finished bidding 0.31 percent weaker at 2.575 per dollar on Thursday, a day after the central bank tightened reserve requirements to soften the impact of heavy capital inflows. 

 The sol is near a 16-year high and the central bank has intervened in the currency market every day since late August to buy dollars, but it did not step in on Thursday.

 Meanwhile, Costa Rica said it will limit lending to limit the attractiveness of an interest rate gap that has sparked a credit boom and drawn in potentially destabilizing foreign capital. 

 The Brazilian real was little changed as the market eyed how far policymakers would let the currency firm.

 The real hit a seven-month high on Tuesday, breaking past the 2-per-dollar mark on bets the central bank will allow further gains as policymakers fret about a recent move higher in inflation.

 But its advance has stalled this week after Finance Minister Guido Mantega warned that the government was ready to correct any excessive moves in the exchange rate. 

 Brazil has used a series of measures to keep the real from gaining too much in recent years. The real  closed at 1.9885 per dollar, 0.05 percent weaker than Wednesday's close.

title: ANALYSIS-Latin America lays out defenses in  currency  war
text:
* Colombia joins Peru and Costa Rica in flows defense

* Pundits predict bumper year for emerging market assets

* Brazil seen on sidelines this time as inflation flares

By Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Latin American policymakers are manning their defenses ahead of what could be a new battle in the "currency wars" as flows of hot money put unwelcome upward pressure on their currencies.

Economists and investors predict that an easing in the euro zone's debt crisis, new economic stimulus measures in Japan and a return of risk appetite will fuel bumper investment flows into Latin America and other emerging markets in 2013.

Some policymakers are already at the barricades.

Colombia cut interest rates on Monday and said it would ramp up dollar purchases. Peru plans to pre-pay up to $1.5 billion in foreign debt this year and is intervening aggressively to curb currency gains. And tiny Costa Rica unveiled a steep hike in taxes on foreign investments this month.

Even Mexico, which has a hands-off approach to currency market intervention, is considering an interest rate cut that some economists believe reflects as much a desire for a weaker peso as it does concerns about growth.

"Much of the region is once again dealing with the impacts of currency wars and QE in the developed world," said Standard Chartered senior strategist Bret Rosen, referring to the extraordinary monetary easing measures undertaken by central banks known as quantitative easing.

Low interest rates in developed economies encourage investors to look for yield elsewhere, pushing up the currencies of countries at the receiving end of their attentions. Stronger currencies make exports less competitive, hurting economic growth.

It is a problem that has battered Brazilian manufacturers for several years. The government pushed back by slashing interest rates and intervening in the currency market to weaken the real, introducing capital controls and offering tax breaks for several industries.

But Brazil has less room for maneuver than other leading Latin American economies this year as policymakers are concerned about inflation, which rose above an annualized rate of 6 percent this month.

Latin American finance ministers complained last month about the impact of stimulus policies in developed economies, and Group of 20 economic policymakers are set to address the impact of monetary policy on currency valuations next month at a meeting in Russia.

Tools to combat appreciating currencies include buying dollars, as Colombia and Peru are doing; capital controls as in Costa Rica; and macroprudential measures, such as Peru's move to raise deposit requirements on dollar bank accounts.

Mark Mobius, who helps oversee $51 billion in emerging market assets at fund manager Franklin Templeton, expects a huge influx of funds into emerging markets this year as investors tire of low-yielding government bonds.

"I think it's going to be enormous, terrific, hundreds of billions. Investors have been penalized with so low rates that they are not making anywhere near what they need," he said.

Global stock markets are up 4 percent already this year, and fund tracker EPFR said it noted a clear preference for emerging market equities over bonds, which attracted most money in 2012. The VIX index, a gauge of investor stress, fell this month to its lowest levels since 2007.

The Institute of International Finance banking group predicts capital flows to Latin America will jump 5.6 percent this year from 2012 to a record $321 billion.

Inflows to the region in 2012, including foreign direct investment as well as stock and bond investment, were already estimated to be about 30 percent higher than the "hot money" period immediately before the global financial crisis in 2008.

WHAT'S HOT?

Brazil and Mexico, as the region's two biggest economies, are likely to attract the bulk of inflows in 2013, although Brazil has managed to deter a lot of speculative investors with capital controls introduced during 2010-2011, when a rush of capital pushed the real up 12 percent against the dollar.

Foreign portfolio inflows into Brazilian stocks and bonds totaled $16.5 billion last year, down from $67.8 billion in 2010.

In its January fund managers' survey, Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch said Brazil had the biggest share of "underweight" ratings in the history of the survey.

Mobius likes small to mid-cap companies in the region and firms exposed to the consumer sector, such as banks. Citigroup, which raised its stock ratings for Latin America to "overweight" as it cut back other emerging markets, likes industrials.

Mexico, for its part, is benefiting from optimism about tax and energy reforms being promised by its new government. That has helped propel stocks and bonds to record high levels.

Pacific Investment Management Co, the California-based firm known as PIMCO that operates the world's largest bond fund, sees opportunities to make money if Mexico's central bank cuts interest rates later this year, pushing up the price of bonds.

Mexico's central bank has made a U-turn from warning of rate hikes to warning of rate cuts, prompting many to suspect it is worried about the peso. The peso hit a 10-month high the day central bankers met to discuss rates, and it only came off those highs when policymakers warned the following morning that they could cut rates. Lower rates would make the peso less attractive to foreign investors.

"It's no surprise that with the peso being weaker in the second half of (last) year that they were a little bit more hawkish, and now we have had a very nice run in the peso year-to-date perhaps they would be more dovish," said Michael Gomez, co-head of emerging markets at PIMCO.

London-based Capital Economics sees Mexico's peso as the currency with the most upside this year, due mainly to the lower risk of intervention by laissez-faire policymakers, in contrast to the record $13.9 billion bought by Peru's central bank in 2012 as the sol hit a 16-year high.

Chile is likely to join Peru and Colombia in intervening to check gains in the peso while shunning capital controls, said Capital's Neal Shearing, while Brazil is in the unusual position of trying to strengthen its currency to fend off rising inflation. A stronger currency cuts the cost of imported goods.

"Inflation concerns are starting to creep back in Brazil, which now marks it out from Colombia, Chile and Peru who seem to be more worried about the strength of the currency and its impact on competitiveness," he said.

The central bank had intervened in the market in recent months to keep the real weaker than 2 per dollar, but this week rolled over currency swaps that mimic the sale of dollars in the futures market - a move with the opposite effect.

The real strengthened past the 2-per-dollar mark on Tuesday for the first time since July, and analysts said they believed policymakers would allow it to firm further if needed.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazilian real gains after  central bank  acts
text:
* Brazil's real up 1.39 pct after auction, swap offers

 * Mexico's peso edges lower, on fiscal cliff concerns 

(Updates prices, adds context)

 By Asher Levine and Alexandra Alper

 SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 26 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real strengthened on Wednesday following heavy central bankintervention in the currency market, while Mexico's peso was little changed as worries over U.S. budget talks weighed.

Brazil's central bankintervened three times in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday in an effort to limit recent weakness in the real, which has dropped nearly 9.0 percent against the U.S. dollar this year. 

 Early on Wednesday, the bank conducted an auction to sell up to $2 billion on the spot market with repurchase agreements, which aims to provide liquidity to the foreign exchange market at year-end.

 The move was followed by two currency swap auctions, both offering 40,000 contracts with a maturity of Feb. 1, 2013. The bank sold a combined total of 37,000 contracts, which are derivatives that emulate the selling of dollars in the futures markets.

 "The central bank wants the dollar around 2.05 reais, considering the market was very calm and there was no reason for it to step in," said Reginaldo Siaca, head of foreign exchange at Advanced Corretora in Sao Paulo. "With the auctions, it is signaling the band it is comfortable with for the end of the year."

 The real strengthened sharply after the interventions, gaining 1.39 percent to close at 2.05 per U.S. dollar.

Brazil's central bank had last carried out a swap auction on Dec. 3, when the real closed at 2.119 per dollar. 

 "The central bank saw that a dollar close to 2.10 reais would be harmful for inflation," said João Medeiros, head of currencies at Pioneer Corretora in Sao Paulo.

 The Mexican peso edged down 0.21 percent to 13.0120 per dollar as anxieties remained over unresolved austerity issues facing the United States, Mexico's biggest trading partner. 

 "Mexico is really the barometer for the reality of the market over the holidays, which is thin (trading) and growing concerns over the fiscal cliff," said RBS economist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky. 

 She pointed to U.S. President Barack Obama's decision to return early to Washington from vacation to tackle the looming package of tax hikes and spending cuts, along with an upcoming debt ceiling debate, as fueling investor concern. 

 The U.S. Treasury on Wednesday announced the first of a series of measures that should push back the day when the government will exceed its legal borrowing authority as imposed by Congress by around two months. 

 Without any action, Treasury said the government is set to reach its $16.4 trillion debt ceiling on Dec. 31. 

 Still, the Mexican peso has performed well this year, firming more than 7.0 percent since 2011, and Cattan-Naslausky warned against reading too much into market moves during periods of light trading.

 Chile's peso edged up 0.08 percent to 479.10 per U.S. dollar.

text:

* Mexico's peso slips 1.43 pct, Chile's peso off 0.67 pct

(Adds comment, updates prices, changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso tumbled by the most in five months on Friday after U.S. budget negotiations stalled and Brazil's real weakened despite efforts by the country's central bank to lift the currency.

Brazil's real shed 0.52 percent to 2.0732 per dollar, while Mexico's peso tumbled 1.43 percent to 12.9444 per dollar. The peso hit its weakest level since early December and headed for its worst one-day loss since late July.

Markets fell on Thursday after a budget plan proposed by a Republican leader failed to win support from his own party, raising the chances that austerity measures kick in next year.

U.S. lawmakers are struggling to come up with a deal to avert $600 billion worth of tax increases and spending cuts, a combination that could push the world's largest economy back into recession next year.

"The risk is rising that (talks) are going to drag into next year," said Delia Paredes, an analyst at Mexico's Banorte-IXE.

A U.S. economic downturn could hit Mexico the hardest among Latin American countries, since it sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

Bets on a deal by U.S. lawmakers before the end of the year had spurred gains in riskier assets, such as Latin American currencies. Mexico's peso hit a two-month high last week.

Brazil's central bankintervened twice earlier in the day, selling up to $4 billion in two auctions with repurchase agreements. The auctions were designed to increase the supply of foreign exchange before year-end, but traders and analysts said they aim at curbing excessive losses in the Brazilian real.

The central bank said after the market close that it will sell up to $2 billion on the spot market on Dec. 26 with a repurchase agreement.

"After all the central bank has done, I think it wants the foreign exchange rate below 2.1 per U.S. dollar. It can even strengthen past 2.05 per dollar," said Reginaldo Siaca, manager at Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo.

* Chile peso up again, some see cenbank intervening

* Mexico peso up 0.5 pct, Brazil real flat

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 11 (Reuters) - Venezuelan bonds rallied for a second session on Tuesday on expectations of a regime change in the oil-exporting nation, while Latin American currencies rose as German data on investor confidence and hopes of a U.S. budget deal supported appetite for risk.

Venezuela's global 2027 bonds, the most actively traded, reached their highest price since early 2008 as President Hugo Chavez underwent surgery in Cuba for a cancer recurrence, raising the prospect of new presidential elections, even as Chavez named a successor.

The 2027 bonds last traded 1.4 points higher at a bid price of 102.367.

Yield spreads between Venezuelan bonds and safe-haven U.S. Treasuries tightened 3 basis points to 749 basis points according to JPMorgan's EMBI+ index, showing investors' appetite for the country's assets was the strongest since September 2008.

Before leaving Venezuela, Chavez named his vice president and foreign minister, Nicolas Maduro, to take over, should he become incapacitated. Chavez, who is due to begin a new six-year term on Jan. 10, urged supporters to vote for Maduro in the event of an election.

"We are encouraged that President Chavez asked for voter support for his candidate since this suggests an electoral transition as opposed to the alternative strategy to allow the VP to finish the entire six-year term," Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies & Co. Inc., wrote in a research note.

CURRENCIES GAIN, EXCEPT REAL

Elsewhere in Latin America, most currencies rose after a key index of German investor sentiment rose sharply in December, supporting optimism about the world economy.

The appetite for risk further grew as the S&P 500 index

ended at its best level since Election Day, buoyed by hopes of a resolution to the U.S. budget impasse.

The Mexican peso rose 0.5 percent to 12.7435 per dollar, while the Chilean peso edged 0.1 percent higher to 475.00 per greenback, its strongest level in nearly two months.

It was the sixth straight winning session for the Chilean peso, which led some traders to believe the country's central bank could soon act to curb currency gains.

On the other hand, the Brazilian real closed practically unchanged at 2.0770 per dollar after the central bank announced two auctions on Wednesday to sell as much as $1.5 billion on the spot market with repurchase agreement.

The announcement added to the market perception that Brazilian policymakers do not want the real to weaken. Confirming that perception, a member of Brazil's economic team said the real was at a satisfactory level when it traded around 2.03 and 2.04 reais per dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso firms, Brazil real wobbles near low
text:
* Mexican peso gains on optimism about U.S. talks

* Brazil real near 3-1/2-year low, intervention eyed

* Chile peso firms, helped by interest rate hike bets

(Updates prices)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso firmed on Tuesday, helped by optimism over U.S. fiscal negotiations, while Brazil's real teetered near a 3-1/2-year low, awaiting signs of central bank intervention.

Mexico's peso, one of the most freely traded emerging market currencies, has whipsawed in tandem with U.S. stocks over worries whether U.S. lawmakers will be able to stave off impending tax hikes and spending cuts that could hobble the economy.

The Mexican peso firmed 0.29 percent to 13.0175 per dollar, its fourth session of gains.

The peso has rallied 2 percent back from a 10-week low last week, on hopes the U.S. would avoid the "fiscal cliff," a combination of spending cuts and tax rises due to be implemented under existing law in early 2013 that may cut the federal budget deficit but also tip the economy back into recession.

Following U.S. President Barack Obama's re-election, the peso slumped and its technical outlook deteriorated sharply, suggesting deeper losses ahead.

But the currency's rally during the past four sessions drove the cost of dollars in pesos below its 200-day and 100 day moving averages.

After its recent rally, Nomura strategist Benito Berber reckons the peso is currently pricing in about a 10 percent to 15 percent chance of failure by U.S. lawmakers, down from about a 20 to 25 percent chance last week.

"There is at least a more amicable tone in the talks, but this is very short term," Berber said, adding the peso could slump back toward 13.50 per dollar if the market starts to bet on failure in Washington.

As the peso weakened, total bets on the Chicago exchange for

a stronger peso fell to $3.7 billion last week from a record high of $5.5 billion in late September.

That still leaves a lot of investors betting on a strong peso, investors who could face stop loss levels above the peso's low last week of 13.29 per dollar.

The Brazilian real traded nearly flat at 2.0805 per dollar, just off its weakest levels since May 2009 that it hit on Friday. Currency trading was low with the local stock market closed for a holiday.

After trading in a narrow range since July, the real last week saw its steepest weekly slump since early June. The currency's tumble could push Brazil's central bank to intervene soon in the foreign exchange market, analysts said.

The Chilean peso firmed 0.4 percent, following a 1 percent surge on Monday, after strong economic data in the third quarter stoked bets that the central bank could raise interest rates. Higher interest rates attract yield-hungry investors.

Chile's economy kept expanding at a fast clip in the third quarter versus the year-earlier period, fueled by a jump in domestic demand, central bank data showed on Monday.

title: FX  Funds Back in the Black in 2012 - but Only Just
text:
-- FX funds gain 0.14% on average in the 10 months to October

-- Timing investor swings has been key to performing well in 2012

-- Central bank easing has made it harder to make money in FX

By Clare Connaghan

Currency funds have barely made a profit in 2012 because the euro-zone crisis and policies of the world's central banks have made it harder for traders to make money investing in the $4 trillion-a-day foreign-exchange market.

But at least they are doing better than in 2011.

After losing more than 6% on average last year, foreign-exchange-focused investment managers on average made a gain of 0.14% in the 10 months to October, according to Parker Global Strategies, a U.S.-based company that tracks the performance of currency funds globally.

That compares with a 2% gain over the same period for all hedge funds, across all financial markets, according to the Dow JonesCredit Suisse Core Hedge Fund Index.

"It's been a frustrating year again--there haven't been any big macro trends out there," said Paul Lambert, head of currency at Insight Investment in London.

Policy easing by central banks globally, from the European Central Bank to the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan, have helped to keep currencies in check by neutralizing the risk of a breakup of the euro zone and squashing interest rate differentials. Along with the efforts made by several emerging market governments, such as Brazil's, to stop their currencies appreciating, that has made it harder for foreign exchange investors to make money.

"There has been a slight improvement this year in the performance of foreign-exchange funds but it's still been quite a difficult year," said Pablo Frei, head of multi-manager programs at Zurich-based funds firm Quaesta Capital.

A key part of the problem is the way in which financial markets have tended to behave, switching between periods of so-called risk-on and risk-off as investors have indiscriminately blown hot or cold in response to the euro-zone crisis.

For foreign exchange markets, that has meant piling into currencies perceived as safe havens, such as the dollar and yen, when confidence is low while selling emerging-market and commodity-linked currencies perceived as risky. And whenever investors have grown upbeat, those flows have reversed. As a result, more traditional and discriminate market drivers such as a country's relative economic fundamentals have taken a back seat.

"You haven't really had a trending market this year so unless you've been able to time the risk-on/risk-off moves correctly then you would have struggled," said Michael DePalma, chief investment officer of currency strategies at AllianceBernstein in New York.

Compared with equities, where the investor can pick between different industrial sectors or even individual stocks, there are fewer choices when it comes to currency investing. As a result, currency investors have been scrambling over an even smaller number of trades.

"The fact is there haven't been a huge number of very good ideas this year, so the money that's found its way into the currency market has crowded itself into a couple of places like the Mexican peso," said Mr. DePalma.

The Mexican peso, which has gained more than 5% this year against the dollar, has been a big favorite of currency investors, who have been encouraged by Mexico's relatively strong fundamentals. The economy is expected by the government to grow 3.5% this year. The Bank of Mexico has also been of the non-interventionist kind.

Currency managers that specialize in higher-yielding emerging market currencies, such as the Mexican peso, are having a better year than most, said Diane Miller, a principal at U.K. consulting firm Mercer.

But overall 2012 has been another difficult year for foreign-exchange funds, which last delivered returns of more than 1% in 2008.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real suffers largest loss in 2 months
text:
* Risk aversion up on concern about delay in Greek aid

* Mexican peso trims early losses

* Brazil real drops 0.9 pct, Mexican peso down 0.1 pct

By Danielle Fonseca

SAO PAULO, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real on Tuesday posted its largest single-day loss in nearly two months on speculation the government would favor a weaker currency to support the economy, while a rebound in U.S. retail stocks supported the Mexican peso.

Latin American currencies in general were pressured by concerns about the so-called U.S. fiscal cliff, as well as growing fears that Greece would not receive international aid in time to avert bankruptcy.

The real closed 0.9 percent lower at 2.0685 per dollar, a four-month low, on market chatter that the government would like to see a weaker currency to boost industrial activity.

"There is some speculation, some market rumors that the central bank would tolerate a currency weaker than 2.1 per dollar," said Flavio Serrano, chief economist at BES Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

The Brazilian real has been stuck within an informal trading band of 2.0 to 2.1 per dollar since early July due to a series of central bank interventions on both ends of that range.

On different occasions, Brazilian policymakers have suggested that such a currency range would be appropriate to support the domestic industry without stoking inflation, but a number of recent economic indicators have showed the economy is taking longer than expected to recover.

FISCAL CONCERNS

Also weighing on Latin American currencies were concerns about the looming U.S. fiscal cliff - a combination of government spending cuts and tax increases scheduled to star in January that could plunge the world's largest economy into another recession.

The Chilean peso lost 0.68 percent to 483.60 per dollar, its weakest level in almost three months.

"What we have is a very discouraging external scenario," said Mario Battistel, a manager at the currency desk of Fair brokerage in Sao Paulo, citing the fiscal cliff fears in the United States and that concerns that Greece's problems are hurting all of Europe.

Fears that the euro zone's debt crisis could flare up again increased as Greece's international lenders clashed over how Athens can bring its debts down to a sustainable level.

The public disagreement highlights risks that Greece may not receive financial aid in time to avert bankruptcy, causing investors to duck for cover in safe-haven assets such as the dollar.

MEXICAN PESO TRIMS LOSSES

Sentiment improved slightly in the afternoon, cushioning the Mexican peso's losses, as key U.S. retail stocks were supported by strong results from Home Depot, the world's largest home improvement company.

The peso edged 0.1 percent lower at 13.2225 per dollar after dropping more than half a percentage point earlier. Mexico greatly relies on the U.S. consumer market to support its exports.

In a sign that Mexico will maintain its non-interventionist policy in foreign-exchange markets, Deputy Finance Minister Gerardo Rodriguez said the government was not worried about the recent currency weakness.

The recent decline in the peso's value, he said, reflects investor worries about the global economic outlook, but does not mean the danger of capital exodus has increased in Mexico.

By Natalia Cacioli and Moises Avila

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Chile's peso gained on Thursday on hopes Chinese factory output will accelerate at the end of the year and boost demand for South America's exports, but an intervention by Brazil's central bank capped gains in the real.

Mexico's peso gave up slight gains to weaken in late trading after weak quarterly earnings from Apple Inc, the most valuable public company in the United States, hit U.S. stock futures and investor appetite for riskier assets.

Chile's peso firmed 0.31 percent after a top Chinese official said the country's industrial output growth may be faster in the final three months of 2012 than in the third quarter.

China is the main consumer of Latin America's commodities exports and the positive outlook for the its economy boosted investors' appetite for risk in general.

The Chilean peso led gains among Latin American currencies, rising half a percentage point to 478.40 per dollar as the comments by the Chinese official boosted prices of copper, Chile's main export product.

"With copper and the euro rising, and stocks in positive territory, the (Chilean) peso could strengthen toward 478 units (per dollar)," said Jose Manuel Briceno, an analyst with GKFX in Santiago.

Chile's peso has appreciated around 8.5 percent so far this year, giving it a ranking as one of the top three performers among the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Chile Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said late on Wednesday in New York that the government is seeking ways to weaken the currency without resorting to capital controls.

Mexico's peso slipped 0.15 percent to 13.01 per dollar and was set to close at its weakest in more than six weeks.

The Mexican currency, the most freely traded in Latin America, usually tracks other liquid risky assets such as U.S. stocks and the euro. The peso weakened in tandem with a drop in U.S. stock futures once Apple reported its results after the U.S. stock market close.

Mexico's peso has been one of the top-performing emerging market currencies this year. But gains have flagged in recent weeks as investors cashed in on the rally.

Alfredo Puig, a trader at brokerage Vector in Monterrey, said the cost of dollars in pesos could weaken past its 200-day simple moving average to 13.20 per dollar if global market jitters persist.

The number of futures contracts betting on a stronger peso on the Chicago exchange hit a record high in late September. That position has fallen a bit, but the peso is still vulnerable to a stampede of investors who may try to get out of bullish bets at the same time.

"People think that the dollar shorts in Chicago are going to cover themselves due to the risk aversion we are seeing," Puig said.

In Brazil, a much stronger government hand has been curbing currency gains and keeping the real at a tight trading range of 2.02-2.05 per dollar for the past several sessions.

The Brazilian central bank reinforced the floor for the real early o n T hursday by intervening in the foreign exchange market for the second time this week.

The real traded nearly unchanged at 2.0240 per dollar after the central bank sold nearly all the 30,000 reverse currency swaps it offered in an auction, completing the early rollover of swaps that expire on Nov. 1.

Reverse swaps, or derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market, became the central bank's favorite instrument to intervene in the currency.

Combined with threats of additional government measures to curb inflows of speculative capital, those interventions have drastically reduced liquidity and volatility in Brazil's foreign exchange market.

"The market is completely stuck. The government has already admitted we have a dirty-floating regime with strong intervention," said Jankiel Santos, chief economist at BES Investimento in Sao Paulo.

"The economic fundamentals point to a stronger real, but this is a market with very low liquidity due to government intervention," he added.
