title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Peru  currency  set to gain in 2013, defying  central bank
text:
(Repeats to widen distribution)

LIMA, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Big mining investments and extra U.S. monetary stimulus are set to extend a rise in Peru's currency that has already taken the sol to a 16-year high despite sweeping official efforts.

Peru's central bank, which has bought a record $11.6 billion this year in interventions on the spot market, faces a dilemma because it has a limited number of tools to avert sharp currency swings in the partially dollarized economy, and the finance ministry has ruled out using capital controls that would limit the sol's advances.

That basically leaves the central bank the option of buying even more dollars on the spot market, allowing pension funds to put more money overseas to boost demand for dollars, or raising reserve requirements for bank deposits or loans.

These tools have been employed in varying doses over the last few years. But they have only slowed the pace of appreciation, not stopped it, and the chief of the central bank says the sol might retreat only several years from now.

Though many Latin American countries face appreciation pressures that hurt export competitiveness, Peru's central bank has a more difficult job than most of its peers.

That's because more than 40 percent of all bank deposits in Peru are denominated in dollars and loans denominated in dollars are widely available. Right now, with the sol gaining, some Peruvian consumers are rushing into loans in dollars - betting their monthly payments will fall over time in domestic currency terms.

But the central bank says it is worried they may eventually get stung and that it must limit volatility to prevent consumers who get paid in soles but owe debts in dollars from being squeezed. This concern among policymakers outweighs complaints from exporters that a stronger sol will dent the country's economic growth streak of 36 straight months.

"Our primary worry is vulnerability from loans in dollars. We don't want the sol to appreciate beyond what fundamentals merit because at some point it will retreat," Central Bank President Julio Velarde told Congress on Wednesday. "This could happen in three, four or five years. We are concerned about what could happen with the financial system when it does retreat ... so it's better to try to prevent (excessive strengthening)."

In addition to the expected impact from more stimulus announced by the Federal Reserve in September, Peru's large fiscal surplus, low inflation and surging domestic demand have attracted new investors. They have been encouraged by surging domestic demand that has offset a dip in the country's vast mineral exports over the past few months.

"There is a restructuring of portfolios going on in favor of the sol. There is a perception among people in the market that the sol is a stronger currency and therefore they're betting on it and holding assets in soles," said Jorge Chavez, a former central bank president and chief of the Maximixe brokerage in Lima.

A Reuters poll on Oct. 4 of 17 emerging market economists showed the sol holding almost steady at 2.57 for the next 12 months.. But the feeling among nearly 10 Peru specialists consulted by Reuters is considerably more bullish, with their median forecast for late 2013 at 2.45 for a gain of 5.3 percent.

Ricardo V. Lago, a former World Bank official who has long been a fan of Peru's economy, forecast the most gains for the sol - 7 percent to 2.40 per dollar by the end of 2013. It is currently at a 16-year-high of about 2.578 per dollar.

It has strengthened 4.4 percent so far this year and is expected to gain another 1.2 percent to 2.55 per dollar by the end of 2012, the local economists said.

The sol has appreciated despite heavy and frequent interventions by the central bank. Those purchases, which Velarde has called the biggest in the region for the size of Peru's economy, have averted gains that might have been larger.

In neighboring Chile, the central bank has refrained from intervening this year and in Mexico it has largely held back from doing so. The peso currencies of both those countries have appreciated about twice as much as the sol in 2012.

In the last decade, the sol has gained 26 percent, helping a "de-dollarization" of the economy. Ten years ago, 7 0 p ercent of Peruvian bank deposits were held in dollar-denominated accounts. Now only 43 percent are.

"I would say the sol will be at 2.40 per dollar at the close of 2013," Lago said. "The sol will continue to appreciate, and even if there were a bump in the road in 2013 because of the European crisis we can expect continued economic growth in 2015 and 2016. Plus, the avalanche of mining projects supports this hypothesis."

Peru has a portfolio of mining projects worth $53 billion in coming years, though some of them have been held up by social protests. Foreign direct investment and portfolio inflows over the last 3.5 years were $30 billion, more than neighboring Bolivia's gross domestic product.

APPETITE FOR SOLES

Velarde said he has been intervening frequently in the local spot market because the "appetite for the sol is amazing" and that, unlike years past, it has become a darling of investors.

"The situation has reversed and now it's the world's most conventional funds, the most conservative ones, that are buying Peru," Velarde said in late September.

Powered by domestic demand, Peru's economy is expected to grow 6 percent this year, the fastest pace in South America, and expand at a similar annual rate through 2014.

International reserves have swollen to $61 billion - equal to a third of GDP. Inflation is mild, running about 3 percent a year, while the fiscal surplus is healthy. It widened to 7 percent of GDP in the first half of this year, and is seen at 1.5 percent of GDP for the year and 1 percent in 2013.

At the same time, investment inflows more than cover the current account gap - forecast at 3.9 percent of GDP this year because of a downturn in mineral exports.

"These are the elements that will determine the exchange rate in the medium term. They suggest the exchange rate will continue to fall," said Hugo Perea, the head of economic research at BBVA Banco Continental.

CENTRAL BANK MEASURES

The sol's appreciation trend is expected to intensify with spillover from the Federal Reserve's decision to buy $40 billion in mortgage securities a month until the labor market improves.

"When these monetary packages are announced, we all know that these flows will end up in the whole world and thus won't be reflected in accelerated inflation in the U.S.," said Chavez, the former Peruvian central banker. "This would tend to intensify the sol's gains."

Economists expect Peru's central bank to announce more measures to keep excessive capital inflows from creating systemic risks or credit bubbles.

The central bank has already raised bank deposit requirements three times this year to stem the impact of foreign capital inflows and reduce the pace of credit growth.

Velarde has said two additional measures are being evaluated, including asking banks to set aside more reserves for home mortgages denominated in dollars, an idea which is being reviewed by the country's banking regulator.

New mortgages in dollars, which carry lower interest rates than loans in soles, lea p t 23.8 percent in July on the year. The central bank has said consumers should not aggressively sign up for new dollar loans by betting their monthly payments will fall in the future as the sol gains. Consumers with mortgages in many [20121017 192631 GMT]

Eastern European countries suffered in recent years when local currencies depreciated.

Another measure, which has been used in the past, would boost demand for dollars by allowing local pension funds to invest more abroad. Current rules limit them to putting 30 percent of their $30 billion in funds overseas. The ceiling might be slowly lifted to 50 percent.

"This is common sense and should be done because it wouldn't require much effort on the part of the central bank and it wouldn't imply inappropriate risks," said Chavez.

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso slips as market eyes Spain
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Hopes for Spanish bailout fail to boost Latam FX again

* Barclays sees buying opportunities in Mexican peso

* Mexican peso down 0.21 pct, Brazil real flat

(Adds comment, update prices)

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Mexico's pesos slipped on Tuesday while Brazil's real pared gains to end flat as investors awaited signs that Spain will request financial aid, a step seen as crucial to stop the spreading of the euro zone debt crisis.

Modestly stronger U.S. economic data and expectations about Spain have been supporting appetite for emerging market assets since euro zone officials said over the weekend that Madrid could request a bailout next month.

On Tuesday, two German coalition lawmakers were quoted as saying Germany was open to a precautionary credit line for Spain, though one of the officials later said his comments had been "over interpreted" in the report and that he was not referring to Spain.

The uncertainty left investors reluctant to drive Latin American currencies much higher, said Alfredo Puig, a trader at brokerage Vector in Monterrey, Mexico.

"The market really thinks (Spain) will be sorted out (with a bailout) in the end, but if there is any real evidence to the contrary, it could be dangerous," Puig said.

Concerns that Europe's debt crisis could set off a global financial crisis have repeatedly hit riskier assets around the world since late 2010.

The Mexican peso slipped 0.21 percent to 12.8420 per dollar while the Brazilian real pared early gains to bid flat at 2.0341 per dollar. Chile and Colombia's pesos dipped slightly.

The real has been weaker than 2.03 per dollar since Oct. 9. Possible central bank interventions to stem currency gains and support exporters have contributed to the weakness of the Brazilian currency.

But even in Mexico, where the government has refrained from intervening in the foreign exchange market, currency gains have been modest.

The Mexican peso has shed some recent gains and now stands roughly at the same level it was before the U.S. Federal Reserve unveiled a third round of its bond-buying program on Sept. 13, which was expected to drive large dollar inflows to emerging markets.

"Since the announcement of QE3, (those gains) have waned, succumbing, in our view, to profit-taking rather than to any re-assessment of risky assets per se," Barclays analysts said in a report, adding they see buying opportunities for the Mexican peso.

"In our view, this suggests still-reasonable entry opportunities for being long the Mexican peso," they said.

text:
MEXICO CITY, Dec 29 (Reuter) - Banco de Mexico said it intervened on the foreign exchange market to support the peso Friday. 

 "Yes it intervened, the amount and the details will be announced in the next accounts report of the (central) bank," a spokeswoman for Banco de Mexico said. 

 Traders estimated the intervention at between $20 million and $40 million. 

 "It intervened with very little, between $20 million and $40 million at most, they wanted it to close around 7.70," one trader said. 

 The widely-watched 48-hour peso closed two centavos stronger at 7.69/7.70 after the intervention. 

 "The dollar selling became apparent after midday and it all corresponded to the central bank," a trader said.

 The intervention was concentrated on the 48-hour contract, which because of a national holiday January 1 will fall due on Wednesday, traders said. 

 Traders said the low amount of the intervention was due to the thinness of the year-end forex market. 

 "There were few real operations, by people who had to square their positions to close their books," one trader said.

title: Mexico Stocks Close Dn 0.4% Despite Late Rally

 The IPC sank to an intraday low of 2,747.28, 1.6% below Thursday's close, around 2010 GMT before some speculative buys surfaced in the final 50 minutes of trading.

title: Mexico's GDP seen rising 3 percent next year.
text:
NEW YORK (Reuter) - Mexican finance minister Giuillermo Ortiz said Tuesday he believed the Mexican economy will resume growth in 1996, predicting the country's gross domestic product (GDP) will rise by 3 percent next year. 

 "We believe 1996 will be a year when economic growth will resume," Ortiz told an audience of businessmen, investors and reporters in New York. 

 Ortiz said his GDP forecast was based on expected 15 percent to 16 percent growth of total exports in 1996 and an expected increase in private investments of 5 percent in real terms next year among other things. 

 "Our inflation forecast for 1996 is 20.5 percent," Ortiz said. 

 Ortiz said the central bank would continue to intervene sporadically in the Mexico's foreign exchange market in a bid to reduce Mexico's peso volatility. Ortiz added, however, that the central bank will not defend any type of foreign-exchange fluctuation band for the country's currency. 

 "The central bank will intervene sporadically (in the foreign-exchange market)...(but) the bank will not be defending any type of band," he said.

title: Mexico's Cetes break downward trend in auction.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Dec 11 (Reuter) - Mexico's Cetes, or treasury bills, broke the downward trend in rates in this week's primary auction because last week's sharp decline was met by pressure on the exchange rate, analysts said. 

 The rate on bellwether 28-day Cetes rose 205 basis points to 50.31 percent, while the 91-day Cetes rate rose 128 basis points to 49.73 percent and the 182-day rate rose 82 basis points to 47.73 percent, Banco de Mexico said. 

 Analysts said they had expected the 28-day rate to rise about 200 basis points above last week's 48.26 percent. They based their expectations on the 190 basis point rise in secondary Cetes rates and in auctions to add liquidity to the market. Same-day Cetes rates closed on Monday at 51.50 percent. 

 Analysts had worried that the central bank was trying to knock down rates too far and too fast after last week's sharp 520 basis point decline in the 28-day paper. 

 "Pressure on the exchange rate was behind this rebound in the interest rates," one market specialist said. 

 In the last few days of trading last, the Mexican peso fell to below 7.80 pesos per dollar -- a key psychological barrier. 

 The Banco de Mexico was forced to intervene in the foreign exchange markets late on Friday to boost the Mexican currency. The peso was also under pressure from year-end demand for dollars. 

 The rates on the 28-day paper had fallen steadily since November 14, when they reached 59.99 percent at the auction. 

 Economists said the rebound in the Cetes rates was probably also due to 48 percent being considered a floor for primary rates, since inflation for December is seen coming in at about four percent for the month, leaving the possibility of negative real rates. 

 The Banco de Mexico assigned 1.10 billon pesos offered at 28 and 91 days and 700 millon at 182 days. 

 The auction took place one day earlier than normal because of a religious holiday in Mexico on Tuesday.

title: Mexico stocks close lower in quiet session.

title: D'Amato Again Calls For Release Of IMF Report On Mexico
text:
WASHINGTON (AP-DJ)--Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato called again Wednesday for the Treasury Department to release a classified report on Mexico that was drafted earlier this year by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 D'Amato, a New York Republican, is demanding Treasury declassify the report covering an internal IMF probe of the circumstances surrounding its surveillance of Mexico in the runup to its December 1994 financial crisis. 

 The crisis prompted the Clinton administration to launch a $20-billion bailout effort, which has sparked a backlash on Capitol Hill, prominently from Republicans, including D'Amato. 

 The senator, speaking on the floor of the Senate, maintained Wednesday that disclosure is increasingly important since currency speculators are now capitalizing on recent peso interventions by Mexico's central bank. 

 D'Amato maintained that intervention is essentially being financed through the $11.8 billion in outstanding U.S. credit to Mexico. 

 General details about the IMF report has been dribbling out, although D'Amato is demanding full disclosure of the document that Treasury classified citing national security concerns. 

 D'Amato has received a copy of the classified report, he confirmed. But he added that he hasn't read the report 'because I'll probably come down to the floor of the Senate and expose the bungling' by the IMF and the U.S. 

 As reported, the internal probe found a range of shortcomings involving IMF staff, the fund's 24-member executive board and the Mexican government into last December's crisis. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus has also maintained that the report's findings weren't surprising and that management had implemented corrective actions.

title: Mexico intervenes  for second time to bolster peso.
text:
MEXICO CITY (Reuter) - Mexico's central bank Tuesday intervened for a second time to shore up the stricken peso after investors ditched the currency in disappointment at a long-awaited budget proposal for 1996. 

 A Banco de Mexico official confirmed the central bank had sold a "small amount" of dollars to support the Mexican peso, as it did last Thursday when the currency hit an all-time low. 

 From a level of around 8.20 per dollar in the peso's closely-watched 48-hour contract, the central bank's action drove the currency back to end the session at 7.79, a three-centavo gain over Monday's close. 

 That was just token respite in a week in which the peso has been hammered by investor fears that the government has lost its way on economic policy. 

 Analysts also were asking how much longer the government could afford to go on intervening to back the peso, given its relatively scanty reserves, the bulk of which have been borrowed from the United States. 

 Peso worries resurfaced Tuesday after the government unveiled a budget proposal for 1996 that analysts said contained unrealistic growth and inflation projections. It also fell short of what they had hoped would be a bold programme to resuscitate the country's crisis-torn economy. 

 Finance Minster Guillermo Ortiz paid no attention to recommendations for a U-turn on economic policy. He said he would stand his ground and not be bossed around by speculators. 

 "I want to emphasise that speculators will not make us change course. That would be equivalent to playing their game, validating the climate of uncertainty that they have sown in recent days," he told Congress. 

 The proposal for a balanced budget was drawn up on assumptions that Mexico's economy would grow 3 percent next year, with an inflation rate of 20.5 percent, Ortiz said. 

 Underpinning that is a projected average exchange rate of 7.7 pesos per dollar, below Tuesday's level and one that many analysts consider wildly optimisitic. 

 "It makes you wonder what country they're living in," one stock trader said. 

 Gray Newman, economist at James Capel in Mexico City, welcomed the government's commitment to what he called responsible fiscal and monetary policy but he said it may fall on deaf ears. 

 "I'm not sure this will help calm the markets because concerns over fiscal policy are not driving the market right now. It's more of a credibility issue," he said. 

 Interest rates have more than doubled to above 70 percent in the last two months as the government battles a speculative attack on the peso by offering almost irresitible returns. 

 The immediate drawback is that Mexican banks are highly vulnerable to the higher rates. In the longer-term, such cripplingly tight monetary policy undermines the very rebound from recession the government says it is aiming to achieve.

title: Mexico investors dig in, see slim hope of US help.
text:
LONDON, Nov 10 (Reuter) - Foreign investors in Mexico are holding steady despite the peso's slide analysts said on Friday, seeing little hope of U.S. help this time round but drawing some cheer from a rare intervention by Mexico's central bank. 

 The United States and the IMF were forced to bail Mexico out a year ago when a bungled peso devaluation saw foreign capital flee emerging markets world-wide. 

 But news that Washington was facing the prospect of a debt default by its own federal government dashed what little hope there was of the U.S. coming to Mexico's rescue a second time. 

 "The idea of using U.S. tax payers' money to support the Mexican peso is simply not on the cards," said Peter West, economic advisor at West Merchant Bank. 

 "Mexico is not particularly popular in the U.S. at the moment," added Rupert White, head of Latin American equity sales at James Capel in London. 

 Foreign investors say the peso's plunge to an all-time low on Thursday was driven by a speculative attack on the foreign exchanges and was not justified by Mexico's economic fundamentals. 

 The Mexican government has done all in its power to set the ecomomy straight. It is running a trade surplus, credit and inflation are under control, it agreed a pact with labour and unions to encourage modest growth and it has even paid back some of its U.S. borrowings. 

 Fund managers and analysts alike said the overnight intervention by Mexico's central bank to support the peso was well-timed and would deter fresh assaults in the short term. 

 "They achieved quite a lot by spending very little," West said. "Quite a lot of people got their fingers caught in the door." 

 Despite limited foreign currency reserves, Mexico spent an estimated $150 million to $200 million in a rare intervention, lifting the peso from its post-war low of 8.30 against the dollar to a more respectable 7.60. 

 But Mexico-watchers warned that the low level of Mexico's foreign currency reserves would not permit unlimited support. 

 Mexico has borrowed some $12 billion out of $20 billion available in U.S. credit facilities agreed by U.S. President Bill Clinton earlier this year. 

 But this is earmarked for paying off debt and Mexico would have an uphill battle renegotiating the terms of the borrowings for permission to use them as a peso war chest. 

 Capel's White said this was not impossible, though the likelihood was small. 

 With the peso weakness weighing on U.S. dollar sentiment, the United States cannot remain unconcerned by what is happening to its neighbour. 

 But with Clinton proposing to shut down the federal government next week amid an increasingly likelihood of default on federal debt, Mexico is not high on the U.S. agenda. 

 And last night longtime critic of U.S. aid to Mexico, Republican Senator Alfonse d'Amato, voiced widespread opposition in Congress. 

 "The Mexican government will spend U.S. taxpayers dollars in a frantic and futile attempt to support the peso," he said. 

 While most foreign funds are not greatly exposed to Mexico, unlike this time last year when many got burned in the "Tequila crisis", some did get tempted back in a rally last March and are taking a big loss now. 

 "Cumulatively though people are underweight in Mexico at the moment," White said, seeing a limit to the impact of this round of currency troubles.

title: Peso calms as market awaits goverment's next move.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 10 (Reuter) - Mexico's peso, which sank to record lows Thursday before being rescued by central bank action, was little changed Friday as traders awaited the government's next move. 

 The peso opened slightly weaker at 7.70 to the dollar in the most-watched 48-hour contract but later firmed to 7.58 in quiet trading, two centavos above Thursday's close. 

 "The peso is too devalued right now, it is at levels which are excessively low and there has to be a correction," one dealer said. 

 Mexico's currency plunged Thursday to an all-time low of 8.30 to the dollar, generating panic in the market, before Banco de Mexico, the central bank, stepped in to sell around $200 million and buy pesos in a bid to support the Mexican currency. 

 Markets have been worried for some time about whether Mexican policy-makers have a clear strategy for hauling the country out of its worst recession in decades. 

 But their concern came to a head this week when the central bank raised interest rates a steep 10 percentage points in an effort to prop up the wobbly peso. 

 Markets saw the move as a mistake because it would deepen the recession and pounced hard on the Mexican currency, pushing it down more than 10 percent in a matter of days. 

 The government did not issue a statement on the peso crisis Friday. 

 President Ernesto Zedillo said on Thursday that "sooner rather than later" financial markets would have to face what he termed the reality of Mexico's imminent economic recovery. 

 "Today we know we have succeeded in quickly leveling the trade balance, that we have practically liquidated all short-term debt and that hyperinflation has been avoided," he said in a speech in Merida, the capital of the eastern state of Yucatan. 

 The central bank said it had not intervened again on Friday to sell dollars and buy pesos. 

 But traders pointed to a sharp hike in money market interest rates as a signal that the bank was intervening there to make pesos more attractive. 

 Banco de Mexico's action on Thursday drew strong criticism from one U.S. senator who has long opposed Washington giving aid to Mexico. 

 Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, attacked President Zedillo's government for spending "U.S. taxpayer dollars in a frantic and futile attempt to support the peso" -- a reference to the $12.5 billion in loans from the U.S. Treasury to Mexico to help it through its economic crisis. 

 Zedillo said in his Merida speech that Mexico had managed to rebuild its international reserves "which guarantees the solvency of our economy" -- a reference to the fact that the official reserves now stand at $14.16 billion. 

 But private economists and financial market analysts were sceptical. They said the reserves were more than outweighed by the dollars Mexico owes in short-term loans to the United States and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 This means the country effectively has negative reserves and will continue to have trouble defending its currency against speculative attacks.

title: Mexican peso steadies after  intervention .
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 10 (Reuter) - Relative calm returned to Mexico's peso market in the wake of Banco de Mexico's intervention Thursday, and the currency rebounded from early lows in thin trade, giving the stock market a boost. 

 Banco de Mexico denied market rumors that it had intervened to give the peso a helping hand Friday morning. 

 Analysts said the market was still trying to fathom the implications of the central bank's first intervention in almost six months, and many players were on the sidelines. 

 One question concerning analysts was to what extent Banco de Mexico would keep liquidity in check in the money market to put upward pressure on interest rates and bolster its defense of the currency. 

 A Banco de Mexico official said late Thursday the intervention in foreign exchange markets was accompanied by a drain on liquidity in the money market to raise rates. 

 "The problem is interest rates lead to a vicious circle. A rise in rates is mortal for banks and for public finances. I'm very scared about the bank problem," said Rodolfo Navarrete, economist at Vector brokerage in Mexico. 

 Treasury bill, or Cetes, rates continued to soar in same-day trade, amid a push by speculators in the money market to see how high Banco de Mexico was ready to let interest rates go in its efforts to attract peso buyers. 

 Their efforts were rewarded. In its daily liquidity auction the central bank sold 42- and six-day credit at 64.81 percent and 67.38 percent, a level that traders said indicated Banco de Mexico would sell benchmark 28-day Cetes above 64 percent in next weeks's primary auction. 

 That's would be a stunning increase of 10 percentage points, hard on the heels of a similar rate hike last week. 

 Investors continue to fret about the impact on Mexico's recession-struck economy of the recent bout of financial market turmoil, worrying that tighter credit will stifle any recovery. 

 Few believe that Banco de Mexico's suprise dollar selling in the markets Thursday is anything but a temporary solution to the peso's woes. 

 Banco de Mexico's reserves are currently in a net negative position, which limits its capacity to dig into its own coffers to sell dollars in support of the peso. 

 Mexico's hands are also tied by a strong anti-Mexican tide of sentiment in the U.S. Congress, that analysts say may prevent Mexico City from borrowing more U.S. money to help bail out the Government. 

 It has already taken $12.5 billion from the U.S. Treasury to support the currency this year. Before this month's round of peso upheaval, Mexican president Ernesto Zedillo had tactfully said he had no plans to borrow more. 

 In the immediate future, analysts said, the market will be waiting for Tuesday's 1996 budget announcement to see whether Zedillo has any more plans up his sleeve to rescue the country from crisis and restore investors' battered confidence.

title: Mexican peso seen lulled by  intervention .
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 10 (Reuter) - Peso trading is expected to be relatively quiet at the opening following Banco de Mexico's surprise intervention in the markets yesterday to boost the currency, analysts said. 

 "If the market opens up with people strongly buying dollars we could be off to the races again. But that's not usually the most likely scenario -- people will watch and wait," said Denis Parisien, an analyst at I.D.E.A. in New York, late Thursday. 

 Banco de Mexico openly intervened for the first time since May 14 Thursday, selling what it described as a "modest" amount of dollars when the peso hit a record low of 8.30 against the dollar, helping it rebound to 7.60. 

 A Banco de Mexico source told Reuters Thursday the intervention in the foreign exchange market was supported by a drain of liquidity in the money market. "Operationally, this was done by reducing the (cash) balances of banks in the central bank." 

 He declined to specify whether there would be further intervention, saying such a move was discretionary. 

 "The wise element of a free-floating exchange rate is that central bankers always leave themselves the possibility of intervening," the source said. 

 Many analysts think the market will test Banco de Mexico again in coming days, pushing the peso down to see how low it can go before there is more intervention. 

 "Once you go out in as visible fashion as they did Thursday, people are going to say 'fine, but what about tomorrow'," said Rob Rauch, head of sales and trading at the Weston Group in New York. "It's not something you can do just once." 

 There were unconfirmed rumors in the currency markets that Banco de Mexico's move followed or coincided with a large and timely peso order by either a U.S. hedge fund or Mexican and U.S. banks. They would have made a fortune if they bought the peso at its lows. 

 But traders who caught the wrong side of the rebound with short peso positions were badly burned, and Parisien expected them to lick their wounds Friday rather than test the central bank's defensive strength anew. 

 A U.S. Veteran's Day holiday Friday could also cool the market, but several analysts said Banco de Mexico is unlikely to enjoy a lull for long. 

 On Tuesday, the government unveils its budget proposals for 1996, and if they fail to contain strong enough measures to rescue Mexico's economy, many believe the peso could come in for a new battering. 

 Also, Banco de Mexico's reserves are still depleted, despite some $12.5 billion in U.S. support received earlier this year. 

 With Washington embroiled in a battle between the White House and Congress over raising the U.S. debt ceiling, it is not considered a good time for Mexico to be liberally spending what it has left to defend its currency. 

 Rauch said the government of President Ernesto Zedillo may have a hard time convincing investors that they have any plans up their sleeve to restore order to the economy, because confidence has sunk so low. 

 He said he would like to see a clearer definition from the Finance Ministry and Banco de Mexico on whether their priority was spurring growth or taming inflation.

title: Banco de  Mexico  statement on  intervention .

MEXICO CITY, Nov 10 (Reuter) - The following is a Banco de Mexico statement issued early Friday on its intervention in the foreign exchange market on Thursday: 

 "Late last year the Bank of Mexico adopted a floating exchange rate regime. Since May 14, the Bank has followed a virtually free float, without intervening in the foreign exchange market.  In recent weeks, and in particular over the last few days and in today's session, the peso had shown considerable volatility and depreciated at a fast rate, reaching the level of N$8.30 per $1 U.S. dollar, a behavior unrelated to the fundamentals of the economy.

As a result, the peso strengthened closing at N$7.60 pesos per $1 U.S.. A small amount of reserves was used in this intervention. 

 "The Foreign Exchange Comission deemed that this intervention, wich does not imply the abandonment of a floating exchange rate policy, is appropiate given current budgetary and monetary policies. The 1996 Budget, to be presented to Congress next week, emphasizes the maintenance of solid public finances.

title: Mixed Reviews On Mexican Central Bk  Intervention : Analysts
text:
MEXICO CITY (DJ-EMR)--Thursday's central bank intervention into Mexican currency markets has drawn criticism in Mexico as the start down a slippery slope of dwindling reserves, but analysts interviewed Friday said the alternative may have been worse. 

 "Intervention is a dangerous policy," said Mexico City economist Jonathan Heath. "But in this situation, you don't have too many alternatives." 

 Mexican currency markets seemed to have stabilized midday Friday, with the dollar closing at at 7.55 pesos, unchanged from Thursday. 

 Volatile trading Thursday drove the dollar as high as 8.25 pesos, prompting the central bank to step in with what analysts estimate was $150 million to $200 million of peso purchases.

title: Mexican new peso under less pressure - officials.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 23 (Reuter) - Speculative attacks on the Mexican new peso have been diminishing in recent days, and Banco de Mexico intervention to shore the currency up has been in very small amounts, a senior Mexican treasury official said. 

 Alejandro Valenzuela, undersecretary for international affairs at the finance ministry, said the failure of the new peso to reach a government target of 6.0 per dollar is something that would be resolved over time as confidence in the government's economic programme strengthens. 

 The peso "without doubt is very undervalued," Valenzuela told a news conference, adding that its weakness in recent days has been in very thin trading. 

 Alejandro Reynoso, a senior central bank official, told the same news conference that interest rates needed to remain high to attract savings, despite the burden this placed on domestic industry. 

 "High interest rates are necessary to maintain domestic savings," he said, adding that a government programme to create inflation-indexed investment units would go some way towards easing the pressure on companies. 

 The officials said there were positive signs that the country is beginning to overcome the worst effects of the December 20 devaluation of the new peso, noting that the trade balance is now positive and that the economy registered a public primary surplus in January. 

 They said that this helped explain why the TIIP interbank interest rate fell more than 18 percentage points to about 91 percent this week. 

 The officials also said that the amount of dollar-denominated Tesobonos in circulation has been reduced to $16.593 billion as of Wednesday. 

 Asked if the International Monetary Fund was dragging its feet on paying out the balance of a $17.8 billion loan promised to Mexico, Valenzuela of the finance ministry said $10 billion would be made available beginning in April. Mexico has already received $7.8 billion on that loan.

MEXICO CITY (AP-DJ)--Mexico's peso continued to perform weaker against the dollar Thursday in mid-morning trading. 

 In Mexico City around 1645 GMT, on the spot dollar market, the dollar was trading at mid rate levels of 7.2700 pesos per dollar against 6.9500 pesos per dollar at Wednesday's close. Spreads were 7.2200/7.3200 pesos per dollar. 

 The peso opened at a mid rate of 6.9550 pesos/dlr Thursday and then began a steep decline that hit a mid rate of 7.4500 new pesos/dlr around 1530 GMT before recovering somewhat. 

 Traders were mixed on whether Mexico's central bank intervened to prompt the rebound, and officials at the Bank of Mexico reiterated they will not comment on interventions. Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said earlier this week monetary authorities will allow the peso to continue floating, but that the central bank will intervene from time to time in an effort to bring stability to the beleagured currency. 

 Trading was light and speculative, added dealers.

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Weaker For Third Straight Day
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP-DJ)--Mexico's peso closed weaker against the dollar Wednesday for the third straight day following an 18% rebound Friday. 

 In Mexico City, on spot and 24-hour dollar markets, the dollar ended at mid rate levels of 6.9500 pesos per dollar against 6.6350 pesos per dollar at Tuesday's close. Spreads were 6.9000/7.0000 pesos per dollar. 

 The U.S. currency hit an intraday high of 7.3500 around 1830 GMT before rebounding in the final hour of trading. Traders said the central bank probably intervened to bring about the late rebound, perhaps with as much as $100 million. The Bank of Mexico would not confirm any intervention, however. 

 Traders added that volume was light to moderate, and that speculation and pessimism continued to be directing many of the transactions in the wake of weeks of market volatility. 

 'Investors are still uneasy,' said one Mexico City trader. 

 'Nobody believes the government anymore,' added another dealer. 

 Traders said more uneasiness was created Wednesday because peso demand was still minimal despite a rise of 24.39 percentage points in 27-day Cetes, or Treasury bills, to yields of 82.38% at Wednesday's primary auction. 

 Although demand outstripped offerings, one dealer said most of the bids came from domestic investors as many foreign investors remained on the sidelines.

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Weaker For Second Straight Day
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP-DJ)--Mexico's peso closed weaker against the dollar Tuesday for the second straight trading day after an 18% rebound last Friday. 

 In Mexico City, on the spot dollar market, the dollar ended at mid rate levels of 6.6350 pesos per dollar against 6.4750 pesos per dollar at Monday's close. Spreads were 6.6100/6.6600 pesos per dollar, compared to spreads of 6.4500/6.5000 pesos/dlr at Monday's close. 

 Traders said downward pressure was created on the peso as holders of maturing dollar-linked government paper known as Tesobonos attempted to increase their yields. A little more than $500 million dollars in Tesobonos mature this Thursday. 

 Dealers said Mexico's central bank intervened in a bid to keep the peso from falling too much ahead of Thursday's amortization. There was no confirmation of the intervention, but Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz conceded during a Tuesday briefing to financial investors and reporters in New York that the Bank of Mexico 'will intervene from time to time' in a bid to lend stability to the Mexican currency. 

 The peso recovered 18% against the U.S. currency Friday to close at 6.3000 pesos/dlr after the government unveiled a tough emergency economic plan that calls for a 50% sales tax hike, double-digit increases in gasoline, gas and electricity, and a tightening of the fiscal belt. 

 But the Mexican currency dropped 2.7% against the dollar Monday in light, short-term profit-taking and investor concern that soaring interest rates could cause a stronger contraction in the economy than originally anticipated, traders said.

title: Mexican peso soars higher vs dlr on economic plan.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 10 (Reuter) - The Mexican new peso rocketed off historic lows against the dollar following the government's announcement of a new economic plan, ending more than a peso higher in 24- and 48-hour contracts. 

 Traders said Banco de Mexico intervention also helped the Mexican currency gain ground. 

 The 24- and 48-hour peso closed a full 1.2 new pesos stronger at 6.25/6.35 per dollar. Earlier the same-day peso closed 80 centavos higher at 6.55/6.75. 

 "The rise wasn't real in as much as Banco de Mxico came in and intervened," one trader said. 

 But others noted that Mexico's drawing on $3 billion of a $20 billion U.S. aid facility Friday added real resources and heft to the central bank's moves and would continue to do so from now on. 

 "The expectation is that the central bank will now be able to use that money to meet its commitments and will have more available to enter the market," another trader said. 

 The peso's gain followed the announcement of a tough fiscal plan to overcome Mexico's economic crisis. Authorities said they are aiming for an exchange rate of about 6 new pesos per dollar. 

 -- Ivette Ceretti, Mexico City Bureau +525 728-9555

title: Banco de Mexico says peso to float for time being.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 9 (Reuter) - The Mexican peso will remain floating for the time being, and no plans have been made yet to change the exchange rate regime, a Banco de Mexico spokesman said. 

 "For the time being, the exchange scheme for Mexico is free floatation with discretionary intervention," the spokesman, who asked not to be identified, said. He denied there were any plans to impose exchange controls, as has been rumoured in the currency markets where the peso plummeted. 

 He said the central bank would only start thinking about possible alternative peso regimes when conditions improve. 

 The spokesman declined to put a timeframe on when the central bank expected conditions to be suitable for a new exchange rate policy, but he suggested the decision was not imminent. 

 Officials, including the central bank spokesman, are expecting the government to announce new emergency measures to deal with the peso crisis by the latest Friday. 

 -- Henry Tricks, Mexico City bureau +525 728-9560

title: Mexico's New Peso Closes Sharply Down At 6.7950 To Dlr

 Traders said it was probable Mexico's central bank intervened Tuesday around 1730 GMT, when the dollar hit 6.8500 new pesos/dlr. The intervention could not be confirmed. 

 Market traders estimated the Bank of Mexico bought $350 million worth of new pesos Monday to bring the local currency below seven pesos to the dollar. That also could not be confirmed. 

 Market volume Tuesday was average, with the peso suffering as investors continued to fret over a seeming lack of economic and political direction, said dealers. 

 'Nobody is bringing dollars to Mexico,' said one Mexico City trader. 'With this kind of volatility, there is no way you can hedge your bets.'

title: Mexico new peso ends sharply down, off worst levels.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 6 (Reuter) - Mexico's new peso closed sharply weaker on continued fears over the Mexican economy, but off its lows after the Mexican central bank stepped in to prop up the faltering currency, traders said. 

 The new peso closed 25 centavos weaker at 6.53/6.58 per dollar in 24-hour and 48-hour contracts, traders said. 

 "It was pure speculation ... everyone began to buy dollars because of the economic and political uncertainty here," one trader said. 

 "Later in the day, the Banco de Mexico entered the market and it stopped the peso's fall," he said. 

 One trader said investors bailed out of the peso on rumors that a government takeover on Friday of Banpais bank could be repeated with a handful of other banks facing debt problems. 

 But some analysts said the peso suffered because of a world-wide speculative attack on currencies that are considered weak following the devaluation Sunday of the Spanish peseta. 

 "The peseta devaluation mixed with ongoing concerns over the Mexican economy, including the health of banks," one Mexico City analyst told Reuters. 

 Traders said they estimated Banco de Mexico spent about $200 million defending the peso. Despite the intervention, there was still heavy dollar demand at the end of the trading day, traders said. 

 The same-day new peso closed 88 centavos weaker at 6.80/6.90 per dollar earlier in the day.

title: Mexico judge's order takes heat off Zedillo.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 6 (Reuter) - A judge on Monday ordered the brother of Mexico's former president to stand trial on murder charges, taking some pressure off embattled President Ernesto Zedillo as his government sought to stop the currency sinking to new lows and Indian rebels from revolting. 

 Judge Diogenes Cruz ruled there was enough evidence to try Raul Salinas de Gortari, the 48-year-old elder brother of ex-president Carlos Salinas, on charges of masterminding the murder last year of the boss of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI). 

 The arrest rocked Mexico where ex-presidents and their families have for generations enjoyed de facto immunity from the law after leaving office. 

 In a separate development, prosecutors said they were seeking the extradition from the United States to Mexico of Mario Ruiz Massieu, brother of the dead party leader, on charges of covering up the murder investigation to favour Raul Salinas. 

 Ruiz Massieu was arrested at the Newark, New Jersey, airport in the northeastern U.S. last Friday for failing to declare to customs officials all of the $46,000 in cash he was carrying in a suitcase on an unexplained flight to Spain. Under U.S. law all people entering or leaving the country must declare currency in excess of $10,000. 

 A U.S. judge on Monday ordered Ruiz Massieu held without bail after Mexico demanded his extradition and his lawyer said his client was seeking political asylum in the United States. 

 Both Ruiz Matthieu and Raul Salinas deny any wrongdoing and say the charges against them are absurd and unproven. 

 The moves against Salinas and Ruiz Massieu were likely to help Zedillo who is facing a currency crisis and a deepening economic recession by showing he was serious about promises to bring high-level wrongdoers to trial, political analysts said. 

 Zedillo's image took a dent over the weekend when he sent an envoy to negotiate a truce with Carlos Salinas who was so upset by unproven allegations that he too was linked to the September 1994 murder of PRI boss Francisco Ruiz Massieu that he started a hunger strike. 

 The truce which involved a public statement from prosecutors making clear Carlos Salinas was not under suspicion for the assassination halted the hunger strike but did Zedillo little good with public opinion or with opposition politicians. 

 Mexico's financial markets kept up the pressure on Zedillo's administration Monday where the peso plunged to a new record low of 6.85 to the dollar on fears the economic crisis would trigger a series of bank collapses. 

Mexico's central bank intervened to calm traders and by late afternoonn peso futures had limped back to a buy-sell rate of 6.53/58, down 25 centavos from their close last Friday. 

 On the political front, Indian rebels in the southern state of Chiapas dealt Zedillo a blow on Sunday night by rejecting his proposals for peace and dialogue in the 14-month conflict as "a real backward step" though they stressed they were still interested in talking rather than fighting. 

 In another reminder of the smouldering tensions in Chiapas, ranchers and right-wingers burnt the symbolic coffins of two pro-dialogue figures in a public square at the weekend to show their opposition to negotiations with the rebels of the Zapatista National Liberation Army. 

 Back in the capital, Zedillo's government faced another test in Congress where politicians this week were due to start picking over the controversial $20 billion U.S. aid package to Mexico agreed by Washington with Zedillo's government at the end of last month. 

 The deal is likely to go through although some Mexicans are unhappy about a clause allowing the Americans first call on their precious oil revenues in the event of a default. Legislators are also concerned the severe austerity measures imposed by the accord would kill economic growth.

title: Mexico's New Peso -2: Down 39% Since Crisis Erupted
text:
Traders said the new peso may slowly be finding its natural level following weeks of volatility and flirtations with the psycholical barrier of 6 pesos to the dollar. 

 'It seems every time we approach six, the market brings the rate down again,' said one Mexico City trader. 

 Traders said, though, that the Mexican central bank intervened Wednesday after the local currency reached the level of 6 pesos to the dollar in intraday trading. They said there was no indication of new intervention Thursday. 

 Bank of Mexico Governor Miguel Mancera said Wednesday he expected the peso to shortly stabilize around 5 new pesos to the dollar.  The new peso strengthened 2.7% against the dollar from Wednesday's close, but still stands 39% down against the dollar since Dec. 20, when Mexico's financial crisis erupted. 

 Mexico was forced to move to a free floating exchange regime when its international reserves dipped to such low levels it could no longer sustain a long-held policy of defending the new peso within a wide trading band with the dollar.

title: Mexico stocks fall to 17-month low, peso weakens.
text:
MEXICO CITY (Reuter) - The Mexican peso plunged and the stock market fell to a 17-month low Wednesday as foreign investors fled the nation, worried about the economy and the indigenous uprising in the southern state of Chiapas. 

 The Mexican peso fell sharply, ending at about 5.97 per dollar after dipping below 6 to the dollar during the day. 

Foreign exchange traders said the Mexican central bank intervened to prop up the peso, selling about $100 million to buy the Mexican currency. 

 "The peso opened the day under heavy pressure from foreign investors, but when it hit 6 (pesos to the dollar), the Bank of Mexico intervened," one trader said. 

 The new peso has shed 42 percent of its value since the government decided on Dec. 20 to devalue the currency and then let it float on world markets. 

 Traders said foreign investors were troubled by the political situation in Chiapas and confused about President Ernesto Zedillo's decision on Tuesday to halt the army's advance on Zapatista rebels there, they added. 

 Stock prices took a tumble for the first time since the announcement two weeks ago of a $50 billion U.S.-led aid package for the Mexican economy. 

 The main stock market index closed at a 17-month low of 1,798.0, down 123.08 points or 6.4 percent. 

 Rumours, later denied, that central bank governor Miguel Mancera would resign hit stock prices. 

 They were then compounded by a statement by Grupo Sidek, a Mexican conglomerate with vast interests in steel and tourism, that it would default on some short-term debt contracted by its subsidiaries -- the first default announcement in the two-month old economic crisis. 

 The share price of Sidek and its subsidiaries Simex and Situr fell more than 20 percent on the news amid concerns that other companies might also face liquidity problems. 

 "This is the tip of the iceberg," one trader said. 

 "The market was sad and bad. It is still reflecting what is happening in the country," one trader said. "There is a complete and utter lack of confidence among investors, and the rumours add to that." 

 Stock prices were also hit by a rise in domestic interest rates in the central bank's weekly auction of government securities. 

 The benchmark 28-day Mexican Treasury bill rate rose 4.8 percentage points to 40 percent in the auction as Banco de Mexico cranked up rates to try and entice investors. 

 Investors' appetite for the bills was weak, with demand for all T-bills falling to 3.45 billion new pesos, less than half of the 7.49 billion new pesos investors sought last week.

title: Mexico stocks, peso reel as foreigners bail out.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 15 (Reuter) - The Mexican currency took a battering Wednesday and stock prices fell sharply as foreign investors pulled out of their Mexican holdings and bought dollars, traders said. 

 The latest round of market turmoil came after a cocktail of news about the financial health of Mexican companies and the indigenous uprising in the southern state of Chiapas that disturbed investors even as the government was moving to reestablish stability on the political and economic fronts. 

 The Mexican new peso -- so called after the government slashed three zeroes off the old currency in 1993 -- fell sharply, ending at about 5.97 per dollar after at one point dipping below 6 to the dollar. 

Foreign exchange traders said the Mexican central bank intervened to prop up the peso, selling about $100 million to buy the Mexican currency. 

 "The peso opened the day under heavy pressure from foreign investors, but when it hit 6 (new pesos to the dollar), the Bank of Mexico intervened," one trader said. 

 Traders said foreign investor uncertainty over the political situation in the troubled state of Chiapas caused some of the pressure. Foreign investors do not know how to interpret President Ernesto Zedillo's decision Tuesday to halt the army's advance on Zapatista rebels there, they added. 

 Stock prices also took a tumble for the first time since the announcement two weeks ago of a $50 billion U.S.-led aid package for the Mexican economy. 

 The main stock market index was down more than 100 points, or over 5 percent, in late trading. 

 Rumours, later denied, that central bank governor Miguel Mancera would resign hit stock prices. 

 They were compounded by steel firm Sidek's statement that it would default on some short-term debt contracted by its subsidiaries -- the first default announcement of the two-month old economic crisis. 

 The share price of Sidek and its subsidiaries Simex and Situr all fell more than 25 percent on the news amid concerns that other companies might also face liquidity problems. 

 "There is a lot of confusion in the market and the foreigners are selling most," one trader said. 

 A Banco de Mxico spokesman said rumours of Mancera's resignation were "totally unfounded". 

 Stock prices were also hit by a rise in domestic interest rates in the central bank's weekly auction of government securities. The benchark 28-day Mexican Treasury bill rate rose 4.8 percentage points to 40 percent in the auction as Banco de Mexico cranked up rates to try and entice investors. 

 Investors' appetite for the bills was weak, with demand for all T-bills falling to 3.45 billion new pesos, less than half of the 7.49 billion new pesos investors sought last week. 

 Analysts said that in the securities market, too, confusion was prevalent about Zedillo's aims in Chiapas after he first sent police and troops to detain rebel leader Marcos and then ordered security forces to halt their advance. 

 "Because there was such a drastic change of signal in the handling of the problem, investors sought higher returns," one analyst said.

title: Camdessus/Mexico -3: Sees Continued Peso Float
text:
Camdessus briefly reviewed Mexico's economic goals for this year and into 1996 as part of the unprecendented credit package approved by the IMF's shareholders overnight. 

 The IMF managing director stressed the Mexico's economic fundamentals currently are far stronger than when its 1982 debt crisis, which also sparked a global crisis in sovereign lending by commercial banks. 

 He said that while the Mexican economy will slow in the first half of this year, authorities are anticipating inflation-adjusted growth of 1.5% this year, reflection a second-half recovery. And he added that growth is expected to recover further in 1996. 

 In terms of inflation, Mexico is 9% by year end. And Camdessus voiced optimist that policies being implemented by Mexico will keep wage growth 'very restrained.' 

 Mexico's current account deficit, which was suprassing 8% of gross domestic product (GDP), is expected to be nearly halved to around 4.5% of GDP by year end, Camdessus said. Further declines to levels around 3% to 3.5% of GDP are expected in 1996. 

 The peso, meanwhile, is expected to continue to float, according to Camdessus, who said that Mexico's central bank will be intervening to on a 'very limited' basis given a policy of floating the currency.

title: U.S. helps prop up peso as Mexico stocks plunge.
text:
MEXICO CITY (Reuter) - The U.S. Federal Reserve intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday to prop up the battered Mexican peso, but while the move helped the peso, Mexican stocks plummeted in the biggest one-day drop in five years. 

 Meanwhile, Mexican officials were seeking support abroad to help the country weather its financial crisis. 

 The flotation of the peso on December 20, which resulted in its losing nearly 40 per cent of its value, led investors to bail out of Mexican investments, sending the stock market skidding. 

 In New York, a spokesman for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which generally acts for the Federal Reserve (Fed) in market interventions, said it bought Mexican pesos for dollars at the request of the Mexican central bank. 

 These operations are consistent with the efforts of the U.S. monetary authorities to assist Mexico in responding to recent financial developments,'' the Fed, as the U.S. central bank is known, said in a statement. 

 Mexico's central bank, Banco de Mexico, said it had made the first drawings on a U.S.-Canada peso support package announced last week, using $500 million from U.S. monetary authorities and C$83 million ($59 million U.S.) from Canada. 

 The peso regained some of its massive losses of the last three weeks, rising as high as 5.0 to the dollar before easing to end with a gain of 30 centavos at 5.30. 

 But the moves to support the peso could not stem the losses in Mexican stocks. 

 The bolsa's IPC index of 37 shares closed down 149.88 points, or 6.65 percent, at 2,104.05. In percentage terms, it was the steepest stock market drop since October 16, 1989, when the bolsa fell 8.05 percent.

 The peso regained some of its massive losses of the last three weeks, rising as high as 5.0 to the dollar before easing to end with a gain of 30 centavos at 5.30. 

 But the moves to support the peso could not stem the losses in Mexican stocks. 

 The bolsa's IPC index of 37 shares closed down 149.88 points, or 6.65 percent, at 2,104.05. In percentage terms, it was the steepest stock market drop since Oct. 16, 1989, when the bolsa fell 8.05 percent. 

 In Japan, Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria, putting a brave face on his country's peso crisis to placate nervous Japanese investors, forecast an end to the upheaval in a few weeks. 

 In meetings with government officials, bankers and business executives in Tokyo, Gurria reiterated Mexico's position that its economy is fundamentally strong and said the crisis is an opportunity, not a setback. 

 "In the next few weeks I expect the pendulum to have swung back to the middle," Gurria said. 

 He forecast the peso would settle around 4.50 to the dollar but gave no timing for such stability to be achieved. 

 Governor Hiroshi Yasuda of The Export-Import Bank of Japan praised the rescue effort Mexico has put in place involving deregulation, monetary controls and privatisation. 

 "The new programme has good substance," he said. "But we want to watch how the new measures take effect for a while. 

 In Mexico, a Finance Ministry official said annualized inflation will soar to 31.1 percent and real growth in the gross domestic product will drop to 1.1. percent in the first three months of 1995. 

 The official, Martin Werner, unveiled figures projecting annualized growth of just 0.2 percent and annualized inflation of 21.2 percent in the second quarter. 

 But he said the economy will then recover, allowing for higher growth in 1996. 

 "The problem of the adjustment is transitory and the economy is going to come out of it with more solid bases to re-establish the path of growth," Werner told a meeting of bankers and investors at the Mexican stock market. 

 One key political opposition party has filed a formal complaint charging former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari covered up Mexico's economic problems to help his bid to become the head of the new World Trade Organisation. 

 The complaint against Salinas, given to the attorney general's office for investigation by the centre-left Democratic Revolution Party, or PRD, blamed the Salinas administration for the country's current crisis, which began with the peso devaluation. 

 It accused Salinas of "crimes against the national wealth" and "improper exercise of public service." 

 In its complaint, the PRD said Salinas and his economic cabinet allowed the country's current account deficit to grow to "an unsustainable level" and failed to take action for fear it would taint Salinas' reputation as the man who brought economic stability to Mexico. 

 It said the peso should have been devalued last April to put a damper on the deficit, which grew to $28 billion by the year's end. 

 Salinas, whose six-year term ended Dec. 1, is on a world tour seeking support for the WTO post and has refused to comment on the accusations. 

 The attorney general's office accepted the PRD complaint but gave no indication of what action it would take. 

 Attorney general Antonio Lozano, a member of the conservative National Action Party, was appointed by Salinas' successor Ernesto Zedillo. Lozano is the first cabinet member in modern Mexican history who is not a member of Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party.

title: (WSJ):U.S. Fed  Intervenes  In  Forex  To Bolster  Mexico 's Peso
text:
WASHINGTON (AP-DJ)--The Federal Reserve, broadening efforts to restore investor confidence in Mexico, intervened in foreign-exchange markets to prop up the reeling peso, Tuesday's Wall Street Journal reports. 

 The intervention was viewed as comparatively light. But it was enough to shore up the sagging currency and to send a critical signal that the U.S. wasn't willing to stand by while the peso continued to slide.

 The intervention was made at the request of Mexico's central bank, Banco de Mexico, which financed the move by tapping an 18-billion-dlr emergency credit facility that was set up by a U.S.-led international group after Mexico's currency began its free-fall last month.

title: Fed moves to support peso as Mexicans seek support.
text:
NEW YORK (Reuter) - The Federal Reserve intervened in the foreign exchange market Monday to prop up the battered Mexican peso as Mexican officials sought support abroad to help the country weather its financial crisis. 

 The flotation of the peso on Dec. 20, which resulted in its losing about a third of its value, led investors to bail out of Mexican investments, sending the Mexican stock market skidding. 

 A spokesman for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which generally acts for the Fed in market interventions, said it bought Mexican pesos for dollars at the request of the Mexican central bank. 

 In a statement, the Fed said it "announced today that it is intervening in the foreign exchange market at the request of and for the account of the Banco de Mexico, purchasing pesos against the dollar. 

 "These operations are consistent with the efforts of the U.S. monetary authorities to assist Mexico in responding to recent financial developments." 

 The peso regained some of its massive losses of the last three weeks, rising as much as 65 centavos to 5.0 to the dollar before easing to 5.30. 

 But Mexican stocks slumped more than 74 points, or 3.28 percent, showing no sign of a turnaround. 

 Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria, putting a brave face on his country's peso crisis to placate nervous Japanese investors, forecast an end to the upheaval in a few weeks. 

 In meetings with government officials, bankers and business executives in Tokyo, Gurria reiterated Mexico's position that its economy is fundamentally strong and said the crisis is an opportunity, not a setback. 

 "In the next few weeks I expect the pendulum to have swung back to the middle," Gurria said. 

 He forecast that the peso would settle around 4.50 to the dollar but gave no timing for the currency stability be achieved. 

 Gurria received a polite hearing. But like much of the financial world, his listeners were not ready to buy his argument completely that a drastic shift in the currency's value was something to cheer about. 

 Japan has agreed to take part in a U.S.-led $18 billion credit arrangement to see Mexico through the immediate crisis. The central Bank of Japan was expected to contribute up to $1 billion, while four private Japanese banks are part of other rescue efforts led by U.S. commercial banks. 

 But bankers and business officials were cautious. 

 Governor Hiroshi Yasuda of The Export-Import Bank of Japan praised the rescue effort Mexico has put in place involving deregulation, monetary controls and privatisation. 

 "The new programme has good substance," he said. "But we want to watch how the new measures take effect for a while. 

 "Having just joined NAFTA, they have a tough road ahead but they have to hang in there," he said, referring to the North American Free Trade Agreement signed by Mexico, the United States and Canada. 

 Asked about fresh lending to Mexico, Yasuda said, "It would be no problem if the Mexican economy heads for better conditions after global financial aid takes effect." 

 At another meeting in London, investors and analysts were told by a high-level Mexican delegation that the Bank of Mexico would not intervene to support the peso, despite the statement to the contrary by the New York Fed. 

 "They said the Mexican central bank was not supporting the peso," said one analyst who attended the meeting. 

 "They said they would not be active but were confident the market would take the peso to 4.5 per dollar," another said. 

 Francisco Gil, vice-governor of Bank of Mexico, Enrique Vilatela, director of Banco Mexicano de Comercio Exterior (Bancomex), Carlos Sales, economic aide to President Ernesto Zedillo, and Rolf Schlettwein, vice-chairman of Mexican Council of Investment, were at the meeting.

title: Argentina Redrado:  Intervention  Not Driving Inflation
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Argentina's central bank president defended his bank's foreign exchange intervention policies and said they are not creating inflation pressures in his country.  

Martin Redrado, at a conference held by the Bank of Mexico in Mexico City Tuesday, said, "I don't see there is a conflict there as long as we sterilize" the bank's moves to buy dollars to build up his nation's foreign exchange reserves.  

Redrado was addressing a question from the audience that sought to understand whether these interventions are fueling price pressures in his nation. Economists expect inflation to come in a 11.2% gain for the year in Argentina, well over the central bank's ceiling of 8%.  

The central banker hung some of the blame for current levels of inflation on the past policies of his bank, and noted that there's a lag before the bank's currently restrictive policies will impact the price pressure environment. He added, "we are exactly on track" in terms of the bank's monetary policy goals.

title: Latin America Stands To Benefit If Asia Budges On  Forex
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--U.S. and European governments are jawboning their counterparts in Asia to revalue their cheap currencies, which could provide a welcome lift to another region that's quietly watching the debate from the sidelines.  

Latin America has long lagged its peers in developing Asia when it comes to export competitiveness, a trend that hasn't been helped by policy decisions in places like Beijing and Seoul aimed at keeping local exchange rates from appreciating too quickly.  

That competitive advantage eventually could narrow, though, if Asian authorities heed Saturday's call by the Group of Seven industrialized nations to allow greater flexibility in exchange rates - a practice already introduced by many Latin American governments in recent years.  

"If we were in a scenario in which (Asian countries) allow currencies to float, that might help Latin America a little bit, especially Mexico," said Carlos Janada, a Latin American economist at the IDEAglobal consultancy.  

While China has kept its yuan fixed against the dollar since 1994 at an exchange rate that is now considered undervalued, Mexico's peso was floated the same year and, after an initial plunge, has strengthened considerably in the intervening period. Recently, China surpassed Mexico as the No. 2 exporter to the U.S., behind Canada, much to the consternation of manufacturers south of the Rio Grande.  

Marc Chandler, a currency strategist at HSBC, said several of his bank's clients have indicated "they'd be happy to" take bigger positions in Mexico if it becomes clear China will agree to loosen its reins on the foreign exchange market and allow the yuan to strengthen.  

Stronger currencies in Asia also could give a boost to other countries in Latin America, which has bet increasingly on export-fueled growth with mixed results since beginning to open up its economies in the 1990s after several decades of protectionist policies.  

Ecuador, El Salvador and Panama would automatically benefit. The three countries have fully dollarized their economies, so their goods immediately would become cheaper on world markets if any Asian countries agree to strengthen their currencies vis-a-vis the greenback.  

But Latin American countries with free-floating currencies also could use a hand as they try to expand a still-shaky export base. After a decade of free-market reforms, Latin America and the Caribbean's percentage of exports to gross domestic product barely budged, to 16.5% in 1999 from 14.1% in 1990, according to World Bank data. By contrast, the percentage in East Asia and the Pacific rose to 38.1% from 26% over the same period.  

It's far from clear if Asian governments will budge on foreign exchange policy. China until now has balked at growing international pressure to revalue its currency, insisting Tuesday that the issue is an "internal affair."  

Guillermo Ortiz, Mexico's central bank governor, told reporters Tuesday that Chinese currency revaluation "isn't a scenario that is likely" and that Mexico should try to ensure greater competitiveness by making its own economy "more flexible."  

Economists agree that countries like Mexico haven't helped their own cause by faltering on long-promised reforms such as overhauling the tax system, increasing private sector investments in the energy sector and easing labor laws.  

"It's hard to compete with China on a number of fronts, and the currency is just one of those problems," said Rafael de la Fuente, a Latin America economist at BNP Paribas.  

While no countries in Latin America boast the size of China's workforce and few can compete with its extremely low labor costs, they also haven't been able to keep pace with other parts of emerging Asia where better-trained workers churn out lucrative technology exports for overseas markets.  

Although countries such as Costa Rica were able to draw significant investments from U.S. computer chip giant Intel in the 1990s, the world's three largest chip foundries are located in Taiwan and Singapore. Latin America's export base, by contrast, still skews predominantly toward commodities and other materials farther down the value-added chain.  

Still, a more evenly balanced playing field when it comes to currencies can't hurt if recent history is any indication.  

Brazil is expected to post a record trade surplus of more than $20 billion this year, prodded along in large part by last year's 35% currency depreciation. South America's biggest country had rung up an uninterrupted string of trade deficits between 1995 and 2000, when its exporters were held back by an overvalued fixed exchange rate designed to slay inflation.  

Neighboring Argentina also has watched its export sector steadily recover since scrapping the peso's decade-old fixed parity with the dollar in January 2002. With the local currency now worth only a third what it was before the devaluation, Argentine exports have jumped 17% in the first seven months of 2003 from the year-earlier period as the country starts to recover from a four-year recession.  

With long-standing inflation pressures ebbing in many corners of Latin America, few central banks have been compelled in recent months to defend their currencies from further depreciation and some - such as Argentina - have even moved to ensure that they don't start to strengthen again.  

A bit of extra help from across the Pacific wouldn't go unnoticed, even if Latin American governments largely have remained silent as the U.S., Europe and Asia increasingly spar over the rules of the currency game.  

"I think the cause of greater competitiveness in Asia than in Latin America is a little more complicated than just the exchange rate," said Sidney Weintraub, a Latin America economist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.  

Nonetheless, many Latin American authorities "would welcome some appreciation of the Asian currencies," added Weintraub, who's based in Washington.  

-By Mike Esterl, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-4026; mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Mexico's Peso Closes At Record Low 11.222/Dlr; Euro Cited

title: Mexico's Fin Min: Opposed To Direct  Forex  Invention
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's Finance Minister Francisco Gil Diaz said Thursday his country remains fully committed to its free-floating currency regime and dismissed the idea that authorities should tap the roughly $50 billion in international reserves to stem the recent slide in the peso. 

 "We think it's a waste of money," Gil Diaz told reporters in a press conference when asked about the possibility of direct intervention in the foreign-exchange market. 

 After strengthening against the dollar for several years, the peso ($1=MXN10.96) weakened more than 10% last year and has slipped further in 2003, reaching historical lows late last month. 

 Gil Diaz praised the central bank, which has tightened monetary policy to lower inflation expectations but refrained from intervening directly in the currency markets. 

 He said Mexico learned its lesson in 1995, when it unsuccessfully tried to halt the peso's depreciation after allowing the currency to float in late 1994. Gil Diaz is meeting with investors in New York City. 

 Gil Diaz said the Finance Ministry is sticking to its original 3% economic growth target for 2003, which would be about three times the expansion posted last year. 

 But he said the 2003 growth target is based on the assumption that there will be no U.S.-led war in Iraq, or if there is one, that it will be short. 

 "If it is a protracted type of event, it would certainly have a negative effect on Mexican growth," he told reporters. A possible U.S. invasion of Iraq is heightening fears of a double-dip recession in the U.S., which absorbs more than 80% of Mexican exports. 

 Gil Diaz said the government is bracing itself for tough global conditions by setting tight spending targets. The 2003 budget calls for a fiscal deficit ceiling equal to 0.5% of gross domestic product. 

 Mexico also completed its 2003 external financing needs in January, when it issued $2 billion in global bonds. 

 Gil Diaz said he met with the ratings agency Standard & Poor's earlier Thursday. He said S&P told him that of the 92 countries that face some fallout risk from a war in the Middle East, Mexico ranks as one of the less vulnerable. 

 Although Mexico has met its 2003 external financing needs, Gil Diaz didn't rule out that the country may return to foreign capital markets to retire its remaining Brady bonds by the end of 2003. 

 "It depends on the windows of opportunity we find," he told reporters. Mexico retired some more Brady bonds in January, and the amount of Bradys left in circulation today is "miniscule," he added. 

 Bradys are restructured sovereign bonds that were issued in the late 1980s and early 1990s and are backed by U.S. Treasury collateral. Over the past several years, Mexico has launched exchange offers in which the bonds are replaced with global bonds. 

 A side effect of the Iraqi war concern has been the surge in the price of oil, a major export commodity for Mexico. 

 Mexican oil currently fetches more than $25 a barrel, above the $18.30-a-barrel assumption contained in the government's 2003 budget. 

 Gil Diaz estimated that Mexico could ramp-up oil exports another 150,000-200,000 barrels a day in the second half of this year, if warranted by global demand. 

 Mexico exports around 1.76 million b/d of oil.
