title: Mexico's Peso Opens At 10.8550/Dlr Vs 10.9450 Wed Close
text:
MEXICO CITY -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's peso opened sharply stronger against the dollar Thursday, buoyed by the dollar's  own rally against the euro. 

 In Mexico City, Banamex quoted the 48-hour spot peso opening at MXN10.8550 to the dollar, stronger from Wednesday's MXN10.9450 close. 

 A Mexico City trader said the peso's gains were tied to the dollar's gains against the euro. 

 The dollar rallied as banks took profits on weeks of euro gains, although the rebound isn't expected to be sustained with concerns over a war in Iraq still weighing on  the U.S. currency. 

 The peso, which has racked up a string of new closing lows in the past week, has been hard hit by the dollar's weakness, given Mexico close trade and investment ties to the U.S. 

 On Wednesday, Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz attributed the peso's weakness largely to dollar losses against the euro, weaker-than-expected U.S. economic recovery, and Mexico's loss of competitiveness with other economies. 

 Ortiz reiterated that the central bank won't rule out use of any mechanisms at its disposal to counter volatility if peso weakness threatens inflation or inflation expectations, but stressed that the ultimate decision to intervene in the foreign exchange market lies with the Finance Ministry, which has the deciding vote in the exchange commission. 

 President Vicente Fox and Finance Minister Francisco Gil  both said at the weekend that Mexico won't intervene by selling dollars in the foreign exchange market, but Ortiz rejected the notion of any rift between the bank and the government. 

 In the local media, his comments were taken by some to mean the bank is ready to intervene if necessary, and by others to mean that it doesn't intend to do so. 

 Bear Stearns, in a report Thursday entitled "Too Many Voices on Peso," said "the government and the Bank of Mexico are sending mixed messages about the peso, and confusion over policies tends to weaken the currency in question." 

 Ortiz reaffirmed Wednesday that the peso's depreciation in the past 10 months has yet to show a clear impact on prices, but said the bank was watching closely for contamination of inflation via the exchange rate.

title: UPDATE 2-Mexico's cenbank says peso not spurring inflation.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 29 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso's swoon to record lows against the dollar has yet to fuel inflation that would force the country's central bank to prop up the currency, the bank's governor said on Wednesday. 

 Banco de Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz said the central bank's mandate dictated that it only be concerned with the peso's volatility if it filters into the economy in the form of inflation, or expectations of future inflation. 

 "The central bank is not concerned about any exchange-rate level," Ortiz told a news conference on the bank's 2003 monetary program. "There is no magic number or magic level" for the peso. 

 The Mexican currency closed at 10.972 to the dollar on Wednesday, its fourth consecutive record low closing against the greenback. Investors are concerned a war in Iraq could damage the U.S. economy, the destination for 90 percent of Mexican exports. 

 Banco de Mexico is closely watching the peso and will act with the "necessary force" if required to quell inflation pressures, Ortiz said. 

 But, he added, an intervention "is not foreseeable under the conditions we're seeing in the markets these days." 

 Banco de Mexico's target for consumer price inflation in 2003 is 3 percent, far below 2002's inflation of 5.7 percent, and the bank has tightened monetary policy recently in its effort to meet this year's target. 

 Mexican prices rose at a moderate rate of 0.32 percent in the first half of January, while the peso shed 1.33 percent of its value against the dollar during the same period. 

 Banco de Mexico has not directly intervened to calm volatility in the local foreign exchange market since 1998. 

 Ortiz noted that any such intervention has to be approved by a so-called exchange commission, on which the finance ministry's representative has veto power. Finance Minister Francisco Gil and President Vicente Fox said this week they have no intention of intervening to support the peso. 

 NERVOUS WORLD MARKETS 

 While declines in Mexico's currency in the past have often been a reflection of worsening domestic economic conditions, economists say the peso's recent weakness is more the result of nervousness across world markets about the possibility of a U.S.-led war against Iraq. 

 Still, economists caution, a prolonged U.S. war against Iraq would hurt the U.S. economy, in turn damaging the Mexican economy, which relies on the United Stats as its main export market and chief source of foreign direct investment. 

 The Mexican peso has weakened by more than 5 percent against the U.S. dollar since the end of 2002. It weakened 12 percent against the dollar last year. 

 In addition to the external factors, economists say some of the recent peso weakness can be attributed to investor concerns over stalled economic reforms in Mexico. Fox has failed to gain congressional support for new laws that would raise more taxes, lower electricity costs and make the local labor market more flexible.

title: Mexico's Peso Ends At Another Low; Mkt Eyes  Central Bank
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 MEXICO CITY -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's peso slipped against the dollar to its third new closing low in a week Monday, as market participants remained nervous over the brewing U.S.-Iraq conflict. 

 In Mexico City on 48-hour spot dollar markets, Banamex quoted the peso closing at a midrate of MXN10.9070 per dollar, weaker from its open of MXN10.8790 and from Friday's MXN10.8750 close. The closing spread was MXN10.8970/10.9170, compared with MXN10.86/10.89 Friday. 

 The continuing weakness of the peso, linked to the euro's gains against the dollar, has drawn differing views of how far the Bank of Mexico will let it go before taking action. 

 Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz said last week that the bank was keeping open all options to confront volatility and speculation hitting the peso, to the extent that it pushes up inflation expectations and threatens the bank's 3% inflation target for this year. 

 But Mexican President Vicente Fox said in Davos this weekend that the government will maintain its free float of the currency. 

 "Our peso has handled this turbulence well and is in good conditions," Fox added. "Precisely because of that, we will continue the floating system, and we are not going to alter it." 

 Fox reiterated that Mexico has close to $50 billion in foreign currency reserves. 

 Finance Minister Francisco Gil Diaz was also quoted in local media Monday as saying the government won't intervene to hold up the peso. 

 In a report Monday, HSBC welcomed the Bank of Mexico's decision Friday not to tighten monetary policy by increasing the size of its liquidity restriction, known as the "corto." 

 "Wisely, the Bank of Mexico left the corto unchanged, realizing that higher interest rates were unlikely to have any effect on protecting the beleaguered peso, " HSBC said, adding to "watch for Bank of Mexicointervention to sell dollars" if the rate goes beyond past MXN10.95. 

 Guillermo Estebanez, a currency analyst at Bank of America, said he had mixed views about the possibility of intervention, which would be the central bank's first since 1998. 

 Gil Diaz was against it, and the Finance Ministry has the deciding vote in decisions taken by the central bank's exchange commission, he said. 

 While noting the government's reluctance to intervene, Estebanez also cautioned that in foreign exchange markets, things can get ugly fairly quickly. 

 The Bital bank noted the continued ties to euro/dollar moves Monday, and saw a short-term trading range between MXN10.70 and MXN11.00 to the dollar. 

 "We consider that under the current situation the Bank of Mexico could intervene directly in the market to contain the speculative rise in the exchange rate, which would be probably in case the rate went above MXN11.00," the bank said in its intraday report. 

 Bank of America's Estebanez said the peso will continue to move with the dollar against the euro, reflecting Mexico's close association with the U.S. economy. 

 "It's not something that FX markets invented," he said. "If euro flows to the U.S. stop, they will also stop to Mexico."

title: Mexico's Peso Opens At 10.8790/Dlr Vs 10.8750 Fri Close

 In Mexico City around 1535 GMT, on 48-hour spot dollar markets, Banamex quoted the peso trading at a midrate of MXN10.8730, stronger from its opening level of MXN10.8790 and from Friday's MXN10.8750 close. 

 Banamex quoted a spread of MXN10.8630/10.8830, compared with MXN10.86/10.89 at Friday's close, which was an all-time  closing low the for peso. 

 Worries about a U.S. attack on Iraq have been at the heart of the recent pressure on the peso, which has been weakening as the dollar loses ground against the euro. 

 "The Mexican peso remains prisoner to the dollar," FXbriefing said in a report Monday. 

 The peso weakened sharply Friday after the Bank of Mexico left its monetary policy unchanged - against the expectations of most participants, who anticipated a tightening. 

 In its policy report, the central bank said it expects the current volatility - which includes a dose of speculation - to be temporary. 

 The report followed comments by central bank Governor Guillermo Ortiz, who said the bank wasn't ruling out any options for countering volatility and speculation. 

 A number of analysts and traders said they expect the market to test the bank's resolve to back the currency as it  aims to bring inflation down to 3% this year. 

 The last time the Bank of Mexico intervened directly in the exchange market was September 1998, during the Russian crisis. 

 President Vicente Fox, speaking in Davos on Saturday, reiterated his government's commitment to a free-floating exchange rate. 

 All Latin American currencies have suffered similarly in  recent days. Over the past two years, Mexico's peso has fared better than other regional currencies, Fox said. 

 "Our peso has handled this turbulence well and is in good conditions," Fox added. "Precisely because of that, we will continue the floating system, and we are not going to alter it."

title: DAVOS-UPDATE 1- Mexico  says will not  intervene  to support peso.
text:
DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Mexico will not intervene in currency markets to support the weakening peso, preferring to allow markets to set the level, Finance Minister Francisco Gil Diaz said on Sunday. 

 "The policy is no intervention whatsoever. We are going to allow the market to work," Gil Diaz said on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum. 

 The Mexico peso has declined about 20 percent in value against the U.S. dollar in the past 10 months, Gil Diaz said. It fell again on Friday after the Mexican central bank held interest rates steady to close at 10.87 percent. Markets had anticipated a rate increase to offset the inflationary impact of a falling currency. 

 But Gil Diaz told Reuters he was confident that Mexico could achieve its inflation and growth targets of 3.0 percent this year despite the weakening currency. 

 He said the government's inflation report earlier this month showed price gains came in below 0.4 percent, which if sustained would mean it would undershoot its 3.0 percent inflation target for the year. 

 Moreover, Gil Diaz said, the potentially inflationary impact from a weakening currency is lessening and the feed-through time lengthening, so he does not see the peso weakness as a threat. 

 "I am confident the central bank will be able to achieve its inflation target," Gil Diaz said. 

 Economists, however, are doubtful. In a survey they forecast a 4.2 percent inflation rate for 2003. Last year Mexico missed its 4.5 percent target, posting consumer price increases of 5.7 percent. The Mexican central bank already has raised interest rates three times from September.

title: Mexico's Peso Closes Weaker At MXN9.8500/Dollar

title: Mexico shares, peso weaken on Wall St, dollar losses.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 24 (Reuters) - Mexican stocks followed Wall Street lower on Monday, while the peso currency weakened with the U.S. dollar with some market analysts predicting the Mexican central bank will intervene to bolster the peso. 

Mexico's benchmark IPC index fell 0.38 percent to 6,477.80. The index which lost 3.4 percent last week and 13 percent since mid-May is at its lowest level this year. 

 Among top losers were shares of America Movil, which is the most actively traded stock on the exchange, shedding 2.16 percent to 6.81 pesos per share, taking its loss to about 23 percent since the start of the year. 

 America Movil's New York-listed American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) fell 2.65 percent to $13.60. 

 In a report to clients after the market close on Friday Merrill Lynch said it is turning positive on the Mexican stock market citing attractive valuations following the recent sell-off in Mexican stocks and what it sees as strong economic growth prospects starting in the second half of 2002. 

 Merrill said historically low interest rates in Mexico and the convergence of the country's economy with that of the United States, its largest trading partner, would attract more funds into the equities market. 

 Merrill's senior country strategist Carlos Peyrelongue said his top picks were Mexico's largest bank BBVA Bancomer, media giant Televisa, the country's biggest retailer Wal-Mart de Mexico (Walmex) and brewer Grupo Modelo. 

 BBVA Bancomer, which is down 16 percent since early April, fell 1.09 percent to 8.15 pesos per share, while Walmex series "C" shares fell 0.52 percent to 22.90 pesos per share. 

 Televisa rose 0.21 percent to 19 pesos per share, 

 Fueling investor caution toward Mexican equities are concerns that falling U.S. equities and currency markets would force investors to trim their Mexican holdings to raise cash. 

 These same concerns have brought down the value of the Mexican peso currency against the U.S. dollar by 9.25 percent since April 4. 

 In Monday trading thee peso shed 1.80 centavo from Friday to 9.9680 per U.S. dollar, while the dollar weakened to 0.98 per euro, its lowest level in two years. 

 Many market analysts predict the Mexican central bank may restrict its daily credit injection in the money market to prevent the peso from falling through 10 per dollar and to calm inflation fears. 

 "It will be important to monitor inflationary expectations and results in the months ahead," said Michael Gavin, Latin American economist at UBS Warburg. "We think the central bank is ready to act if pass-through to prices becomes evident." 

 The Mexican central bank is scheduled to release later on Monday inflation figures for the first half of June. 

 A Reuters survey of 31 private-sector economists predicted on average that consumer prices rose 0.15 percent during the period. The figures are scheduled to be released at 2:30 p.m. 1930 GMT), half an hour before the market close.

title: Mexico stocks down following Nasdaq, peso stable.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 5 (Reuters) - Mexican stocks followed the U.S. Nasdaq lower early on Wednesday with blue-chip retailer Walmex, telephone giant Telmex and mining shares topping losers, while the peso was slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar, traders said. 

 Mexico's IPC index of 36 leading shares fell 0.65 percent to 6,970.83 points. 

 Topping the list of percentage losers were shares of Mexico's largest retailer Wal-Mart de Mexico (Walmex) , a favorite of foreign investors, falling 1.94 percent to 28.75 pesos. 

 Shares of Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) , which account for about 16 percent of the IPC, fell 1.80 percent to 16.40 pesos. 

 Among other losers were shares of Mexican copper mining company Grupo Mexico , falling 2.29 percent to 16.20 pesos after the company said on Tuesday it shut down its Cananea copper mine in northern Mexico because it couldn't meet workers' wage demands. 

 In a report to clients on Wednesday, UBS Warburg said the closure of Cananea would reduce Grupo Mexico's cash flow and put it under pressure in servicing its heavy debt load. 

 "We maintain our cautious view and believe debt restructuring is key for Grupo Mexico, said Tom Meyer, analyst at UBS Warburg in New York. 

 Also weak were shares of Mexico's Industrias Penoles , the world's largest silver producer, falling 2.08 percent to 23.50 pesos. 

 Although analysts believe many Mexican stocks are attractive at current levels after last week's sell-off, investors are cautious and are looking for more evidence the Mexican economy - and that of its largest trading partner the United States - are on course for a recovery. 

 The IPC lost 4.5 percent last week and is down 6 percent since the start of May. 

 "We will continue to look to the United States for direction," said Jose Alberto Galvan, head of equities research at Finamex in Mexico City. 

 On Wall Street, stocks were mixed in late morning trade after an earlier report showed the U.S. services sector posted its fourth straight month of growth in May, expanding at its fastest pace since August 2000. The Dow Jones industrial average was last up 0.24 percent while the Nasdaq composite index was down 0.72 percent. 

 In the local currency market, the peso weakened 0.60 centavo from Tuesday to 9.7390 per U.S. dollar after losing about 1 percent against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday. 

 "Continued peso volatility is likely to maintain pressure on short-term rates," said Deutsche Bank on Wednesday. 

 The peso has been hurt in recent days by the U.S. dollar's losses against the Japanese yen and euro. 

 The market's view that the peso will weaken further lifts interest rate expectations as investors believe Mexico's central bank may intervene in the money market to restrict liquidity, which will boost the peso. 

 At Tuesday's Cetes auction of local Treasury bills, the rate on Mexico's benchmark 28-day Cetes rose seven basis points to 7 percent.

title: Mexico exporters bemoan "super peso", tight policy.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 15 (Reuters) - Mexican business leaders have stepped up calls for the country's central bank to take action to weaken the local currency, saying the so-called "super peso" is threatening to kill off exporters. 

 But Banco de Mexico has thus far held steady amid the latest wave of public pressure from manufacturers and speculation in local markets. On Friday it dampened the speculation further by keeping its monetary policy unchanged in its daily money market intervention. 

 "It's time for Banco de Mexico to loosen up its monetary policy, to support industry at this difficult time of economic slowdown," Claudio Gonzalez, the head of the Business Coordinating Council, told reporters on Thursday. 

 Gonzalez spoke after business and banking leaders held a closed-door meeting with Banco de Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz and Finance Minister Francisco Gil to discuss the country's monetary and economic policies. 

 Mexico's export-oriented industry is in the midst of a sharp slowdown as the economy of the United States, which buys some 90 percent of Mexican exports, cools. Industrial production fell 3.1 percent in April after a 1.9 percent drop in March. 

 Exporters argue they are being made less competitive by the peso, which has strengthened about 6 percent against the dollar this year while other Latin American currencies, including Brazil's real and Chile's peso, are at new lows against the greenback. 

 A strong peso means companies' sales in dollars bring in fewer pesos in profits, unless the companies raise their prices in dollars abroad. However, despite the strong peso, Mexico's exports totaled $56 billion in the first four months of 2001, up 7.8 percent from the same 2000 period. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso finished on Friday 6.3 centavos stronger at 9.012 pesos to the dollar, firming 0.5 percent in the week. 

 Economists say the chief reason for the peso's strength has been the heavy influx of foreign investment into Mexico, whose economy is viewed as a relatively safe haven compared to other emerging markets such as recession-plagued Argentina. 

 PESO BOGEYMAN 

 But manufacturing industry leaders have targeted Banco de Mexico as their main peso bogeyman. 

 They argue the central bank is sacrificing Mexican industry in its bid to drive inflation to 6.5 percent this year from 8.96 percent in 2000, and to U.S. levels of about 3.0 percent a year starting in 2003. 

 "What's clear is that we're not going to be around to enjoy the lower inflation," Rufino Salinas, head of the Glass Industry Association, said this week. He said many small-and medium-sized exporters will go out of business before the end of the year under current conditions. 

 Last month the central bank eased its monetary policy for the first time after three years of tightening. It did so by reducing its so-called money-market "short" from 400 million pesos to 350 million pesos. 

 News of modest inflation in May - which saw the smallest rise in the May consumer price index since 1972 - followed by the weak industrial production data, fueled speculation this week Banco de Mexico would ease monetary policy anew. 

 Diminishing inflation expectations have dropped local interest rates to their lowest levels since 1994. Benchmark 28-day Cetes, or T-bills were auctioned at 9.51 percent on Tuesday, down almost nine percentage points from their 2001 peak in mid-January. 

 But Banco de Mexico appears to be unwilling to be too aggressive in loosening its monetary policy given lingering inflationary pressures in the economy, and particularly since consumer spending remains strong despite the production slowdown. 

 The Finance Ministry on Friday reported private consumption in the first quarter of 2001 rose 6.5 percent compared to the same 2000 period. 

 Economists, meanwhile, say Mexican businesses have granted wage increases this year that have outpaced productivity gains, a factor that has also reduced their competitiveness. 

 Unlike Banco de Mexico policy, "...this is a factor that is under the businessman's control," Jonathan Heath, chief economist at Latin Source consultants wrote in the Reforma daily.

 A corrected version of the story follows: 

MEXICO CITY, May 18 (Reuters) - With Mexico's peso hovering at its strongest level since 1998, Mexico's Central Bank on Friday cut the amount it withholds daily from the money market, its first cut in three years. 

 The Banco de Mexico said in its daily report that it slashed the so-called "short" to 350 million pesos ($38.8 million) from 400 million pesos, the first reduction since current restrictive monetary policy was put in place in March 1998. 

 The Central Bank's daily intervention in the local money market is its main mechanism for defending the value of the peso currency against the dollar. The measure also holds local interest rates relatively high by keeping liquidity in the money markets lower than the market's estimated need. 

 Since 1998 the Central Bank had been gradually raising the so-called short, or intervention, tightening its monetary screws in a bid to combat inflation through relatively high interest rates aimed at keeping domestic consumption in check. 

 Mexico's interest rates have been ebbing in recent months, with the rate on the benchmark 28-day Cetes - or T-bill - government paper falling to a seven-year low at the government primary auction on Tuesday. 

 For 2001, Mexico has set an official inflation goal of no higher than 6.5 percent, compared with 8.96 percent inflation in 2000.

title: Mexico Peso Closes Stronger At 9.3520/Dollar On `Short'
text:
MEXICO CITY -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's peso closed stronger against the dollar Monday after the central bank tightened monetary policy. 

 Banamex quoted the peso closing at a midrate of MXN9.3520 to the dollar on 48-hour spot dollar markets, stronger from its open of MXN9.3650 and from its close of MXN9.3800 Friday. Spreads at the close were MXN9.3470/9.3570 compared with MXN9.3650/9.3750 Friday. 

 The Bank of Mexico raised its money-market "short" to MXN280 million from MXN230 million, signaling that it continues to worry about inflation. The bank said it found "various factors" that could impede its goal of lowering inflation to a rate similar to that of the U.S. and Canada by 2003. 

 The move came as no surprise, following central bank Governor Guillermo Ortiz's comments last week that additional monetary restrictions were likely. The short - which is the daily shortfall that the Bank of Mexico holds with commercial banks - was introduced as the bank's main monetary policy tool in March 1998. It has been raised 10 times since then, most recently on June 26. 

 "It's becoming less effective," Guillermo Estebanez, currency strategist at Bank of America in San Francisco. "The first time, it was taken seriously, but the 10th time...? This is a very marginal instrument in terms of monetary policy." 

 Expecations that the central bank would intervene in the money market heightened after the rate on Mexico's overnight Cetes, or Treasury bill, slid to 11.25% Friday.

title: Mexican peso rises, helped by Mexican, U.S. rates.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 28 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso rebounded on Wednesday to nearly erase the week's losses as the U.S. Federal Reserve met expectations, leaving interest rates alone. 

 The Fed decision, released 15 minutes before the close of peso trading in Mexico City, came on the back of Mexican central bank intervention to buoy the currency ahead of the July 2 presidential election. 

 "It's the combination of factors and a rebound from selling that's strengthened us here," said one trader. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso rose 11.3 centavos to 9.9600/9.9650 to the dollar, trimming some of its early gains but bouncing back after dropping a total of 13.3 centavos on Monday and Tuesday. The 24-hour contract gained 11.4 centavos to 9.9570/9.9620. 

 Traders said the Fed decision to leave interest rates unchanged and rising yields on Mexico's T-bills after a government auction on Tuesday were helping the local currency to recoup part of the ground lost against the dollar in recent sessions.

title: Mexican peso strengthens at close.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 28 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso rebounded on Wednesday to nearly erase the week's losses as the U.S. Federal Reserve met expectations, leaving interest rates alone. 

 The Fed decision, released 15 minutes before the close of peso trading in Mexico City, came on the back of Mexican central bank intervention to buoy the currency ahead of the July 2 presidential election. 

 It also came as yields on Mexico's T-bills rose, helping to boost the currency to recoup ground lost against the dollar in recent sessions, traders said. 

 "It's the combination of factors and a rebound from selling that's strengthened us here," said one trader. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso rose 11.3 centavos to 9.9600/9.9650, trimming some of its early gains, but bouncing back after dropping a total of 13.3 centavos on Monday and Tuesday. The 24-hour contract gained 11.4 centavos to 9.9570/9.9620. 

 The same-day peso contract, used mostly by foreign investors to jump quickly in and out of the market, strengthened 11.2 centavos to 9.9500/9.9550. 

 "The raising of the 'short' and rising rates (on Mexican T-bills) are in some way taking a little pressure off the currency," said Francisco Blanco, analyst at the Arka brokerage, referring to the Mexican central bank intervention on Monday. 

 "Here, also, I believe that the statements from the finance ministry, as well as from Banco de Mexico, in the sense that they could be open to more tightening in monetary restrictions if the markets continue to show volatility, is a factor that contributed to making the currency better." 

 The peso has fluctuated throughout the month amid uncertainty about the presidential elections, viewed as the most hotly contested in recent Mexican history. Trading volume has been light, leaving the market vulnerable to exaggerated moves, traders said. 

 With Wednesday's gains, the currency is now down roughly 4.5 percent so far this month. As of Tuesday, it had dropped more than 5.6 percent from the start of June. 

 Economists, market analysts and fund managers say Mexico's currency and economy should remain relatively stable whatever the outcome of the vote, which would represent a clear departure from recent history. 

 Since 1976, nearly every presidential succession has been accompanied by a peso crisis, the last being the 1994 devaluation at the start of President Ernesto Zedillo's term. 

 Before trading closed Wednesday, the U.S. central bank opted to leave interest rates unchanged, but signalled another increase could come in the future. The Fed has boosted rates six times since June 1999 in its campaign against inflation. 

 Higher U.S. rates are a bearish sign for emerging nations because companies find it harder to access credit abroad. 

 On Tuesday, primary rates on the Mexico's benchmark 28-day Cete, or T-bill, rose to 17.01 percent, its highest since Nov. 25, 1999, at a government auction. 

 ((-Kristin Roberts, Mexico City newsroom, +525 728 9549)).

title: Mexican peso falls after  central bank intervention .
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 26 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso tumbled in late trading on Monday despite an afternoon intervention by the country's central bank to buoy the sliding currency ahead of Sunday's presidential election. 

 The peso has weakened steadily since late last week, fluctuating on shaky volume ahead of the July 2 vote and the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting on interest rates. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso lost 10.5 centavos to 10.0300/10.0500 to the dollar while the 24-hour contract weakened 10.3 centavos to 10.0250/10.0450. 

 Just after midday in Mexico City, Banco de Mexico tightened its monetary policy, raising the amount of liquidity it withholds from the local money market each day to 230 million pesos from a prior 200 million pesos. The mechanism, known as leaving the money market "short," is aimed at raising local interest rates to bolster the peso. 

 Before the central bank's move, the 48-hour peso contract was 8.9 centavos weaker in trading against the dollar.

title: UPDATE 2-Mexican peso drops on election jitters.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 6 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso fell by 1.89 percent on Tuesday amid increasing uncertainty over the outcome of the July 2 presidential and congressional elections, traders said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso contract closed 18.5 centavos weaker at 9.67/9.68 to the dollar, down 1.89 percent against the Monday close, as market players took up positions in greenbacks ahead of the polls. 

 The market was less concerned about who wins the election than how the results of the hotly contested election is taken by the loser, analysts and traders said. 

 "The market has incentives to hold (long dollar positions), above all before the elections," one trader said. "The electoral problem is not who wins, but how the losing candidate reacts." 

 The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is facing its stiffest challenge in its 71-year hold on the Mexican presidency, with its candidate Francisco Labastida in a tight race with Vicente Fox of the conservative National Action Party (PAN). 

 Labastida, holding a slim lead over Fox in the latest opinion polls, said on Monday Mexico could face social unrest if the PRI wins the elections by a small margin. 

Mexico's central bank may intervene to prop up the sliding currency, said analyst Eligio San Juan at BBV-Probursa. 

 "The exchange rate can move other variables," said San Juan. "If it depreciates too much, the authorities will have to intervene and the central bank could increase the 'short'," he added. 

 The "short" is an instrument the central bank uses to regulate market liquidity. It has been tightened twice so far this year. 

 "The proximity of the election is complicating the peso market, owing to the possibility of a very close result," said Cesar Castro, director of analysis at the Centre of Analysis and Economic Forecasts for Mexico (CAPEM). 

 He said the election nerves would probably last until a month after the election. 

 The peso fall undermined Mexican stocks, with the leading IPC index dropping about 273 points, or 4.2 percent.

title: UPDATE 2-Mexican peso drops on election jitters.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 6 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso fell by 1.89 percent on Tuesday amid increasing uncertainty over the outcome of the July 2 presidential and congressional elections, traders said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso contract closed 18.5 centavos weaker at 9.67/9.68 to the dollar, down 1.89 percent against the Monday close, as market players took up positions in greenbacks ahead of the polls. 

 The market was less concerned about who wins the election than how the results of the hotly contested election is taken by the loser, analysts and traders said. 

 "The market has incentives to hold (long dollar positions), above all before the elections," one trader said. "The electoral problem is not who wins, but how the losing candidate reacts." 

 The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is facing its stiffest challenge in its 71-year hold on the Mexican presidency, with its candidate Francisco Labastida in a tight race with Vicente Fox of the conservative National Action Party (PAN). 

 Labastida, holding a slim lead over Fox in the latest opinion polls, said on Monday Mexico could face social unrest if the PRI wins the elections by a small margin. 

Mexico's central bank may intervene to prop up the sliding currency, said analyst Eligio San Juan at BBV-Probursa. 

 "The exchange rate can move other variables," said San Juan. "If it depreciates too much, the authorities will have to intervene and the central bank could increase the 'short'," he added. 

 The "short" is an instrument the central bank uses to regulate market liquidity. It has been tightened twice so far this year. 

 "The proximity of the election is complicating the peso market, owing to the possibility of a very close result," said Cesar Castro, director of analysis at the Centre of Analysis and Economic Forecasts for Mexico (CAPEM). 

 He said the election nerves would probably last until a month after the election. 

 The peso fall undermined Mexican stocks, with the leading IPC index dropping about 273 points, or 4.2 percent.

title: Mexico's Ortiz: April Inflation Likely Below 0.6%
text:
LONDON -(Dow Jones)- Mexico's inflation is expected to be below 0.6% in April and will allow the country to meet its 10% annual inflation target this year, Guillermo Ortiz, governor of the Mexican central bank, told Dow Jones Newswires Friday. 

 Ortiz said the central bank has an inflation target of 3% by 2003 but he couldn't reveal what the inflation targets for 2001 and 2002 would be. 

 "We are going to have a change in government and a lot will depend on who wins," Ortiz said. 

 Ortiz added that both presidential frontrunners, Vincente Fox of the National Action Party and Francisco Labastida of the Ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, endorsed the target of 3% by 2003. 

 Ortiz said the government's overall fiscal position had worked well alongside the central bank's monetary policy and was partly responsible for bringing annual inflation down from 50% in 1995. 

 Ortiz dismissed intervention in foreign exchange markets to weaken the peso. "Mexico's central bank hadn't intervened since 1998, during the worst moments of the Russian crisis," he said, adding that the bank would only intervene again in similarly dire circumstances.

title: Mexico's exports may rise 13 pct in 2000-Ortiz.
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 10 (Reuters) - Mexico's exports could rise 13 percent this year compared with 1999 to reach $155 billion as the robust economy remains on its current path, said Banco de Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz on Monday. 

 "If we think that in 1994 the total exports of the country were $60 billion, we've seen an expansion with few precedents worldwide," said Ortiz, at a meeting of Mexican and Japanese executives. 

 In 1999, Mexico's exports were $136.7 billion. 

 In the first two months of the year, Mexico's exports grew at a 33.1 percent clip compared with the same 1999 period, while imports surged 31.6 percent. 

 While Mexico's trade is soaring, the country is still heavily dependent on the United States for an export market. In 1999, the Latin American nation sent $109.75 billion in goods and services to its northern neighbour - more than 88 percent of its total exports for the year. 

 Mexico's preliminary trade deficit for January and February was $889 million, close to the gap it reported in the first two months of last year. 

 "Despite the strong appreciation in the exchange rate, during 1999 and also in 2000, the exports continue to react with great vigour," Ortiz said. 

 Ortiz on Monday also repeated his firm denial that Mexico is intervening in the country's exchange rate, repelling charges from presidential candidate Vicente Fox that economic authorities are manipulating the peso to keep it strong. 

 "The central bank does not manipulate the exchange rate," Ortiz told reporters after the executives' meeting. "It is the reduction in the country's credit risk that has fostered the peso's strengthening." 

 Mexico's credit rating was lifted to investment grade by Moody's last month, buoying markets and prompting the peso to climb to a 19-month high. The currency, which rose 2.6 percent during the first quarter, has since slid and closed around 9.32 to the dollar on Monday. 

 Fox, the candidate for the conservative National Action Party (PAN), said last week the current administration might be allowing the peso to strengthen to convince the population that the economy is faring well ahead of July's presidential elections. 

 Finance Minister Jose Angel Gurria also responded to the charges from Fox, saying he backed the free-floating system now in play. 

 "We really have no problem of manipulation or intervention by the government in the markets, and on the other side, the free-floating regimen is a strength of the Mexican economy," Gurria told reporters. 

 Fox is running second in the polls ahead of the July 2 vote, trailing closely the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party's candidate Francisco Labastida.

title: Mexico money market "short" won't change-Cenbank.
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 5 (Reuters) - Mexico's Central Bank said on Wednesday it has no plans to change the amount of cash by which it keeps the money market short each day, quelling speculation that it might intervene to weaken the peso. 

 "The Bank of Mexico is not contemplating measures related to the 'short,'" said Armando Baqueiro, head of economic studies at the central bank. 

 Mexico drains the money market by 180 million pesos ($19.2 million) daily to keep liquidity tight, part of an effort to fight inflation. It last changed the policy in January, when it raised the amount from 160 million pesos. 

 In recent days, markets have speculated that the Central Bank might step in to weaken the peso. 

 The currency hit a 19-month peak of around 9.2 to the dollar in late March on optimism over the strong economy and an upgrade of the nation's credit rating by firms Moody's and Standard & Poor's. 

 The 48-hour peso slipped in Wednesday's trading to 9.3950 to the dollar.

title: Brazil's Fraga sees similarities with Mexico.
text:
BRASILIA, March 4 (Reuters) - The new president of Brazil's Central Bank said on Thursday that Brazil's floating foreign exchange system and its plan to set inflation targets was similar to Mexico's strategy after the peso's devaluation in 1994. 

 "We are not adopting a regime identical to Mexico's, although some similarities exist given that Mexico also has inflation targets and a floating foreign exchange. The operational details will be different, but the general principle is not very different," Fraga told a news conference. 

 He was answering a question from a reporter about whether Brazil would adopt Mexico's system of automatic intervention in the foreign exchange market whenever the peso falls or rises by more than 2 percent against the dollar. 

 Fraga said earlier that the Brazilian Central Bank would intervene in foreign exchange markets when necessary and the interventions would "discrete and limited." 

 He also said Brazil would use overseas borrowing to help provide local foreign exchange markets with liquidity. 

 While private markets remain closed to Brazil as it scrambles to recover from a 40 percent-plus devaluation, a second instalment of loans from the International Monetary Fund, currently under discussion in Washington, would also be used partly to fund the country's balance of payments deficit, he said.

title: Mexico short-end T-bills pressured by Brazil fears.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 2 (Reuters) - Renewed jitters over Brazil's sinking real currency pushed short-end Mexican Cetes or T-bill rates slightly higher at Tuesday's weekly primary auction, analysts said. 

 Short-term rates also rose slightly because the market felt it was time to level off after five consecutive weeks of declines, economic analysts said. 

 "The resurgence of external pressures, like the greater depreciation of the real and its impact on the (Mexican) peso, caused the slight rise in the 27-day Cetes," said Martin Delgado, analyst at Value brokerage in Mexico City. 

 The bellwether 28-day Cetes - a 27-day paper at Tuesday's auction - rose seven basis points to 26.78 percent compared with the previous week. 

 Other maturities continued to decline on favourable longer term inflation prospects, with the 91-day Cetes sinking three basis points to 27.04 percent, the 161-day Cetes down 34 basis points to 26.52 percent and the 343-day paper five basis points lower at 26.96 percent. 

 Carlos Samano, director of analysis at Bancomer brokerage, said the "marginal increase in the short-term rate was because the time had come to find a floor after five auctions with consecutive declines." 

 "It's not an important rebound; it's just an adjustment," he added. 

 The Brazilian real, allowed to float in January after overwhelming pressure from markets, slipped to a new low of 2.17 per dollar on Tuesday, forcing the country's central bank to intervene. 

Mexico's peso was dragged down a notch too, with the benchmark 48-hour peso contract shedding 1 centavo to end at 9.945/9.95 per dollar after paring heavier earlier losses. 

 Analysts said primary Cetes rates on Tuesday were also affected by a sharp 38.8 percent fall in demand to 14.22 billion pesos, compared with demand the week before. 

 "Demand fell for all maturities because investors preferred to stay on the sidelines with the uncertainty over external factors," said Mireya Gomez, an analyst at Bursametrica Management.

title: Brazil monetary policy aims to control inflation.
text:
BRASILIA, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Brazil's current monetary policy is designed to keep inflation in check following a sharp devaluation of the domestic currency, the real, Central Bank President Francisco Lopes said Friday. 

 The Central Bank may set targets for inflation after the real lost more than 41 percent of its value against the dollar in barely two weeks, stoking fears of a return of hyper-inflation, Lopes told foreign correspondents in an interview. 

 The Central Bank planned to start publishing the level of its foreign currency reserves daily from Feb. 1 to quash the perception that continued high daily dollar outflows are sapping its foreign cash reserves, he said. 

 "We are going to start publishing them from Monday, given this situation, this absurd thing of people reading the (dollar) flow statistics in completely the wrong way," Lopes said. 

 "Clearly, any intervention on our part will be known on the following day. For us to give the market security, it is good to give it transparency," he added. 

 Brazil's foreign currency reserves remained around $36 billion, which includes about $9 billion from an international rescue package sponsored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), he said. 

 The country would have to adopt a logical model for interventions such as the one used in Mexico, where the Central Bank automatically intervenes if the peso fluctuates by more than a certain percentage level, said Lopes. 

 In a bid to increase the flow of dollars to local currency markets, drained by weeks of massive dollar outflows, the Central Bank may again raise the limit of dollars local banks are allowed to sell as it did earlier this week, he said. 

 Lopes also dismissed growing speculation that Brazil might default on its local currency debt due to the devaluation and high interest rates. The Central Bank Friday raised the benchmark market rate to 37 percent from 35.5 percent in what economists said was a bid to control the real's slide. 

 "To think that we will have rollover problems demonstrates you don't understand anything about Brazil," he said.

title: Fresh dollar auction unlikely - Banco de Mexico.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank said it would continue operating within the terms of its scheme of contingent dollar sales to support the peso and was not considering fresh intervention for Wednesday. 

 The central bank would have to alter the terms of its contingency scheme in order to carry out a fresh dollar sale, but a central bank source said that was not currently on the cards. 

 "I insist, today that is not the theme," he told Reuters. "I don't want to say it is ruled out or not ruled out,...but the bank is continuing to operate under the established scheme." 

 Banco de Mexico intervened on the foreign exchange market on Wednesday, auctioning $200 million at an average exchange rate of 10.6321 pesos per dollar. 

 That took place under the terms of an automatic mechanism set up to support Mexico's floating currency should it shed more than 2.0 percent of its value against the previous day's official fixing rate. 

 The scheme allows the central bank to sell a maximum of $200 million per day over three auction opportunities. 

 The central bank sold its full $200 million quota at 9:15 a.m. (1515 GMT), when the benchmark 48-hour peso was trading at 10.75 to the dollar.

title: FOCUS - Mexico peso crawls back from abyss.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso has crawled back from its mid-September abyss, taking advantage of recent calm in international financial markets to stand under 10 to the dollar on Thursday. 

 But analysts said they did not expect the currency to advance much further in coming weeks as concerns over Latin America's economic giant Brazil and the Mexican Congress's budget debate keep investors timid. 

 On Thursday the benchmark 48-hour peso contract closed below the 10-to-the-dollar level for the first time since September 2, ending the day at 9.96/9.97 per dollar. 

 The currency has recovered about 7.6 percent of its value since tumbling to a record low of 10.73 to the dollar on September 10, when investors fled Latin American markets amid fears Brazil would be the next emerging economy to succumb to an Asian-style meltdown. 

 Mexico's free-floating currency made the peso especially vulnerable to the fear and loathing that gripped Latin American markets in the late summer. 

 "I think now we're unwinding that part of the move that was not justifiable by (Mexico's) economic fundamentals," said James Barrineau, Latin America strategist at Salomon Smith Barney. 

 The peso on Thursday still stood down about 19 percent from its 1998 starting point of 8.065 to the dollar. 

 This year's declining oil revenues and increased inflation expectations meant the peso had reason to cede some ground to the dollar, analysts said. 

 But Mexican monetary officials took steps to limit what they saw as an unwarranted run on the money as Latin American financial markets appeared on the verge of unravelling. 

 As the peso hit all-time lows in early September, Banco de Mexico tightened its monetary screws a fifth time this year by raising the amount it leaves the local money market short each day to 100 million pesos. The prior daily short was 70 million pesos. 

 There was talk in Mexican markets on Thursday that the central bank may soon loosen monetary policy, a move that could lower local interest rates and take some pressure off the economy. 

 In the event Banco de Mexico did not alter the short when it intervened in the money market on Thursday, however it may still review its policy after weighing Thursday's release of first-half October inflation data, analysts said. 

 Banco de Mexico said the consumer price index rose 0.78 percent in the first two weeks of October, in line with analysts' forecasts. 

 But the forthcoming debate on the 1999 budget, which President Ernesto Zedillo's government has to present to Congress by November 15, will keep a lid on further gains in the peso. 

 Analysts said they expected a budget deal would be reached, but not after public wrangling that will make for nervous markets. 

 "We think there could be a little more volatility because of the debate over the budget, (bank-bailout fund) Fobaproa and the series of decisions that have to be made between now and the end of the year," said Alfredo Thorne, head of economic research at J.P. Morgan's Mexico operation. 

 But he said he expected the peso to end the year at 9.8 to the dollar. 

 Investor expectations that Brazil will adopt fiscal measures paving the way for securing multibillion dollar loans have been key to the peso's recent recovery. 

 But if Brazil were to disappoint markets or if the U.S. economy falters despite recent Federal Reserve interest-rate cuts, the peso will come under renewed fire, analysts said. 

 "I'm optimistic (about the peso's outlook) but there is still some room for disappointment," said Javier Maldonado, chief economist for Latin America at Bank of Montreal. 

 ((Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559 mexicocity.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Mexican  central bank  wages war on speculators.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The guardians of Mexico's battered peso have a fight to the finish on their hands as they seek to bolster the latest currency to become a victim of the world's emerging market woes. 

 Because Mexico has one of the most liquid currency markets of any emerging market country, the peso has become a soft target for speculators seeking to place proxy bets against other currencies - such as Brazil's real - which they believe are heading for a fall. 

 "It's the biggest most liquid emerging market currency market," said a New York banker who asked not to be named. 

 "If you want to bet on Brazil's currency weakening you simply short the (Mexican) peso," he added. 

 The peso closed at an all-time low for the third day running on Friday with the benchmark 48-hour peso shedding seven centavos to end at 10.58/10.62 against the dollar. 

 But for Mexico's monetary authorities there is more at stake than national self-respect. As the peso has plunged, the central bank has hiked interest rates, fuelling fears that the economy will be tipped into recession. 

 "The peso has become one of the thermometers of emerging market sentiment," said Juan Pablo Chavez at IDEA in New York. 

 Some funds have been using the peso as a hedging device against other emerging market instruments. 

 "You buy-high yield Thai bonds or Ukrainian treasury bills and then hedge it by shorting the peso," an economist with a large investment bank in New York. 

 The peso's role as a punching bag for nervous investors in emerging markets has driven down the currency's value to a point that it is widely seen as undervalued in relation to the real state of health of the Mexican economy. 

 "The peso has reached levels that have stopped reflecting economic fundamentals" said Chavez. 

 The Bank of Mexico, ever sensitive to the threat to inflation posed by a fallen peso, has tightened liquidity and hiked interest rates in recent weaks in an effort to brake the currency's fall but to no avail. 

 But now the central bank appears to be ready to take off the gloves and to mix it up with the currency speculators. 

Central Bank governor Guillermo Ortiz declared on Thursday he was prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market whenever he saw fit. The Bank of Mexico did as much earlier in the day with a discretionary sale of $278 million outside a pre-settled automatic intervention mechanism in which it sold an additional $200 million. 

 The prospect of random interventions by the central bank to support the peso appears to have put the hedgers on the defensive. "The Mexican forex market may cease to be an efficient hedge against emerging market risk, said Chavez. 

 One trader said on Friday: "right now nobody wants to buy excessive (dollar) positions because it could turn out to be very expensive if Banco de Mexico intervenes." 

 "This latest intervention has altered the rules of the game and ... this should increase the cost of this hedge," he said. 

 One of the most alarming aspects of the slide in the peso, which has lost 23 percent of its value against the dollar this year, has been its tendency to feed on itself as Mexican investors take fright and dump the currency. 

 Mexico's long history of currency instability has instilled strong survival instincts among Mexicans who tend to take to their heels as soon as they sense that the currency is coming under strong pressure. 

 "You also have an overreaction in Mexico because those people who did not switch into dollars in time in the past got burned," said Jonathan Heath, an independent economist based in Mexico City. 

 "You can't blame them, it's perfectly rational behaviour," he added.

title: WRAP: Mexico Signals More Active Role To Bolster Peso
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--As recently as three months ago, President Ernesto Zedillo said Mexico shouldn't spend "a nickel" of international reserves to fight speculation. That was before turmoil in global markets sent the peso into a tailspin. 

 The Bank of Mexico on Thursday intervened in the currency market for the first time since December 1995, apart from the $200 million auctions it holds when the peso weakens 2.0% against the dollar from the previous day's fix. The central bank said it sold $278 million, in addition to the $200 million auction. 

 Economists predicted the central bank would spend more reserves - and guide interest rates higher - if the market continued to deteriorate, marking another departure from its passive approach to the foreign exchange market since the government floated the peso in December 1994. 

 Bank of Mexico Governor Guillermo Ortiz and Finance Minister Jose Angel Gurria insisted they weren't defending a specific exchange rate and only sought to inject liquidity into an unusual, disorderly market. 

 "By not having to defend a determined exchange rate, we're not subject to a constant, unforseen bleeding of international reserves," Ortiz told a news conference. "What's fundamental is to give the market liquidity in these difficult circumstances and try to reduce volatility to the extent we can." 

 The peso has declined 16% against the dollar since the beginning of August and hit a sixth straight all-time closing low Thursday, ending at a mid-rate of 10.6000 to the dollar. The Mexican currency fluctuated wildly between 10.3200 and 10.7300 during the session.

title: Banco de Mexico says sold $278 mln to support peso.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank said the "discretional intervention" it undertook earlier on Thursday to support the peso totalled $278 million pesos. 

 "The foreign exchange market suffered unusual pressure today derived from a deterioriation in the international financial situation," Banco de Mexico said in a statement. 

 "Given this situation the (central bank's) Exchange Commission, made up of members if the Finance Ministry and the Banco de Mexico, instructed the central bank to directly sell $278 million in the market in order to give it liquidity and reduce its volatility," it said. 

 The intervention, in the form of a dollar sale, came in addition to an automatic $100 million auction that was triggered earlier in the session when the peso lost 2.0 percent of its value against the greenback. 

 The central bank undertook the intervention as the Mexican currency shed 40 centavos to a record low of 10.73 pesos per dollar after the automatic auction took place. 

 The extra dollar sale pushed the peso back up to 10.35 per dollar, leaving it two centavos weaker than Wednesday's close. 

 It ended Thursday at 10.55 pesos to the dollar. 

 During the morning the central bank auctioned $100 million at an average price of 10.577 pesos per dollar. 

 A second dollar auction, scheduled for 11 a.m. local (1600 GMT), did not take place because the peso had not fallen another two percent after the earlier auction. 

 Separately, the central bank moved to tighten monetary policy a fifth time this year, increasing the amount by which it keeps the money market short each day to 100 million pesos from 70 million pesos 

 In a separate statement Banco de Mexico said this was designed to contain currency volatility. 

 "The Governing board repeats its conviction that the referred to volatility is out of line with the basic conditions of the Mexican economy," it said. 

 "In order to counteract this volatility and bring order to the country's financial markets, to preserve sustained economic development and inflation objectives congruent with this objective, the governing board of Banco de Mexico has decided to restrict monetary policy further. 

 "Banco de Mexico is aware of the impact the increase in the cost of credit has on various key parts of the economy, but it feels that this is a necessary stabilising factor given current circumstances," it said. 

 Turbulence emanating from Russia and Asia has hit all emerging markets including Mexico, which has been trying to minimise the impact on its economy as its floating peso bears the brunt of the storms.

 By Rosario Torres Limon 

MEXICO CITY, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank on Thursday sold a heap of dollars and moved for the fifth time this year to tighten monetary policy, but analysts said the measures were unlikely to save the currency from global turmoil. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso hit an intraday low of 10.73 per dollar, but dollar sales by Banco de Mexico of a total $478 million in two automatically triggered auctions and one "discretionary" sale helped lift the peso to a close of 10.52/10.55 per greenback. 

 Banco de Mexico also announced it was increasing the amount it leaves the money markets short by every day to 100 million pesos from 70 million pesos previously. 

 Traders said a meltdown in Brazilian shares, which closed 15.82 percent down amid heavy dollar outflows over devaluation fears, and jitters over the fate of "Sexgate"-plagued U.S. President Bill Clinton, hammered market confidence. 

 "Banco de Mexico is trying to contain the pressures, but the truth is they are so big and of such an international nature that they are beyond the bank's influence," said the director of analysis at Bancomer brokerage, Carlos Samano. 

 With Thursday's plunge, the free-floating Mexican peso has depreciated by 23.5 percent against the dollar this year. 

 Despite the central bank moves, analysts said they saw further downside for the peso as investors continued to desert Brazil, Russia staggered on in indecision and the U.S. Congress pondered a possible impeachment of Clinton for allegedly trying to cover up a sexual relationship with a White House intern. 

 "The short-term perspective remains pessimistic due to volatility, uncertainty over Brazil, Russia and the Clinton situation," said Hector Velez, analyst at Cargill de Mexico. 

 "The great risk we face is that Brazil won't hold out. The outflows of capital from Brazil in recent days have been high," Velez added. 

 Traders said Brazil lost more than $2.0 billion on Thursday. Earlier in the day, the country's central bank said its foreign reserves had slipped around $12 billion so far in September to about $55 billion. 

 "I find it hard to believe the peso will recover until markets stabilise," said Sergio Garcia, director of analysis at the Value brokerage.

text:

Meanwhile, the rate on overnight Cetes soared 650 basis points on the secondary money market	   to 40 percent and Mexican stocks were off more than five percent, flirting with the psychological 3,000-point barrier on the IPC index	 .

 Banco de Mexico said it offered $200 million at auction between 9 a.m. and 9:15 a.m. (1400 and 1415 GMT) but received only $100 million in bids. The remaining $100 million would be offered from 11 a.m. to 11:15 a.m. (1600 to 1615 GMT), it said.

title: Mexico peso closes at record low on Brazil,Clinton.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso		    closed at a historic low versus the dollar on Thursday after a tumultuous day in which the central bank took three separate steps to shore up the ailing currency.



The benchmark 48-hour peso ended 22 centavos weaker at 10.52/10.55 per dollar after financial haemorrhaging in Brazil soured investors on the rest of Latin America and U.S. President Bill Clinton's political woes spread to Wall Street stocks, dealers said.


 The 48-hour peso has lost 23.55 percent of its value versus the dollar this year. It had been even lower at one point in the morning, setting a new intraday low when it had shed 40 centavos to 10.73 per dollar. 

 The 24-hour peso fell even further at the close, losing 33 centavos to end at 10.55/10.65 per dollar. 

 The central bank twice offered dollar sales in order to prevent the slide and then tightened monetary policy in a bid to increase interest rates and thus protect the peso. 

 "Brazil is exerting a lot of pressing on the Mexican currency because of a possible devaluation and the falling share prices there," one forex dealer said. 


Brazil's Bovespa index	   was off 12.5 percent in late trade amid a massive capital outflow from the country.



"Clinton's problems are hitting the peso hard," another trader said as pressure mounted in Washington to begin impeachment hearings because of the Monica Lewinsky scandal.



When the peso lost two percent of its value versus the dollar in early trade, that triggered an automatic central bank auction of dollars, and $100 million was injected into the banking system.



Banco de Mexico later exercised a "discretional intervention" by adding an undisclosed amount of dollars to the system.



Then it announced it was tightening monetary policy for the fifth time this year by reducing liquidity in the secondary money market.



The central bank now will leave the market "short" each day by 100 million pesos instead of the previous 70 million.

title: Bank Of Mexico/Dollar -2: Up To 3 Auctions A Day
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Mexico has altered the mechanism for intervening in the foreign exchange market in support of the peso, although it maintains the daily limit of $200 million, the central bank said. 

 In a press release late Wednesday, the bank said that instead of a single auction of $200 million when the spot peso-dollar rate moves 2.0% above the previous day's fix, the bank will hold up to three auctions in a given session. 

 The $200 million auctions were instituted in February 1997. Under the original plan, the bank held the auction between 1 p.m. and 1:15 p.m. local time (1800-1815 GMT), selling dollars at a minimum of 2.0% above the previous day's fix, which is set by the bank the previous day based on a sample of spot rates. 

 The central bank said the Exchange Commission decided to allow up to three auctions a day, from 9 to 9:15 a.m., from 11 to 11:15 a.m. and 1 to 1:15 p.m. The amount of dollars to be auctioned will remain at $200 million, with subsequent auctions offering only dollars unsold at the earlier auctions. 

 If auctions are held on successive days, the minimum sale rate is 2.0% above the previous day's minimum auction price. 

 The Bank of Mexico placed $200 million at an auction Wednesday, as the peso continued to feel pressure from Russia's financial crisis and the plunging ruble. The peso closed Wednesday at 9.7550 per dollar on 48-hour spot markets.
