title: US attache's weekly "Hot Bites from Mexico" report.
text:
WASHINGTON, June 17 (Reuters) - The following is a weekly "Hot Bites from 

 Mexico" report by the agricultural attache at the U.S. embassy in Mexico City. 

     The report, dated May 28, was released Wednesday by the U.S. Agriculture 

 Department. 

     Attache reports are not official USDA data. 

 Welcome to Hot Bites from Mexico, a weekly review of issues of 

 interest to the U.S. agricultural community. The topics covered 

 in this report reflect developments in Mexico that have been 

 garnered during travel around the country, reported in the media, 

 or offered by host country officials and agricultural analysts. 

 Readers should understand that press articles are included in 

 this report to provide insights into the Mexican "mood" facing 

 U.S. agricultural exporters. Significant issues will be expanded 

 upon in subsequent reports from this office. 

 DRY WEATHER CONTINUES 

 - 

 Mexico's annual rainfall level through April 1998 was 52.3 

 percent less than last year and 41 percent less than the annual 

 average. According to the press, Mexico experienced the driest 

 April and May on record. The GOM says the lack of normal 

 precipitation is expected to reduce overall agricultural 

 production, but has stopped short of declaring a disaster. The 

 lack of normal rainfall is said to have reduced reservoir levels 

 throughout the country, especially in the northwest where they 

 are at a reported 19.3 percent of capacity compared to the 

 average for this time of year of 29.3 percent. Reservoirs in the 

 state of Sinaloa are reportedly among the lowest at only 2.9 

 percent of capacity. Although most of Mexico is experiencing 

 drier than normal conditions, two states - Baja California Sur 

 (in the north) and Quintana Roo (in the south) - have 

 experienced above normal rainfall. (Sources El Economista 

 5/26/98, l Financiero 5/27/1998) 

 FAS/MEXICO COMMENT: The current El Nino-driven dryness continues 

 to plague Mexico. Although 1998/99 grain production is forecast 

 to be 5 percent above last season, rainfall is needed within the 

 next few weeks to permit planting the grain crops. The outlook 

 for the coarse grain crop remains dependent upon rainfall 

 arriving in late May to early June. Meanwhile, poor pasture 

 conditions and water shortages in the north have caused 

 "distress" sales of cattle. 

 DUMPING CLAIMS BY MEXICO'S BEEF AND PORK INDUSTRIES 

 - 

 Mexico's beef and pork industries are said to be increasingly 

 close to filing separate antidumping petitions against U.S. 

 growers, processors and exporters. Speaking for Mexico's beef 

 industry, leaders of the National Cattlemen's confederation (CNG) 

 recently said that, while they don't necessarily blame U.S. 

 cattlemen, imports of U.S. beef have soared in 1997 and 1998 

 relative to 1996 levels, when a similar antidumping claim was 

 settled with a bilateral agreement between the two countries' 

 cattle groups. They also blame the Mexican government for 

 allowing in "low quality" beef and "old, sick cattle" which has 

 reduced live weight prices to about 8.50 pesos/kg (US$0.45/lb) 

 for Mexican cattle. 

 Meanwhile, Mexico's pork industry is now said to be close to 

 filing its own petition against U.S. pork.  The president of the 

 Mexican Pork Council (CMP) is quoted as saying "We aren't 

 bothered by the volumes imported as long as they are not priced 

 below the cost of production, known as dumping".  The CMP alleges 

 that since October 1997, falling U.S. pork prices have caused 

 Mexican pork prices to drop from 12 pesos to 9.50 pesos per kilo 

 (currently US$1.41 to 1.12).  The CMP's antidumping petition has 

 reportedly already been prepared, asking for a halt to Mexico's 

 favourable in-quota TRQ duties under NAFTA.  At the same time, 

 however, both the cattlemen and hog growers admit that their 

 biggest problem is that they are uncompetitive due to much higher 

 feed and credit costs.  (Sources: Reforma, 5/25/98; El 

 Financiero, 5/26/98) 

 MEXICAN COFFEE PRODUCTION AT RISK FOR LACK OF WATER 

 ---------------------------------------------------- 

 According to the Mexican Confederation of Coffee Producers (CMPC) 

 certain coffee production areas in the states of Chiapas, Oaxaca 

 and Puebla are at risk of losing coffee trees due to the severe 

 dryness and lack of normal rainfall.  CMPC estimates that if 

 rains are delayed beyond the next two weeks, production could be 

 reduced by 500,000 60-kg bags for 1998/99.  The seriousness of 

 this situation is not the immediate reduction in production, but 

 the long term effects this phenomenon will have on small coffee 

 producers who make a marginal living from coffee.  New coffee 

 plants take from 3 to 4 years before they produce, and many small 

 producers are concerned because they have no other means for 

 their livelihood but coffee production.  (Source:  Reforma 

 5/27/98) 

 FAS/MEXICO COMMENT:  Although extreme dryness, fires and lack of 

 rainfall will undoutably affect coffee production in some areas, 

 it is still too early to quantify.  Therefore, we will maintain 

 the current production estimate of 5.55 million 60-kg bags for MY 

 1998/99.  Furthermore, some sources indicate that coffee 

 producers and exporters are somewhat between "a rock and a hard 

 place".  Producers and exporters are likely to "cry wolf" that 

 production will be limited in order to obtain better prices on 

 the international market and, on the other hand, producers have 

 to convince the Mexican authorities and coffee processors that 

 there is sufficient supply to cover domestic demand, thus 

 avoiding imports of coffee beans like last year.  For further 

 coffee information, refer to our annual coffee report MX8043 

 dated 5/15/98. 

 ATO EXPHOTEL PRESS CONFERENCE 

 ----------------------------- 

 On Thursday, May 28, the Director of the Agricultural Trade 

 Office (ATO) hosted a meeting with key members of the Cancun 

 press to present details on the first ATO-sponsored U.S. Pavilion 

 at the second annual EXPHOTEL trade show in Cancun on June 10-12. 

 The focus of EXPHOTEL is on top quality food, products and 

 equipment used by the hotel, restaurant, industrial cafeteria and 

 hospitality (HRI) industries. The U.S. Pavilion includes 25 U.S. 

 private companies and trade organisations which will feature an 

 impressive selection of value-added U.S. food and agricultural 

 products, including U.S. poultry, meats and speciality products, 

 peanuts, fresh and processed fruits and vegetables, juices, dairy 

 products and grocery products. At EXPHOTEL 97, 109 Mexican and 

 international companies exhibited their products to over 3,000 

 decision makers in the food service industry. Based on the 

 success of last year's show, EXPHOTEL 98 will feature twice as 

 many exhibitors. For more details on the U.S. Pavilion, contact 

 Lourdes Guzman at the ATO at TEL: 011-525-202-0168; FAX: 

 011-525-202-0528. (Source: ATO/Mexico) 

 ATO BULLISH ON MEXICAN MARKET 

 - 

 The Agricultural Trade Office (ATO) in Mexico City is preparing 

 to launch an aggressive campaign through outreach efforts to 

 various U.S. companies and trade organisations and local 

 Mexican-American business interests about new export 

 opportunities in Mexico for U.S. food and agricultural products. 

 The ATO is bullish on the Mexican market for a number reasons, 

 including Mexico's increased focus on exports, better bank 

 regulation, improved management of the exchange rate, a growing 

 population of young consumers, and an expanding tourism and 

 restaurant sector, among others. 

 In particular, Mexico's tourism industry is booming-various 

 marketing reports and research studies show that the number of 

 five, four, and three star hotels has increased, on average, 24, 

 13, and 10 percent, respectively, every year from 1992 to 1996. 

 During this same period, the number of foreign visitors to Mexico 

 grew three percent. On average, these tourists stayed in Mexico 

 for 10 days, during which time they spent a lot of money: in 

 1997 alone, foreign visitors spent over US$7.6 billion in Mexico. 

 ATO/Mexico sees the growth in this sector as a prime opportunity 

 for increased exports of U.S. food and agricultural products, and 

 is actively participating in trade events, like EXPHOTEL 98, to 

 maximize the exposure of the U.S. food sector in Mexico. (Source: 

 ATO/Mexico). 

 QUOTA FOR CHILEAN APPLES FILLED 

 ------------------------------- 

 The Secretariat of Commerce (SECOFI) announced on May 22, 1998 

 that the tariff-rate quota for Chilean apples was filled for 

 1998. Under the Free Trade Agreement between Mexico and Chile, 

 imported apples from Chile to Mexico are charged a 13.3 percent 

 duty for the 1998 in-quota quantity of 2,156.7 metric tons. 

 With the quota now filled, the duty snaps back to the normal 

 tariff rate of 20 percent. According to official Mexican trade 

 data, imports of Chilean apples totalled about 2,422 MT in 1994, 

 zero in 1995, 137 MT in 1996 and 43.7 MT in 1997. This year, 

 however, Chilean apples had a better opportunity in the Mexican 

 market due to the absence of most U.S. apples until the 

 suspension agreement reached earlier this month which ended the 

 101 percent duty under Mexico's antidumping action against U.S. 

 red and golden delicious apples. See our reports MX8046 and 

 MX8007 for further information. (Source: Diario Oficial 5/22/98) 

 FAS/MEXICO COMMENT: Since the suspension agreement, the duty for 

 1998 on imported U.S. apples are now 10 percent for the in-quota 

 safeguard volume of 61,901.97 MT and 20 percent for any imports 

 above that level. 

CENTRAL BANK STABILISES PESO 

 - 

 On Wednesday, Mexico's Central Bank reportedly intervened in the 

 market with US$10 million to help stabilise the peso, which 

 closed that day at US$1.00 = 8.86 pesos. The relatively sharp 

 decline was attributed to nervous international investors pulling 

 out of emerging markets like Mexico. Mexico's free-floating 

currency is said to often be subject to speculation by investors 

 who like Latin America. (Source: The News, 5/28/98) 

 MORE ON HFCS 

 - 

 Local newspapers reported that the National Chamber for the Sugar 

 and Alcohol Industries (CNIAA) claims that imported high fructose 

 corn syrup (HFCS) from the United States continues and that such 

 imports indicate a persisting dumping issue. In fact, reminds 

 the press, what Mexico wants is to gain greater access for sugar 

 exports to the U.S. above the current annual quota of 25,000 MT. 

 Mexico has already a sugar surplus of about 1.0 MMT and sugar 

 production of approximately 5.1 MMT for MY 1997/98, which is 

 slightly higher than previous CNIAA forecast due to good weather 

 conditions. Such claims are in the midst of the announcement of 

 the initiation of an unfair trade investigation by the U.S. 

 Department of Commerce on the Mexican HFCS anti-dumping 

 decisions. (Sources: El Nacional 5/20/98, El Financiero, 

 5/26/98) 

 TABLE EGG QUOTA AUCTION FOR 1998 

 - 

 SECOFI has announced in the Diario Oficial an auction for quota 

 certificates to import 1,004 MT (1.5 million dozen) of fresh U.S. 

 table eggs during 1998. These imports are part of the 

 tariff-rate quota (TRQ) for all shell eggs established under 

 NAFTA. The total TRQ for all shell eggs in 1998 is 7,315.80 MT 

 (20.8 million dozen), including fertilised eggs. The auction 

 will take place on June 1, 1998 and will be conducted by SECOFI. 

 See our recent report MX8051 for additional information. 

 (Sources: USAPEEC/Mexico; Diario Oficial 4/29/98). 

 NUEVO LEON TO IMPROVE BORDER INFRASTRUCTURE 

 ------------------------------------------- 

 The Mexican border state of Nuevo Leon announced this week that 

 it will invest US$200 million to improve and expand the 

 infrastructure of its only inland border crossing point at 

 Colombia. The Colombia-Solidaridad bridge is one of three 

 bridges servicing Laredo, TX, the most important U.S. border 

 crossing point with Mexico. The Nuevo Leon government is 

 planning to build a highway between Monterrey and the bridge, a 

 cargo airport and a railroad bridge. This ambitious project will 

 begin with the 240-kilometre highway. A request for bids to 

 construct the highway will go out in June. Currently 2,500 

 trucks cross at Colombia, northbound and southbound combined, but 

 U.S. Customs reports the bridge could easily handle twice that 

 much traffic. The bridge, since its opening in 1993, has been 

 badly underutilized, in part, because of a lack of infrastructure 

 on the Mexican side of the border. (Source: OAA/NL from El 

 Maqana, 5/26/98) 

 TEX-MEX RAILROAD INVESTS IN A NEW FACILITY 

 - 

 The Texas Mexican (Tex-Mex) Railway Co. has announced it will 

 invest US$19.5 million to increase its rail yard capacity in 

 Laredo, TX. The project will give Tex-Mex the largest rail yard 

 facility on the U.S.-Mexico border. Tex-Mex has already broken 

 ground and begun construction at the 408-acre site east of 

 Laredo. The project will help to meet the expected growth in 

 rail traffic over the next three years, as well as help alleviate 

 congestion problems within the city of Laredo. The new facility 

 will include office space and areas for U.S. Customs, INS and 

 USDA to conduct inspections. Tex-Mex is currently crossing over 

 9,000 railcars per month on average, up from around 2,000 

 railcars per month in 1994. (Source: OAA/NL from Laredo Morning 

 Times, 5/22/98) 

 TAMAULIPAS ORANGES AFFECTED BY DRY WEATHER 

 - 

 According to the President of the Tamaulipas Citrus Producer's 

 Association (TCPA), the state's orange crop is feeling the 

 effects of the high temperatures throughout the state. The TCPA 

 estimated 1998 production at approximately 150,000 MT prior to 

 the dry spring. TCPA's President also said, local producers 

 cannot harvest their oranges now because there is no market, but 

 if they wait, they run the risk of losing a large portion of the 

 harvest to the dry weather. He also indicated that, like other 

 local producers, i.e. cattlemen, orange producers are waiting for 

 a government emergency support programme. If granted, it would be 

 used for marketing activities and improving irrigation systems. 

 (Source: OAA/NL from El Diario de Nuevo Laredo, 5/26/98). 

 SUPERMARKET'S LARGE STAKE SOLD 

 ------------------------------ 

 Grupo Gigante, Mexico's third largest retailer, said recently it 

 received US$ 192.4 million in cash for the sale of its fifty 

 percent stake in a joint venture with France's Carrefour. When 

 Gigante announced in February that it would sell its stake in 

 "Grandes Superficies de Mexico" to Carrefour, analysts predicted 

 that the Mexican company would receive US$120-140 million. Since 

 joining in the venture with Carrefour in 1993, Gigante had 

 reportedly invested about US$142 million in "Grandes 

 Superficies", which owns 13 supermarkets. (Source: The News, 

 5/24/98) 

 NEW FOOD STORE OPENS 

 - 

 H.E. Butt Grocery, seeing the Mexican market as a fast-growing 

 alternative to a saturated U.S. market, opened its second food 

 store on May 24 in the northern industrial city of Monterrey and 

 is said to be planning to open two more this year. The San 

 Antonio, Texas-based company known as H.E.B. wants to carve out a 

 niche in an increasingly competitive northern Mexico retail 

 industry by focusing on food and giving customers a taste of 

 U.S.-style shopping. The U.S. supermarket business is said to be 

 saturated. "It's a mature industry", said Charles Butt, chairman 

 and chief executive of the closely held company. "We see this as 

 an opportunity, particularly with the name recognition we have in 

 northern Mexico". (Source: The News, 5/24/98) 

 MEXICAN BREAD IN SOUTH AMERICA 

 - 

 According to local news reports, last Monday Mexico-based Bimbo, 

 Inc. has started bread production in its new 25 million-dollar 

 bakery in Peru. Bimbo, said to be the third largest bread 

 producer in the world, with more than 80 production plants 

 serving 550 million people throughout the Americas, has formed a 

 strategic alliance with the food company, Alicorp, to produce in 

 Peru. The Bimbo group reported overall sales of US$2.3 billion 

 in 1997. (Source: The News 5/26/98).

title: Mexico business group opposes more peso tightening.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 16 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank should not tighten monetary policy further despite the recent slide by the peso on the back of Asia's financial woes, a top employers' group said on Tuesday. 

 "We think that the currency should float, and in that sense, if it has weakened a bit now, once this international situation is over, we expect it to recover some," Gerardo Aranda, president of Mexican employers' federation Coparmex. 

 "We prefer a floating (exchange rate) rather than a strong intervention," Aranda told reporters. 

 Banco de Mexico adopted a restrictive monetary policy in March, leaving the money market short by 20 million pesos a day. The policy has not returned to neutral since. 

 Some analysts have said that the central bank should tighten further given the recent weakness in the peso. 

 Through Tuesday Mexican currency has lost 10 percent on the year versus the dollar this year. The benchmark 48-hour peso ended Tuesday 3.0 centavos firmer at 8.9920/9.000 per dollar. ((Veronica Galan, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9553, mexicocity.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Mexican peso pares losses, but still weaker.
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 27 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso lifted off its early lows Wednesday on the prospects of central bank intervention but was still sharply weaker at mid-morning due to contagion in emerging markets from Asia's ongoing crisis. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso was down 9.15 centavos to 8.876/8.8815 per dollar after hitting early lows of 8.89/8.905 per dollar. 

 "It moderated its losses after stock markets in the United States, Brazil and here recovered slightly," one dealer said. "But the outlook is not very good." 

 Dealers added that the likelihood of central bank intervention helped the currency bounce off lows. 

 Banco de Mexico usually sells $200 million when markets are thin and the peso falls more than 2 percent in a single 24-hour period. 

 "If the spot (48-hour) rate is weaker than 8.8823 per dollar at midday, Banco will sell $200 million," one dealer said. Tuesday's midday value for the peso was set by the central bank at 8.708 pesos. 

 ((Miguel Angel Karim, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9555 mexicocity.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Mexican overnight Cetes close lower on firm peso.
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 17 (Reuters) - Mexican overnight Cetes rates closed 40 basis points lower at 19.30 percent on Friday, driven down by foreign investors who were attracted by the strength of the peso, dealers and analysts said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso closed 0.9 centavos stronger at 8.4830/8.4850 to the dollar, riding a buying spree on the stock exchange to ward off speculation about a change in monetary policy and other factors that could weaken the currency. 

 "There was a little more action from foreigners, which was directly reflected in the appreciation of the peso and the bolsa and some of those resources were directed toward the money market," one analyst said. 

 Rates, which move in the opposite direction to price, also came down when the central bank injected 356 million pesos of liquidity during its daily intervention. 

 ((Fatima Escobar, Mexico City newsroom, +525 728-7916, mexicocity.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: FOCUS - Mexico trade deficit invokes crisis deja vu.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Mexico's surprisingly high December trade deficit of $722 million, announced late Monday, evokes unsettling memories in Mexico: rampant imports, a strong currency, a growing current account deficit. 

 Dare anyone bring up the specter of December 1994? 

 Not yet, according to economists. The country is far from the dangerous balance of payments troubles that led to Mexico's worst economic disaster since the Great Depression when a swelling trade deficit contributed to the end-1994 peso crash. 

 However, the alarming trade deficit for December, which was half a billion dollars higher than what was forecast in a Reuters survey of 10 financial institutions, renewed concern among economists and traders about potential fallout from a widening trade gap. 

 The December figure was the highest monthly trade deficit since $1.69 billion in December 1994 and it almost wiped out the trade surplus for the year, which ended at a thin $582 million -- sharply down from $6.145 billion dollars for 1996. 

 The government was quick to blame plummeting world prices for oil, which accounts for 11 percent of Mexico's exports. 

 Still, Mexican officials and investors will keep close watch on the peso, seeing whether it weakens enough to boost exports and keep rising imports at bay, economists said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso lost 3.4 centavos to 8.213/8.218 per dollar on Tuesday, while Mexican stocks fell 1.7 percent on the IPC index. 

 "Mexico is very aware of what it was that led to the crisis," said Felipe Garcia of IDEA in New York. "I think it's too early to say Mexico is in trouble with its current accounts. But the trend is what worries the market." 

 Economists already are revising their 1998 trade balance figures because of oil prices, and most are predicting a trade deficit in the range of $5 billion for 1998. 

 That compares with some $18.5 billion for 1994. 

 Surging imports and fallout from Asia's recent competitive devaluations were also to blame, analysts said. 

 Optimists shrugged off Mexico's import growth, saying it is a sign of a vibrant recovery with inflation under control. 

 Moreover, Garcia noted that most of the import growth was for capital and intermediate goods, which are bought largely by exporters gearing up for more production. 

 The biggest difference between now and December 1994 is that the peso now trades freely. The December 1994 crisis blew wide open when the government removed controls on the currency, prompting its near free-fall before it later stabilized. 

 But if oil prices remain depressed -- and there are mixed opinions on this point -- while consumer demand for imports stays strong, the peso again will draw serious scrutiny. 

 The issue could be the first test for former finance minister Guillermo Ortiz, now chief of the central bank. Mexico-watchers already are wondering whether Banco de Mexico might intervene should the peso remain strong. 

 "That's the $29 billion question for Mr. Ortiz," said Gray Newman, chief economist for Latin America at HSBC James Capel, in a sly reference to the default-prone Tesobonos, a now-defunct dollar debt instrument in vogue at the time of the devaluation. 

 Newman said he's inclined to think the government won't need to intervene as long as there is some healthy weakening of peso. His year-end projection is 8.8 to the dollar. 

 "We're a long way from 1994 levels," Newman said, noting that the current account deficit then was about seven percent of GDP compared to a rough 2.5 percent projection for year-end 1998. He also predicts the monthly trade deficits will come down as the year progresses. 

 Others are not so sure. 

 "The peso weakening late last year was not sufficient to halt imports," noted Ignacio Catalan, a well-known economic commentator. 

 "If we project the trends for imports and exports, the trade deficit could reach $7.5 billion this year and it could get serious," Catalan said. "That would be much higher than government projections." 

 ((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9507)) 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1998

title: Ortiz unlikely to change exchange policy - analysts.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz, newly appointed as head of the Mexican central bank, is unlikely to make in any radical changes in monetary policy, particularly to the exchange rate, economists said Monday. 

 President Ernesto Zedillo named Ortiz to become the new governor at Banco de Mexico on January 1, replacing retiring longtime central bank chief Miguel Mancera, who oversaw a policy of a freely floating peso. 

 In his announcement late Sunday, Zedillo said he would propose that the central bank gain more say in setting exchange rate policy. 

 The finance minister now casts the deciding vote on the Exchange Commission, the joint central bank finance ministery body that sets exchange rate policy. It was not clear if this structure would change. 

 Some financial analysts speculated that Ortiz might move his country away from the free float the currency went to in late 1994. 

 Since the peso crash of December 1994, the currency has freely floated, with the Banco de Mexico occasionally intervened up until late 1996 to curb wild swings in the currency. 

 The economic think tank I.D.E.A. said in a market commentary that concern over Ortiz may increase in times of market crisis. 

 "The concern stems from the potential contradiction between the need for the central bank to maintain its perception of independence and Ortiz's recent history as a proponent of a weaker peso and higher growth," I.D.E.A said. 

 Many major Mexican exporters have complained that the peso is overvalued, eroding their foreign sales. However, the central bank has been loath to weaken the peso versus the dollar, fearing that it could fuel inflation. 

 Even so, all economic analysts consulted by Reuters were confident the the current foreign exchange rate policy is likely to remain in place. 

 Most economists played down the possibility of Mexico moving to a fixed rate system, perhaps based on the Chilean real trade weighted exchange rate band. 

 "Some people have said that Ortiz would want a system of bands for the exchange rate. Maybe he had that idea three or four yers ago, but I don't think he will keep to that idea given what has happened to that type of exchange rate regimes, particularly in Asia," said ING Barings economist Sergio Martin. 

 "If he had that idea, he has abandoned it. Besides we (Mexico) don't have enough reserves for it," Martin added. 

 "If this move was meant to make Banco de Mexico more independent, which I think it is, then a exchange rate band or any type of fixed exchange rate would subvert that. The minute the Banco de Mexico intervenes in the exchange rate they lose power, so I would suspect they will keep the current policy," Paribas economist John Welch said. 

 "Some of the talk that we are hearing is that Ortiz might be more inclined to intervene to weaken the peso. In fact our view, and I think the central bank's view, is that the peso doesn't need to be weakened," said Lawrence Krohn, head of Latin American economic and equity research for UBS Securities. 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: Mexico  central bank  lies low amid market turmoil.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Mexico's central bank has taken a low profile during the turmoil that has whipped Mexican financial markets recently, economists said Thursday. 

 In the past Banco de Mexico has sanctioned interest rate increases and other measures to buffet the Mexican currency from internal or external shocks. By contrast, the central bank has kept to a neutral stance during the current turbulence, they said. 

 "I think that what the Banco de Mexico has seen is that interest rates are going in the direction they have to, so that there is no reason why they should intervene," independent Mexico City economist Jonathan Heath told Reuters. 

 "It is letting the market find its own level on interest rates and the exchange rate, and they are trying to keep to their neutral policy stance," he said. 

 In September, the central bank went so far as to announce it might leave money markets in a long position, aiming to lower interest rates and rein in some of the strength of the currency. 

 As things turned out, the bank was able to sit back and watch market forces do the job for it. The peso, which defied forecasts that it would weaken on various occasions this year, was felled by global market turmoil that began in Asia. 

 On Oct. 21, the 48-hour spot peso opened at 7.71 per U.S. dollar, a year-high. A week later, the market had pushed it to nine pesos to the dollar, its weakest ever. The free-floating currency has since gained some strength to about 8.40 per dollar on the 48-hour contract. 

 Rates on government treasury bills, or Cetes, have also bounced around in the last month, with a rise of more than 300 basis points on one-month paper at one recent primary auction. A week later, the bellwether rate dropped almost 200 basis points. 

 During previous bouts of market volatility, particularly in 1996, the central bank intervened to leave money markets short of liquidity, a signal it wanted higher interest rates to support the currency. 

 J.P. Morgan economist Alfredo Thorne reads the central bank inactivity in the markets as a signal it is aiming to curb increases in real interest rates by allowing the exchange rate to take the brunt of external shocks. 

 "The Finance Ministry as well as Banco de Mexico want to give the message that from now on they want to absorb external shocks via a greater depreciation of the real exchange rate and a smaller increase in real interest rates," he said in a call to investors late on Wednesday. 

 The recent market volatility was the first time this year the peso has come under sustained attack, and the decision of the central bank to leave the amount of its daily liquidity objective unchanged was fundamental to its message, he said. 

 In March this year when the U.S. Federal Reserve lifted its key interest rate by 25 basis points, the real rate on three-month Mexican Cetes rose to 12 percent by the end of March from four percent at the end of February. 

 "In October what happened was just the opposite," Thorne said. "The government is giving a clear signal, and that is that external shocks are to be absorbed by a greater volatility in the exchange rate." 

 Banco de Mexico Director of Research Agustin Carstens said during a conference in Miami this week that the government was "comfortable" with the peso's current level. 

 He declined to give a preferred level for the peso but said: "When we felt there were inflationary pressures, we would tighten monetary conditions." 

 ((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559. e-mail mexicocity.newsroom@reuters.com)) 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: Mexico  unlikely to  intervene  to help peso-official.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Mexico will not intervene in the foreign exchange market to help the bruised peso unless market volatility darkens future economic prospects, Finance Ministry chief spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela said on Monday. 

 "We are committed to a free-floating exchange rate. Wherever the market sets the level, it sets the level," Valenzuela told Reuters in an interview. 

 But he said the central bank would step in if volatility continued unchecked and began showing up in other key variables of the economy, such as long-term interest rates and inflation. 

 "Right now, that has not been the case. But if volatility prevails in a sense which does not correspond to reality, yes, we will intervene openly, transparently, showing clearly that what the market is showing in the short-term does not coincide with fundamentals," he said. 

 Mexico's peso, after months of strength, suffered its worst fall since the 1994 peso devaluation on Monday and sank to record lows amid worldwide markets turmoil. Mexico's stock market fell nearly 14 percent before trading was halted. 

 The country has some $25.4 billion in foreign reserves but has been wary of fighting losing battles against well-heeled currency speculators. 

 Valenzuela defended the country's economic fundamentals and said he was not overly concerned about the latest bout of market instability, which plagued Mexico following the 1994-95 peso crisis. 

 "We believe the market fundamentals are okay. In Mexico, we are confident, in contrast to other years like 1994, that the economy is on very solid ground ... it's doing well. 

 "We suppose that once when this volatility fades away, people will look again at the Mexican market and come back, because in essence the valuation and the economy are very solid. This economy is a good buy," he said. 

 Valenzuela said the market jitters will likely lead to higher short-term interest rates and could have a "small" impact on inflation in a few months time. 

 "The most important thing on the inflation front is to continue to have a sound fiscal and monetary policy," he said. 

 He said Mexico was unlikely to tap markets for debt in the coming weeks, but added that the country had met its funding needs for this year. 

 "We are in a very solid position right now. We have no humps of short-term liabilities that we have to deal with right now," he said. 

 ((--David Luhnow, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9565)) 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: Mexico peso ends firm as brokers enter money mkt.
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 17 (Reuter) - The Mexican peso extended early firmness at the close of trade on Thursday due to local and foreign brokers switching from dollars to invest in the domestic money market, traders said. 

 "It is better for brokers to sell their dollars to have pesos to invest at very high rates in the money market," a trader said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso and its 24-hour stablemate ended 1.05 and two centavos firmer, respectively, at 7.8750/7.8775 and 7.8625/7.8650 per dollar. 

 "As interest rates are so attractive, it is better to go short on dollars, and as that means the peso firms up, you win both ways," the trader said. 

 Dealers said reduced pressure from the U.S. bond market had also shored up the peso.  The U.S. 30-year Treasury bond was down 10/32 to yield 7.07 when the foreign exchange market was closing in Mexico.  "Dealers are seeing that the time is ripe for switching to pesos.  The outlook is still for U.S. rates to go up, but not in the short term," another trader said, referring to the May 20 Federal Open Market Commitee meeting to review U.S. interest rates. 

 Same-day peso contracts had earlier closed two centavos firmer at 7.8660/7.8700 per dollar. 

 Dealers estimated the peso could remain at current levels until domestic interest rates begin to decline. 

 "Some banks are very short on dollars and will stay that way until Banco de Mexico lowers interest rates," a trader said.  "But we need to look out for how the central bank intervenes in the secondary money market." 

 (( --Alexis Quiones, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9555)) 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: FEATURE - Latin  currency  regimes face U.S. rate rise.
text:
NEW YORK, March 13 (Reuter) - After two years of warm glow nurtured by generous foreign capital, the currencies of four major Latin American countries may face a stress test if rising U.S. interest rates reverse the capital influx. 

 Economists and currency analysts anticipate no serious disruptions in the short term, but they say the Mexican peso could trade in a wider range and the Venezuelan bolivar could head into rougher waters, if U.S. credit becomes tighter. 

 Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and Venezuela, the four countries that together account for two-thirds of the Latin economy, are each pursuing a different currency regime with varying degress of rigidity and ties to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Argentine peso is pegged at parity with the U.S. dollar. Brazil's real moves in a band that is fixed periodically. Mexico follows a managed floating regime, and Venezuela sets a reference rate with targeted depreciation. 

 All four regimes have worked well in controlling inflation and boosting investors' confidence, which has prompted many market watchers to hail it as the dawn of a new era for Latin America. 

 But some analysts argue that the disadvantages of the regimes were not showing up because the weak balance of payments is supported by the flow of investment funds. 

 "In the rampant euphoria of 1996 and early 1997, any exchange rate policy you can devise will probably lead to a relatively stable, strong currency," said Ernest Brown, Latin America economist at Morgan Stanley. 

 The question arises how a currency can climb down without wreaking havoc on the economy, he said. 

 MEXICAN PESO 

 The Mexican peso, whose devaluation sent shock waves through emerging markets in December 1994, came under instant fire when U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan testified in Congress this month. His warning about soaring equity prices was seen as preparing financial markets for a monetary tightening. But in the second leg of his address, Greenspan tempered his hawkish tone. 

 The peso fell from 7.74 per dollar before the first part of the testimony to a low of 8.10 in the subsequent days. But the decline sparked no panic, traders said. 

 "The peso was slightly overvalued based on the inflation differential between Mexico and the U.S.," said Peter Allen, director of emerging markets research at BancBoston Securities, who saw the peso's weakening as on target. 

 The Bank of Mexico, which announced last month that it would sell $200 million of reserves if the peso falls by more than 2.0 percent in one day, did not intervene. 

 Robert Hodrick, Nomura Professor of International Finance at Columbia University's Graduate School of Business, said that while central bank intervention may smooth short-term volatility, it does not change the currency's value. 

 "It is the monetary growth in conjuction with the demand for pesos and what's happening to the monetary policy in the U.S. that determines the peso value of the dollar," he said. 

 Jaime Valdivia, vice president of emerging market fixed income research at Morgan Stanley, said he was "encouraged" that Bank of Mexico did not intervene. "It showed that the central bank was not concerned enough to implement the brake." 

 Mexico's economy grew a surprisingly strong 5.1 percent in 1996 and the improving credit fundamentals provide the underpinning of the country's currency, he said. 

 But the peso should slide to nine per dollar by year end, assuming an annual inflation rate in Mexico at 18.1 percent, according to his forecast. 

 BOLIVAR MORE PRECARIOUS 

 Compared to Mexico, Venezuela's bolivar is in a more precarious state, Valdivia said. 

 If the trend of deteriorating fiscal balance, loose monetary policy and stubbornly high inflation continues, the bolivar could see more turbulence ahead, he said. 

 Walter Molano, director of emerging market research at SBC/Warburg, said the bolivar is at least 20 percent overvalued, but the Venezuelan government has to maintain a strong currency to reduce inflation. 

 With a weak fiscal base and a shaky banking sector, the government has few alternatives to manage inflation, he said. "They have to rely on the exchange rate." 

 David Malpass, an economist at Bear, Stearns and Co, said Venezuela was following its neighbours' lead by keeping the currency stable against the dollar. 

 "It is a positive and dramatic departure from the past when the government printed money and had control over the exchange rate," he said. 

 But he refrained from predicting whether the government had the political will to pull it through. 

 "It is too early to tell," he said. 

 ARGENTINE, BRAZILIAN CURRENCIES LIKELY TO KEEP VALUE 

 The currencies of Argentina and Brazil are likely to keep their value in the face of rising U.S. interest rates, experts said. 

 The value of the Argentine peso hinges entirely on the credibility of the currency board, which Argentine leaders, regardless of their political stripes, are firmly committed to, they said. 

 Because of the currency, Argentine short rates will rise with U.S. rates, said Morgan Stanley's Brown. "The currency is safe, but asset values will be hit hardest." 

 In Brazil, tight monetary policy implies a strong and stable currency, experts say. 

 But the country's huge current account deficit makes the economy highly vulnerable to foreign capital flow, said Molano, who estimates that half of Brazil's $32 billion current account deficit is financed by foreign direct investment and the rest by portfolio investment. 

 Brazil has to raise interest rates more to match a rise in U.S. rates, if U.S. monetary policy changes, he said. 

 Molano does not expect a knock-on effect to Latin currencies if one buckles under the strain because trade integration in the region is low -- about 15 to 20 percent. 

 "Whatever correlation they have with each is due to their link with the U.S. dollar," he said.

title: Mexico peso ends stronger on certification hopes.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 28 (Reuter) - The Mexican peso clawed back some lost ground at the close on Friday. 

 Traders said the peso recovered as banks that had gone long on dollars stepped in to sell them ahead of expected recertification by the U.S. government of Mexico as an ally in the the war on drugs. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso and its 24-hour stablemate ended 3.4 and 2.5 centavos firmer, respectively, at 7.9400/7.9460 and 7.9350/7.9450 per dollar. 

 "The peso recovered as the market has already discounted Mexico's certification," a trader said. 

 News that U.S. Secretary of State Albright recommended recertification for Mexico came just five minutes after the close of trade in Mexico's foreign exchange markets. 

 Traders noted Banco de Mexico did not intervene in the market as speculation had eased considerably since Thursday. 

 The central bank was expected to accept bids from banks to buy dollars if the peso reached a rate of 7.9925 per dollar by 1200 local time/1800 GMT, or two percent weaker than the official fixing rate published in Friday's edition of the Mexican Government Official Gazette. 

 This rate was surpassed in early trade, but the peso began to firm up mid-morning so the criteria for central bank intervention never crystallized. 

 Traders said they expected more banks to sell more long dollar positions on Monday after certification was confirmed. 

 "Yesterday's (peso) onslaught was out of order. Dealers overbought dollars and they dumped part of their positions today," another dealer said. "So now we have certification, they will certainly offload the rest on Monday." 

 Same-day peso contracts had earlier closed 14 centavos weaker at 7.9550/7.9650 per dollar, after lagging the market.

title: FOCUS-Mexico peso takes long-awaited tumble.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 27 (Reuter) - Mexico's peso suffered its largest fall in more than a year on Thursday due to an explosive mix of low Mexican interest rates, rising long-term U.S. rates and political jitters. 

 The peso lost 17.6 centavos, or 2.1 percent, to 7.98 per dollar in key 48-hour contracts. It was the peso's weakest level since late October, 1996. 

 "Panic gripped the market. Dealers began talking about the peso hitting eight per dollar," one trader said. 

 Nervous foreign banks and a few locals began selling the peso in early trade due to rising U.S. long bond yields and worries about Mexico's recent drug scandals and their effect on Washington's certification of Mexico's cooperation in the war on drugs. 

 Speculators swooped in soon after, seizing the opportunity to sell pesos in the most skittish foreign exchange market in months. Once the peso hit certain levels, programmed sell orders by banks worsened the losses. 

 "Speculation snowballed once foreign banks began to dump pesos on programmed stop losses," another local dealer said. 

Mexico's central bank did not intervene in the market despite having outlined a plan in recent weeks to sell dollars on days when the peso fell by more than two percent. 

 A Banco de Mexico spokeswoman said the bank did not intervene because the peso had not fallen by more than two percent before 1215 p.m. local/1815 GMT -- the time limit for the central bank to sell dollars. 

 Most economists had been expecting the peso to fall for some months after it had slowly gained strength during the past 15 months on foreign flows into Mexican securities. 

 As foreigners hunted for bargains in the country's stocks and bonds following the 1995 crisis, they sparked a virtous cycle that strengthened the peso and boosted dollar returns, prompting Economists said a correction was only a matter of time, but said the peso should resist a uncontrolled fall. 

 "The correction is here," said I.D.E.A. in a market commentary. Local banks may unwind some of their remaining short positions on the dollar and extend the correction slightly, I.D.E.A. added. 

 Trouble began on Wednesday, when comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan forced U.S. long-term interest rates higher at a time when Mexican interest rates had fallen to their lowest levels since before the 1994 peso devaluation. 

 Political worries have also mounted in recent weeks following back-to-back drug corruption scandals, including the arrest of Mexico's anti-drug czar on allegations he was linked to a powerful drug lord. 

 Although Washington could decertify Mexico's anti-drug efforts, a move that means sanctions, most observers believe the United States will waive decertification on national security grounds. Mexico is the U.S.'s third-largest trade partner.

title: Mexico peso battered by Greenspan, certification.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 27 (Reuter) - The Mexican peso plunged in late trade to end sharply weaker on Thursday after a speculative onslaught in a skittish market, traders said. 

 Traders said gains in U.S. long bond yields following Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony on Wednesday coupled with the certification process of Mexico's cooperation in the war on drugs were the main causes of market anxiety. 

 "Looking at it in the cold light of day, what happened was that speculation snowballed once foreign banks began to dump pesos on stop losses," a dealer said. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso and the 24-hour contract closed 17.6 and 17 centavos weaker, respectively at 7.9600/7.9800 and 7.9500/7.9700 per dollar. 

 Same-day peso contracts had earlier closed 4.9 centavos weaker at 7.8220/7.8250 per dollar. 

 Banco de Mexico did not intervene in the markets despite the fact an announcement on February 19 that it would inject up to $200 million if the peso slid by more than two percent. 

 A spokeswoman for the central bank said it only sold dollar put options to local banks until 1215 local time/1315 EST/1815 GMT, or 75 minutes before the foreign exchange market closes. 

 "Since the peso was not more than two percent weaker at that time, Banco de Mexico did not intervene," said the spokeswoman, who wished to remain anonymous. 

 In a February 19 release, Banco de Mexico said that if the peso fell more than two percent, it would auction $200 million among banks at a minimum price two percent above the exchange rate of the previous working day. 

 The spokeswoman was unable to say whether the central bank would sell dollars at the start of trade on Friday. 

 An analyst said the confusion among traders probably arose as they were considering trading levels as a reference rate, rather then the central bank's official fixing rate. 

 The fixing rate to be published in Friday's edition of the Mexican Government Official gazette will be 7.8358 pesos per dollar. 

 This means, the analyst said, that the peso would have to reach a trading rate of 7.9925 per dollar before 1215 local time for the central bank to begin to accept bids from banks to purchase dollars. 

 Traders said nervousness escalated in late trade. 

 "Panic gripped the market, dealers began to speak of pesos changing hands at eight per dollar," one trader said. 

 "Speculators had a field day with Greenspan's testimony, higher U.S. long bond yields and the certification process," he added. 

 Yields on U.S. 30-year Tresury bonds gained to 6.81 percent in late trade, compared to 6.67 percent before Greenspan spoke on Wednesday. 

 Among other things, Greenspan said he could not rule out increased U.S. interest rates in order to curb inflationary pressures.

title: Banco de  Mexico  says no  intervention  in peso mkt.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Feb 27 (Reuter) - Mexico's central bank said Thursday it did not intervene in the country's foreign exchange market to support the peso, which was badly hit during the day by economic and political concerns. 

 A Banco de Mexico spokeswoman said the central bank only sells dollar put options to local banks until 1215 p.m. local/1815 GMT, slightly more than an hour before the market closes. 

 "Since the peso was not more than 2 percent weaker at that time, the Banco de Mexico did not intervene," said the spokeswoman, who wished to remain anonymous. 

 The peso ended down 17.6 centavos in key 48-hour contracts at 7.96/7.98 per dollar -- more than two percent lower on the day. 

 Banco de Mexico recently unveiled a plan to build reserves and dampen exchange rate volatility, promising to intervene in the forex market with up to $200 million if the peso falls more than two percent in a given day. 

 "In case the (dollar) exchange rate rises on a given day by more than two percent from the exchange rate of the previous working day, $200 million will be auctioned among banks with a minimum price two percent above (the exchange rate) on the prior working day," Banco de Mexico said at the time in a statement. 

 The spokeswoman was unable to say if the central bank would sell dollars at the start of trade on Friday.

title: Bank Of Mexico/Auctions-3:Could Thwart Speculative Attacks
text:
If the dollar-buying mechanism doesn't prompt the peso to depreciate gradually in line with inflation, many analysts say sharper adjustment pressures could resurface by April. And that's when the central bank's program to sell dollars to stem big exchange rate swings could become a useful tool - especially if the swings take place amid thin, speculative trading as they did during late 1995. 

 'It could cut down on speculative attacks,' said Hector Chavez, economist with Santander Investment in Mexico City. 'In 1995 and even in 1996 there was a game with the central bank to see when and where they would intervene. This is different, because they're not signalling an exchange rate target.' 

 At least one observer, though, questions why the Bank of Mexico would not opt for the more traditional tool of intervening directly in the foreign exchange market. 

 'Oftentimes limited intervention could be more effective,' said Lawrence Goodman, economist with Salomon Brothers in New York. 'It could dampen those pressures without disclosure of dollar sales.' 

 But others argue that Mexico's newly independent central bank really has no choice, because it's still busy trying to build a solid track record in the wake of the December 1994 peso devaluation and ensuing turmoil. 

 'Group of Seven countries don't have credibility problems, but the Bank of Mexico has to be as transparent as possible,' said Jonathan Heath, a Mexico City-based economist. He added that the undisclosed intervention practices of other central banks 'would be a disaster' for Mexico at this time.

title: Mexico Cetes rate ends up for third straight day.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Jan 10 (Reuter) - Mexican overnight Cetes rates closed up 60 basis points at 24.80 percent, their third consecutive gain, after zigzagging through a session fraught by speculation in the wake of volatile international markets, traders said. 

 "Although the system was supposed to be liquid, some are still witholding their cash, and the fact that the central bank is draining liquidity helps them," a trader said. 

 Banco de Mexico drained 1.602 billion pesos of liquidity by offering to purchase paper through three auctions on the secondary market. 

 Overnight rates on bank paper meanwhile closed up 65 basis points at 25.75 percent. 

 Dealers noted that volatility in yields on U.S. long bonds triggered jitters and instability in the foreign exchange market which thus affected the money market. 

 Other traders said secondary rates were gaining on a technical adjustment. 

 "Some big banks sold paper at the beginning of the week, when secondary rates fell substantially, and now they're climbing back up," another dealer said. 

 No credit maturities were expected for Monday, however, 602 million pesos was expected to return to the system following Friday's central bank intervention.

title: FOCUS - Mexico's Mancera defends peso policy.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Nov 14 (Reuter) - Banco de Mexico Governor Miguel Mancera on Thursday defended his policy of maintaining a free-floating peso, arguing that a permanently undervalued exchange rate may do as much harm as good. 

 At the end of a year of relative exchange-rate stability, in which he was criticised by some sectors when the peso's margin of undervaluation against the dollar shrank, the central bank chief stressed his prime duty was controlling inflation. 

 For instance, when the peso began a slide in October, Banco de Mexico left the money markets short of 20 million pesos to push up interest rates to stop the currency from fueling inflation. 

 "The Bank of Mexico made this decision because large and abrupt increases in the exchange rate bring about inflationary consequences that, in the end, make it more difficult to bring rates down," Mancera said. 

 In October, the peso slid from around 7.5 pesos per dollar to eight pesos. On Thursday, the benchmark 48-hour or spot contract closed at 7.9050/7.9080 per dollar. 

 Giving his reasons for the steep October peso drop, Mancera said uncertainty ahead of the signing of an economic recovery pact, problems with petrochemical and rail privatizations, and accumulated inflation differentials between the United States and Mexico played their parts. 

 But wheras some sectors, such as exporters, had argued that a steep peso drop was long overdue, Mancera indicated that he did not favor maintaining a permanently undervalued exchange rate to foster economic growth. 

 "Even though there are some groups that apparently benefit from a permanently undervalued exchange rate, there are also those who would suffer from such a situation," he said. 

 "It should be recalled that an ever undervalued exchange rate perpetuates the depression of real wages and the existence of high inflation and interest rates. This effects consumption, investment and, consequently, economic performance as a whole." 

 "The idea that a permanently undervalued exchange rate fosters economic growth, or that it is beneficial to all, is not persuasive," he said. 

 On the other hand, he said Banco de Mexico had not intervened this year to stop gradual depreciations brought on by market forces. 

 "It must also be emphasized that the current monetary and exchange-rate policies are in no way designed to forestall the depreciation of the domestic currency, should the fundamental conditions of the economy so warrant," he said. 

 Referring to the performance of the economy, he reiterated that it was expected to achieve at least four percent growth this year and next, noting that as well as export growth, "in 1996 it is already possible to recognize the positive contributions of consumption and investment." 

 Export momentum continued strong, he said, and year-end inflation was expected to be around half last year's level of 52 percent.

title: Mexico peso fights back but still ends off.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 (Reuter) - The Mexican peso recovered some ground lost to return to below its support at 7.80 per dollar by the close on Wednesday, but was still reeling from an early speculative onslaught, traders said. 

 "There were dealers who had surplus dollar positions and began to sell them when they saw the peso was recovering," a trader said, explaining the fight-back from early session lows. 

 The benchmark 48-hour peso and the 24-hour contract closed 5.6 and 5.9 centavos weaker, respectively, at 7.7800/7.7850 and 7.7750/7.7950 per dollar. 

 The same-day peso had earlier closed 6.5 centavos weaker at 7.7850/7.8000 per dollar.Traders said that foreign buyers stepping into the Mexican stock market also prompted local dealers to sell dollars. 

 The 48-hour peso earlier reached its weakest level this year, at 7.8250/7.8450 per dollar, as panic and speculation seized the market in early trade. 

 Traders said expectations that Tuesday night's substantial primary interest rate hikes might shore up the peso were dashed when traders realized that those holding dollars were not very willing to part with them in an uncertain situation. 

 The market was already nervous as the peso had weakened considerably in recent sessions and foreign investors had shunned the Mexican markets following a watering down in the government's petrochemical privatization plans. 

 Other traders pointed to comments made by U.S. economist and MIT professor Rudiger Dornbusch to the local press criticising the cental bank's policies. 

 "Banco de Mexico is bad news for the peso, not people who predict there will be difficulties," Dornbusch was quoted as saying on the front page of the Reforma newspaper, which many traders read. 

 In a Reuters interview, Dornbusch said he had not accused the Banco de Mexico of intervening directly in the currency markets, but of using monetary policy as a brake on peso depreciation. 

 "I have not said that (Banco de Mexico has intervened in the currency market directly). I said that if you allow me to control the (monetary) aggregates, I control the interest rates, which controls the peso," he said. 

 On Monday, Banco de Mexico had announced it would allow the secondary money market to close on Tuesday with a liquidity shortfall of 20 million pesos, as opposed to balancing liquidity flows exactly, as it had done since August 16. 

 Many traders saw this move as designed to push up interest rates and shore up the peso, which had already begun to totter. 

 Dornbusch said this move was valid as a temporary move, but should not aim to help the peso recoup lost ground. 

 "That is alright for a brief moment, just to stabilize expectations and to say we are not looking for big drop... But if they want to bring the peso back, that is lunacy," he said. 

 Traders said they did not spot any central bank intervention in the market on Wednesday, although several said they expected the Banco de Mexico to step in selling dollars if the peso nudged up to levels around 7.85 per dollar.

title: Mexican peso could hit 8 per dollar soon - analysts.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 (Reuter) - Battered over the past week, Mexico's peso will likely fall further against the dollar in the next few weeks before recovering slightly towards the year end, economists said on Wednesday. 

 Although it had been one of the world's strongest currencies this year against the dollar, the peso has suddenly fallen victim to growing worries about its value and domestic seasonal factors such as inflation. 

 In the past week, the peso has fallen from about 7.52 per dollar to 7.80 per dollar -- a slide that has worried traders who still remember the turbulent months that followed its spectacular December 1994 crash. 

 On Wednesday, the peso was down 8 centavos at midday to 7.79/7.805 per dollar in its widely-watched 48-hour contracts. 

 Some Mexican economists were sanguine about the peso on Wednesday, saying they had expected the currency to begin adjusting toward year-end expectations of about 8.00 per dollar. 

 A survey of Mexican economists by Reuters MXAAP forecasts a year-end peso at 7.86 per dollar -- only slightly below current levels. Analysts had originally forecast a lower level for the peso, but many adjusted their predictions in recent weeks, thinking the peso might stay strong. 

 "This is a temporary thing...we had a similar situation during this time last year, but our fundamentals are much better right now," said a top economist at a top Mexican bank. 

 The economist expects the peso to test 8.00 per dollar in the coming weeks as investors buy dollars to protect themselves against any surprises in the government's economic plan for 1997, which is due to be unveiled before November 15. 

 The government plan will include public sector price rises for next year that could affect inflation expectations. 

 "We are in a turbulent area. Until the new government plan is announced, we cannot discount new shocks," said Enrique Quintana, a columnist for Mexico City daily Reforma. 

 Threat of interest rate or currency intervention by the Banco de Mexico will likely prevent an all-out speculative attack, however. Last year, the Banco de Mexico ended a run on the peso in November by selling dollars. 

 Economists said the peso's current weakness can be explained also by fundamentals. Interest rates in Mexico had fallen most of this year and were their lowest in both real and nominal terms since before the devaluation. 

 Declining trade surpluses during August and September, meanwhile, added weight to comments by U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch that the peso was in danger of becoming overvalued. 

 "This is a natural cycle for the peso under the current system...interest rates fall until some exogenous factor causes the peso to fall and rates to back up," said Ernesto O'Farrill, director of Mexico City consultant Bursametrica. 

 The government's move to scale back its privatization of the petrochemicals industry also had a psychological effect on investors -- giving some an excuse to sell pesos. 

 O'Farrill said the peso's ups and downs will likely continue until the Banco de Mexico can build enough reserves to credibly defend the currency. Net central bank assets remain below $4 billion, according to latest official figures. 

 "The central bank should have been more aggressive in building reserves this year. That would avoid these types of shocks," he said. 

 O'Farrill sees a year-end peso at 8.10 per dollar. He expects interest rates to rise again in the coming weeks as the central bank tries to defend the peso.

title: Dornbusch says "essential" for Mexico peso to slip.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 (Reuter) - Economist Rudiger Dornbusch said on Wednesday it was "essential" for the Mexican peso to decline over time in tandem with the country's inflation rate. 

 In an interview with Reuters, the MIT professor said he is comfortable with the current level of the peso, which has declined sharply in recent days and weakened again today after strengthening for much of this year. 

 But he warned that the currency needs to continue to weaken in line with Mexico's high inflation rate. 

 "The peso over time has to accompany the rate of inflation. That is what is important. The current level is OK -- not glorious, but not perilous. But that the peso should decline over time, that is essential," Dornbusch said. 

 Dornbusch, who correctly predicted the 1994 peso crash, unleashed a storm of controversy here recently by warning the Banco de Mexico was allowing the peso to become overvalued -- as it was before the devaluation. 

 He said he has not accused the central bank of intervening directly in the foreign exchange market to shore up the peso, but does blame the Banco de Mexico for encouraging peso strength this year by keeping high real interest rates in Mexico. 

 "I have not said that (Banco de Mexico has intervened in the currency market directly). I said that if you allow me to control the (monetary) aggregates, I control the interest rates which control the peso," he said. 

 Mexico's peso has fallen from about 7.60 to 7.80 per dollar in the past few sessions due in part to increasing worry about whether or not it was getting too strong. 

 In midday trade on Wednesday, key 48-hour contracts were off 8 centavos at 7.79/7.805 per dollar. 

 Dornbusch said he did not think his recent comments on the peso sparked the recent sell-off, saying that investors were concerned about high inflation in Mexico and recent news that the government decided to scale back its sell-off of the country's secondary petrochemicals industry. 

 "...people are uncertain about what the Pemex news really is -- is it good, or is it as one suspects, less good. I think those uncertainties have a lot more to do with it than my comments," he said before attending an Institute for International Research conference in Mexico City. 

 Dornbusch said the Banco de Mexico's recent tightening of liquidity in the secondary money market was aimed at calming jitters on the foreign exchange market. 

 But he said it should only be a temporary move and should not be aimed at helping the peso recover lost ground. 

 "That is alright for a very brief moment, just to stabilize expectations and to say we are not looking for a big drop ... But if they want to bring (the peso) back, that is lunacy," he said. 

 -- Robert Kozak, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9559

title: No risk of Mexico devaluation - business leader.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 2 (Reuter) - The head of Mexico's top business group Hector Larios Santillan ruled out Wednesday any risk of a new devaluation in Mexico. 

 "No, absolutely not", he told reporters. "Here what we need to be watching is solely and exclusively that our currency has the balance and the competitivity which is needed so that (other countries') products don't end up being cheaper abroad than what we are exporting." 

 Larios, president of the Business Coordinating Council, was speaking after Massachusetts Institute of Technology economics guru Rudiger Dornbusch caused a stir here by saying that Mexico did not have a truly free-floating peso because Banco de Mexico was intervening to stop it from moving. 

 Larios said business leaders were sure that the central bank was not intervening.  "I repeat, what we need to is to ensure that our currency is competitive. The president himself has committed himself to not letting our currency overvalue and this is very important," he said. 

 Larios said he believed predictions that the peso would be around eight to the dollar by the year end, a level which he said would "cover perfectly the undervaluation which is needed for the currency to be competitive."

title: Mexico's peso -- heading into trouble?.
text:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 2 (Reuter) - Is Mexico's peso heading for a fall? 

 U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch thinks so. He stirred up a hornet's nest of reaction when he said this week that Mexico was heading for a repeat of its disastrous 1994 devaluation by letting the peso become overvalued. 

 "There was a problem last time and they didn't listen and there is going to be another problem this time if in the next months they don't start moving towards a real exchange rate policy," Reforma newspaper quoted him as saying at a seminar in the resort of Cancun. 

 The comments, from a man who correctly predicted the 1994 peso crash, come at a delicate time. 

 The peso has barely moved in nominal terms in a year. The most-watched 48-hour contract was trading Wednesday at 7.52 to the dollar, against 7.49 a year ago. 

 Because of Mexico's high inflation -- about 30 percent over the past 12 months -- this has meant a substantial appreciation in real terms. 

 Voices in the key export sector, in brokerages and in politics are starting to be heard urging central bank Banco de Mexico to nudge the peso down to avoid a loss of competitiveness and a swing back into the red on the trade balance. 

 Export growth has slowed sharply as the peso appreciates. In August, total exports grew 10.1 percent over the same month in 1995 -- their lowest growth since July 1993, according to Interacciones brokerage. 

 The head of the Finance Committee in Mexico's Congress, Francisco Suarez Davila, told Reuters a "yellow warning light is flashing" over the peso because of its gain in value. 

 Yet many analysts here say the peso is not overvalued at its current levels. They are more concerned about what would happen if the currency continues appreciating at its present pace and then trips over. 

 Using a base year of 1990, independent economist Jonathan Heath said his calculations showed the peso to be 3.3 percent undervalued at the end of August, compared to a trough of 28.2 percent undervalued in March of last year and a peak of 34 percent overvalued in February 1994. 

 "The peso is probably now about where it should be," he said. "But the exchange rate is not the problem. The real problem is the structural problem of the balance of payments which means that even with a huge devaluation like we had in 1994/5, imports only fell back slightly." 

 Heath says that unless Mexico tackles its chronic dependence on imports to feed its large "screwdriver" exports of assembled goods, balance of payments problems are likely to reemerge -- regardless of the exchange rate. 

 The government is standing firmly behind its free market line, insisting that debate about a "correct" level for the peso is futile in a free-floating exchange regime. 

 One senior government source, speaking on condition he not be identified, told Reuters Dornbusch's assertion the central bank was intervening to keep the peso high was "a lie". 

 "If Banco de Mexico were intervening to maintain a certain exchange rate, you could argue about whether the peso was over- or undervalued," he said. "But in an absolutely free market, the peso's level is dictated by supply and demand." 

 But some economists say that although the bank may not have intervened by selling dollars on a large scale, it has influenced the peso's strength by keeping interest rates higher than they might otherwise need to be. 

 Dollar returns on Mexican Cetes in the first half of this year have been over 30 percent a year -- a big incentive for hot foreign money. 

 The bank's own report on monetary policy to Congress, issued at the end of September, says that the peso's stability in the first eight months of this year "has been the result of market behaviour". It then adds: 

 "However, that does not mean that on some occasions Banco de Mexico does not try to influence, through its posture on monetary policy, both interest rates and the exchange rate. This (is) with the objective of helping to achieve the inflation goal and to order prevailing conditions in the exchange and money markets". 

 The United States, which had to bail Mexico out last time it got its sums wrong on the peso, has kept publicly silent on the delicate issue of the peso. 

 But U.S. officials have privately expressed concern about whether the peso will be able to achieve a soft landing over the next few months from its current firm levels towards what they term more realistic levels of below 8.20 to the dollar by the year end.

title: Mexico News: Dornbusch Says Peso Not Free Floating
text:
MONTERREY (Dow Jones)--The following news summary is based on Tuesday's editions of the Monterrey dailies El Norte, El Diario and El Financiero's Northeast Edition. 

 -- Rudiger Dornbusch, the influential and controversial economics professor from the Massachussetts Institute of Technology, accused the Mexico's Central Bank of intervening to keep the peso strong against the dollar. 

 "It's wrong to say that in Mexico there exists a free float of the currency, since the Bank of Mexico controls it so it won't move," El Norte reported Dornbusch as saying in a conference in the resort city of Cancun. 

 Bank of Mexico officials have repeatedly said this year they haven't interfered with the value of the peso. 

 Dornbusch said in his accusation that the Central Bank's efforts to prop up the peso were "very irresponsible" and could damage Mexico's effort to grow its export industry. Exports, in four or five years, should account for 30% of economic production in order for Mexico to achieve 6% annual growth. 

 "... which will only happen with a competitive exchange rate," El Norte quoted Dornbusch as saying. 

 Mexico's peso closed at 7.53 pesos to the dollar on Monday, which is stronger than the year-end close of 7.69 pesos to the dollar, despite inflation so far in 1996 of 18.5%. 

 -- The debtors' rights group, El Barzon, demonstrated in several cities against the Mexican banking system and vowed to protect their properties from foreclosure on the day a government program to restructure debts and give interest rate reductions ended, Monterrey dailies reported. 

 Barzon members used different protest techniques to call attention to their cause, including riding elephants through Mexico City streets, smashing tomatoes in front of the Mexico's Banking Association building, painting signs in blood in Chihuahua and handing out packets of basic foodstuff in Nuevo Leon.

title: Risks mount as Mexican peso powers on - Kleinwort.
text:
LONDON, Sept 16 (Reuter) - Persistent strength of the Mexican peso will spell trouble next year if the authorities do not intervene to counteract it soon, Kleinwort Benson warned on Monday. 

 The currency, converted from a crawling peg to a free float after December 1994's traumatic devaluation, has appreciated by around 23 percent against the dollar this year. 

 Trade surpluses, successful forays into the international capital markets and a boost to sentiment from the government's delivery on promises of fiscal and monetary firmness, have all contributed to the peso's strength this year. 

 But in a note to investors, Kleinwort Benson estimated the peso was overvalued by about 9.0 percent against the dollar on a purchasing power parity basis and said strong action was needed in the next four months. 

 "If the exchange rate depreciation does not take place this year, it will simply be a case of storing up the problem for a later date," said Neil Dougal, Latin America analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities. 

 "The longer the delay, the bigger the required adjustment." 

 He said using interest rate policy to influence the exchange rate was the only practical tool in the short term, but this was causing sharp fluctuations in real rates. 

 While active intervention could have an expansionary effect on money supply, there was space for this without exerting undue upward pressure on interest rates. 

 "The current undershoot on monetary base targets means there is ample scope for non-sterilised intervention," he said. 

Mexico's central bank has intervened on the foreign exchanges, buying dollars on the open market last month for the first time since the devaluation. But the $130 million purchase was comparatively small and was aimed at rebuilding reserves rather than weakening the currency. 

 Analysts would like to see more. 

 "In our view, there is now a strong case for more explicit and aggressive action," Dougal said. 

 The announcement by the Mexican authorities at the start of August, that they would modify the policy of a free floating peso by buying limited quantities of dollars from local commercial banks, was a postive first, Dougal said. But more action was needed. 

 "A clear signal and more aggressive action are required if problems for the peso at the end of this year or in the first half of 1997 are tO be avoided," he said. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734

title: Bear Stearns praises Mexico's monetary policy.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 20 (Reuter) - Mexico's monetary policy is working well and is no longer the Achilles' heel in the country's return to economic growth following the peso crash, Bear Stearns said on Thursday. 

 "In meetings this week with senior government officials in Mexico City, we confirmed our sense that Mexico's monetary policy is operating well and is no longer the weak link in Mexico's economic program," Bear Stearns' economist David Malpass wrote in a statement. 

 Malpass said Mexico is using tight monetary policy to keep the peso strong and ensure lower interest rates. 

 "Mexico's formal policy is still to use its net domestic credit targets to guide monetary policy while floating both interest rates and the exchange rate. In practice, however, it wants to use peso strength to assure steadily lower interest rates," Malpass said in the statement. 

 The latest example of this was two weeks ago, when peso instability caused interest rates to rise and the Banco de Mexico to drain liquidity from the money market, Malpass said. The peso recovered. 

 He said Banco de Mexico has no plans to intervene in the forex markets to keep the peso strong or build reserves. 

 "By leaving international reserves at minimum levels, the central bank hopes to avoid the artificially high interest rates which occur when a central bank sells local currency debt to avoid an expansion of the money supply while it is buying dollars to accumulate reserves," Malpass wrote. 

 Mexico's peso-focused policy should allow interest rates to fall, occasionally rebounding to control any peso weakness. At some point, however, Mexico will have to weigh the benefits of a relatively stronger peso to inflation versus the cost to exporters and market sentiment, Malpass said.

title: Mexico  cenbank  intervened  in  forex  26 times in '95.
text:
MEXICO CITY, June 11 (Reuter) - Mexico's central bank intervened 26 times in the foreign exchange market during 1995, selling a total of $4.935 billion to buy pesos. 

 According to the bank's full 1995 report, made available Tuesday, most of the intervention came between the start of the year and March 14. 

 These dollar sales, "were in great measure due to the sales carried out on Monday and Tuesday of each week to compensate for the demand for foreign currency deriving from the amortization in pesos of the Tesobonos, which were coming due at that time", the bank said. 

 Once holders of Tesobonos were allowed to receive payment in U.S. dollars, there was no more reason for those interventions in the currency market, the bank added. 

 Twenty of the interventions came before March 14, according to the detailed figures provided by the bank. After that date the interventions came on March 20 ($5.0 million), May 30 ($15 million), November 9 ($175 million), November 14 ($125 million), December 8 ($160 million) and December 29 ($45 million). 

 During November in particular, the peso was buffeted by incorrect rumours about government instability. Bank officials say they have not intervened at all so far in 1996.
