title: Once a laughingstock, Mexican peso could be too strong.
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 24 (Reuter) - Once it was embarrassingly weak. Now it's uncomfortably strong. 

 Economists here are starting to worry about the rise of Mexico's peso, which has gained sharply against the dollar this year in real terms. 

 Some even want Mexico to start selling pesos for dollars on the open market to keep the currency down and to build reserves -- something that was unthinkable last year, when the peso wobbled with every economic worry. 

 "Now would be as good a time as any to purchase dollars at a fairly attractive price," said Gray Newman, an economist at James Capel in Mexico City. 

 Banco de Mexico may intervene in the markets to keep the peso from appreciating above current levels at 7.38 per dollar, believes Denis Parisien, an analyst at consultants I.D.E.A. in New York. 

 After losing nearly half its value in 1995 after the bungled December 1994 devaluation, the peso has staged a quiet comeback this year amid growing confidence that Mexico is on the verge of recovery. 

 According to market traders, the peso has gained about 16 percent against the dollar in real terms since January, at a time when the dollar has been at its strongest level in years against other benchmark currencies like the German mark and Japanese yen. 

 "It depends on how you look at the peso, but I think it has crossed the line and has become a touch overvalued," Parisien said. 

 Burned by the devaluation, Mexican officials avoid making comments about desirable peso levels. 

 A central bank official, who declined to be identified, said in an interview he was not concerned about the recent peso strength. He said it was understandable after abnormal peso weakness at the end of last year. 

 "Our message to the markets is very clear: that we are in a free-floating market and we intend to stick to it," said the official. 

 But some officials have conceded that Mexico could conceivably at some point in the future buy dollars to prevent the peso from becoming overvalued again. 

 Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television on May 9 that the peso was still competitive and he did not believe Mexico would see sustained large financial flows to strengthen the peso. 

 But he added, "In the unlikely case of having very strong flows that tend to produce undesirable and very long-lasting (peso) appreciation, then the Banco de Mexico could start accumulating reserves or something like that." 

 Ortiz's view that the peso is still competitive has been backed up by Mexico's recent trade figures, which show exports are still strong, economists said. 

 "Mexico is not running into the same problems it did before the devaluation," said Damian Fraser, head of the Mexico City's Caspian Research office. 

 But, Fraser said, Mexico should use current peso strength as a means to build reserves. "Reserves haven't increased in a significant way this year," he said. 

 Mexico's net international assets -- the country's reserves net of loans from the United States and International Monetary Fund to help it through the peso crisis -- have grown from $1.357 billion on Jan. 12 to just $1.582 billion as of May 17. 

 A stock of reserves and a slightly weaker peso now might help Mexico weather any future peso weakness, if foreign inflows to Mexico dry up. 

 Economists also warn about the longer-run dangers of allowing a currency to become overvalued, especially in a country like Mexico with a history of currency crises. 

 Mexico has in the past found it politically easy to have a strong peso, which makes imports cheaper and helps consumer purchasing power, economists said. 

 The government might again be tempted to boost employment through a strong peso ahead of 1997 mid-term elections, they added.

title: Mexico experts say peso strength should be curbed.
text:

 Banco de Mexico may intervene in the markets to keep the peso from appreciating above current levels at 7.38 per dollar, believes Denis Parisien, an analyst at consultants I.D.E.A. in New York. 

 "If the peso continues to challenge the 7.38 level, Mexican authorities are very likely (to intervene), given the need to accumulate reserves," Parisien said. 

 After losing nearly half its value in the year that followed the bungled December 1994 devaluation, the peso has staged a quiet comeback this year amid growing confidence that Mexico is on the verge of recovery. It closed Friday at 7.386.

 Most economists say the peso was overvalued by about 20-25 percent before the devaluation so peso gains have sparked a debate about whether Mexico's money is again overvalued. 

 "It depends on how you look at the peso, but I think it has crossed the line and has become a touch overvalued," Parisien said. 

 Burned by the devaluation, Mexican officials avoid making comments about desirable peso levels. 

 A central bank official, who declined to be named, told Reuters he is not concerned about the recent peso strength. He said it was understandable after abnormal peso weakness at the end of last year. "Our message to the markets is very clear: that we are in a free-floating market and we intend to stick to it," said the official. 

 But some officials have conceded Mexico could conceivably buy dollars in the future to stop the peso from becoming overvalued again and stalling the export-led recovery. 

 Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz told Reuters Financial Television on May 9 the peso was still competitive and did not believe Mexico would see sustained large financial flows strengthen the peso. 

 But he added: "In the unlikely case of having very strong flows that tend to produce undesirable and very long-lasting (peso) appreciation, then the Banco de Mexico could start accumulating reserves or something like that." 

 Economists pointed out that Mexico sold pesos during 1993 in order to keep the currency within its trading band amid heavy foreign inflows. The trading band was abandoned in 1994.

 "Mexico is not running into the same problems it did before the devaluation," said Damian Fraser, head of the Mexico City's Caspian Research office.

 Mexico's net international reserves have grown from $1.357 billion on January 12 to $1.582 billion on May 17. 

 "A country in Mexico's position would be well advised to build a significant stock of net reserves ... through cautious, transparent peso selling," added Paulo Leme, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York. 

 Higher reserves and a slightly weaker peso would help weather any future peso weakness if foreign inflows dried up. 

 Economists also warn about the longer-run dangers of allowing a currency to become overvalued, especially in a country like Mexico with a history of currency crises. 

 Mexico has in the past found it politically easy to have a strong peso, which makes imports cheaper and helps consumer purchasing power, economists said. The government might again be tempted to boost employment through a strong peso ahead of 1997 mid-term elections. 

 Economists say they are unsure what President Ernesto Zedillo will do. "I sense there is no agreement on what the policy should be," said one Mexico City economist.

title: Mexico's Ortiz says peso very competitive.
text:
TOKYO, May 9 (Reuter) - Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz told Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo on Thursday that he was not concerned about the current situation of the peso and that the currency was very competitive. 

 Asked whether the recent rise in the peso's value was a concern for the government, Ortiz said in an interview: "I don't think that we will see a repetition of very large financial flows that will cause undesirable lasting (peso) appreciation...so I'm really not concerned. 

 "We're still in a situation in which the peso is very competitive," he said when asked if Mexican exporters had complained about the strong peso, which might stall the country's export boom. 

 Asked whether the government had set any target range for the peso, Ortiz said Mexico was not targetting any range. 

 "In the unlikely case of having very strong flows that tend to produce undesirable and very long-lasting (peso) appreciation, then the Banco de Mexico could start accumulating reserves or something like that," he said. "But we are comfortable in the way the Banco de Mexico is managing the foreign exchanges and the money markets." 

 So far this year, the peso has gained about 3.0 percent against the U.S. dollar. 

 On Wednesday, Finance Ministry spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela said in Mexico City that Mexico wants the peso to remain competitive but stable. He also said the central bank, the Banco de Mexico, had not intervened to support the peso so far this year. 

 Asked whether the government was considering issuing more bonds, such as 10-year bonds, after placing a global $1.75 billion issue of 30-year bonds last week, Ortiz said: "I think we're looking for opportunities to strengthen our debt structure." 

 But he added that Mexico has no definite plans yet.

title: Competitive, stable Mexican peso important - gov't.
text:
MEXICO CITY, May 8 (Reuter) - Mexico wants its peso to remain competitive but stable, Finance Ministry spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela told a news conference on Wednesday. 

 Valenzuela also told reporters that Mexico was committed to a floating peso regime. 

 "We want the peso to remain competitive," he said. "It is very important that the peso is stable." 

 "We will keep a floating currency, it is important to underline that." 

 Valenzuela said that Banco de Mexico has not intervened to support the peso so far this year. 

 He added that the stable peso has allowed Banco de Mexico to rebuild its foreign reserves. 

 On May 3, Mexico's international reserves rose to $15.894 billion from $15.642 billion on April 30. 

 The last official central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market was in December 1995. 

 So far this year, the peso has appreciated by 3.0 percent against the U.S. dollar.

title: Peso strength seen easing Mexico's interest rates.
text:
MEXICO CITY, March 19 (Reuter) - Mexico's battered peso has shown a surprising resilience this year and economists say its underlying solidity could allow interest rates to gradually decline. 

 After a year of harrowing volatility, some improving economic fundamentals and better financial conditions are helping the peso shine this year. 

 "We see the peso being stable and that continuing even as interest rates decline," said Rodolfo Navarrete, economist with brokerage house Vector. 

 Bancomer economist Javier Maldonado said, "Basically we see the peso being reasonably stable in 1996, with interest rates dropping and inflation better than last year." 

 The peso is reaping the benefits of better fundamentals in Mexico after a year of harsh market shocks that followed the December 1994 devaluation. 

 The current account deficit has narrowed dramatically to $654 million in 1995 from $24.42 billion in 1994, diminishing the need to borrow abroad. The government has redeemed all of its outstanding dollar-denominated Tesobonos, which had risen to about $29 billion at their height. 

 Strength in the stock market, as investors foresee an eventual end to the recession, has helped create foreign demand for the peso. 

 The Banco de Mexico has also been discreetly intervening in support of the peso through intermediaries and agencies for some time, analysts said. 

 The central bank has refrained from overtly intervening in the exchange market so far this year. 

 Also last year's inflation spiral is expected to end once an expected bubble in April is past. 

 April prices are expected to rise three percent, and then inflation is seen tapering off for the rest of the year. 

 The main weapon in steadying the peso over most of last year has been very high interest rates. But analysts now see the peso decoupling somewhat from rates and drawing more on the improved fundamentals for stability -- a trend they see continuing. 

 "The peso has been one of the more stable currencies in the world this year," one Mexico City economist noted. 

 Despite its good behavior so far this year, economists do expect some nominal depreciation in the peso later this year as lower interest rates cut its attractiveness. 

 But they add that the real appreciation in the peso against the U.S. dollar will be greater than the nominal depreciation, as price increases in Mexico outstrip those in the U.S. 

 The private sector sees inflation in Mexico easing to between 25 percent and 35 percent in 1996, after the stunning devaluation of the peso caused inflation to skyrocket to 51.97 percent in 1995. 

 But economists add the currency could still be vulnerable to a series of unexpected factors: higher-than-expected inflation, turbulent politics and a too rapid decline in interest rates. 

 "We expect lower interest rates, and the problem is that any (large) drop in interest rates could weaken the peso," one Mexico City-based economist said. 

 Vector economist Navarrete forecasts the peso at 8.8 or 8.9 per dollar by the end of 1996, at the high end of forecasts made by other economists in the Mexican capital. 

 Interest rates are expected to slip to between 30 to 38 percent by year-end on the bellwether one-month Cetes bill. At Monday's primary auction, the one-month Cetes rate fell to a still-lofty 41.55 percent. 

 After the currency was allowed to float on December 22, 1994, it took a fall from 3.47 to a low of 7.90/7.94 against the U.S. dollar on November 15 last year. It closed today at 7.5130/7.5175 per dollar.

title: Mexico  could  intervene  if markets unruly - Guemez.

 Guemez expressed satisfaction over the fact Mexico did not intervene to shore up its currency so far this year but he did not rule out that this could happen again.

 He cited chiefly an increase in foreign reserves as a result of Mexico's long-term borrowing on the capital markets, and the virtual elimination of the government's short-term dollar-denominated liabilities, securitized in so-called Tesobonos.

title: Mexico Peso -4: Economist Dornbusch Urges Weaker Peso
text:
The senior Mexican central banker, who presented a paper on the crisis at the AEA convention, generally explained Mexico's problems in 1994 as rooted in efforts to maintain a fixed exchange rate and in external developments, prominently U.S. interest rate hikes that drew investors away. 

 Dornbusch countered at the AEA panel discussion that Mexico - which has been intervening to support the peso in recent months - was being overly aggressive in fighting inflation and should be more concerned about inflation-adjusted or 'real' appreciation of the peso. 

 He suggested that the central bank shouldn't be as concerned about inflation, calling its attempts to curb price gains 'super dogma.' 

 Dornbusch maintained that the central bank is failing to take into account inflation-adjusted appreciation of the currency because authorities are 'stubbornly attached to inflation fighting.' And he suggested political pressures still exist to strengthen the peso every time a presidential election year rolls around. 

 'The question in Mexico is why is growth in Mexico not at 6%?,' Dornbusch said, compared to official forecasts of up to 3% growth this year. And he maintained that authorities shouldn't be seeking to lower Mexico's inflation rate, which ran at 50% last year, to U.S. norms, which are around 3% or less. Rather, Dornbusch said Mexico should look more for levels around 6% to 7% annual inflation. 

 Gil rebuked Dornbusch, saying that there is 'no substance in the comments.' And the central banker added during the panel discussion, 'I certainly hope, Rudy, you always find central bankers obsessed with inflation. I would really worry if they were not.'

title: Mexico's Peso -2: Interest Rate Drops Boost Confidence
text:
The peso closed 0.3% stronger against the dollar from Wednesday's close, and is down 54% against the dollar since Dec. 20, 1994, when Mexico's financial crisis erupted. The spot dollar ended 1995 at 7.6950 pesos. 

 Traders and analysts say continued drops in interest rates have boosted hopes that Mexico's economy will begin to recover in 1996 after a horrendous recession last year. 

 Secondary money market rates traded in stable fashion Thursday, after the central bank reported Wednesday that the interbank lending rate, or TIIP, dropped 2.8308 percentage points to 45.9715%. Bellwether 28-day Cetes rates fell 2.11 percentage points to 44.70% at the central bank's primary Treasury bill auction late Tuesday - the third straight decline. 

 Even beforesthe recent rate drops, economists were calling for the economy to grow 2% to 3% this year after a 1995 GDP contraction that some estimate was as large as 7%. 

 In other news, the central bank reported after markets closed Wednesday that international reserves as of Dec. 29 stood at $15.741 billion, down $315 million from the week before. It said it spent $45 million to intervene in the currency market last week. The Bank of Mexico confirmed intervention in last Friday's market, when the spot dollar flirted with the 7.75-peso mark.  The central bank also reported that the base monetary supply ended 1995 at 66.809 billion pesos, up from 56.935 billion pesos at the close of 1994. Mexico stayed within its target of a 17.5% increase in its monetary base, although it did not meet its target for expansion of net domestic credit due to lower-than-expected international reserves.

title: Mexico's Peso -2: One_Year Cetes Back On Auction Block
text:
Although drops in interest rates often hurt a currency, others pointed out that the trend might also be spawning optimism in the prospects of an economic recovery. 

 'What's perhaps very important is the idea that the government is offering one-year Cetes, which gives confidence for long-term prospects,' said Felix Boni, director of equities research with James Capel in Mexico City.
